Prosodics: intonation (rising = tentativeness or question, falling = assertion), pitch, stress - especially contrastive stress ('I didn't say HE stole it') - tempo, volume, pausing and rhythm; paralinguistic effects (laughter, voice quality) and non-fluency features (fillers, false starts, repair, micropauses). AQA's transcription key marks micropauses (.) and timed pauses (2.0) - analyse where they fall, not just that they exist. Graphology: layout (columns, sections, white space), typography (font, weight, size, case), colour, images with captions, bulleting and headings. In multimodal texts (Kress & van Leeuwen, 2006) analyse compositionally: information value (left/right = given/new, top/bottom = ideal/real), salience (what the eye is drawn to first) and framing (what is connected or separated). A captioned photograph anchors an image's meaning; bold weight gives a claim authority before it is read. Applying the frameworks - the method (AO1/AO2/AO3): Read twice: first for genre, audience, purpose and what is represented or presented; second for quotations banked against each level. Plan by angle, not by level: representational angle for AQA 7702/1 Q1/Q2 (25 marks each), point of comparison for Q3 (20) and OCR H470/01 Section C (36). Push every point through the chain: quotation → terminology → effect → context . An effect without a quotation is assertion; a quotation without effect is description; context bolted on at the end caps AO3. Let mode filter the levels: speech → prosodics and turn-taking; print → grammar and graphology; electronic → multimodality and engagement features. For AO2, evaluate concepts: name the framework (Grice, Austin/Searle, Brown & Levinson, Halliday, Kress & van Leeuwen), apply it, then judge what it reveals and what it misses in this text. Timing: AQA Paper 1 Section A is 70 marks in roughly 90 minutes - about 25 per text question and 20 for the comparison, after reading time. OCR H470/01 gives two hours for 80 marks: roughly 15 minutes per microscope item (Section A), 35 for the directed writing (Section B) and 55 for the comparison (Section C). Selection beats coverage every time. Common errors that cap marks: (1) catalogue mode - listing devices with no representation claim; (2) context dump - a paragraph of production facts with no link to a linguistic choice; (3) theorist name-dropping - 'Grice' appended to a point the theory does not explain; (4) cross-mode comparison error - comparing prosodics against a printed text. For OCR's 'Language under the microscope' (H470/01 Section A, 2 x 10 marks), compress the chain: the item names the levels to analyse, so lead with the most significant feature, quote precisely, explain the effect in context, and stop - depth in ten marks, not coverage.

topics.name: Language and Gender
topics.subject: english-language
topics.searchText: english-language English Language Language and Gender Outline and evaluate the deficit model (Jespersen; Lakoff 1975) with its criticisms of evidence and scope (AO2). Evaluate dominance research - Zimmerman & West (1975), Fishman (1983) - including the interruption/overlap distinction and O'Barr & Atkins' (1980) 'powerless language' critique (AO2). Assess the difference model (Tannen 1990) against diversity and dynamic approaches - Cameron (2007), Butler's (1990) performativity, Eckert & McConnell-Ginet's communities of practice (AO2). Analyse how unseen media texts represent women and men through marked lexis, semantic derogation, agency and multimodal choices (AO1/AO3). Deploy two or three theorists woven into an argument rather than listed, matching the AQA AO2 'evaluate the idea' essay demands (AO1/AO2). Explain how contextual factors - era, domain (public/private), publication - shape gendered language use (AO3). Lakoff (1975) 'women's language': hedges, tag questions, empty adjectives, intensifiers, superpolite forms, hypercorrect grammar, rising intonation on declaratives. O'Barr & Atkins (1980): courtroom 'powerless language' correlates with social status, not sex - the standard AO2 critique of the deficit model. Zimmerman & West (1975): men made almost all recorded interruptions in cross-sex conversations; Fishman (1983): women do the 'housework' of talk - topic-raising, questions, minimal responses. Tannen (1990): report talk vs rapport talk; difference is cultural mismatch, not domination. Cameron (2007): differences are small, within-gender variation exceeds between-gender; the difference model is a 'zombie' statistic recycled by publishers. Butler (1990): gender is performed through repeated stylistic acts; Eckert & McConnell-Ginet: styles emerge in communities of practice. AQA 7702/2 Section A = one 'Evaluate the idea that...' essay, 30 marks; OCR H470/02 Section B (Language in the media) = investigate how language features and contextual factors construct meanings, 24 marks. Deficit model Early framework holding that women's language is weaker or less effective than men's - Jespersen (1922); formalised as 'women's language' by Lakoff (1975). Dominance model Approach treating language as a site where men control conversation and women are silenced - Zimmerman & West (1975); Fishman (1983). Difference model Tannen's (1990) cross-cultural account: men and women speak different but equal subcultures (report vs rapport talk), so miscommunication is cultural mismatch, not domination. Diversity (dynamic) model Later approach treating gender as one variable among many, with language use varying by context and community of practice - Cameron (2007); Eckert & McConnell-Ginet. Gender performativity Butler's (1990) claim that gender identity is constituted through repeated stylised acts - including speech - rather than expressed from a fixed inner essence. Interruption vs overlap Interruption intrudes before a current speaker's turn is complete (potentially dominance); overlap is simultaneous talk that supports or completes the other's turn (Tannen: often affiliative). Report talk vs rapport talk Tannen's (1990) pair: men's public, information- and status-focused talk vs women's private, connection-focused talk. Semantic derogation Schulz's (1975) finding that lexical pairs pejorate for the female term over time (master/mistress, bachelor/spinster). Marked term The form that carries extra semantic weight against an unmarked norm - 'female surgeon' marks sex where 'surgeon' defaults to male (Spender's 1980 male-as-norm). Community of practice Eckert & McConnell-Ginet's (1992) unit: a group with shared practices and goals, within which gendered styles emerge - not innate, but built jointly. Gender sits within Language diversity (AQA 7702 Paper 2, Section A) and surfaces in unseen media texts on OCR H470/02 Section B (Language in the media, 24 marks). The models are an evaluation toolkit - but examiners reward critique , not citation-listing. Deficit - Jespersen (1922): his chapter 'The Woman' claimed women's vocabulary was smaller and more conservative while men innovated; it set the deficit frame that later research inherited, with no systematic data behind it. Deficit - Lakoff (1975), Language and Woman's Place : 'women's language' comprises hedges ('sort of'), tag questions ('isn't it?'), empty adjectives ('divine'), intensifiers ('so'), superpolite forms, hypercorrect grammar and rising intonation on declaratives. Her claim: women are socialised into tentative speech, and the language reflects - and reproduces - social powerlessness. Lakoff critiqued: anecdotal evidence with no recorded corpus; a trivial feature list that invites caricature; women treated as a single homogeneous group. The killer AO2 move is O'Barr & Atkins (1980) : courtroom language showed 'powerless language' (including Lakoff's own features) correlates with social status , not sex - high-status women spoke like high-status men. Lakoff's markers are markers of powerlessness, not of gender. Dominance - Zimmerman & West (1975): in recorded informal cross-sex conversations, men made almost all the interruptions, while same-sex conversations (male and female) showed few. Their claim: conversation is a resource men control, silencing women's contributions. Dominance - Fishman (1983): analysing taperecorded couple conversations, women did the 'housework' of talk - raising topics (often dropped by male partners), asking more questions, producing minimal responses ('mm', 'yeah') to keep talk going - while men set the topics that developed. Women's linguistic labour produced men's conversational power. Dominance critiqued: small, self-selected samples; and interruption is not automatically dominance - Tannen distinguished intrusive interruption from supportive overlap, so the same phenomenon can be read two ways. West & Zimmerman's later 'Doing Gender' (1987) reframed the data: participants perform gender in interaction, pointing towards the diversity model. Spender (1980): 'male as norm' - language encodes men as the standard and women as the marked deviation, a bridge from dominance research into representation analysis (below). Why the early frameworks still earn marks: deficit and dominance are not museum pieces - they are the foil every later model is measured against, and AQA AO2 rewards exactly that measurement. A paragraph that names Lakoff's features, cites O'Barr & Atkins' courtroom evidence and states the consequence ('the features mark powerlessness, not sex') is a complete AO2 unit: claim, evidence, evaluation. The same paragraph structure serves dominance: Zimmerman & West's finding, Fishman's extension, then the interruption/overlap distinction as the critique. Examiners' reports repeatedly flag candidates who list six models without evaluating any - three well-worn models, each collapsed into claim-evidence-critique, outscore them every time. Difference - Tannen (1990), You Just Don't Understand : the cross-cultural communication model. Men favour report talk - public, informational, status-building; women favour rapport talk - private, connection-building, supportive. Miscommunication ('Different Words, Different Worlds') is cultural mismatch, not domination; overlap, for instance, is reframed as affiliative rather than intrusive. 'Different but equal' - deliberately softer than the dominance model. Tannen critiqued: Hyde's (2005) gender similarities hypothesis - a meta-analysis finding males and females similar on most communication variables; and Cameron (2007) argued the difference model is a 'zombie' statistic that keeps being recycled because it sells books: it naturalises stereotypes as science and excuses inequality ('that's just how men/women are'). Diversity/dynamic - Cameron (2007), The Myth of Mars and Venus : measured gender differences are small; within-gender variation exceeds between-gender variation; style shifts with context, role and audience - the same woman in a boardroom, on the phone to a friend and online produces three distinct registers. Performativity - Butler (1990), Gender Trouble : gender is not expressed but constituted through repeated stylised acts, including speech - there is no pre-linguistic 'feminine essence' that language merely reports. This reframes the whole debate: gendered language is something speakers do , repeatedly, in context. Communities of practice - Eckert & McConnell-Ginet (1992): gendered styles emerge within groups with shared practices and goals - e.g. a sports team, a workplace, a friendship group - so 'masculine' directness may be a team norm, not a male trait. This unit of analysis allows intersectional work (gender + class + region + age) that deficit and difference models cannot handle. Exam synthesis: the strongest AQA essays treat the models as a historical arc rather than rival truths - deficit and dominance as early lenses with fragile evidence, difference as a popularisation that dodges power, diversity and performativity as the current lens that handles context and within-group variation. Weigh each model against the data and against its social consequences (AO2), and anchor claims in the contexts where gendered language is produced: public vs private domains, media, workplace, online (AO3). Two or three theorists woven into an argument beat six listed in a paragraph. OCR's Language in the media question (H470/02 Section B, 24 marks) asks you to 'investigate how language features and contextual factors construct meanings in this text' - frequently a media text representing women, men or gender roles. AQA Paper 2 texts about gender appear as discourses to analyse and evaluate. The method is the representation method (see Textual Variations topic) pointed at gender. Marked lexis: 'female surgeon', 'male nurse', 'career woman' - the modifier marks sex against an unmarked male default (Spender's male-as-norm). Ask in every text: which terms are marked, which unmarked, and what that asymmetry assumes? Semantic derogation: Schulz (1975) showed paired terms pejorate for the female member over time - master/mistress, bachelor/spinster. Where a text uses one side of such a pair, the history of the word rides with it. Generic and gendered forms: 'mankind', 'chairman', generic 'he' - and reform attempts ('chair', 'firefighter', singular 'they'), which link gender representation to language change and prescriptivism: a productive AQA link between the diversity and change strands of Paper 2. Goffman (1979), Gender Advertisements : the ritualisation of subordination in visual representation - women depicted lying down, smaller, 'licensed withdrawal', averted gaze. Use it as the multimodal parallel: who does the grammar of the image empower? Asymmetry of evaluation: media texts typically judge women by appearance and men by action - evaluative adjectives ('glamorous', 'family-first') applied asymmetrically to otherwise parallel figures. Method for the unseen media text: (1) state what gender group is represented and how ('Text B represents women professionals as exceptional rather than ordinary'); (2) work the levels - lexis (marked terms, evaluative and appearance-focused adjectives, semantic fields), grammar (agency: who acts, who is acted upon; passives concealing perpetrators or crediting subjects), pragmatics (presuppositions about roles - 'working mothers' presumes motherhood is the default that needs qualifying), discourse (who is quoted, foregrounded, given the anecdote), graphology (image roles, captioning, layout); (3) tie each finding to contextual factors - publication era, readership, genre - because the OCR mark scheme awards context for explaining the construction, not for decorating it. End by evaluating the representation: perceptive answers say what version of reality the text is selling and who benefits from it. Media discourses and attitudes: beyond representing gender groups, media texts also carry discourses about language itself - anxiety about singular 'they', mockery of vocal fry or uptalk, nostalgia for 'proper' English. These are evaluative texts to analyse (how the attitudes are linguistically constructed: evaluative lexis, modality, presupposition) and evaluate (whose interests the attitude serves - AQA Paper 2's discourses questions do exactly this). The link is productive in both directions: gender representation draws on language change (pejoration, reform), and language attitudes draw on gender (which speakers get policed). Weaving the two strands is what makes a top-band answer look synoptic rather than topic-bound. AQA 7702/2 Section A offers a choice of two 'Evaluate the idea that...' statements, 30 marks each - e.g. June 2017: 'Evaluate the idea that a person's language use is completely determined by the social groups they belong to.' Gender is one such social group; occupation and region are others, so the same essay mechanics serve this topic and the Language and Power topic. Command word: evaluate - a verdict is compulsory. Structure as thesis, counter-evidence, refined verdict: e.g. determinism fails because Cameron's within-gender variation and Butler's performativity show speakers exceeding their categories, but social groups still constrain access to registers and to power (O'Barr & Atkins' status effect). Theorist deployment: two or three, woven: Lakoff's features to open the deficit frame, O'Barr & Atkins to collapse it, Cameron or Eckert & McConnell-Ginet to rebuild. Name the study, its finding and its limitation in one sentence each - a paragraph per theorist listing biographies scores AO2 at the bottom of the scale. AO3: contexts decide the verdict - public vs private domains (Fishman's couple data is domestic; phone-ins are broadcast), era (1970s samples predate the online audience), and medium (interruption behaves differently on air and in chat). Use context to explain why the research found what it found. OCR H470/02 Section B (24 marks): investigate language features and contextual factors - deploy gender concepts (marked lexis, derogation, agency) plus the representation method, and credit the text's production context and audience. About 45 minutes: budget three or four developed analytical strands rather than exhaustive coverage. Directed writing (OCR H470/01 Section B, 24 marks; AQA 7702/2 Section B): when writing about a gender issue, avoid recycling the stereotypes the theories critique - the examiner notices when a script about gendered language performs the deficit model it claims to evaluate. A worked verdict chain for the essay: thesis ('social groups constrain but do not determine language use') - so for ('Lakoff's features show socialisation into tentative styles') - so against ('but O'Barr & Atkins show the same features track status, not sex') - so refined ('groups condition access; speakers exceed the conditions') - so context ('and the 1970s samples that founded the field predate the online contexts where style-shifting is most visible'). Each link is one sentence with a theorist attached; the whole chain is the essay's spine, and the remaining paragraphs flesh out each link with data. That is the difference between an essay that has theorists and an essay that uses them.

topics.name: Language and Power and Technology
topics.subject: english-language
topics.searchText: english-language English Language Language and Power and Technology Distinguish power in discourse from power behind discourse (Fairclough 1989) and instrumental from influential power, with textual evidence for each (AO1/AO2). Apply Goffman's (1967) face and Brown & Levinson's (1987) politeness theory - positive/negative face, FTAs, mitigation strategies - to transcripts and media texts (AO1/AO3). Analyse occupational power using Wareing (1999): vertical vs horizontal power, jargon as gatekeeping, and workplace discourse features (AO1/AO2). Use the CDA three-dimensional method (description, interpretation, explanation) to link textual features to ideology and institutional power (AO1/AO3). Analyse electronic language: multimodality (Kress & van Leeuwen 2006), CMC features (synchronicity, permanence, interactivity) and power online (AO1/AO3). Deploy politeness and power concepts in directed writing for electronic and specialist audiences (AQA 7702/2 Q4; OCR H470/01 Section B) (AO1/AO2). Fairclough (1989): power in discourse (visible in the encounter) vs power behind discourse (institutions setting conventions); instrumental vs influential power. CDA method: description (text) - interpretation (discursive practice) - explanation (social practice/ideology). Brown & Levinson (1987): positive face (approval) vs negative face (autonomy); FTAs mitigated by bald on-record, positive politeness, negative politeness, off-record, or avoidance. Goffman (1967): face = the positive social value claimed in interaction; face-work maintains it. Wareing (1999): vertical (hierarchical) vs horizontal (peer) occupational power; jargon gatekeeps; Koester (2004): phatic talk builds workplace solidarity. Sinclair & Coulthard (1975): IRF/IRE - the teacher controls classroom turns and topics. Crystal (2001): e-language as a third mode blending speech and writing; synchronous vs asynchronous CMC. Electronic power: gatekeeping lowered (anyone can publish) but re-concentrated in platforms, algorithms and moderation; synthetic personalisation scales online. AQA 7702/2 Section A = one 'Evaluate the idea...' essay (30); Q3 analyse discourses (40); Q4 directed writing (30). OCR H470/02 Section B Language in the media (24). Power in discourse Power exercised within the language event itself: who asks the questions, who interrupts, what can be said and by whom - visible in the text (Fairclough, 1989). Power behind discourse The social and institutional power that determines the conventions, participants and order of discourse - who may speak, write or set the agenda (Fairclough, 1989). Instrumental power Power that enforces authority and compliance - law, court directives, institutional rules; backed by formal sanction. Influential power Power that persuades rather than enforces - media, advertising, politics, charity appeals; no formal authority, so it works on attitudes. Face Goffman (1967): the positive social value a participant claims in interaction; face-work maintains it against threat. Positive vs negative face Brown & Levinson (1987): the desire to be approved and included (positive) vs the desire for autonomy and freedom from imposition (negative). Face-threatening act (FTA) An act threatening face - requests and orders threaten negative face; criticism and disagreement threaten positive face. Speakers choose a mitigation strategy accordingly. Politeness strategies Brown & Levinson's (1987) options for handling FTAs: bald on-record, positive politeness (solidarity), negative politeness (deference, hedging), off-record (indirectness), or no FTA. Jargon (as gatekeeping) Specialist terminology that compresses meaning for insiders and excludes outsiders - efficiency and exclusion simultaneously; a marker of occupational power. Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA) Fairclough's method: description of the text, interpretation of its production and consumption, explanation of its social practice - linking language to ideology and power. Power appears across both boards: in AQA's diversity essays (occupation as a social group, 7702/2 Section A, 30 marks), its discourses questions (Q3, 40 marks: analyse how texts present views) and directed writing (Q4, 30 marks); in OCR through Language in the media (H470/02 Section B, 24 marks). Fairclough's (1989) Language and Power is the anchor text. Power in discourse: power exercised within the encounter and therefore visible in the transcript or text - who asks the questions, who interrupts, whose turns are allocated, what may be said. In a doctor-patient consultation the doctor's questions set the agenda; the patient's answers are structurally compelled. Analyse it through turn-taking, topic control, IRF sequences and constraints on contribution. Power behind discourse: the institutional machinery that decides the conventions themselves - who may enter the discourse (membership criteria), which register counts as legitimate, who owns the outlet. A courtroom's 'address the bench as your Honour' is power behind discourse: the rule exists before any interaction. In media texts, editorial policy and platform rules are the invisible layer. Instrumental vs influential power: instrumental enforces (statutes, directives, warnings backed by sanction); influential persuades (advertising, political rhetoric, charity appeals). The distinction is examinable in both directions - a workplace email can be instrumental ('submit by Friday or the audit fails') or influential ('it would be great if...'), and the politeness choice marks which. Synthetic personalisation (Fairclough 1989): mass-audience texts address each member as an individual ('you'), simulating intimacy at scale - the standard bridge between influential power and audience design. CDA - the three-dimensional method: (1) description : the text's linguistic features (lexis, grammar, modality, presupposition); (2) interpretation : the discursive practice - how the text was produced, distributed, consumed, and by whom; (3) explanation : the social practice - the ideology and power relations the text serves. The method turns a feature-spotting exercise into an argument about whose interests the language advances - which is precisely what OCR's 'investigate how language features and contextual factors construct meanings' and AQA's discourses questions reward. Presupposition is CDA's sharpest tool: covert assumptions ('yet another pointless delay') smuggle ideology in as common ground, and modality marks authority (deontic 'must' vs epistemic 'perhaps'). A worked contrast, hypothetical but methodologically exact: a court directive ('The defendant shall attend on the 14th') and a charity appeal ('Will you help one child tonight?'). The court text is instrumental power: deontic 'shall', formal register, no negotiation - power backed by sanction. The charity text is influential power: interrogative, direct address, emotional lexis - no formal authority, so the language works on attitude. Two sentences, two power types, the grammatical markers that distinguish them: that density is the standard for any paragraph on power. It also shows why the instrumental/influential split is examinable in unseen texts - the distinction is recoverable from the grammar alone, and the strongest answers recover it without being told the text's function. Face - Goffman (1967), Interaction Ritual : face is the positive social value a participant claims for themselves in interaction; interaction is face-work - a constant, delicate maintenance of one's own and others' face. Losing face is not metaphorical: threats to face disrupt the encounter itself. Politeness theory - Brown & Levinson (1987): two faces per participant. Positive face : the desire to be approved, liked, treated as a member of the group. Negative face : the desire for autonomy, to be unimpeded. Every face-threatening act (FTA) hits one or both: requests, orders and reminders threaten negative face; criticism, disagreement and bad news threaten positive face. The strategy set: (1) bald on-record - no mitigation, justified by urgency or high power ('Sit down'); (2) positive politeness - solidarity: in-group markers, compliments, inclusive 'we' ('Come on, we're all friends here'); (3) negative politeness - deference: hedges, indirectness, deferential modality ('I wondered whether you might possibly...'); (4) off-record - hint or implicature ('It's rather cold in here' meaning 'shut the window'); (5) no FTA - silence or topic shift. Choice is governed by power (P), social distance (D) and the ranking of the imposition (R): high P and D push towards negative politeness; low P and D license baldness or positive politeness. Critiques: culturally specific - some speech communities prioritise deference or solidarity differently, so the P/D/R calculus is not universal; it idealises the speaker as a rational strategist, underweighting institutional constraint (scripts, protocols) and emotion; and politeness is not only about power - reciprocity and routine matter too. Exam use: in transcripts (manager-worker, doctor-patient, teacher-pupil), identify the FTAs and the mitigation chosen, then infer the power relations - a bald on-record order from a subordinate is analytically interesting precisely because it breaks the predicted pattern. In media texts, politeness strategies manufacture brand intimacy: positive politeness plus synthetic personalisation is the standard combination in advertising and customer-facing copy. A worked chain in a media text, using a hypothetical customer email: 'We know you've been busy - whenever you get a chance, your account needs updating.' The FTA is a negative-face threat (the imposition of the update); the mitigation stacks two strategies - positive politeness ('We know you've been busy' - claimed empathy, in-group 'we') and negative politeness ('whenever you get a chance' - hedged imposition); and synthetic personalisation ('your account') scales the intimacy to a mass audience. Three strategies in one sentence - and the analysis says what each does, not just what each is called. That chain, pointed at whichever face is threatened, is the examinable core of politeness theory. Wareing (1999): occupational language divides by vertical power (exercised down a hierarchy - manager to worker, surgeon to nurse) and horizontal power (across peers - colleague to colleague, professional to professional). The same register serves both: jargon signals expertise horizontally and enforces hierarchy vertically. Jargon as gatekeeping: specialist terminology compresses meaning for insiders ('We'll escalate the SLA breach') and excludes outsiders - efficiency and exclusion simultaneously. In unseen texts, ask what the jargon assumes about the reader: a customer-facing letter that keeps the jargon is asserting institutional authority over the layperson; one that translates it is managing face. Workplace discourse features: directives (imperatives, obligation modality - 'we need this by Friday'), topic control in meetings, turn allocation, documented procedures; Koester (2004) showed phatic talk - small talk, banter, personal asides - is not off-task noise but builds solidarity and softens hierarchy, doing real relational work in institutional settings. Doctor-patient and teacher-pupil: the classic unequal encounters. Doctor controls the agenda through questions and topic shifts; patient supplies minimal responses - power in discourse backed by power behind it (institutional legitimacy, gatekept knowledge). Teacher-pupil talk runs on Sinclair & Coulthard's (1975) IRF/IRE structure: teacher initiates, pupil responds, teacher evaluates - the feedback slot is where the control lives. Critiques worth deploying: the 'informed patient' discourse shift has flattened some of the asymmetry; collaborative classroom talk redistributes the IRF slots. Exam use: AQA's diversity data sets include occupational data, and occupation is one of the social groups the June 2017 essay statement targets. In any workplace transcript, label the power through three moves: IRF or turn allocation (structure), FTA and mitigation choice (politeness), jargon and modality (register) - then explain each through the institutional context (AO3). A worked chain in a workplace transcript, hypothetical: 'Right, team - we need the figures by Friday. Sarah, can you chase finance?' The topic control ('we need') asserts vertical power through obligation modality; the inclusive 'we' softens it with positive politeness; the direct allocation ('Sarah, can you...') reserves the directive force for a named subordinate while hedging it as a question - power in discourse, strategy choice and hierarchy in one move. Where a text shows the reverse (a subordinate balding on-record, a superior hedging everything), that deviation is the analysis: it breaks the P/D/R prediction and therefore reveals the actual relations rather than the assumed ones. Electronic language cuts across every question type: AQA pairs electronic texts in Paper 1 Section A, targets electronic audiences in directed writing, and OCR's Language in the media texts are frequently digital. Treat e-language as a mode in its own right with its own affordances - Crystal's (2001) Language and the Internet frames it as a hybrid of speech and writing rather than degraded either. CMC features: synchronicity (live chat and video calls vs asynchronous email and forums), permanence and searchability, interactivity (comments, reactions, shares), audience reach (one-to-one to mass), and brevity economy (abbreviation, emoji, fragmented syntax). Asynchronous CMC borrows written planning; synchronous CMC borrows spoken turn-taking - the blend is the analysis, and claims like 'email is formal' should be evaluated against the informal workplace email that exists precisely because tenor overrides mode. Multimodality: Kress & van Leeuwen (2006) - image, colour, layout and typography carry meaning alongside words. In unseen digital texts, analyse composition: salience (what is biggest, boldest, most central), reading paths (headlines, hyperlinks, scroll order), and image anchoring (captions fixing what a photograph means). Typography is lexis by other means: a bolded claim, an ALL-CAPS warning, a lowercase aesthetic each signal attitude before any word is read. Power online: the gatekeeping power behind discourse has weakened - anyone can publish - but re-concentrated in platforms: algorithms rank, moderation deletes, terms of service constrain. Instrumental power in CMC includes moderation messages and platform rules; influential power scales through influencers and viral copy, with synthetic personalisation industrialised ('your journey', 'we picked this for you'). Anonymity and audience distance shift politeness: trolling is bald on-record FTAs at scale, while moderation notices perform institutional face repair. Hashtags aggregate topics and perform stance - influence in one token. Exam use - directed writing: AQA Q4 (30 marks) and OCR H470/01 Section B (24 marks) ask you to write for a specified audience - often a blog, script or article. Apply the theory in the writing itself: positive politeness and synthetic personalisation for an electronic audience, hedging for a non-specialist one, jargon only where the brief licenses it - and assess the ideas and issues of the source texts as the AQA command requires. A worked multimodal chain, using a hypothetical article: headline 'Remote work is killing teamwork' (bold, sans-serif), standfirst in grey, stock image of an empty office, pull-quote mid-article. The headline asserts the thesis with a present-tense declarative and a dysphemistic verb ('killing'); the typography and salience give it authority before any evidence is read; the grey standfirst subordinates the qualification; the empty office anchors the claim visually; the pull-quote re-foregrounds the most emotive source. Composition, typography and lexis carrying one representation claim - Kress & van Leeuwen's (2006) multimodality applied as analysis, not name-dropped. That is the density to reproduce on any electronic text: every layout choice is a linguistic choice by other means.

topics.name: Child Language Acquisition
topics.subject: english-language
topics.searchText: english-language English Language Child Language Acquisition Sequence the stages of spoken development - pre-verbal, holophrastic, two-word, telegraphic, post-telegraphic - and label the stage in unseen data from linguistic evidence, not from age alone (AO1). Analyse phonological development (substitution, deletion, assimilation, cluster reduction) and link phonological processes to lexical and grammatical growth (AO1). Categorise virtuous errors - overextension, underextension, overgeneralisation - and explain why they evidence rule formation rather than failed imitation (AO1/AO2). Evaluate theories critically: Chomsky's LAD and its critiques, Skinner's behaviourism, Piaget's cognitive model, Vygotsky's ZPD, Bruner's LASS and Halliday's functions (AO2). Analyse reading and writing development (emergent literacy, Kroll's phases, Britton's modes) and compare spoken and written trajectories (AO1/AO2). Apply the data-analysis method for AQA 7702/1 Section B (30 marks, AO1 15 + AO2 15) and OCR H470/02 Section A (20 marks, AO1 10 + AO2 10) within exam timing. AQA 7702/1 Section B = 30 marks: a discursive essay, choice of two questions, data may be spoken, written or multimodal (June 2024: a child transcript and children's writing). The June 2024 mark scheme splits Section B as AO1 15 + AO2 15: half data analysis, half critical evaluation of theories and the given statement - theory description alone cannot pass. OCR H470/02 Section A = 20 marks (AO1 10 + AO2 10): the language development stage of a child aged 0-7, analysing phonology, grammar and meaning, with the IPA provided in the paper. Label stages from evidence - utterance length, grammatical completeness, phonological processes - never from the child's age; mixed-stage data is normal and expected. Theories work best in evaluation pairs: nature (Chomsky) vs nurture (Skinner); cognition-first (Piaget) vs interaction-first (Vygotsky/Bruner); functions (Halliday) cut across all four. Virtuous errors are the single strongest classroom argument: systematic, rule-governed errors absent from adult input cannot be products of imitation alone. Holophrastic stage The single-word stage (roughly 12-18 months): one word may express a whole proposition (a holophrase); Nelson (1973) found over 60% of first words are nominals. Two-word stage From roughly 18-24 months: subject-verb and verb-object pairs ('daddy gone') with emerging word order; Braine analysed it as pivot + open-class grammar, with function words still absent. Telegraphic stage From roughly 24-36 months: content words only, with articles, auxiliaries, prepositions and inflections missing; measured by rising mean length of utterance (MLU - Brown, 1973). Post-telegraphic stage From roughly 36 months: grammatical function words acquired; remaining errors concentrate on inflection and agreement ('goed', 'sheeps'); subordinate clauses and auxiliary questions consolidate. Virtuous error A systematic, logical error produced by applying a rule too generally ('goed', 'foots'); crucially absent from adult input, so it evidences grammar construction rather than imitation (links to Chomsky). Overextension Applying a word beyond its adult meaning ('dog' for all four-legged animals); Rescorla (1980) distinguishes categorical, analogical and statement overextensions. Underextension Restricting a word to a subset of its adult meaning ('dog' used only for the family pet); shows meaning-building in progress in the opposite direction to overextension. LAD Chomsky's Language Acquisition Device: an innate faculty containing universal grammar; children exposed to imperfect, 'degenerate' input still acquire grammar rapidly - the poverty-of-stimulus argument. ZPD Vygotsky's zone of proximal development: the gap between what a child can do alone and what they can do with a more knowledgeable other; scaffolding (Wood, Bruner & Ross, 1976) bridges it. Child-directed speech (CDS) Caregiver speech adapted for the child - higher pitch, exaggerated intonation, simplified lexis, recasts, expansions, question loops; the input side of Bruner's Language Acquisition Support System (LASS). Both boards anchor this topic in data. AQA's Section B discursive essay (7702/1, 30 marks) supplies a Data Set and asks you to evaluate a given statement against it; OCR's H470/02 Section A (20 marks) asks you to examine the language development stage of the child-participant in a transcript. Either way, the stages are the spine - but treat them as descriptive guides, not universal checkpoints, because a top answer labels the stage from linguistic evidence and acknowledges overlap. Stage Rough age Features Exam anchor Pre-verbal 0-12 months Vegetative sounds, then cooing (4-7 months), then babbling - reduplicated strings ('mamama'); Jakobson argued babbling is universal across languages. Proto-words with consistent meaning ('baba' for bottle) mark the transition into lexical development. Holophrastic 12-18 months Single-word utterances where one word may express a whole proposition; Nelson (1973): 60%+ nominals, then action words, modifiers, personal-social words. Overextension and underextension typically begin here. Two-word 18-24 months Subject-verb and verb-object pairs ('daddy gone', 'want juice'); emerging word order; Braine's pivot + open-class grammar; function words absent. Word-order consistency is evidence of grammar construction - useful against pure imitation claims. Telegraphic 24-36 months Content words only: articles, auxiliaries, prepositions and inflections missing, like a telegram; MLU rises (Brown, 1973). Name which grammatical items are missing - precision beats the label. Post-telegraphic 36 months+ Function words acquired; errors concentrate on inflection and agreement; subordinate clauses, auxiliary questions and consolidated negatives appear. Link to Bellugi's negative and question stages for the grammar evidence. Deploy stages as evidence, not assertion: 'the utterances show telegraphic features - auxiliaries and articles are systematically absent - so the child sits at the telegraphic/post-telegraphic boundary' beats 'the child is 2, so telegraphic'. Mixed-stage data is normal: performance varies by context, task and fatigue; the transcript may show post-telegraphic syntax in one turn and holophrastic nouns in another - say so, and use it (the variation itself is analysable). Metrics: MLU (mean length of utterance) and the percentage of grammatically complete utterances are quick quantitative hooks that earn AO1 credit in a discursive essay. Where the marks are: in AQA's discursive essay the stage labels are scaffolding for the evaluation - the examiner rewards what you do with them: evidence of rule construction, of caregiver scaffolding, of the gap between perception and production. In OCR's Section A the stage is the question itself, so the opening sentence should commit to a stage and the closing paragraph should return to it. OCR's Section A question explicitly requires phonology, grammar and meaning - three levels, one answer - so have the detail ready at each. Phonological development: the phonemic inventory grows from vowels and plosives to fricatives and affricates; late-acquired sounds (/θ/ in thumb , /ʃ/ in shoe ) drive the classic processes: substitution ('fumb' for thumb), deletion ('ca' for cat), assimilation ('gog' for dog), consonant cluster reduction ('tee' for tree) and addition . The processes are systematic, which is the point: the child is operating a rule-governed system, not producing random error. Berko & Brown (1960) 's fis phenomenon - a child says 'fis' for fish but rejects an adult's 'fis' - shows perception running ahead of production. Lexical development: Nelson's category data (nominals dominant) at first-word stage; then semantic organisation - overextension (categorical: 'apple' for all round fruit; analogical: 'ball' for the moon; statement-type tied to context - Rescorla, 1980) and underextension ('dog' only for the family pet). Clark's (1973) semantic feature hypothesis explains the direction of error: meanings are built feature by feature. Note the comprehension-production gap: children understand more than they can say. Grammatical development: Brown (1973) tracked 14 grammatical morphemes in acquisition order - progressive -ing first, then articles, then regular past -ed (with overgeneralisation 'goed'), then third-person -s . Bellugi (with Brown) staged negatives (external 'no' + X, then external 'don't'/'can't', then internal negation 'I don't want') and questions (intonation-only, then wh-words without inversion, then auxiliary inversion). These sequences are ready-made analytic frames for any transcript. Pragmatics: turn-taking learned through CDS games and routines; politeness formulas ('please', 'sorry') early; Gricean implicature, irony and audience design much later, through the school years - a useful contrast when a question targets what children cannot yet do. Child-directed speech (CDS) threads through all three levels: higher pitch, exaggerated intonation, simplified lexis, slower tempo, recasts and expansions, question loops. In AQA's discursive essay CDS is usually the fastest route to the interaction side of the evaluation - but always tie the feature to a pattern in the data. Theory earns its AO2 marks only when evaluated against the data: give the claim, the support, the challenge and a judgement. Memorise each theory as a pair of arguments, not a paragraph of description. Chomsky - LAD (1965 onwards): an innate language faculty with universal grammar; the poverty-of-stimulus argument holds that adult input is imperfect and incomplete, yet children acquire grammar rapidly and uniformly. Evidence for: virtuous errors ('goed', 'foots') are never heard in adult speech, so they cannot be imitated; milestones are strikingly uniform across languages. Critiques: the LAD is a black box - no mechanism is specified; it underestimates input quality (CDS is more structured than Chomsky assumed); it has little to say about reading and writing development; and it treats grammar as the whole of acquisition, sidelining pragmatics and functions. Skinner - behaviourism (1957): language learned through imitation, reinforcement and habit formation. Evidence for: children demonstrably copy intonation contours, lexical items and CDS recasts. Critiques: the decisive one is Brown & Hanlon (1970) - caregivers respond to the truth value of utterances, not their grammatical form, so 'doggy bringed it' passes uncorrected while a true but ungrammatical utterance is approved; reinforcement cannot explain rule formation. Piaget - cognitive first: language maps onto cognitive development - object permanence (around 8 months) precedes naming, so thought precedes speech. Critiques: some lexical and pragmatic competence appears to precede the relevant cognitive stage, and the model underplays social interaction. Vygotsky - ZPD and the more knowledgeable other: development happens in the gap between independent and supported performance; scaffolding (Wood, Bruner & Ross, 1976) is the mechanism, and Bruner's LASS supplies the formats - routines, games, picture-book reading - in which CDS does its work. Evidence for: recasts and expansions in caregiver data; turn-taking skills built through CDS games. Critique: less explanatory for phonological detail, which develops with striking independence from input style. Halliday - functions (1975): seven functions of early language - instrumental (I want), regulatory (do as I say), interactional (me and you), personal (here I come), heuristic (tell me why), imaginative (let's pretend), representational (informative) - later regrouped into the mathetic (learning) and pragmatic (doing) phases. In a discursive essay, categorise data utterances by function and evaluate which dominate: infant speech is often more interactional and heuristic than the 'get things' stereotype suggests. The virtuous-error argument - why it kills pure imitation If language were learned by imitation alone, every child error would be a copy of adult speech. But 'goed', 'foots' and 'fis' never appear in adult input - the child has constructed a rule (add -ed for past tense; final devoicing) and applied it generally. That construction is exactly what Chomsky's LAD predicts and Skinner's reinforcement loop cannot explain. It is the highest-value three-line argument in this topic: name the error, state the rule, name the theory it supports. AQA's Section B can set written or multimodal data (June 2024's Question 5 asked about writing development), so the written strand is examinable, not optional. Reading: emergent literacy begins with environmental print and grapheme-phoneme awareness; the phonics (decoding) vs look-and-say (whole-word) debate frames instruction, and decoding typically precedes comprehension - Chall's stages run from prereading through initial decoding and fluency to reading for learning and multiplicity. For data analysis, note which words a child reads accurately and which they guess from shape or context. Writing: Kroll's (1981) phases - preparation (motor control, letter formation), consolidation (writing as they speak, strings of clauses), differentiation (genre awareness, punctuation), integration (audience and purpose control) - plus Britton's expressive → poetic → transactional progression. Invented spellings ('becos', 'wos') are orthographic virtuous errors: phonetic logic applied to spelling, evidence of systematic hypothesis-testing rather than carelessness. Multimodal development: children compose with emoji, capitals and formatting in messages - graphology as meaning-making, and a modern contrast to Kroll's print-based phases. The data-analysis method (AQA 7702/1 Section B, 30 marks = AO1 15 + AO2 15): Read the data twice. Note mode, context and the child's age - then set the age aside and identify the stage(s) from evidence: utterance length, grammatical completeness, phonological processes. Collect AO1 evidence level by level: phonology (use the transcription key; OCR supplies the IPA), lexis/semantics (Nelson's categories, over/underextension), grammar (Bellugi's negatives and questions, inflections, MLU), pragmatics (turn-taking, Halliday's functions, caregiver scaffolding visible in the data). Evaluate (AO2): match theories to patterns - CDS features → Vygotsky/Bruner; virtuous errors → Chomsky vs Skinner; functions in utterances → Halliday - and weigh both sides of the given statement with counter-examples. Write discursively: balanced paragraphs, each theory point anchored in quoted data ('Referring to Data Set 1 in detail' is a literal instruction), and an explicit judgement in the conclusion. OCR H470/02 Section A (20 marks = AO1 10 + AO2 10): the question names what it wants - the stage , then phonology, grammar and meaning, with theories supporting interpretation. Roughly 40 minutes: identify the stage with evidence in your opening, then one paragraph per level, theory woven into each, terminology throughout. OCR also expects you to read the phonemic transcription actively: pauses, stressed syllables and simultaneous speech in the key are analysis opportunities, not decoration.

topics.name: Language Change
topics.subject: english-language
topics.searchText: english-language English Language Language Change Distinguish internal change (analogy and regularisation, phonological erosion) from external change (borrowing, contact, technology) and illustrate both with dated examples (AO1/AO2). Apply the lexis processes of change - borrowing, coinage, compounding, blending, clipping, backformation, conversion - and recognise archaisms and their discourse uses (AO1). Analyse semantic shift through broadening, narrowing, amelioration and pejoration, with ready-made example pairs (AO2). Trace the standardisation chronology - Caxton 1476, Johnson 1755, Lowth 1762, Alford 1864, the 1870 Education Act, the BBC and OED - and evaluate Johnson's prescriptivism in aims and practice (AO2). Evaluate the prescriptivism vs descriptivism debate - Aitchison's models, Cameron's verbal hygiene, the Beale/Partridge prescriptive tradition - and avoid nostalgia arguments (AO2). Analyse change data: the OCR H470/02 Section C two-text comparison (36 marks) and the AQA 7702/2 evaluative essay (30 marks, AO1 10 + AO2 20). AQA 7702/2 Section A = 30 marks: a choice of two evaluative essays - language diversity or language change - marked AO1 10 + AO2 20 (June 2023 mark scheme). OCR H470/02 Section C = 36 marks: two texts from different periods (1600s to present), analysing variations and how contextual factors construct meaning; roughly 15 minutes preparation plus 50 minutes writing. Johnson (1755) was prescriptive in ambition - to 'fix' and 'ascertain' the language - but descriptive in practice: his Dictionary records usage with literary citations and 'offers no law'. Aitchison's three models (damp spoon, crumbling castle, infectious disease) are straw men to dismantle, not theories to accept - each fallacy has a named counter-argument. Every change needs a cause (internal or external), a route (S-curve diffusion, lexical diffusion, waves) and an attitude (prescriptivist or descriptivist) - structure essays around that triad. The semantic-shift quadrants - broadening/narrowing crossed with amelioration/pejoration - supply dateable examples: 'silly', 'pretty', 'meat', 'dog', 'villain'. Internal change Change generated within the language system itself - analogy and regularisation (holp to helped, kine to cows), phonological erosion of unstressed inflections - independent of external contact. External change Change driven by contact with other languages and societies - invasion, trade, colonialism, technology - most visibly through borrowing: Norse 'skirt', Norman French 'beef', modern 'sushi'. Semantic broadening A word's meaning widens over time: 'dog' once named a specific breed, 'holiday' once meant a holy day; now both cover far wider ranges. Semantic narrowing A word's meaning contracts: 'meat' once meant food of any kind, 'deer' any wild animal; both now name a specific category. Amelioration A word acquires more positive meaning: 'pretty' moved from crafty or cunning to attractive; 'sophisticated' from adulterated to cultured. Pejoration A word acquires more negative meaning: 'silly' moved from blessed to foolish; 'villain' from farm worker to criminal; 'notorious' from simply famous to infamous. Borrowing Adopting words from other languages; English borrowing is layered by historical contact - Norse, Norman French, Latin and Greek, colonial and global loans. Backformation Creating a new word by removing a supposed affix from an existing one: 'edit' from 'editor', 'burgle' from 'burglar'. Archaism A word or form no longer in ordinary use ('thou', 'prithee', 'anon'); in modern discourse texts archaisms build mock-formal or nostalgic registers. Prescriptivism The view that language should conform to fixed rules of correctness, promoted through grammars, usage guides and public comment (Lowth, Alford, Beale); opposed by descriptivism. Standardisation is the process by which one variety is selected, codified and accepted as the norm - Milroy & Milroy (1999) stress it is an ongoing ideological process, not a single event. The chronology is the backbone of any AQA 7702/2 essay or OCR H470/02 Section C answer that discusses attitudes to change, because dated anchors separate top-band evaluation from assertion. Date Event Exam anchor 1476 Caxton sets up the printing press in Westminster. Selection : the East Midlands dialect of the London area becomes the print standard; Caxton's own prefaces complain of spelling variety - orthography is still unstable. 1755 Johnson publishes his Dictionary of the English Language. Codification : prescriptive in ambition ('fix' and 'ascertain' the language), descriptive in practice - entries record usage with literary citations. 1762 Lowth publishes his Short Introduction to English Grammar. Prescriptive rules fossilise in schools: double negatives condemned, 'between you and I' policed - rules born as style advice become 'correctness'. 1864 Alford publishes A Plea for the Queen's English. Victorian prescriptivism at its most censorious - the register of complaint later satirised by descriptivists. 1870 Forster's Education Act. Mass literacy entrenches the standard and spreads prescriptive norms through schooling. 1922-28 BBC founded; first edition of the OED completed. RP becomes the broadcast standard (accent, not grammar); the OED records rather than legislates - descriptive lexicography. Johnson in detail: his 1747 Plan promised to 'ascertain' the language; his preface admits the futility of trying 'to enchain syllables, and to lash the wind' - the tension between prescriptive aim and descriptive practice is a ready-made evaluation point, and his letter refusing Chesterfield's patronage marks the lexicographer's independence. Lowth in detail: he aimed at errors , not elegance, and did not invent the split-infinitive ban (that is Alford, 1864) - correcting a common misattribution earns credit. Deployment: when a question targets prescriptivism, date the anxiety: the schoolroom grammar tradition (Lowth 1762, Murray's later grammars, Alford 1864, the Beale-revised Partridge usage guides) is a different phenomenon from institutional standardisation (Caxton, Johnson, the OED). Standard language ideology is the attitude that survives after codification: the belief that the standard variety is inherently 'correct' and 'proper' while regional and social varieties are deficient. Distinguish the two in every essay - standardisation is an institutional achievement (a shared print and educational norm), while the ideology is a social belief with real consequences (accent and dialect judgement, educational gatekeeping). AQA essay questions about attitudes to change are usually testing whether you can separate the achievement from the belief - and evaluate the belief with evidence rather than accepting or mocking it. Internal change is generated by the system itself: analogy and regularisation sweep irregular forms - 'holp' yields to 'helped', 'kine' to 'cows', and English verbs continue to regularise in speech ('strived' alongside 'strove'); phonological erosion wears away unstressed inflections once word stress fixed to the word-initial syllable, collapsing the case system that Old English carried. External change is driven by contact, and English borrowing is layered by it: Norse loans in the Danelaw ('skirt'/'shirt' doublets, the pronouns 'they', 'them'), Norman French after 1066 (law, government and cuisine registers - the 'beef'/'cow' prestige split), Latin and Greek scholarly borrowings in the Renaissance inkhorn controversy, colonial loans ('shampoo', 'bungalow'), and modern global and technological coinage ('sushi', 'karaoke', 'selfie'). Jean Aitchison's contribution is less a theory of why change happens than a demolition of the myths around it (Language Change: Progress or Decay?, 1981; her 1996 Reith lectures The Language Web). Each model is a metaphor to dismantle, with a counter-argument ready to hand: Damp spoon (slovenliness): the claim that change comes from laziness. Counter: change is systematic and rule-governed - nobody accuses speakers of sloppiness for pronouncing 'sandwich' as 'samwich' when the process is regular assimilation. Crumbling castle (golden-age fallacy): the claim that English was once at a peak and is decaying. Counter: there never was a golden age - older forms were neither more logical nor more expressive, and the Old English case system was its own burden. Infectious disease (catching change): the claim that change spreads contagiously through peer pressure. Counter: speakers adopt changes selectively and knowingly, like fashion - exposure does not guarantee uptake. Alongside the models sit the routes of change: the S-curve (a change starts slowly, accelerates, then completes - lexical diffusion, Chen 1972; Aitchison), the waves model (Bailey - innovations spread outward from centres like ripples), functional theory (language changes to fill a need - 'brexit' exists because the concept did) and random fluctuation (Hockett, 1958) - the weakest explanation, useful mainly as a contrast to strike down in an evaluation. Change in progress is examinable: contemporary examples - 'th' fronting in London ('fink' for think), 'whom' retreating to fixed registers, intensifier bleaching ('literally'), regularisation in speech ('strived') - let an answer argue that change is observable now , not just in the archive. Substratum theory (contact between varieties reshaping the incoming language - multi-ethnic London English as the textbook case) bridges the internal/external divide: contact supplies the trigger, but the changes follow regular internal patterns. The lexis-level toolkit supplies the AO1 evidence in every essay, and the semantic-shift categories supply the most dateable examples. Word-formation processes: borrowing (layered by contact: Norse, Norman, Latin, global - 'sushi'); coinage or neologism ('selfie' - OED Word of the Year 2013); compounding (two free morphemes: 'laptop', 'deadline', 'brexit'); blending (fused fragments: 'brunch', 'infotainment', 'chillax'); clipping ('blog' from weblog, 'fridge', 'exam'); backformation ('edit' from editor, 'burgle' from burglar); conversion (a brand name becomes a verb: 'to google'); affixation with productive suffixes ('-gate' generating scandal terms, '-core' generating aesthetic labels). Archaisms: 'thou', 'thee', 'prithee', 'anon' survive in fixed registers - prayer, wedding vows, fantasy - and in modern discourse texts they build mock-formal or nostalgic voices; archaic grammar (second-person inflections, 'ye') is a quick spot in OCR's historical texts. Broadening: 'dog' once named a specific (now extinct) breed; 'holiday' moved from holy day to any break; 'butcher' from one who slaughters goats to any meat-seller. Narrowing: 'meat' from any food to animal flesh; 'deer' from any wild animal to one species; 'hound' from any dog to a hunting breed. Amelioration: 'pretty' from crafty or cunning to attractive; 'knight' from boy or servant to noble rank; 'sophisticated' from adulterated to cultured. Pejoration: 'silly' from blessed to innocent to foolish; 'villain' from farm worker to criminal; 'notorious' from simply well-known to infamous; 'hussy' from mistress of a household to its dismissive opposite. Also useful: semantic weakening or bleaching ('very' from 'veray' true to a bare intensifier; 'literally' losing literal force), euphemism ('pass away', 'let go'), and metaphor as a change mechanism (grasp an idea, run a meeting). Causes to cite: social prestige (borrowing from high-status contact - Norman French loans survive because the conquerors held power), taboo avoidance (euphemism cycles: each replacement weakens and is replaced in turn), functional need (new concepts demand new words - functional theory), metaphorical extension, and institutional standardisation itself (which slows some changes and fixes others). In the AQA essay, each process should appear with a dated example and an etymological note - precision is the AO1 currency. In the OCR comparison, the processes are the fastest route to level-by-level differences: quote a clipped or blended coinage in the modern text against an archaism in the earlier one and the lexis paragraph writes itself. The prescriptivism vs descriptivism debate is where AO2 marks concentrate. The descriptivist case : change is natural, systematic and ongoing (Aitchison's demolition of the three myths); dictionaries and corpora record rather than legislate (the OED tradition); 'all living languages change' (Crystal). The prescriptivist case : a shared standard aids clarity, education and social mobility; institutional standardisation was deliberate policy, not accident. Deborah Cameron (Verbal Hygiene, 1995) reframes the debate: prescriptivism is a real social practice worth studying - the question is not 'is it wrong to police language?' but 'why do people care, and whose interests do the rules serve?'. The prescriptive tradition has its own voice: Paul Beale , editor of Partridge's Usage and Abusage (1994), guards 'correct' usage; media prescriptivists - Kingsley Amis (The King's English), John Humphrys, Lynne Truss (Eats, Shoots & Leaves, 2003), Nevile Gwynne (Gwynne's Grammar, 2013) - supply quotable alarmism, and each is a straw man for Aitchison's crumbling castle. A top answer holds both truths: standardisation is real and useful; purist nostalgia is false. Change data analysis - the AQA essay (7702/2 Section A, 30 marks = AO1 10 + AO2 20): Define the key term in the question ('contact', 'change', 'decay') - the evaluation cannot start until the claim is precise. Evaluate in two movements: support the claim with external-contact or internal examples, then challenge with counter-causes - each example dated, each linguist named. Judge: contact is a powerful but partial cause; internal forces (analogy, erosion), functional need and S-curve diffusion operate regardless; standardisation reshapes the outcome. Avoid the two common traps: nostalgia (the crumbling-castle fallacy - there was no golden age) and descriptivist dismissal (mocking prescriptivists without engaging their claims - Cameron's point is that the anxiety is worth studying ). Both sides evaluated is what AO2 20 looks like. OCR H470/02 Section C (36 marks, June 2024: two texts from the early 20th and 21st centuries; 15 minutes preparation, about 50 minutes writing): compare level by level - lexis (archaisms vs neologisms; clipped, blended modern coinage), semantics (shifted meanings of shared words - the semantic-shift quadrants in action), grammar (inflections and spelling variance in the earlier text; modal density and sentence complexity), orthography (capitalisation, long 's' in older eras), discourse conventions (period genres and structures). Attribute each difference to contextual factors - the progress of standardisation, mass education, technology, media era - and integrate: point of comparison, Text C evidence, Text D evidence, explicit link. Use the 15-minute preparation to build the comparison grid before writing a word.

topics.name: Language Discourses
topics.subject: english-language
topics.searchText: english-language English Language Language Discourses Identify language discourses - texts debating language use, change, diversity, gender and power - and connect them to the wider debates they draw on (AO2). Analyse attitudes and perspectives: how texts represent language, construct the producer's identity and position the reader (AQA spec 4.2.3; AO1/AO3). Deploy the discursive-device catalogue - prescriptive claims, anecdotes, appeals to authority, modality, evaluative lexis, metaphor, hyperbole - as evidence of stance (AO1/AO3). Compare how two texts present views on a language issue, evaluating how effectively each presents its case (AQA 7702/2 Question 3, 40 marks: AO1 10 + AO3 15 + AO4 15). Write a directed or opinion piece for a non-specialist audience: assess ideas from the texts, refer to ideas from language study, argue a view (AQA 7702/2 Question 4, 30 marks: AO2 20 + AO5 10). Adapt to OCR's discourse tasks: Language in the media (H470/02 Section B, 24 marks: AO2 12 + AO3 12) and the topical-issue directed writing (H470/01 Section B, 24 marks). AQA 7702/2 Section B: Question 3 = 40 marks (AO1 10 + AO3 15 + AO4 15) analysing how two texts present views; Question 4 = 30 marks (AO2 20 + AO5 10) - an opinion article. AQA spec 4.2.3: discourse texts represent language, construct an identity for the producer, position the reader and connect to wider discourses about language - four bullets, four jobs. Devices double as stance evidence: high modality + evaluative lexis + hyperbole + anecdote = prescriptive; hedging + corpus citation + named linguists = descriptivist. June 2023's texts were both on the full stop (The Conservative Woman and MailOnline, 2020) - same issue, opposing personas: the examiner tests how each presents, not what they claim. OCR places discourses in H470/02 Section B (Language in the media, 24 marks - multimodal text, AO2 12 + AO3 12) and H470/01 Section B (topical statement directed writing, 24 marks, ~500 words). Question 4's three bullets are a checklist: assess the ideas and issues raised in Text A and Text B, refer to ideas from language study, argue your own views - hit all three or lose marks. Language discourse A way of talking or writing about language: the attitudes, debates and representations circulating about language use, change or variety - the topic of the texts, not their grammar alone. Prescriptivism The view that language should conform to fixed rules of 'correctness'; in discourse texts, prescriptive claims assert decline, error or threat ('texting is destroying English'). Descriptivism The view that language should be described as it is used, without legislating correctness; in discourse texts, descriptivists cite corpora, dictionaries and linguists against alarmism. Standard language ideology The belief that one standard variety is inherently superior and 'proper'; the backdrop to most prescriptive discourse and to debates about accents and dialects. Verbal hygiene Cameron's (1995) term for the everyday and institutional practices by which people debate and attempt to 'clean up' language - prescriptivism studied as a real social practice rather than dismissed. Appeal to authority A discursive move citing experts, dictionaries or institutions ('the OED now lists...') to license a claim about language; the descriptivist's favourite device, often cherry-picked by prescriptivists. Anecdote A personal story used as pseudo-evidence ('I recently overheard...'); marks conversational register, positions the writer as relatable, and substitutes narrative for data. Modality The grammar of certainty and obligation ('must', 'surely', 'arguably'); high modality marks a prescriptive stance, hedged modality a tentative or evidence-led one. Evaluative lexis Words carrying judgement of language itself ('sloppy', 'decadent', 'vibrant', 'lazy'); the fastest lexical route to a writer's stance. Metalinguistic commentary Language used to talk about language - corrections, quotations treated as objects of complaint ('so-called innovations'), and labels applied to other speakers' usage. Language discourses are texts about language: newspaper columns, letters pages, blogs, Mumsnet threads, radio phone-ins, speeches and public statements that debate language use, change, diversity, gender and power. AQA assesses them in Paper 2 Section B (7702/2) - a 40-mark analysis of two texts presenting views (June 2023: both articles on the full stop, from The Conservative Woman and MailOnline, 2020) plus a 30-mark opinion article - and the diversity/change essay in Section A also demands 'social attitudes to, and debates about, language' (spec 4.2.1). OCR places discourses in H470/02 Section B (Language in the media: a multimodal media text analysed with theories of power, gender or technology - 24 marks) and H470/01 Section B (directed writing on a topical statement - June 2024: 'Americanisms are taking over the English language.' , a speech for an English class, ~500 words - 24 marks). AQA's spec (4.2.3) lists four things discourse texts do - and each is a line of analysis: they represent language (as decaying organism, as property, as living thing), they construct an identity for the producer (the exasperated purist, the amused descriptivist, the concerned parent), they position the reader and seek to influence (direct address, inclusive 'we', rhetorical questions), and they connect to discourses about language (the decline narrative, the gendered critique of 'vocal fry' and 'uptalk', the Americanism panic, the political-correctness debate, apostrophe protection). Recurring topics: Americanisms and borrowing (the 'taking over' narrative - Crystal's Txtng: The Gr8 Db8 is the classic descriptivist counter to the texting panic), accent hierarchies and prestige (link to the Language Diversity strand), politically correct language, punctuation panics (Truss's Eats, Shoots & Leaves ), and generational complaint ('young people are ruining English'). Gender and power discourses are tested too: the 'vocal fry' and 'uptalk' panics target young women's speech and recycle prescriptive anxiety in gendered form - the descriptivist counter is that the criticism is about the speakers, not the phonetics. Political-correctness debates position 'the woke' as language vandals; the counter is that all institutional language change (titles, terminology) has always been negotiated. Power discourses - political spin, euphemism, institutional jargon - draw on the Language and Power strand, and the same device catalogue applies: nominalisation concealing agency, modality asserting authority. Electronic discourses: social media threads (Mumsnet, X) as discourse venues - direct address, escalation, and screen-based register; comment sections make reception visible, so writers design language for engagement as much as argument. The two texts are usually paired around one issue with opposing or complementary stances - so the analysis target is how each presents , not a verdict on the linguistics. Stance identification is a method, not an impression. Work the levels systematically, and anchor every attitude claim to a quoted device: Lexis: evaluative load ('sloppy', 'vibrant', 'decadent', 'lazy') reveals stance before any argument is made; semantic fields build the representation - decay ('ruin', 'erode', 'slide') vs growth ('evolve', 'enrich', 'borrow'). Modality: high modality and declaratives ('texting is destroying', 'we must resist') mark prescription; hedging and evidence-conditional phrasing ('arguably', 'the evidence suggests') mark descriptivism. Pronouns and positioning: inclusive 'we' recruits the reader into the stance; 'us and them' divides defenders from vandals (young people, institutions, Americans); synthetic personalisation (Fairclough) simulates intimacy in mass-audience texts. Metaphor: the decline/decay/infection frame vs the evolution/growth frame - Aitchison's three models (damp spoon, crumbling castle, infectious disease) are themselves discourse metaphors: spot the metaphor in the text, name the model it echoes, and dismantle its fallacy in your evaluation. Hyperbole and numbers: inflated claims ('everyone knows', 'completely destroyed') and empty quantifiers substitute volume for evidence; precise corpus figures (Google ngrams, OED citations) are the descriptivist counter. Producer identity: the persona built through anecdote, self-deprecation or authority-citing - the exasperated purist's persona licenses complaint; the amused descriptivist's persona licenses mockery of the complaint. Irony and sarcasm: stance markers that invert surface meaning - quote them and read both layers. Media context (AO3): producers and audiences shape the register of complaint - a niche blog (The Conservative Woman) can be more polemical than a mass tabloid (MailOnline), whose online mode forces shorter, bolder syntax and clickable headlines; mode and era are the fastest context marks. Deployment: every paragraph should name the attitude, quote the device that constructs it, and tie both to the text's purpose and audience - an attitude asserted without a quotation is assertion, and a quotation without an attitude claim is description. Positioning in detail earns the AO3 top band: ask of every text who is given authority (the writer? a quoted expert? 'common sense'?), who is cast as the problem (young people, institutions, Americans, 'the woke'?), and what the reader is invited to feel (alarm, amusement, superiority, solidarity). The answers usually explain the text's structure: an anecdotal opening gives the writer eyewitness authority; an authority citation transfers it; a rhetorical question hands the turn to the reader. A discourse text is an argument about language built entirely through positioning - read it as persuasion, not information. Memorise the devices as evidence of stance - each carries a recognisable effect and reveals what the writer wants from the reader. Device Example form Effect and what it reveals Prescriptive claim High-modality declarative + evaluative lexis: 'Texting is destroying the English language.' Asserts decline as fact; reveals standard language ideology - the claim assumes one 'correct' English exists. Anecdote 'I recently overheard a teenager say...' Pseudo-evidence; positions the writer as relatable eyewitness; substitutes narrative for data. Appeal to authority 'The OED now lists...'; 'linguists agree that...' Licenses the claim institutionally; descriptivists cite corpora and named linguists, prescriptivists cherry-pick. Empty quantifier 'Everyone knows', 'no one says anymore' False consensus substitutes for evidence; a hyperbole marker of prescriptive alarmism. Slippery slope 'Next it will be...' Projects a single change into total collapse; the decline narrative in miniature. Golden-age nostalgia 'English used to be spoken properly.' Aitchison's crumbling castle - there never was a peak; dateable counter-evidence exists in any historical text. Straw man 'Descriptivists think anything goes.' Misrepresents the opposing case to demolish it; descriptivists in fact describe systematic variation. Corpus/data citation 'Google ngrams show usage rising since 1990.' The descriptivist counter-move: evidence replaces anecdote; precision signals expertise. Faux-informal intimacy Direct address, asides, contractions in blogs Builds reader rapport in opinion pieces; the register design of the directed-writing task. Structural devices: anecdotal openings (foregrounding the complaint), listicle format (a modern media convention), rhetorical questions as topic shifts, and punchy conclusions that restate the stance - structure evidences purpose, so analyse it. Deployment: in the 40-mark comparison, pair devices across the two texts - the same device (an anecdote) doing different work in each text is a ready-made AO4 point. From catalogue to analysis: the device list is a starting inventory, not the answer. The top band comes from connecting devices to stance and stance to discourse: a single paragraph should move from quotation ('I recently overheard...') to device (anecdote as pseudo-evidence) to stance (prescriptive, nostalgic) to the wider discourse it echoes (the decline narrative - Aitchison's crumbling castle). That four-step chain, repeated across both texts and then compared, is what 'examine any similarities and differences... explore how effectively the texts present their views' rewards. AQA Question 3 (40 marks = AO1 10 + AO3 15 + AO4 15): 'Analyse how language is used in Text A and Text B to present views about changing uses of language. In your answer you should: examine any similarities and differences you find between the two texts; explore how effectively the texts present their views.' For each text: the representation of the language issue, the stance (prescriptive/descriptivist or a blend), and the devices constructing both - anchored in quotation. Compare (AO4): points of similarity and difference in how the views are presented - persona, register, evidence type, structure - not just what the views are. Evaluate effectiveness (the second bullet): does the evidence support the claim? does the persona engage or alienate the reader? does the register fit the audience? - judgement earns the top band. Timing: Section B is 70 marks in roughly 90 minutes - about 50 for Question 3 and 40 for Question 4, after 15 minutes reading the texts. AQA Question 4 (30 marks = AO2 20 + AO5 10): 'Write an opinion article on views about the changing uses of language. In your article you should: assess the ideas and issues raised in Text A and Text B; refer to ideas from language study; argue your own views.' The three bullets are a checklist: assess (weigh the texts' claims - where they hold, where they fail), refer to ideas from language study (original examples beyond the texts - Aitchison's models, Crystal's descriptivism, standard language ideology - this is the AO2 20), and argue your own views (a thesis, not a summary). Craft for the non-specialist audience: headline, accessible but informed register (OCR targets a 'reasonably well-educated, non-specialist audience'), counter-arguments addressed, and an engaging voice - that voice is the AO5 10. OCR's versions: H470/01 Section B (24 marks) gives the statement, format and audience - 'Write a speech for an English class arguing for or against the statement. Aim for 500 words': plan a stance, three arguments with named examples from language study, address the class audience directly, use rhetorical devices sparingly. H470/02 Section B (24 marks = AO2 12 + AO3 12) asks you to 'investigate how language features and contextual factors construct meanings' in a multimodal media text: apply theories (language and power - Fairclough; gender; technology) to linguistic and graphological features, and tie each to the media context - it is a discourse-analysis task, not an opinion piece.
