Obtaining the target gene : (1) reverse transcriptase - isolate mRNA for the target protein (abundant in specialised cells, e.g. β-cells for insulin), use reverse transcriptase (from retroviruses) to make cDNA ; cDNA contains no introns , so bacteria (which cannot splice) can translate it, and single-stranded cDNA is made double-stranded with DNA polymerase; (2) restriction endonucleases - cut the gene from DNA at a specific palindromic recognition site , leaving staggered sticky ends ; (3) a gene machine synthesises the gene directly from a known sequence (from genome databases). Inserting into a vector : the same restriction enzyme cuts a plasmid at a single site, producing complementary sticky ends; gene and plasmid anneal by complementary base pairing, and DNA ligase seals the sugar-phosphate backbones with phosphodiester bonds, producing recombinant DNA . Transforming cells : plasmids are returned to host bacteria (e.g. E. coli) via Ca²⁺ and heat shock (or electroporation), making membranes permeable; marker genes identify successful uptake - fluorescent markers (GFP), antibiotic-resistance markers (survivors grown on antibiotic agar carry the plasmid) or enzyme markers; replica plating distinguishes plasmids with the target gene. Fermenters culture transformed bacteria to mass-produce protein (insulin, factor VIII, vaccines). In vivo (vectors, bacteria) vs in vitro (PCR) comparison is a standard six-marker: in vivo is slow but accurate (proof-reading enzymes, low error rate), copies large fragments, produces modified proteins (post-translational modification possible in bacteria is limited - note insulin is made as pro-insulin), and carries little risk of contamination; in vitro (PCR) is rapid, automatable, needs only tiny DNA samples, but has a higher error rate (Taq lacks proof-reading) and produces many identical copies without modification. Ethics of recombinant DNA and transgenic organisms: benefits (mass cheap insulin, GM crops with higher yield/nutrition, gene therapy); concerns (antibiotic-resistance marker genes spreading to pathogens, GM gene flow to wild populations, animal welfare, corporate control of seeds); evaluation questions want both sides plus a justified conclusion. PCR (polymerase chain reaction) amplifies DNA in vitro in three repeating stages: (1) denaturation at ~95 °C - hydrogen bonds break, separating the double helix into single strands; (2) annealing at ~55 °C - short single-stranded primers bind complementarily to the 3' ends of the target sequences, providing the starting point for DNA synthesis (and preventing re-annealing of the template strands); (3) extension at ~72 °C - Taq polymerase (thermostable, from the bacterium Thermus aquaticus ) adds free nucleotides (dNTPs) to synthesise complementary strands. Each cycle doubles the DNA (2ⁿ after n cycles: ~1 billion copies after 30 cycles). A thermal cycler automates the temperature cycling. Exam questions ask for the role of primers and Taq exactly as above, and why Taq is needed (does not denature at 95 °C). Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by size: DNA fragments are negatively charged by their phosphate groups , so in an agarose gel with an electric current they migrate towards the anode (+) ; shorter fragments travel further/faster through the gel pores, separating fragments by length; fragments are visualised under UV with a fluorescent dye. Combined with PCR, electrophoresis underlies DNA profiling (genetic fingerprinting) : amplify variable number tandem repeat (VNTR) regions, electrophorese, and compare banding patterns between individuals - used in forensics, paternity testing and diagnosis. DNA probes : short single-stranded DNA fragments labelled with radioactive or fluorescent tags ; they hybridise to complementary target sequences on a membrane or gel, locating specific alleles - the basis of screening for mutated alleles (e.g. BRCA1) in medical genetics. DNA sequencing : chain-termination (Sanger) or modern high-throughput methods determine the exact base order of fragments; allele sequences from genome projects let probes be designed. AQA and OCR may also expect allele frequency screening and personalised medicine as applications. Genome projects sequence the entire DNA of organisms (Human Genome Project completed 2003). Proteomics - the study of the complete set of proteins an organism produces - reveals that the ~20,000 human genes produce far more proteins via alternative splicing and post-translational modification , so knowing the genome does not fully predict the proteome. Sequencing pathogen genomes enables rapid vaccine/drug design and epidemiology; comparative genomics maps evolutionary relationships and identifies disease genes. Medical applications of sequencing and probes: screening for mutated alleles before symptoms (predictive testing), personalised medicine (drug choice and dosage by genotype), prenatal and preimplantation diagnosis, and locating genes for gene therapy. Ethical evaluation is a guaranteed 5-6 marker on AQA (3.8.4) and Edexcel (T8) - structure it as benefits, concerns, conclusion. Benefits: earlier diagnosis and treatment; personalised medicine; gene therapy for inherited diseases (CF, SCID); GM crops addressing food security; forensic accuracy. Concerns: genetic discrimination (insurers/employers using screening data); privacy of genetic databases; consent and ownership; embryo use in therapy and screening (destruction of embryos, designer babies); safety of gene therapy (insertion mutagenesis, immune reactions); GM organisms escaping into ecosystems. Gene therapy : supplementing or silencing faulty genes - somatic therapy (body cells only, not inherited, e.g. CF inhalation therapy) vs germ-line therapy (germ cells, heritable, currently illegal in humans on ethical grounds). Screening ethics questions expect you to discuss autonomy, confidentiality, and the right not to know, with a justified judgement - quote the spec point that decision-making is an individual and societal matter.

topics.name: Immunity
topics.subject: biology
topics.searchText: biology Biology Immunity Describe non-specific defences (barriers, inflammation, phagocytosis) and antigen presentation (AQA 3.2.4; OCR 4.1.1) Describe cell-mediated immunity: T-helper and T-cytotoxic cells and clonal selection/expansion (AQA 3.2.4; OCR 4.1.1) Describe humoral immunity: B cells, plasma cells, antibody structure and action (AQA 3.2.4; OCR 4.1.1) Compare primary and secondary responses and explain vaccination and herd immunity (AQA 3.2.4; Edexcel A T6) Distinguish active and passive immunity and describe monoclonal antibody uses (ELISA, pregnancy tests, targeted therapy) Describe HIV structure and replication and explain antibiotic action and resistance (AQA 3.2.4/3.8; OCR 4.1.1) Non-specific: skin, mucus, lysozyme, inflammation; phagocytosis: chemotaxis → phagosome → lysosome fusion → hydrolysis → antigen presentation Cell-mediated: APC activates complementary T-helper cells → clonal expansion → T-cytotoxic cells kill infected/tumour cells with perforin Humoral: T-helper activates B cells → clonal expansion → plasma cells (antibodies) + memory B cells Antibody: 2 heavy + 2 light chains, disulfide bridges; variable region complementary to antigen; forms antigen-antibody complex; agglutination/opsonisation Primary response: slow (clonal selection), antibody rises then falls; secondary: faster, stronger, longer (memory cells) Vaccines: weakened/inactivated pathogens or antigens → active immunity; herd immunity protects the unvaccinated HIV: RNA + reverse transcriptase in capsid; infects T-helper cells; reverse transcription → DNA → host transcription → viral proteins → budding Antibiotics: target bacterial structures (cell wall, ribosomes); resistance via mutation + selection pressure Pathogen A disease-causing microorganism (bacterium, virus, fungus, protoctist) that triggers an immune response. Antigen A cell-surface molecule (usually a glycoprotein or glycolipid) that the immune system recognises as foreign (non-self), triggering an immune response. Phagocytosis Non-specific engulfment of pathogens by phagocytes: the pathogen is enclosed in a phagosome that fuses with lysosomes so hydrolytic enzymes digest it; the phagocyte then presents the antigens. Antigen-presenting cell (APC) A phagocyte (or infected body cell) that displays foreign antigens on its cell-surface membrane after digesting a pathogen, activating specific T cells. Clonal selection and expansion The process by which a specific complementary B or T cell is selected by an antigen, then stimulated to divide by mitosis into many genetically identical cells (a clone). Plasma cell A B cell differentiated during the primary response that secretes large quantities of specific antibodies; short-lived. Memory cell A long-lived B or T cell formed in the primary response that remains in the blood; on re-exposure it enables a faster, stronger secondary response. Antibody A Y-shaped protein (immunoglobulin) of two heavy and two light polypeptide chains joined by disulfide bridges; variable regions form complementary antigen-binding sites, the constant region binds phagocytes. Herd immunity When a sufficiently high proportion of a population is vaccinated (or immune) that pathogens cannot spread easily, protecting unvaccinated individuals. Active immunity Immunity from the production of antibodies by the person's own immune system after exposure to an antigen (natural infection or vaccination); slow but long-lasting with memory cells. The body's first lines of defence are non-specific - they respond to any pathogen the same way. Physical barriers: the skin (keratinised, impermeable, flora outcompete pathogens), mucus in the airways (secreted by goblet cells, traps pathogens, moved by cilia), lysozyme in tears and saliva (hydrolyses bacterial cell walls), stomach acid (pH ~2 kills most ingested pathogens), and blood clotting sealing wounds. Inflammation at a wound: histamine release from mast cells causes vasodilation (redness, heat) and increased capillary permeability (swelling), bringing phagocytes and plasma proteins to the site. Phagocytosis is the key non-specific cellular defence and a guaranteed sequence question (from the existing site content): (1) phagocytes (e.g. macrophages, neutrophils) are attracted to pathogens by chemicals they release ( chemotaxis ); (2) the phagocyte extends its cell-surface membrane around the pathogen, engulfing it into a phagosome ; (3) lysosomes fuse with the phagosome, releasing hydrolytic enzymes (e.g. lysozyme) that digest the pathogen ; (4) soluble products are absorbed into the cytoplasm; (5) the phagocyte becomes an antigen-presenting cell (APC) , displaying the pathogen's antigens on its cell-surface membrane. Antigen presentation is the bridge to the specific immune response: these antigens stimulate complementary T-helper cells , which in turn activate specific B cells. When answering, always link the non-specific phase to the specific phase through the APC - that connection is where most marks are lost. Inflammation deserves the detail the mark schemes list: damaged tissues and mast cells release histamine , which causes arterioles to vasodilate (redness, heat) and capillaries to become more permeable (swelling, oedema), delivering plasma proteins and phagocytes to the infection; the increased blood flow raises the local temperature, slowing pathogen reproduction. Blood clotting seals wounds: platelets adhere to damaged tissue, a cascade of clotting factors activates thrombin, which converts soluble fibrinogen to insoluble fibrin, trapping erythrocytes in a mesh; the scab then protects while repair occurs - positive feedback in the platelet activation step, so it is a stock example of amplification. Cell-mediated immunity responds to cells displaying foreign antigens - body cells infected by viruses, cells altered by mutation (cancer cells), transplanted cells and APCs. Sequence: (1) a complementary T-helper cell binds to the antigen displayed on an APC (via its CD4 receptor and specific antigen receptor); (2) the APC activates the T-helper cell, which clonally expands by mitosis into a clone of active T-helper cells and memory T cells ; (3) active T-helper cells stimulate specific B cells (humoral response) and phagocytes (enhanced phagocytosis) by releasing cytokines; (4) T-cytotoxic (killer) cells bind to complementary antigens on virus-infected or tumour cells and destroy them by releasing perforin , which makes pores in the target membrane so water flows in and the cell lyses. T-cytotoxic cells are the only cells that kill infected body cells directly - a key distinction from B cells (which produce antibodies against free pathogens). Memory T cells provide rapid cell-mediated secondary responses. HIV destroys T-helper cells, collapsing both arms of specific immunity (see below) - explaining why AIDS leaves patients vulnerable to opportunistic infections. Humoral immunity responds to antigens free in body fluids (blood, lymph). Sequence: (1) specific B cells with complementary antibodies on their surface bind the antigen; (2) activated T-helper cells release cytokines that stimulate the B cells to clonally expand by mitosis (clonal selection and expansion); (3) most differentiate into plasma cells , which secrete large quantities of specific antibodies into the blood (up to 2000 per second); (4) some become memory B cells , long-lived, providing the secondary response. Antibody structure : a Y-shaped protein of two heavy and two light polypeptide chains joined by disulfide bridges ; the variable regions at the tips of the Y have a tertiary structure complementary to one specific antigen (like a lock and key), forming an antigen-antibody complex ; the constant region binds phagocyte receptors and complement. Antibody action: agglutination (clumping pathogens so phagocytes engulf many at once), opsonisation (marking pathogens for phagocytes), neutralisation of toxins , and preventing pathogens binding to host cells . Always state the complementarity of the variable region to the antigen - the mark scheme rewards the specificity link, not just 'antibodies kill pathogens'. Clonal selection and expansion is the process the mark schemes dissect: each naive B cell carries antibodies of one specificity on its surface; when a complementary antigen binds, that B cell is selected ; cytokines from T-helper cells stimulate it to divide by mitosis , producing a clone of genetically identical cells; the clone differentiates into plasma cells (antibody secretion) and memory B cells (secondary response). This is why the response is specific and why vaccination works - the vaccine antigen selects the complementary clones without disease. Antigen-antibody complexes are then cleared: agglutinated pathogens are engulfed by phagocytes, and the complexes can also activate complement proteins that lyse bacteria - quote agglutination, opsonisation and neutralisation of toxins as the three antibody actions. Interpret antibody concentration graphs : the primary response is slow - clonal selection and expansion take days to weeks; antibody concentration rises gradually, peaks, then falls as plasma cells die. The secondary response on re-exposure is faster, stronger and longer-lasting : memory B cells divide rapidly into plasma cells without needing T-helper activation of naive B cells, so high antibody concentrations are reached before symptoms develop (pathogen destroyed before it causes disease - the basis of immunity). Learn to read the graph axes and label both peaks; questions ask you to explain the difference in terms of memory cells, not just 'faster'. Vaccination provides active artificial immunity : weakened, inactivated or fragment pathogens (or antigens/toxoids) are injected/taken orally, triggering the primary response so memory cells form without the person suffering disease; on natural exposure, the secondary response prevents symptoms. Herd immunity : when a high proportion of the population is vaccinated, pathogens cannot spread easily because most contacts are immune - protecting unvaccinated individuals (newborns, immunocompromised). The herd immunity threshold depends on how contagious the pathogen is (measles ~95%). Vaccination data interpretation (effectiveness, changing strains, uptake rates) appears on all boards. Active vs passive immunity : active - own immune system produces antibodies (infection or vaccination); slow onset but long-lasting with memory cells ; passive - antibodies received from another organism (placental transfer, breast milk, antivenom, injected immunoglobulin); immediate but short-lived, no memory cells (antibodies are broken down). Learn the 2×2 grid: natural/artificial × active/passive, with one example each - a guaranteed definition-style question. Vaccine types and interpretation : vaccines contain live attenuated pathogens (MMR - strong, long-lasting immunity), inactivated pathogens (flu - weaker, needs boosters), fragment/antigen vaccines (subunit - safest) or toxoids (inactivated toxins - tetanus); mRNA vaccines deliver genetic instructions for host cells to make the antigen. Herd immunity threshold depends on transmissibility (R₀): highly contagious pathogens (measles) need ~95% coverage, less contagious ones less - interpret vaccination-uptake and outbreak data from graphs, and evaluate why some vaccines fail (antigenic drift in flu and HIV, requiring updated vaccines annually) and why booster doses are needed (memory cell numbers decline over time). Monoclonal antibodies are antibodies of one specificity produced by cloned B cells: a B cell (from a mouse immunised with the target antigen) is fused with a myeloma (tumour) cell to form a hybridoma , which divides endlessly and secretes identical antibodies; clones are screened and mass-cultured. Uses: ELISA tests (antibody-linked enzyme produces a colour change when the target antigen/antibody is present - pregnancy tests with HCG, HIV and pathogen testing, allergen testing), targeted therapy (monoclonals attached to toxic drugs/radioactive isotopes deliver treatment directly to tumour cells, reducing side effects), diagnosis (blood typing, cancer markers), and research. Ethics : animal use in production (mice immunised, tumour cells), informed consent in trials, and safety of attaching toxins. The ELISA sequence (capture antibody, antigen, detection antibody with enzyme, substrate) is examinable on AQA and OCR - know the wash steps and why controls are needed. HIV is a retrovirus: RNA genome + reverse transcriptase inside a protein capsid, with a lipid envelope carrying attachment proteins (gp120). Replication: (1) gp120 binds complementary receptors (CD4) on T-helper cells ; (2) the capsid enters the cell and uncoats; (3) reverse transcriptase converts viral RNA to DNA; (4) the DNA integrates into the host genome; (5) host enzymes transcribe viral RNA and translate viral proteins; (6) new viruses bud off, destroying or disabling the T-helper cell. Over years the T-helper count falls, collapsing both specific immune arms - AIDS - leaving opportunistic infections (TB, pneumonia) and cancers. HIV is transmitted in body fluids (blood, sexual contact, needles); initial infection may be asymptomatic for years, which is why testing (ELISA) matters. There is no cure (antiretroviral drugs slow replication); antibiotics do not work because viruses have no cell wall, ribosomes or bacterial metabolism to target. Antibiotics target bacterial-specific structures: cell wall synthesis (penicillin - prevents peptidoglycan cross-linking, so bacteria lyse osmotically), ribosomes (70S - tetracycline, protein synthesis blocked), DNA/RNA enzymes. Resistance arises by random mutation (e.g. penicillinase production) and spreads by natural selection and plasmid transfer: resistant bacteria survive antibiotic courses, reproduce and pass resistance genes vertically (binary fission) and horizontally (conjugation/plasmids). Overuse and incomplete courses increase the selection pressure - the standard evolution link (AQA 3.8, 3.7.3; OCR 4.1.1), and the basis of AQA RP6 (aseptic technique, antibiotic discs on bacterial lawns).

topics.name: Photosynthesis
topics.subject: biology
topics.searchText: biology Biology Photosynthesis Describe chloroplast structure and photosynthetic pigments; interpret absorption and action spectra (AQA 3.5.1; OCR 5.1.1) Describe the light-dependent reaction: photolysis, electron transport chain, photophosphorylation and NADP reduction (AQA 3.5.1; OCR 5.1.1) Describe the light-independent reaction (Calvin cycle): RuBisCO, GP/TP, and the uses of triose phosphate (AQA 3.5.1; OCR 5.1.1) Explain limiting factors (light, CO₂, temperature) and interpret limiting-factor graphs (AQA 3.5.1; OCR 5.1.1) Describe the required practicals: chromatography of pigments (Rf values) and dehydrogenase activity (AQA RP7/RP8; OCR PAG11) Apply the compensation point and agricultural optimisation of photosynthesis to exam scenarios Chloroplast: thylakoid membranes (photosystems) stacked into grana; stroma contains Calvin-cycle enzymes; own DNA/ribosomes Pigments: chlorophyll a (PSI/PSII reaction centre, blue-red absorption), chlorophyll b, carotenoids (accessory); absorption vs action spectra LDR (thylakoid): photolysis 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ + O₂; ETC pumps H⁺ into thylakoid lumen; ATP synthase makes ATP; NADP + H⁺ + e⁻ → NADPH Calvin cycle (stroma): CO₂ + RuBP → 2 GP (RuBisCO); GP reduced to TP (ATP + NADPH); 5/6 TP regenerates RuBP, 1/6 makes glucose Limiting factors: light (plateaus - other factors limit), CO₂ (plateaus), temperature (enzyme kinetics); greenhouse optimisation Practicals: chromatography of pigments with Rf values (AQA RP7); DCPIP dehydrogenase activity (AQA RP8); OCR PAG11 Photosynthesis The synthesis of organic molecules (glucose) from CO₂ and water using light energy, producing oxygen: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. Photosystem A protein-pigment complex in the thylakoid membranes (PSI and PSII) that absorbs light energy and transfers excited electrons to an electron transport chain; each has a primary pigment (reaction centre). Photolysis Light-dependent splitting of water in photosystem II: 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ + O₂, replacing electrons lost from chlorophyll and providing protons for NADP reduction. Photophosphorylation Phosphorylation of ADP to ATP using light energy, via the proton gradient generated by the electron transport chain in the thylakoid membranes (chemiosmosis). RuBisCO Ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase - the enzyme in the stroma that catalyses the fixation of CO₂ with ribulose bisphosphate (RuBP) to form two molecules of glycerate 3-phosphate (GP). Glycerate 3-phosphate (GP) The 3-carbon product of CO₂ fixation in the Calvin cycle; reduced to triose phosphate using ATP and NADPH from the light-dependent reaction. Triose phosphate (TP) The 3-carbon sugar produced by reduction of GP; used to regenerate RuBP and to synthesise glucose, starch, cellulose, lipids and amino acids. Limiting factor The factor in shortest supply that determines the rate of photosynthesis; usually light intensity, CO₂ concentration or temperature. Light compensation point The light intensity at which the rate of photosynthesis equals the rate of respiration, so net gas exchange is zero. Rf value In chromatography, the distance moved by a pigment ÷ distance moved by the solvent front; each pigment has a characteristic Rf used to identify it. Photosynthesis occurs in the chloroplast : a double-membraned organelle with thylakoid membranes stacked into grana connected by lamellae, suspended in the stroma . Structure-function links to quote: thylakoid membranes hold the photosystems (PSI and PSII) and electron transport chain for the light-dependent reaction; their stacking (grana) gives a large surface area for light absorption; the stroma contains the Calvin-cycle enzymes (RuBisCO), sugars and starch grains for the light-independent reaction; chloroplasts have their own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes (endosymbiotic origin) so they can make some photosynthetic proteins quickly. Pigments absorb light: chlorophyll a is the primary pigment at the reaction centre of both photosystems (absorbs blue-violet and red, reflects green); chlorophyll b and carotenoids (xanthophylls, carotene) are accessory pigments broadening the wavelengths absorbed, transferring energy to the reaction centre. The absorption spectrum (light absorbed per wavelength) matches the action spectrum (photosynthesis rate per wavelength) - their overlap is evidence that the pigments absorb the light that drives photosynthesis. Chromatography separates pigments (AQA RP7; OCR PAG11): crush leaves in solvent, spot on chromatography paper/silica TLC plate, run in solvent; pigments separate by solubility and affinity for the stationary phase; calculate Rf = distance moved by pigment ÷ distance moved by solvent front and identify against known Rf values. Exam questions ask for the method, the Rf calculation and why pigments separate (different solubilities/adsorption). Chlorophyll appears red under UV fluorescence when excited - occasionally examinable as evidence of energy absorption. The light-dependent reaction (LDR) occurs in the thylakoid membranes and produces ATP and NADPH (reduced NADP) plus oxygen - all for the Calvin cycle. Sequence: (1) photolysis : light energy (absorbed by PSII) splits water - 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ + O₂ - replacing electrons lost from chlorophyll, releasing protons into the lumen and oxygen as a waste product; (2) light excites electrons in the chlorophyll a reaction centre of PSII to a higher energy level; (3) excited electrons pass along an electron transport chain of carriers from PSII to PSI, losing energy; (4) this energy pumps H⁺ from the stroma into the thylakoid lumen , building a steep proton gradient (also fed by photolysis protons); (5) H⁺ flow back into the stroma through ATP synthase , driving photophosphorylation of ADP + Pi to ATP ( chemiosmosis - exactly parallel to mitochondria); (6) at PSI, electrons are re-excited and, along with H⁺ from the stroma, reduce NADP to NADPH (NADP + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → NADPH). NADP is the terminal electron acceptor - the direct analogue of oxygen in respiration, a favourite comparison question (compare chemiosmosis in mitochondria vs chloroplasts: membrane, proton source, acceptor, products). Herbicide questions test the same sequence: DCMU/atrazine block electron transport at PSII, so photolysis stops, no proton gradient forms, no ATP/NADPH - the Calvin cycle stops; DCPIP (blue → colourless when reduced) substitutes for NADP as the electron acceptor in the dehydrogenase practical (AQA RP8), letting you measure electron transport rate by the rate of decolourisation. Cyclic photophosphorylation (electrons return to PSI producing ATP only, no NADPH) is examinable on some boards (OCR/WJEC) as balancing the ATP:NADPH ratio. The light-independent reaction (Calvin cycle) occurs in the stroma and uses ATP and NADPH from the LDR to fix CO₂ into carbohydrate. Sequence: (1) carbon fixation : RuBisCO catalyses CO₂ combining with ribulose bisphosphate (RuBP, 5C) to form two molecules of glycerate 3-phosphate (GP, 3C) ; (2) reduction : each GP is reduced to triose phosphate (TP) using ATP and NADPH from the LDR (ATP provides energy, NADPH provides H/electrons); (3) regeneration : five of every six TP molecules regenerate RuBP (using ATP), so the cycle continues; (4) the remaining one in six TP is the product used to synthesise glucose (hexose: two TP combine), starch (storage), cellulose (walls), lipids and amino acids (with nitrogen). Balance the numbers: 3 CO₂ fixed → 6 GP → 6 TP → 5 TP regenerate 3 RuBP + 1 TP surplus. Interpretation questions are the highest-value skill: in darkness, GP accumulates (cannot be reduced without NADPH/ATP) while RuBP and TP fall ; when light returns, TP recovers first. If CO₂ is removed, GP and TP fall (no fixation) while RuBP accumulates (cannot be used) - learn both directions and which molecule moves which way under each change; this distinguishes candidates who memorise from those who understand the cycle. RuBisCO is the most abundant enzyme on Earth and is inefficient - it also catalyses oxygen fixation (photorespiration), reducing yield; the 6-marker often asks why RuBisCO's oxygenase activity wastes fixed carbon. Regulation and yield : the cycle's output depends on the balance between carboxylation (using RuBP) and reduction (using ATP/NADPH) - if either runs short, TP is diverted away from RuBP regeneration and sugar synthesis slows; stromal phosphate concentration and stromal pH also regulate the cycle, since ATP synthase needs a proton gradient maintained by the LDR. RuBisCO's inefficiency is a high-value point: it works slowly (~3 reactions per second) and also catalyses the reaction of O₂ with RuBP ( photorespiration ), wasting fixed carbon and ATP with no sugar gain - explaining why crop yields are limited and why C4 plants (maize) with CO₂-concentrating mechanisms outperform C3 plants in hot, dry conditions. The limiting factor is the factor in shortest supply determining the rate. Three are examinable: light intensity - rate increases linearly at low light (light is limiting), then plateaus at high light because another factor (CO₂ or temperature) becomes limiting; the plateau level depends on CO₂ concentration and temperature. CO₂ concentration - atmospheric CO₂ (~0.04%) is usually the main limiting factor for C3 crops; increasing CO₂ (greenhouses at ~0.1%) raises the rate until light or temperature limits. Temperature - rate follows enzyme kinetics: increases to an optimum (~25-30 °C for most plants), then falls as enzymes (RuBisCO) denature; also increases photorespiration and transpiration. Graph interpretation is the standard exam skill: on a light-response curve, the initial gradient shows the photosystems' efficiency, the plateau shows the next limiting factor, and the x-intercept is the compensation point - the light intensity at which photosynthesis rate = respiration rate , so net gas exchange is zero; below it, plants respire more than they photosynthesise and lose biomass. Two curves at different CO₂ concentrations: the higher CO₂ curve plateaus higher - identify which factor limits on each section (low light = light; plateau at low CO₂ = CO₂; plateau at high CO₂ = temperature or another factor). Agricultural optimisation (glasshouse questions, AQA/Edexcel): commercial glasshouses control light (supplementary lighting, reflective surfaces), CO₂ (burners/enrichment to ~0.1%), temperature (heating, ventilation) and water (hydroponics) to raise yields; the economics matter - added CO₂/light must raise yield enough to pay for it (marginal cost vs marginal yield), an A* evaluation point. Application to exam scenarios : given a glasshouse scenario, identify the limiting factor from the data (e.g. yield rises with CO₂ enrichment until it plateaus - then light or temperature limits), and suggest the next intervention. Photosynthesis and global carbon : net primary productivity feeds ecosystems (see ecology topic), and increased atmospheric CO₂ can raise photosynthesis (CO₂ fertilisation) but is limited by other factors - linking this topic to climate-change questions. CO₂ fertilisation and crop data : raising CO₂ raises photosynthesis until another factor limits - interpret two-curve graphs by identifying the limiting factor on each segment (initial slope = light; plateau at low CO₂ = CO₂; plateau at high CO₂ = temperature/enzymes). Economics is the evaluation angle: enrichment only pays if the marginal yield increase exceeds the marginal cost of fuel/lamps - so commercial glasshouses enrich CO₂ during daylight when light is not limiting, and supplement light only when natural light falls below the compensation point; ventilation prevents overheating. Global context: elevated atmospheric CO₂ raises NPP slightly (CO₂ fertilisation) but the effect is limited by nutrients and water - linking photosynthesis to ecosystem productivity questions. AQA RP7 (chromatography of leaf pigments) : crush leaves in propanone (solvent), spot onto chromatography paper or a TLC plate, run in a suitable solvent, then calculate Rf values for each pigment (Rf = pigment distance ÷ solvent distance) and identify chlorophyll a, chlorophyll b, carotene and xanthophyll. Marks for: safe solvent handling, applying small concentrated spots, keeping the origin above the solvent line, and correct Rf calculations with comparison to reference values. AQA RP8 (dehydrogenase activity in chloroplasts) : isolate chloroplasts in cold isotonic buffer (cold - slows enzyme damage; isotonic - prevents osmotic lysis), add DCPIP, and illuminate; DCPIP (blue) accepts electrons from the electron transport chain and decolourises , substituting for NADP; the rate of decolourisation (measured by colorimetry against a calibration curve, or by time to decolourise) estimates the rate of electron transport. Variables to test: light intensity (distance from lamp), wavelength (coloured filters), herbicide presence (DCMU stops decolourisation). Controls and errors : keep a dark control tube (should not decolourise - confirms light-dependence), keep temperature constant, use the same chloroplast concentration; quote sources of error (variation in chloroplast concentration, lamp heating the samples - use a water bath/heat filter). OCR PAG11 covers measuring photosynthesis rate: pondweed ( Elodea ) oxygen production (counting bubbles or collecting O₂ in a gas syringe - volume per minute), or data-logging CO₂/pH. Bubbles are imprecise (size varies, some dissolve); gas-syringe collection is more accurate. Interpretation : rate ∝ oxygen produced; compare with respiration at night; the compensation point explains why plants grown indoors need supplementary light. Isotope evidence (occasionally examinable): ¹⁸O-labelled water shows the oxygen evolved in photosynthesis comes from water (photolysis), not CO₂ - a classic experiment supporting the LDR mechanism.

topics.name: Homeostasis and Nervous System
topics.subject: biology
topics.searchText: biology Biology Homeostasis and Nervous System Explain homeostasis principles: set points, receptors, effectors, negative and positive feedback (AQA 3.6.1; OCR 5.1.1) Describe blood glucose control by insulin and glucagon, including cAMP second messengers; compare type 1 and type 2 diabetes (AQA 3.6.4.2; OCR 5.1.2) Describe kidney structure and osmoregulation: ADH action and the loop of Henle counter-current multiplier (AQA 3.6.4.3; OCR 5.1.2) Describe neurone structure, resting potential and action potential phases (AQA 3.6.2; OCR 5.3.1) Explain synaptic transmission, summation and inhibition at cholinergic synapses (AQA 3.6.2; OCR 5.3.1) Describe thermoregulation by the hypothalamus and interpret physiological control graphs Homeostasis: set point → receptors → coordination (hormonal/nervous) → effectors → correction; negative feedback restores, positive amplifies Blood glucose: insulin (β-cells, lowers - uptake, glycogenesis), glucagon (α-cells, raises - glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis via cAMP); T1: no insulin; T2: resistance Kidney: nephron (Bowman's capsule, PCT, loop of Henle, DCT, collecting duct); loop of Henle: counter-current multiplier creates medullary gradient; ADH adds aquaporins in DCT/CD Resting potential -70 mV (Na⁺/K⁺ pump, K⁺ leak); action potential: threshold -55 mV, depolarisation (Na⁺ in), repolarisation (K⁺ out), refractory period Synapse: Ca²⁺ → vesicle fusion → ACh → postsynaptic receptors → depolarisation; acetylcholinesterase clears ACh; summation: temporal/spatial Thermoregulation: thermoreceptors (skin + hypothalamus) → hypothalamic centre; cooling: vasodilation, sweating; warming: vasoconstriction, shivering, thyroxine/adrenaline Homeostasis The maintenance of a stable internal environment within set limits, using negative feedback loops of receptors, coordination and effectors. Negative feedback A control mechanism in which a deviation from the set point triggers responses that reverse the deviation, restoring the original value (e.g. blood glucose, temperature, water balance). Positive feedback A control mechanism in which a deviation triggers responses that amplify it further (e.g. oxytocin in childbirth, blood clotting). Glycogenesis Conversion of glucose to glycogen for storage in liver and muscle cells, stimulated by insulin. Glycogenolysis Breakdown of glycogen to glucose, stimulated by glucagon via the cAMP second-messenger system. Gluconeogenesis Synthesis of glucose from non-carbohydrate sources (e.g. glycerol, amino acids), stimulated by glucagon. Osmoregulation Control of blood water potential by the kidney: ADH increases water reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct. ADH (antidiuretic hormone) Hormone released by the posterior pituitary on hypothalamic stimulation; binds receptors on collecting duct cells, adding aquaporins and increasing water permeability. Resting potential The potential difference across a resting neurone membrane, about -70 mV, maintained by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump (3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in) and K⁺ leak channels. Action potential A rapid, all-or-nothing depolarisation and repolarisation of the neurone membrane (from -70 mV to ~+40 mV and back) that transmits an impulse along the axon. Homeostasis maintains a stable internal environment (blood glucose, temperature, water potential, pH, ion concentrations) within set limits around a set point . Every control loop has four components: (1) receptors detecting the deviation (e.g. thermoreceptors in skin and hypothalamus, osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus, glucose-sensing β/α cells in the pancreas); (2) a coordination centre (usually the hypothalamus or endocrine gland) comparing the value with the set point; (3) hormonal or nervous signalling ; (4) effectors (muscles, glands) producing the response. Negative feedback is the master principle: any deviation triggers responses that reverse the deviation , returning the value to the set point - e.g. high blood glucose triggers insulin release which lowers it; low glucose triggers glucagon which raises it. Because feedback loops need a deviation to act, homeostasis oscillates slightly around the set point rather than holding it perfectly - a subtlety the exam rewards. Positive feedback amplifies deviations : oxytocin release during childbirth intensifies uterine contractions (more stretch → more oxytocin → stronger contractions); blood clotting (platelet activation attracts more platelets); the sodium influx surge in an action potential. The exam tests whether you can distinguish the two: negative restores, positive amplifies - quote one example of each. Homeostatic imbalance supplies the application scenarios: blood glucose outside set limits (hyperglycaemia damages vessels; hypoglycaemia starves the brain), core temperature outside limits (proteins denature above ~40 °C; enzymes slow and hypothermia sets in below 35 °C), and blood pH shifts altering enzyme and haemoglobin function. Set points differ between individuals and change with time of day (circadian rhythm) - body temperature peaks in the evening and falls overnight, so the hypothalamic set point is not fixed but cycles; exam questions reward recognising that homeostasis maintains conditions within narrow ranges , not exact values, and that oscillation around the set point is normal because feedback responds to deviations with a lag. Blood glucose is controlled by the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas: β-cells (secrete insulin ) and α-cells (secrete glucagon ), both working by negative feedback around ~90 mg per 100 cm³. When glucose rises (after a meal): β-cells detect it and secrete insulin, which increases glucose uptake into cells via GLUT transporters (more transporters in muscle/fat membranes), promotes glycogenesis (glucose → glycogen) in liver and muscle, raises the rate of respiration of glucose, and converts excess glucose to fat. When glucose falls (fasting, exercise): α-cells secrete glucagon , which binds receptors on hepatocytes and activates adenylyl cyclase , producing cAMP (second messenger) ; cAMP activates phosphorylase for glycogenolysis (glycogen → glucose) and gluconeogenesis (glucose from glycerol/amino acids). Adrenaline also raises glucose via the same cAMP pathway in fight-or-flight. The second-messenger cascade is the A* detail: one glucagon molecule activates many adenylyl cyclase molecules, each producing many cAMP molecules, each activating many phosphorylase molecules - amplification explaining why tiny hormone concentrations have large effects. Diabetes : type 1 - autoimmune destruction of β-cells, so no insulin is produced ; onset in childhood; treated with insulin injections and blood-glucose monitoring; glucose cannot be taken up without insulin, so blood glucose rises (hyperglycaemia) and glucose appears in urine. type 2 - insulin resistance : receptors/transporters respond weakly, β-cells eventually decline; associated with obesity, age and inactivity; treated first with diet, exercise and metformin (increases insulin sensitivity), later insulin. Exam questions ask for the differences in cause, onset and treatment - learn the 3-row comparison. Response curves (glucose tolerance tests) and negative-feedback graphs are standard interpretation questions. Osmoregulation controls blood water potential. The kidney contains ~1 million nephrons : Bowman's capsule (ultrafiltration), proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) , loop of Henle , distal convoluted tubule (DCT) and collecting duct (CD) . Ultrafiltration : high blood pressure (from the afferent arteriole being wider than the efferent) forces water, glucose, ions, urea and amino acids out of the glomerulus through the basement membrane into the capsule - proteins and cells are too large to pass (hence protein in urine indicates kidney damage). Selective reabsorption in the PCT : all glucose and amino acids (co-transport with Na⁺, as in the ileum), most ions and much water are reabsorbed (microvilli, many mitochondria). The loop of Henle is a counter-current multiplier (from the existing site content): the descending limb is permeable to water but not ions - water leaves by osmosis into the increasingly concentrated medulla; the ascending limb is impermeable to water - Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are actively transported out, concentrating the medulla and diluting the filtrate; because flow runs in opposite directions, the gradient is maintained and multiplied down the medulla (deepest at the tip); urine leaving the collecting duct equilibrates with the medullary gradient - long loops (desert mammals) produce more concentrated urine. ADH control : osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect low blood water potential; the hypothalamus signals the posterior pituitary to release ADH ; ADH binds receptors on DCT/collecting-duct cells, activating cAMP and causing vesicles of aquaporins to fuse with the membrane, increasing water permeability ; more water is reabsorbed, producing small volumes of concentrated urine; high water potential suppresses ADH, producing dilute urine - negative feedback. Kidney failure questions: dialysis (filtering blood against a dialysate with the right gradient) vs transplant (immune rejection, immunosuppressants). Neurones: sensory (receptor → CNS; cell body in a dorsal root ganglion), relay/intermediate (within CNS), motor (CNS → effector); myelinated axons (Schwann cells) conduct faster by saltatory conduction (impulse jumps between nodes of Ranvier), up to ~120 m s⁻¹ vs ~2 m s⁻¹ unmyelinated. The resting potential of about -70 mV is maintained by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump (actively transports 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in using ATP) and K⁺ leak channels (K⁺ diffuses out down its gradient, making the inside negative); the membrane is impermeable to Na⁺ at rest. The action potential (from the existing site content): (1) a stimulus depolarises the membrane to threshold (~-55 mV) ; (2) voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open - Na⁺ floods in, depolarising to ~+40 mV (positive feedback: more Na⁺ in → more channels open); (3) voltage-gated Na⁺ channels close and K⁺ channels open - K⁺ leaves, repolarising the membrane; (4) brief hyperpolarisation (below -70 mV) before the refractory period resets the channels; (5) the Na⁺/K⁺ pump restores the resting potential. The impulse is all-or-nothing : sub-threshold stimuli produce no impulse; stronger stimuli increase frequency , not amplitude - the standard explanation for how intensity is coded. The refractory period ensures one-way transmission (the section behind cannot fire) and limits maximum frequency - a guaranteed explanation point. Myelination, axon diameter (larger = faster) and temperature (faster to a point) all increase conduction speed - know all three for the comparison questions. Saltatory conduction earns its own marks: myelin (Schwann cell membranes wrapped around the axon) insulates the axon, so depolarisation can only occur at the nodes of Ranvier ; the impulse jumps node to node , travelling much faster (~120 m s⁻¹) and using less ATP (fewer Na⁺/K⁺ pumps active over the length); demyelinating diseases (multiple sclerosis) slow or block conduction - the standard application question. All-or-nothing needs the precise statement: a stimulus below threshold produces no impulse at all; at or above threshold, a full-sized action potential fires; stimulus strength is therefore coded by frequency of impulses, not their amplitude - larger stimuli also recruit more neurones. Axon diameter increases conduction speed (less internal resistance) and temperature increases speed to a point (faster diffusion) before proteins denature. Synaptic transmission at a cholinergic synapse (from the existing site content): (1) the action potential arrives at the presynaptic knob, opening voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels ; (2) Ca²⁺ enters, causing synaptic vesicles to fuse with the presynaptic membrane, releasing acetylcholine (ACh) by exocytosis; (3) ACh diffuses across the cleft and binds receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, opening Na⁺ channels ; (4) depolarisation above threshold generates a new action potential; (5) acetylcholinesterase hydrolyses ACh into choline and ethanoic acid (choline is reabsorbed to reform ACh), preventing continuous stimulation . Synapses are unidirectional (vesicles only on one side, receptors only on the other) and show summation : temporal (rapid repeated releases from one neurone add up) or spatial (simultaneous releases from several neurones) can together reach threshold - the basis of integration. Synapses also allow inhibition (inhibitory neurotransmitters open Cl⁻/K⁺ channels, hyperpolarising) and amplification (few molecules release many ions). Neuromuscular junction : same mechanism but the postsynaptic membrane is the muscle sarcolemma (always excitatory, ACh). Drugs act on synapses: nicotine (mimics ACh), curare (blocks receptors), SSRIs (block serotonin reuptake) - a standard application question. Thermoregulation (AQA 3.6.1.2; OCR 5.1.1): thermoreceptors in the skin (peripheral) and hypothalamus (central, monitoring blood temperature) feed the hypothalamic thermoregulatory centre , which compares core temperature with the set point (~37 °C). Cooling responses (temperature above set point): vasodilation of skin arterioles (more blood near the surface, more heat radiated), sweating (evaporation loses heat), less metabolic activity, hairs flatten (erector muscles relax). Warming responses (below set point): vasoconstriction , shivering (involuntary muscle contraction releases heat), raised metabolic rate via thyroxine/adrenaline , hairs erect (trapping insulating air). Both arms are negative feedback - identify receptors, coordination and effectors in any scenario. Hypothermia (core below 35 °C) and fever (set point reset by pyrogens) are the standard application scenarios: in fever the set point rises, so normal temperature feels cold and the body warms itself until the fever breaks. When answering, always name the receptor, the coordination centre and the effector with the specific response - three linked marks per mechanism.

topics.name: Ecology and Ecosystems
topics.subject: biology
topics.searchText: biology Biology Ecology and Ecosystems Define ecosystems, habitats and niches; describe trophic levels and food webs (AQA 3.5.3, 3.7.4; OCR 6.3.1) Explain energy flow: GPP, NPP, ecological efficiency and pyramids of number/biomass/energy (AQA 3.5.3; OCR 6.3.1) Describe the carbon and nitrogen cycles including saprotrophs, fixation, nitrification and denitrification (AQA 3.5.4; OCR 6.3.1) Explain population dynamics: growth curves, carrying capacity, limiting factors and predator-prey cycles (AQA 3.7.4; OCR 6.3.2) Describe succession (primary/secondary, climax, deflected) and apply mark-release-recapture and quadrat sampling (AQA RP12; OCR PAG12) Evaluate conservation strategies and human impacts: eutrophication, climate change, sustainable management GPP = total energy fixed by producers; NPP = GPP − R; efficiency between trophic levels typically ~10% Energy pyramids always upright; biomass/number pyramids can invert; energy lost as heat (respiration), faeces, urine, uneaten parts Carbon cycle: photosynthesis, respiration, combustion, decomposition, ocean uptake; Nitrogen: fixation (Rhizobium, Azotobacter), nitrification (Nitrosomonas, Nitrobacter), assimilation, denitrification (Pseudomonas) Growth curve: lag, log, stationary, death; carrying capacity K set by limiting factors; predator-prey cycles lag and oscillate Succession: pioneer → intermediate → climax; deflected succession (grazing/mowing) → plagioclimax Eutrophication: nitrates/phosphates → algal bloom → light blocked → decomposition → O₂ depletion → dead zones Sampling: quadrats (abundance, % cover, ACFOR), belt transects, mark-release-recapture (N = n₁n₂/n_marked) Ecosystem A community of organisms (biotic) interacting with each other and their abiotic environment, with flows of energy and cycling of nutrients. Habitat The place where an organism lives, defined by its abiotic and biotic conditions. Niche The role of an organism in its ecosystem: its habitat, interactions and use of resources; two species cannot occupy the same niche (competitive exclusion). Gross primary productivity (GPP) The total chemical energy fixed by producers in photosynthesis per unit area per unit time. Net primary productivity (NPP) The chemical energy remaining in producers after respiratory losses: NPP = GPP − R; available to primary consumers and for producer growth. Carrying capacity (K) The maximum population size an ecosystem can support sustainably, determined by limiting factors (food, space, water, light). Succession The progressive change in a community over time from pioneer species to a climax community; each stage modifies the environment, enabling the next. Climax community The stable final community of a succession, in dynamic equilibrium with the climate and soils of the area. Deflected succession Succession halted or redirected by human activity (e.g. grazing, mowing, burning), maintaining a plagioclimax community. Mark-release-recapture Method estimating mobile animal population size: N = (n₁ × n₂) ÷ n_marked, assuming random mixing, no migration, and equal catchability. An ecosystem is a community plus its abiotic environment, with energy flowing through it and nutrients cycling within it. Trophic levels : producers (autotrophs) → primary consumers (herbivores) → secondary consumers → tertiary consumers, with decomposers (saprotrophs) recycling nutrients at every level by extracellular digestion - secreting enzymes onto dead matter and absorbing the products. Food webs show interlinked food chains; removing one species ripples through the web (keystone species questions). Energy flow starts with gross primary productivity (GPP) - the total chemical energy fixed by photosynthesis per area per time. Producers use some of that in respiration (R): NPP = GPP − R ; NPP is what is available to primary consumers and for producer growth/reproduction. Similar equations apply to consumers: energy ingested = energy lost in faeces + energy assimilated (respired or made into new biomass). Why only ~10% transfers between trophic levels (the guaranteed four-marker): energy is lost as heat from respiration (most energy), faeces (undigested material, egestion), urine (excretion of nitrogenous waste) and uneaten parts (bones, roots); only the energy in consumed, digested, assimilated biomass becomes new biomass for the next level; the second law of thermodynamics means entropy increases so transfers are never 100% efficient. Consequences: food chains rarely exceed 4-5 trophic levels (insufficient energy left), pyramids of energy are always upright (energy always decreases), and human diets based on plants feed more people per hectare (less energy wasted between levels). Pyramids of number and biomass can invert (one tree supports many aphids; phytoplankton biomass drops momentarily before a zooplankton bloom) - know when each pyramid type is appropriate and their limitations. Calculations: percentage efficiency = (energy transferred ÷ energy available) × 100%; NPP calculations from GPP and R are standard. Nutrients cycle between abiotic reservoirs (atmosphere, soil, ocean) and living biomass; energy flows one-way but nutrients are recycled. Carbon cycle : photosynthesis fixes atmospheric CO₂ into organic molecules; respiration returns CO₂ (plants, animals, decomposers); combustion of fossil fuels/wood releases CO₂; decomposition by saprotrophs returns carbon to soil and CO₂; ocean uptake dissolves CO₂ (and carbonate shells); methane (CH₄) from anaerobic decomposition and livestock also contributes. Anthropogenic enhancement : fossil fuel combustion and deforestation raise atmospheric CO₂, driving climate change (greenhouse effect) - link to conservation questions. Nitrogen cycle - know each stage with its bacteria: (1) nitrogen fixation : Rhizobium (mutualistic, in root nodules of legumes) and Azotobacter (free-living in soil) use nitrogenase to reduce atmospheric N₂ to ammonia (NH₃/NH₄⁺); Rhizobium gains carbohydrates from the plant; (2) nitrification : Nitrosomonas oxidises ammonia to nitrite (NO₂⁻), Nitrobacter oxidises nitrite to nitrate (NO₃⁻) - nitrates are the form plants assimilate; (3) assimilation : plants absorb nitrate by active transport and build amino acids/nucleotides, which pass through food chains; (4) ammonification : saprotrophs decompose dead matter and waste, releasing ammonia; (5) denitrification : Pseudomonas (anaerobic, waterlogged soils) reduces nitrate back to N₂, depleting soil nitrogen. Lightning fixes small amounts of nitrogen directly. Exam questions test whether you link each process to its bacteria and conditions (aerobic nitrification vs anaerobic denitrification) and to agriculture (crop rotation with legumes, fertiliser use). Carbon sinks and budgets : the oceans are the largest carbon sink (dissolved CO₂, carbonate sediments, phytoplankton), soils store more carbon than vegetation, and forests fix carbon rapidly in growth - deforestation releases stored carbon and removes the sink, so it contributes doubly to rising atmospheric CO₂. Agricultural links : crop rotation with legumes exploits Rhizobium to add nitrogen without synthetic fertiliser; ploughing increases aeration, boosting nitrification but also decomposition and CO₂ release; waterlogged paddy fields favour denitrification and methanogenesis (CH₄), so rice and livestock farming increase methane - quote these when asked to link nutrient cycles to farming or climate-change questions. A population is all the individuals of one species in a habitat at a time; the community is all species; the habitat is the place; the niche is the role (two species cannot share the same niche - competitive exclusion ). Population growth curve : lag phase (few individuals, slow growth while adapting); log/exponential phase (unlimited resources, maximum growth rate); stationary phase (limiting factors bite - birth rate = death rate); death/decline phase (resources exhausted, waste accumulates). The carrying capacity (K) is the maximum sustainable population size, set by limiting factors : abiotic (temperature, light, water, space) and biotic (food, predation, competition, disease). Limiting factors questions: identify from data which factor limits a population, and predict the effect of adding/removing it. Predator-prey cycles (Lotka-Volterra): predator and prey populations oscillate out of phase - prey rise, predator numbers follow after a lag (time to reproduce); rising predation reduces prey, which then reduces predators; fewer predators let prey rise again. Explain the lag and the phase difference - the standard interpretation question. Sampling methods (AQA RP12; OCR PAG12): quadrats (random placement with random number coordinates to avoid bias; measure abundance as frequency, % cover or ACFOR scale) and belt transects (along an environmental gradient - distribution questions); mark-release-recapture for mobile animals: capture, mark (non-harmful), release, recapture - N = (n₁ × n₂) ÷ n_marked ; assumptions: population closed (no migration), random mixing, marks do not affect survival/catchability, constant population. Know the assumptions - evaluation questions ask what happens if they fail (overestimates if marked animals less catchable, etc.). r/K selection explains population strategies: r-selected species (many small offspring, little parental care, rapid reproduction - mice, insects) exploit unstable environments and recover fast; K-selected species (few offspring, heavy parental investment - elephants, whales) sit near carrying capacity in stable environments and recover slowly - conservation of K-selected species is harder because populations recover slowly from decline. Sampling evaluation : quadrat estimates are only as good as their sample size - larger quadrats and more samples reduce error; random placement avoids bias toward convenient areas; along a gradient, belt transects with quadrats at regular intervals (or interrupted) show distribution change; mark-release-recapture overestimates if marked animals are easier or harder to catch again, and fails if the population changes between samples - state the assumption being violated in evaluation questions. Succession is the progressive, directional change in a community over time, driven by each stage modifying the environment for the next. Primary succession starts on bare substrate with no soil (lava, dunes, retreating glaciers): (1) pioneer species colonise - lichens/mosses adapted to harsh conditions (tolerate drought, low nutrients, fix nitrogen); (2) pioneers die and decompose, building soil , retaining water and nutrients; (3) intermediate communities - grasses, then shrubs, then fast-growing trees (each outcompeting the previous by growing taller, shading them out); (4) climax community - the stable end community in equilibrium with the climate (e.g. oak/beech woodland in the UK); biodiversity and biomass rise through succession and stabilise at the climax. Secondary succession starts where soil already exists (after fire, clearing) - faster, skipping pioneer stages. Deflected succession : human activity (grazing, mowing, burning, trampling) halts succession , maintaining a stable intermediate ( plagioclimax , e.g. grazed grassland, heather moorland); if the activity stops, succession resumes. Conservation applications : managing succession maintains early-stage habitats for species that need them (e.g. grazing to keep chalk grassland, cutting to maintain heath); understand why climax woodland is not always the conservation goal - species diversity peaks at intermediate stages. Exam questions: sequence the stages, explain why each stage enables the next (soil depth, water retention, shelter), and define/apply deflected succession to a scenario. Eutrophication (the guaranteed sequence question): (1) excess nitrates/phosphates from fertiliser runoff or sewage enter water; (2) algal bloom at the surface blocks light; (3) submerged plants die from lack of light; (4) saprobic bacteria decompose the dead biomass aerobically, depleting dissolved O₂ ; (5) aerobic organisms (fish, invertebrates) die from oxygen shortage; (6) anaerobic bacteria flourish, releasing toxic products (H₂S) - dead zones with very low biodiversity. Explain each step as a chain of cause and effect; the BOD (biochemical oxygen demand) rises as O₂ falls - occasionally examinable. Climate change : enhanced greenhouse effect from CO₂ (combustion, deforestation) and CH₄ (livestock, anaerobic decomposition, rice paddies); impacts - species range shifts, phenology mismatches (earlier flowering), coral bleaching, ocean acidification (CO₂ + H₂O → carbonic acid, lowering pH and dissolving carbonate shells). Conservation maintains biodiversity (species, genetic, ecosystem diversity) by managing ecosystems sustainably : in situ methods (nature reserves, habitat restoration, managing succession, legal protection) are preferred - conserve whole ecosystems and the evolutionary context; ex situ methods (zoos, seed banks, captive breeding, gene banks) back up in situ for critically endangered species. Sustainable management : using resources without depleting them - e.g. fishing quotas (maintain breeding stock), coppicing (regrowth without succession to woodland), rotational forestry (replanting). Evaluation questions want both sides: economic development vs conservation (tourism income vs habitat loss); conflict between local needs and global biodiversity; the value of keystone species and ecosystem services (pollination, water purification, carbon storage). Biodiversity measurement : species richness (number of species) vs species evenness (relative abundance) - Simpson's diversity index D = 1 − Σ(n/N)² (higher D = more diverse); OCR and Edexcel expect the calculation and interpretation, and the comparison of two habitats (which is more diverse and why).

topics.name: Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table
topics.subject: chemistry
topics.searchText: chemistry Chemistry Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table Describe subatomic particles and use atomic number and mass number to deduce numbers of each particle Define isotopes and calculate relative atomic mass from mass spectra of elements Explain the four stages of time-of-flight mass spectrometry and perform time-of-flight calculations Write electron configurations including transition metal ions, applying the 4s-removed-first rule and Cr/Cu exceptions Explain trends in first ionisation energy across a period and down a group in terms of nuclear charge, distance and shielding Interpret successive ionisation energy graphs as evidence for electron shells and deduce the group of an element Predict and explain 3:1, 9:6:1 and 1:1 isotopic peak patterns for chlorine and bromine Isotope Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons (same Z, different A). Relative atomic mass (Ar) The weighted mean mass of an atom of an element compared with 1/12 of the mass of one atom of carbon-12. Relative isotopic mass The mass of one atom of an isotope compared with 1/12 of the mass of one atom of carbon-12. Orbital A region within an atom that can hold up to two electrons with opposite spins. Sub-shell A group of orbitals of the same type (s, p, d or f) within a shell; s holds 2, p 6, d 10 electrons. First ionisation energy The enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous 1+ ions is formed from one mole of gaseous atoms. Successive ionisation energy The energy required to remove each further electron from a gaseous ion; a large jump indicates electron removal from a new inner shell. Shielding The repulsion of outer-shell electrons by inner-shell electrons, reducing the effective nuclear attraction they experience. Atoms consist of a nucleus of protons and neutrons surrounded by electrons in orbitals. Protons and neutrons each have a relative mass of approximately 1 (the neutron is very slightly heavier at 1.0087), while the electron has a relative mass of 1/1836 — effectively all the mass sits in the nucleus. Protons carry a charge of +1, electrons carry −1 and neutrons are neutral, so an atom is neutral because the number of protons equals the number of electrons. Particle Relative mass Relative charge Proton 1 +1 Neutron 1 0 Electron 1/1836 −1 The atomic (proton) number Z defines the element and fixes its position in the periodic table; the mass number A is protons plus neutrons. Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons — same Z, different A. Isotopes have identical chemical properties (same electron configuration, so same bonding and reactions) but different physical properties such as mass, density and diffusion rate. Radioactive isotopes additionally have unstable nuclei. Relative atomic mass (A r ) is defined as the weighted mean mass of an atom of an element compared with 1/12 of the mass of one atom of carbon-12. Relative isotopic mass is the mass of one isotope compared with the same standard — for light isotopes this equals the mass number. Relative molecular mass (M r ) is the sum of the relative atomic masses in a molecule; relative formula mass is used for ionic compounds. Mass spectrometry of elements: a time-of-flight (TOF) instrument works in four stages. (1) Ionisation: in electron impact (EI) the vaporised sample is bombarded with high-energy electrons which knock one electron off each atom to give M + (g) ions; in electrospray ionisation the sample is dissolved and protonated to MH + , a gentler method suited to fragile biological molecules. (2) Acceleration: an electric field accelerates all ions to the same kinetic energy. (3) Ion drift: ions enter a field-free tube where lighter ions travel faster — time of flight is inversely proportional to √(mass), since KE = ½mv². (4) Detection: ions strike a detector producing a current proportional to their abundance. Exam calculations often ask you to find a time of flight ratio or the A r : take each isotopic mass, multiply by its relative abundance (signal area), total these and divide by total abundance. Electrons occupy orbitals — regions of space that can hold a maximum of two electrons with opposite spins. An s orbital is spherical; there are three p orbitals (p x , p y , p z ) shaped like dumbbells at right angles; there are five d orbitals and seven f orbitals. Sub-shells group orbitals of the same type: s holds 2, p holds 6, d holds 10 electrons. Sub-shell energies increase in the order 1s Two rules govern filling: the Pauli exclusion principle (no orbital holds more than two electrons, and they must have opposite spin) and Hund's rule (within a sub-shell electrons occupy orbitals singly with parallel spins before pairing up, minimising repulsion). Two exceptions must be known: chromium is [Ar]3d 5 4s 1 and copper is [Ar]3d 10 4s 1 , because a half-filled or filled d sub-shell is more stable than the expected arrangement. For ions, remember the rule: 4s electrons are removed first . Although 4s fills before 3d, once the 3d sub-shell is occupied it drops below 4s in energy, so the 4s orbital is emptied first during ionisation. Fe (Z=26): 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d⁶4s²; Fe²⁺: 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d⁶; Fe³⁺: 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d⁵ (a stable half-filled d sub-shell, which is why Fe³⁺ is more stable than Fe²⁺). Other examples: Cl⁻ is 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶ (isoelectronic with Ar); Ca²⁺ is [Ar]; Na⁺ is [Ne]. Writing configurations from a noble gas core saves time: Al = [Ne]3s²3p¹. Exam tip: when asked for the full electron configuration of a transition metal ion, always write the 3d before 4s in the final answer even though 4s filled first — most boards penalise 3d written after 4s for ions. First ionisation energy is the enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous 1+ ions forms from one mole of gaseous atoms: Na(g) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻, ΔH = +496 kJ/mol. It is always endothermic — energy must be supplied to overcome the attraction between the nucleus and the electron. Successive ionisation energies measure removal of electrons one after another from the same atom, and each is larger than the last because the same positive charge attracts fewer electrons more strongly and the ion is increasingly positive. Three factors control ionisation energy. Nuclear charge: more protons pull electrons harder. Distance: the further the outer electron is from the nucleus, the weaker the attraction. Shielding: inner shells repel outer electrons and screen them from the nuclear charge. Trends: ionisation energy increases across a period — nuclear charge rises while shielding stays roughly constant because electrons enter the same outer shell, so Z eff increases. Small dips break the trend and are standard A*/explain questions: aluminium (3s²3p¹) has a lower first IE than magnesium (3s²) because the highest-energy electron is in the higher-energy 3p sub-shell, which is easier to remove; sulfur (3p⁴) has a lower first IE than phosphorus (3p³) because sulfur's paired 3p electrons repel each other, so one is easier to remove. Ionisation energy decreases down a group — each element has an extra full inner shell, so atomic radius and shielding both increase and outweigh the rise in nuclear charge. Graphs of log(successive IE) against electron number provide the classic evidence for shells: within one shell the increase is gradual, but a large jump occurs when the next electron comes from a new, inner shell because it is much closer to the nucleus and far less shielded. Counting the number of electrons before the first big jump tells you the number of outer-shell electrons, hence the group. For example, an element with a huge jump after the fourth ionisation energy is in Group 4. A mass spectrum of an element shows one line per isotope: the position on the m/z axis gives the isotopic mass and the height gives the relative abundance. From this you calculate A r . Worked example: chlorine gives peaks at m/z 35 (75.0%) and m/z 37 (25.0%), so A r = (35 × 75.0 + 37 × 25.0) / 100 = 35.5. Two diatomic patterns are examined constantly. Chlorine (³⁵Cl 75%, ³⁷Cl 25%) gives molecular-ion peaks for Cl₂⁺ at m/z 70, 72 and 74 in the ratio 9:6:1 (0.75² : 2 × 0.75 × 0.25 : 0.25²), while any fragment containing one Cl atom (e.g. CH₃Cl⁺) appears as a doublet at m/z 49/51 or 35/37 in a 3:1 ratio. Bromine (⁷⁹Br 50%, ⁸¹Br 50%) gives 1:1 doublets, and Br₂⁺ peaks at m/z 158, 160, 160, 162 in the ratio 1:2:1 . These ratios let you deduce how many halogen atoms a fragment contains — a favourite AS-level question. TOF calculation style: two ions of the same charge given the same kinetic energy — the heavier ion flies more slowly. If ion A (mass m A ) takes time t A and ion B takes t B , then t B /t A = √(m B /m A ). Rearrange to find the unknown mass, then identify the isotope. Always work in kg for mass (divide by 1000 from gmol⁻¹ × 10³ to match SI joules) unless the question asks for a ratio. Mass spectra and ionisation energy graphs reward precise method writing. For TOF calculations, state the principle first — same charge, same kinetic energy, so velocity depends on mass — then apply t B /t A = √(m B /m A ). For A r calculations from abundance data, show the weighted-mean expression with all terms before evaluating; the expression itself carries method marks even if arithmetic slips. When asked to identify an element from successive ionisation energies, count the electrons before the large jump, state the number of outer-shell electrons, then name the group — three separate reasoning steps, three marks. For ionisation energy trend questions, the mark scheme expects the three factors named explicitly: nuclear charge (number of protons), distance of the outer electron from the nucleus, and shielding by inner shells. 'More protons attract more strongly' alone scores one mark; adding 'same shell so shielding unchanged, so effective nuclear charge increases' scores the rest. For discontinuity explanations, name the sub-shells of both elements compared — Mg 3s² vs Al 3s²3p¹, or P 3p³ vs S 3p⁴ — before giving the reason (higher-energy sub-shell, or paired-electron repulsion). Electron configuration answers: write full configurations in the order asked (AQA asks ascending order 1s first; for transition metal ions, 3d before 4s in the final answer), use superscript notation correctly, and double-check the electron count against the charge — an Fe²⁺ answer with 24 electrons is a silent error that costs a mark. Common traps: writing 4s² in a transition-metal ion's configuration; forgetting the Cr/Cu exceptions; treating isotopes as chemically different; giving ionisation energy as exothermic. Practise writing the causal chain — extra inner shell → more shielding and greater distance → weaker attraction → lower IE — because chained explanations are what separate A* scripts from A/B.

topics.name: Bonding and Structure
topics.subject: chemistry
topics.searchText: chemistry Chemistry Bonding and Structure Draw dot-and-cross diagrams for ionic, covalent and dative bonded species Explain properties of ionic, metallic, giant covalent and simple molecular substances from their structure and bonding Use electronegativity differences to predict bond polarity and whether a molecule is polar overall Describe London forces, dipole-dipole forces and hydrogen bonding, and predict which occur between given molecules Predict shapes and bond angles using VSEPR, explaining deviations caused by lone pairs Compare melting points, boiling points and conductivity of substances using the forces that must be overcome Ionic bonding The electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions formed by electron transfer from a metal to a non-metal. Covalent bond The strong electrostatic attraction between a shared pair of electrons and the nuclei of the bonded atoms. Dative (coordinate) bond A covalent bond in which both electrons of the shared pair come from the same atom. Metallic bond The electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons. Electronegativity The ability of an atom to attract the pair of electrons in a covalent bond (Pauling scale). Intermolecular force An attractive force between molecules: London (induced dipole-dipole), permanent dipole-dipole, or hydrogen bonding. Hydrogen bond A strong dipole-dipole attraction between an electron-deficient H bonded to N, O or F and a lone pair on a neighbouring N, O or F. Delocalised electrons Electrons not associated with any one atom or bond, free to move through the structure (metals, graphite). Giant covalent lattice A structure of atoms bonded covalently throughout, e.g. diamond, graphite, SiO₂. Ionic bonding occurs between a metal and a non-metal: electrons are transferred from the metal to the non-metal, forming positive and negative ions held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction in all directions. Every ion attracts oppositely charged neighbours, producing a giant ionic lattice — the diagram convention is a regular 3D array of alternating cations and anions. A dot-and-cross diagram shows outer-shell electron transfer: the metal's electron(s) are drawn as dots moved onto the non-metal's crosses. Lattice strength depends on ionic charge and ionic radius : MgO (Mg²⁺, O²⁻) melts at 2852 °C versus NaCl (Na⁺, Cl⁻) at 801 °C because ±2 charges and smaller ions give a higher charge density and much stronger electrostatic attraction. This explains trends in melting points and is the same reasoning used for lattice enthalpies (see Thermodynamics and Born-Haber cycles). Properties of ionic compounds follow directly from the lattice: (1) high melting and boiling points because strong electrostatic forces must be overcome throughout the lattice; (2) conduction only when molten or dissolved — then ions are mobile and carry charge, whereas in the solid the ions are fixed in place; (3) solubility in polar solvents like water, which hydrate and stabilise the ions. Exam answers must state the force broken on melting: it is electrostatic attraction between ions, not covalent bonds, and it is attraction not repulsion that is overcome. Covalent bonding is the strong electrostatic attraction between a shared pair of electrons and the nuclei of the bonded atoms — found between non-metals. A single bond shares one pair, a double bond two pairs, a triple bond three; bond enthalpy rises and bond length falls in the order single > double > triple. In dot-and-cross diagrams shared pairs overlap the two atoms; outer shells only are drawn, and you should state that both nuclei attract the shared pair. A dative (coordinate) covalent bond forms when both electrons in the shared pair come from the same atom: the donor must have a lone pair and the acceptor an empty orbital. Examples: NH₄⁺ (N donates its lone pair to H⁺), H₃O⁺, the [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ complex, CO (one normal C–O plus one dative). Dative bonds behave exactly like ordinary covalent bonds once formed — same length, same strength. Metallic bonding is the attraction between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons — a lattice of cations in a sea of mobile electrons. Delocalisation explains properties: high melting points (strong attraction, rising with ion charge — Mg melts higher than Na because Mg²⁺ attracts two electrons per ion), electrical and thermal conductivity (mobile electrons carry charge and heat), and malleability/ductility (layers of ions can slide without breaking the bonding because delocalised electrons hold the structure together in any arrangement). Simple molecular substances (H₂, H₂O, CO₂, NH₃, I₂) contain strong covalent bonds within molecules but weak intermolecular forces between them: low melting and boiling points (only IMFs overcome), poor conductivity (no mobile ions or electrons), and solubility varies with polarity. This within/between distinction earns marks constantly — melting a molecular solid breaks intermolecular forces, never covalent bonds. Electronegativity is the ability of an atom to attract the bonding electrons in a covalent bond, measured on the Pauling scale. It increases across a period (nuclear charge rises, radius falls) and decreases down a group (radius and shielding rise). Fluorine is the most electronegative element (4.0), then O (3.5), N and Cl (3.0). If two bonded atoms have similar electronegativity the bond is non-polar covalent; a large difference gives ionic character (rough guide: difference > 1.7 ionic, molecule is polar depends on shape: symmetrical molecules (CO₂, CCl₄, BF₃, CH₄) have dipoles that cancel, giving non-polar molecules despite polar bonds; asymmetrical ones (H₂O, NH₃, CHCl₃) are polar overall. Three intermolecular forces (weakest to strongest): (1) London (induced dipole-dipole) forces — exist between all molecules; caused by instantaneous fluctuations in electron distribution inducing dipoles in neighbours; strength increases with number of electrons (higher M r ) and with surface contact (long straight-chain alkanes boil higher than branched isomers). (2) Permanent dipole-dipole forces — between polar molecules only, in addition to London forces. (3) Hydrogen bonding — the strongest IMF, occurring when H is bonded directly to N, O or F (small, highly electronegative atoms with lone pairs); shown as a dashed line from the H to the lone pair of N/O/F on a neighbouring molecule. Consequences to quote: H₂O boils at 100 °C far above H₂S (−60 °C) despite H₂S having more electrons, because water hydrogen-bonds; ice is less dense than water because H-bonds hold molecules in an open lattice; ammonia's high solubility in water involves H-bonding.
