The New Right applies functionalist logic politically: Murray (1994) blames the breakdown of the nuclear family — welfare dependency, lone parenthood — for crime and educational failure; Marsland claims welfare has undermined the family's self-reliance. Marxism : Engels (1884) traced the monogamous nuclear family to the need to pass private property to legitimate heirs; Zaretsky (1976) argued the family offers a private sanctuary from alienating capitalism but is also a unit of consumption absorbing advertising and debt; Ansley (1972) called wives 'takers of shit' — absorbing the frustration male workers bring home, so the family stabilises capitalism rather than individuals. Feminism : liberal feminists (Oakley) seek equal sharing of domestic labour within existing structures; radical feminists (Delphy and Leonard 1992) see the family as the main site of patriarchal oppression — women's unpaid domestic work benefits men; Marxist feminists (Ansley) link women's subordination to capitalism. Personal life perspective (Smart 2007): 'family' means more than blood and law — fictive kin, friends, pets and chosen families (Weeks 1999 on same-sex households) show relationships are what people define as significant. AO3: functionalism is criticised for ignoring conflict and the dark side of family life; Marxism is economically deterministic; radical feminism treats all families as equally oppressive, which personal life research disputes. AQA 4.2.2.2 links the family to the social structure and social change, with particular reference to the economy and state policies. Industrialisation restructured the family: Parsons argued pre-industrial extended families gave way to the nuclear unit that suited geographic and social mobility; Laslett's household-size data (1972) showed the extended family was never universal in pre-industrial England; Anderson (1971) found working-class families in 1850s Preston used extended kin as a mutual insurance system against poverty — evidence the family adapts to economic conditions. State policy shapes family life directly: the Divorce Reform Act 1969 made divorce easier; the Civil Partnership Act 2004 and the Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013 extended legal recognition to same-sex couples; child benefit, Sure Start and free childcare support child-rearing. Evaluations of policy: the New Right criticises welfare for rewarding lone parenthood and weakening incentives (Murray); Donzelot (1977) argued professionals — doctors, social workers, health visitors — 'police the family' through surveillance targeted at the poor and working class; Fletcher (1976) counters that the welfare state supports the family in performing its functions better. Feminists note policy remains gendered: childcare provision and tax systems have historically assumed a male breadwinner, and Thatcherite policy reinforced women's domestic role. Exam point: a 30-marker on policy needs a perspective debate — functionalists see policy as helping the family perform functions; Marxists see it as relieving capitalism of costs (Donzelot's surveillance protecting the workforce); feminists see it as patriarchal in design and effect — with a weighed conclusion. AQA 4.2.2.3 expects the trends and their sociological explanations. Trends (ONS): the marriage rate has roughly halved since the early 1970s; the average age at first marriage has risen to over 30; cohabitation has risen steeply (over 3 million cohabiting couple families); around 40% of marriages end in divorce; births outside marriage have risen to about half of all births; lone-parent families are around a quarter of families with children, about 90% headed by women; families are smaller and stepfamilies have grown. Secularisation: with church attendance in decline (Wilson), marriage loses its religious status and divorce its stigma — couples see cohabitation as legitimate. Declining stigma and changing attitudes: divorce and lone parenthood are now normalised (Weeks 1999) — media and policy treat them as ordinary. Rising expectations: Fletcher (1966) argued couples expect more from marriage (companionship, romance), so they are less willing to tolerate unhappy marriages — higher standards, more divorce. Individualisation and the pure relationship: Beck (1992) and Giddens (1992) argue late-modern relationships are chosen, negotiated and retained only while they satisfy — divorce becomes a route to new family types (Stacey). Women's economic independence: Wilkinson (1994) called the change a 'genderquake' — women with careers and welfare rights need not tolerate unsatisfying marriages. New Right counter: Murray (1994) blames welfare dependency for rising lone parenthood — a political, not cultural, explanation that feminists dispute (benefits are modest and single mothers face poverty). Consequences — family diversity: Chester (1985) argued the nuclear family remains the dominant arrangement (the neo-conventional family: dual-earner but nuclear); the Rapoports (1982) identified five types of diversity — organisational, cultural, class, life-course and cohort. AO3: the A* answer weighs cultural explanations (secularisation, attitudes) against economic ones (genderquake, welfare) and judges which better explain the data. AQA 4.2.2.4 covers the domestic division of labour, power relationships and resources. Housework: Oakley (1974) treated housework as work — monotonous, unrewarding, done mostly by women and largely dissatisfying. Willmott and Young (1973) claimed the symmetrical family with joint conjugal roles was emerging among home-centred couples; Boulton (1983) rebutted this: men may 'help', but women remain responsible for housework and childcare in practice. Gershuny (1994) found a lagged adaptation — men increase housework as wives enter full-time work, but slowly; Kan (2001) showed the gap narrows with women's earnings but never closes. Dual burden and triple shift: Duncombe and Marsden (1995) found women in paid work carry paid work, housework and emotional work — men neglect the emotional shift. Same-sex households: Dunne (1999) found lesbian couples divide labour more equally, supporting the claim that inequality is gendered, not natural. Decision-making: Edgell (1980) found men dominate important decisions (moving house, finances) and women the routine ones. Money: Pahl (1993) and Vogler showed pooling has grown with dual-earner households, but men usually control it when they are the main earner. Domestic violence: Dobash and Dobash (1980) interviewed 109 women in refuges: violence was systematic male control, often triggered by challenges to male authority; Mirrlees-Black (1999, BCS) found around one in four women had experienced domestic violence — many incidents unreported. AO3: functionalists (Young and Willmott) see growing symmetry; Marxists (Zaretsky) blame capitalism's strains; radical feminists see patriarchy persisting regardless of employment; the personal life perspective asks whose meanings count — e.g. the woman who insists she 'chooses' domesticity. The strongest answers weigh symmetry evidence (Gershuny) against continued responsibility (Boulton) and reach a judgement. AQA 4.2.2.5 — childhood: Pilcher (1995) defines childhood by separateness — a distinct status with its own laws, dress and institutions. Aries (1960), studying medieval paintings, argued childhood is a recent invention: in the 10th-13th centuries children were 'miniature adults' working and mixing with adults from an early age. Childhood varies culturally (Punch 2001 — Bolivian children take adult responsibilities early), so it is socially constructed. Change: the March of Progress view holds childhood has improved — compulsory education, child protection (Children Act 1989; UN Convention 1989), shorter working hours. Conflict and postmodern views disagree: Firestone saw children as oppressed by adult control; Hillman called the control an 'age patriarchy'; Postman (1994) argued TV is blurring the adult-child boundary and childhood is 'disappearing'; Palmer (2006) blames a 'toxic childhood' of screens, junk food and marketisation. Childhood also varies by class, gender and ethnicity — not all children enjoy the same protected status. AQA 4.2.2.6 — demography since 1900: the birth rate fell from about 28 per 1,000 (1900) to about 11 today, with baby booms after the world wars and in the 1960s; total fertility is around 1.5 — well below replacement (2.1). The death rate fell from about 19 to about 9 per 1,000 as sanitation, nutrition (McKeown) and medicine improved; life expectancy rose from under 50 to over 80. Consequences: an ageing population (Hirsch 2005 — rising pension and health costs, changing dependency ratios), smaller families, and migration-driven diversity: record net migration in recent years has produced transnational families and greater ethnic diversity of family forms (globalisation). AO3: link demographic change to theory — ageing supports Hirsch's policy warnings and postmodern accounts of diverse life courses. Exam technique for families essays AQA Paper 2 : each optional topic carries 4- and 6-mark items, a 10-mark 'outline and analyse two...' and a 30-mark 'outline and evaluate...' — roughly AO1 8 / AO2 8 / AO3 14, so evaluation dominates. 30-mark skeleton: (1) define the claim and its key concepts; (2) three or four developed points, each with a named study and date; (3) three or four evaluations with counter-theorists; (4) a conclusion with a weighed judgement answering the exact question. Pitfalls: describing statistics without sociological explanation; citing Murdock's universality claim without evaluating it (polygamy, single-parent households); confusing the symmetrical family claim (Young and Willmott) with its rebuttal (Boulton); omitting the synoptic link to socialisation, education and the economy that 30-markers reward.

topics.name: Education
topics.subject: sociology
topics.searchText: sociology Sociology Education Set out functionalist, Marxist and feminist views of the role of the education system (AQA 4.1.1.1) Explain class differences in achievement through external (material and cultural) and internal factors (AQA 4.1.1.2) Explain ethnic and gender differences in achievement with named studies and dates (AQA 4.1.1.3-4) Analyse relationships and processes within schools: labelling, streaming, pupil subcultures and pupil identities (AQA 4.1.1.5) Evaluate the significance of educational policies from 1944 to the present, including marketisation, parentocracy, privatisation and globalisation of policy (AQA 4.1.1.6) Deploy education content in 10- and 30-mark essays and in the Methods in Context question (AQA 4.1.2) Functionalist: Durkheim (school as society in miniature), Parsons (1961, bridge and meritocracy), Davis and Moore (1945, role allocation). Marxist: Bowles and Gintis (1976, correspondence principle), Althusser (1971, ISA), Willis (1977, lads resist). Class — external: material deprivation (Smith and Noble 1995), cultural capital (Bourdieu 1984; Sullivan 2001); internal: labelling (Becker), streaming (Lacey 1970, Ball 1981). Ethnic: Gillborn and Youdell (2000, educational triage), Coard (1971), Fuller (1984), Mirza (1997), institutional racism (Gillborn 2008). Gender: girls' improvement (Gorard et al 2001; Sharpe 1994), boys' underachievement (Mitsos and Browne 1998), laddish subcultures (Sewell). Policy: 1944 tripartite, comprehensives, 1988 ERA marketisation, parentocracy (Ball, Bowe and Gewirtz 1994), privatisation (Ball and Youdell 2008), PISA policy borrowing (Ball 2008). Meritocracy The claim (Parsons) that education sifts and sorts pupils by ability and effort, so success reflects talent — the 'myth of meritocracy' for Bowles and Gintis. Correspondence principle Bowles and Gintis (1976): school hierarchies, punctuality and reward systems mirror the workplace, reproducing a passive, obedient workforce for capitalism. Cultural capital Bourdieu (1984): the knowledge, tastes and language middle-class parents pass on, which the education system values and rewards, converting class advantage into qualifications. Material deprivation Lack of physical necessities — housing, diet, income — that hinders attainment; statistically linked to free school meals eligibility and class gaps. Labelling Becker: teachers judge pupils against an 'ideal pupil' image (middle-class) and attach labels that shape how pupils are treated and how they respond. Self-fulfilling prophecy Rosenthal and Jacobson (1968): teacher expectations, once communicated, cause pupils to internalise labels and act them out. Streaming Separating pupils into ability groups across subjects; Lacey (1970) and Ball (1981) show it pushes lower-stream pupils into anti-school subcultures. Pupil subculture A group whose members share values and status derived from response to school — pro-school (high stream) or anti-school (low stream) subcultures (Lacey). Marketisation The 1988 Education Reform Act policy of creating an education market: formula funding, league tables, open enrolment and competition between schools. Parentocracy Miriam David's term for the marketised claim that parental choice drives standards; Ball, Bowe and Gewirtz (1994) call it a myth. Ideological state apparatus Althusser (1971): institutions such as education and media transmit ruling-class ideology, reproducing and legitimating class inequality. Ethnocentric curriculum A curriculum centred on one culture (Coard 1971: white, British, Christian) that devalues minority-ethnic pupils' identities and lowers their self-esteem. AQA 4.1.1.1 (also OCR H580/03 Section B) expects competing views of what education is for. Functionalism: Durkheim argued school is 'society in miniature' — teaching shared norms and values creates the social solidarity modern society needs; Parsons (1961) saw school as the focal socialising agency, a bridge between family's particularistic values and society's universalistic ones, operating through meritocracy; Davis and Moore (1945) added role allocation — education sifts and sorts the most able into the most functionally important (best-rewarded) roles. Marxism: Bowles and Gintis (1976) claimed the correspondence principle mirrors workplace hierarchy in school — subservience, motivation by external rewards, fragmentation — producing a passive workforce; the claim that education is meritocratic is a myth that legitimises inequality by making class advantage look like talent. Althusser (1971) called education an Ideological State Apparatus reproducing and legitimating class inequality. Willis (1977) supplied the classic evaluation: his 12 'lads' formed a counter-school culture, partially seeing through school ideology yet still drifting into manual work — resisting, but not escaping, class reproduction. Feminism: education historically channelled girls into domestic subjects; girls still face gendered subject choice and the devaluation of feminine achievement. Evaluation of each view Functionalism: assumes a value consensus that may simply reflect dominant groups; explanations risk teleology ('schools exist because they have functions'); ignores inequality of opportunity. Marxism: economically deterministic — Willis shows pupils resist; the correspondence principle overstates workplace similarity (many jobs are not hierarchical); ignores gender and ethnicity. Interactionism (Becker): focuses on meanings and everyday processes but ignores structure — a pupil's poverty shapes attainment regardless of teacher meaning. AQA 4.1.1.2 splits explanations into external (home and background) and internal (school processes). External — material deprivation: poor housing affects study space and health; Smith and Noble (1995) listed housing, diet and income as barriers to schooling; Tanner et al (2003) showed the cost of books, uniforms and transport burdens low-income families; Flaherty (2004) found free school meals carry stigma that discourages uptake. External — cultural factors: Bernstein (1975) distinguished restricted and elaborated speech codes — schools use and reward the elaborated code middle-class pupils arrive with (criticised by Labov as language difference, not deficit); Douglas (1964) linked parental interest to attainment; Feinstein (2003) showed educated parents' children do better from the earliest years; Bernstein and Young (1967) found middle-class mothers buy more educational toys; Sugarman (1970) identified working-class subcultural values — fatalism, immediate gratification, present-time orientation. Cultural capital: Bourdieu (1984) argued middle-class parents pass on cultural capital (knowledge, tastes, language) which schools reward; Sullivan (2001) measured it — pupils with wider reading and cultural knowledge did better, supporting Bourdieu over pure cultural deprivation theory. Internal — labelling and streaming: Becker (1971) found teachers' 'ideal pupil' image was middle-class; Rosenthal and Jacobson (1968) demonstrated the self-fulfilling prophecy in 'Pygmalion in the Classroom'; Hargreaves (1967) showed differentiation and polarisation — streaming pushes lower-stream working-class pupils into anti-school subcultures; Lacey (1970) found the same in Hightown Grammar; Ball (1981) at Beachside showed even banding (not full streaming) produced the same polarisation. Archer et al (2010) analysed working-class pupil identities — 'Nike identities' — showing schools devalue working-class taste, and pupils respond with symbolic violence. AQA 4.1.1.3 — ethnic differences: external factors include material deprivation and racism in wider society (Rex 1986 — racial discrimination in housing and work); internal factors matter more in exam answers: Gillborn and Youdell (2000) found 'educational triage' — schools under pressure from league tables sort pupils into those who will pass anyway, hopeless cases and borderline A-to-C candidates, with black pupils over-represented in the lower groups; the A-to-C economy drives it. Coard (1971) argued the curriculum is ethnocentric, devaluing black culture and lowering self-esteem; Troyna and Williams (1986) agreed the curriculum gives priority to English and European culture. Pupil responses: Fuller (1984) found black girls rejected labels and channelled anger into achievement; Mirza (1997) found teachers' racism produced 'failed strategies' — girls avoided teachers who labelled them, costing attainment; Sewell (1997) found black male peer groups valued rebellion, but this is not inevitable. Gillborn (2008) argues institutional racism pervades the system — the 'assessment regime' disadvantages ethnic minorities systematically. AO3: some pupils resist labels (Fuller) and Chinese pupils outperform all groups, complicating single explanations. AQA 4.1.1.4 — gender differences: girls now outperform boys at GCSE and in university entry. Girls' improvement: the impact of feminism since the 1970s; changing ambitions — Sharpe (1994) found 1970s girls prioritised love and marriage, 1990s girls careers; assessment changes — Gorard et al (2001) showed the gender gap opened with GCSE coursework (1988), then stabilized; equal opportunities policies (GIST, WISE, the National Curriculum) removed formal barriers; teacher attention — Swann (1998) found girls receive more interaction because reading is valued. Boys' underachievement: Mitsos and Browne (1998) blamed poor literacy, laddish subcultures and the feminisation of schooling (Sewell 2006); Francis (2000) found boys' identities conflict with schoolwork. AO3: radical feminists note girls still face patriarchy — subjects remain gendered and the pay gap awaits them. Evaluation: class, gender and ethnicity interact The A* answer treats class, gender and ethnicity as interacting, not separate: working-class black boys face both class disadvantage and racialised labelling (Archer et al 2010 — 'Nike identities'); Chinese pupils outperform all groups, undermining single-cause explanations; and girls' success coexists with gendered subject choice and the eventual pay gap. Interactionists (Becker) explain in-school meanings but not out-of-school causes; structural theories explain patterns but not why individual pupils respond differently. Examiner tip: in 'outline and evaluate' questions on ethnic or gender differences, always weigh external against internal factors and end with a judgement about which better explains the pattern. AQA 4.1.1.5 — processes within schools: teacher-pupil relationships shape achievement through labelling (Becker 1971), expectations and the self-fulfilling prophecy (Rosenthal and Jacobson 1968); streaming creates pupil subcultures through differentiation and polarisation (Hargreaves 1967; Lacey 1970) — pro-school subcultures gain status from achievement, anti-school subcultures from rebellion; Keddie (1971) found teachers denied lower-stream pupils knowledge, not ability, driving failure; pupil identities (Archer et al 2010) show class, gender and ethnicity interact — 'ideal pupil' images shift by context, and working-class pupils' 'Nike identities' invite symbolic violence. AQA 4.1.1.6 — policies: the 1944 Education Act created the tripartite system — grammar, secondary modern and technical schools selected by the 11-plus, embodying functionalist meritocracy claims; Ford (1969) showed streaming in a comprehensive simply reproduced the same differences. From 1965, comprehensives replaced selection. The 1988 Education Reform Act introduced marketisation: national curriculum, formula funding (per-pupil budgets), league tables and open enrolment — Miriam David called the claimed result a parentocracy; Ball, Bowe and Gewirtz (1994) called it a myth: privileged-skilled choosers (middle-class, mobile) capture the best places, disconnected choosers (working-class) take what remains; Bartlett (1993) showed cream-skimming (schools selecting high-achievers) and silt-shifting. Chubb and Moe (1990) supported marketisation, arguing parental choice raises standards. New Labour (1997-2010): academies, specialist schools, Education Action Zones, Education Maintenance Allowances, Sure Start — aimed at both standards and equality. Coalition 2010 onwards: free schools (Allen 2010 questioned their benefit), the pupil premium, academy expansion. Privatisation: Ball and Youdell (2008) distinguish endogenous (private sector involvement in state education) and exogenous (education sold as a commodity abroad) privatisation. Globalisation of policy: PISA rankings and international comparisons drive policy borrowing (Ball 2008). AO3: functionalists see marketisation promoting choice and standards; Marxists see it reproducing class inequality under a parentocracy myth. Policies — evaluation points to deploy Use these AO3 points in any policy essay: (1) Ball, Bowe and Gewirtz (1994) — the parentocracy is a myth; middle-class 'privileged-skilled choosers' capture the best places, so marketisation widens class gaps. (2) Gillborn and Youdell (2000) — league tables create educational triage, penalising schools with disadvantaged intakes. (3) Allen (2010) — free schools are untested and may widen inequality. (4) Functionalists (Chubb and Moe 1990) — competition raises standards where parents can choose. (5) The New Right — welfare and comprehensive schooling undermined standards; marketisation restored discipline and choice. Pair each with the policy it evaluates. On AQA 7192 Paper 1 , education appears as 4- and 6-mark item questions, a 10-mark 'outline and analyse two...', and the 20-mark Methods in Context question (Q5); on OCR H580/03 as item-based questions plus a 30-mark assess essay; on Eduqas as extended 'discuss' essays. Command word What it demands AO focus Outline and analyse two Two developed points, each applied to the question AO1 + AO2 Outline and evaluate Knowledge plus sustained debate with a reached judgement AO1 + AO2 + AO3 Assess / discuss how far Weigh evidence for and against a claim AO3-heavy 30-mark skeleton: (1) define the claim (e.g. what counts as 'inside school'); (2) three or four developed points, each with a named study and date; (3) three or four evaluations with counter-theorists; (4) a conclusion with a weighed judgement answering the exact question. Common pitfalls: confusing external (home, background) and internal (school process) factors; describing policy without evaluating it; citing Murdock-style universality or Parsons' meritocracy without critique (Bowles and Gintis); ignoring Willis' counter-evidence that pupils resist; listing material and cultural deprivation without studies; ending without a judgement. Timing: 30 marks ≈ 30 minutes — plan 4, write 24, check 2. For 10-markers, two developed points with application suffice — do not spend evaluation credit early.

topics.name: Crime and Deviance
topics.subject: sociology
topics.searchText: sociology Sociology Crime and Deviance Set out functionalist, strain and subcultural theories of crime and deviance with named theorists (AQA 4.3.1.1) Explain interactionist and labelling theory, including secondary deviance and the dark figure (AQA 4.3.1.2) Analyse the social distribution of crime by class, gender, ethnicity, age and locality, including recent patterns (AQA 4.3.1.4) Evaluate explanations of globalisation and crime, green crime, state crime and the media-crime relationship (AQA 4.3.1.5) Assess crime control, prevention and punishment, victims, and the role of the criminal justice system (AQA 4.3.1.6) Deploy crime content in 10- and 30-mark essays and Methods in Context (AQA 4.3.2; 4.4.4) Durkheim: crime is inevitable and universal; functions include boundary maintenance, adaptation and change; too much crime produces anomie. Merton (1938): five adaptations to strain — conformity, innovation, ritualism, retreatism, rebellion; Cohen (1955) status frustration; Cloward and Ohlin (1960) criminal, conflict, retreatist subcultures; Miller (1958) focal concerns; Matza (1964) drift. Interactionist: Becker (1963) labelling, Lemert (1951) secondary deviance, Cicourel (1968) negotiated justice, Braithwaite (1992) reintegrative shaming. Distribution: dark figure — victim surveys (CSEW) reveal unrecorded crime; self-reports show smaller gender and ethnic gaps (Graham and Bowling 1995; Sharp and Budd 2005). Global: Hobbs and Dunningham (1998) glocal crime, Castells (1998), Beck (1992) risk society; green crime (South 1998; White 2008); state crime (Green and Ward 2004). Control: situational prevention (Clarke 1997), broken windows (Wilson and Kelling 1982), left realism (Lea and Young 1984), Foucault (1977) panopticon, Garland (2001) culture of control. Dark figure The volume of crime that goes unreported and unrecorded, so official statistics understate the true extent of offending. Moral panic Cohen (1972): an exaggerated media-driven overreaction to a group or event, creating 'folk devils' and amplifying the problem it responds to. Strain theory Merton (1938): deviance arises from the gap between culturally approved goals (wealth) and the legitimate means of achieving them. Delinquent subculture Cohen (1955): a working-class youth subculture offering an inverted status hierarchy in which delinquency earns the respect blocked by school failure. White-collar crime Sutherland (1949): crime committed by middle-class or professional people in the course of their occupation — e.g. fraud, tax evasion. Corporate crime Crime committed by companies or their employees for the company — e.g. health and safety violations, false accounting (Tombs and Whyte 2003). State crime Crime or deviance committed by, or with the approval of, state agencies — defined through human rights by Green and Ward (2004), e.g. torture, genocide. Green crime Crime against the environment (South 1998; White 2008) — primary (direct harm, e.g. illegal dumping) and secondary (state or corporate rule-breaking, e.g. unsafe practices). Secondary deviance Lemert (1951): deviance that follows from being publicly labelled — the label becomes the person's master status and a self-fulfilling identity. Situational crime prevention Clarke (1997): reducing opportunity through target hardening — locks, CCTV, surveillance — rather than tackling root causes. Panopticon Foucault (1977): the prison design in which inmates are always potentially watched, so they discipline themselves — a metaphor for modern surveillance power. Chivalry thesis Pollak (1950): the claim that male police and courts treat female offenders more leniently, so female crime is under-recorded. AQA 4.3.1.1 expects the consensus tradition and its critics. Durkheim argued crime is inevitable and universal — not everyone is socialised effectively, and modern societies of organic solidarity leave room for deviance. Crime is also functional: boundary maintenance — punishment publicly reaffirms shared values (as in trials); adaptation and change — deviance allows society to evolve (Durkheim praised Socrates); and a safety valve for strain (Davis argued prostitution protects the family; Polsky agreed pornography channels frustration). But too much crime produces anomie — the breakdown of regulation. Merton's strain theory (1938) : deviance arises from the gap between culturally approved goals (the American Dream of wealth) and the legitimate means of achieving them. Five adaptations: conformity (accept both), innovation (goals yes, means no — property crime), ritualism (means yes, goals abandoned), retreatism (reject both — alcoholics, vagrants) and rebellion (replace both). Evaluation: explains working-class property crime but not all crime — it assumes everyone shares the same goals, ignores white-collar and female crime, and takes statistics at face value. Subcultural theories : Cohen (1955) argued working-class boys facing school failure suffer status frustration and form delinquent subcultures with inverted success values — spite, malice, vandalism earn the status blocked by the middle-class measuring rod. Cloward and Ohlin (1960) added illegitimate opportunity structure : criminal subcultures (stable networks — professional crime), conflict subcultures (gang violence where no networks exist) and retreatist subcultures (double failures turn to drink and drugs). Miller (1958) dissented: working-class focal concerns — toughness, smartness, excitement, fatalism, autonomy — originate in working-class culture itself, not in reaction to middle-class goals. Matza (1964) argued most delinquents drift in and out of crime, using techniques of neutralisation (Sykes and Matza 1957) — denial of responsibility or injury — to excuse it. AO3: feminist critics note the neglect of female deviance (Heidensohn); interactionists note these theories take official statistics at face value. AQA 4.3.1.2 : Becker (1963) argued deviance is not a quality of the act but the consequence of social reaction — 'deviant behaviour is behaviour people so label'. Moral entrepreneurs (police, media, politicians) apply labels; once labelled, the person is viewed through the label. Lemert (1951) distinguished primary deviance (acts not publicly labelled — trivial, widespread) from secondary deviance (deviance caused by being caught and labelled, which becomes a master status — 'thief' — and a self-fulfilling identity). Cicourel (1968) showed juvenile justice is negotiable: officers' typifications of the 'delinquent' (working-class, black) meant middle-class youths were less likely to be arrested, and their parents' intervention deflected prosecution — so statistics reflect labelling, not behaviour. Young (1971) studied hippies and marijuana: police labelling of drug users created the deviant subculture the police had imagined. Braithwaite (1992) distinguished reintegrative shaming (punish the act, not the person — Japan's low crime) from disintegrative shaming (stigmatise the person — pushing them into deviant subcultures). Goffman (1961) showed asylums strip inmates of identity through mortification. Official statistics and the dark figure: police-recorded crime omits unreported and unrecorded offences. Victim surveys — the Crime Survey for England and Wales (Mayhew and colleagues' design) — measure the dark figure: victims report large volumes of crime the police never record. Farrington and Dowds (1986) showed recorded crime rose in one Lancashire area partly because of changed police recording practices. AO3: labelling theory is criticised as deterministic — many people resist labels (Fuller 1984; Braithwaite); it ignores the origins of primary deviance; Marxists argue labels reflect wider class power, not individual bias; realists argue some differences are real, not labelling artefacts. AQA 4.3.1.4 expects patterns by social group and the debates about them. Class: official statistics over-represent the working class — but Marxism points to white-collar crime (Sutherland 1949) and corporate crime (Tombs and Whyte 2003; Snider 1993) committed by the powerful, largely invisible in statistics; Pearce (1976) called this 'crimes of the powerful'. Murray's underclass thesis (1994) blames welfare dependency — disputed by left realists who see poverty and relative deprivation as structural causes. Gender: men are over-represented in statistics as offenders and victims. The chivalry thesis (Pollak 1950) claims female crime is under-recorded because male agents of control treat women leniently — supported by self-report studies (Graham and Bowling 1995: almost identical rates of admitted offending among young white and black men; Sharp and Budd 2005). The liberation thesis (Adler 1975) claims women's crime rises as patriarchy weakens. Heidensohn (1985) used control theory: women are controlled at home, work and in public, so they have fewer opportunities for crime. Carlen (1988) interviewed 39 working-class women offenders: crime results from the failure of class and gender deals — poverty plus the collapse of the rewards of domesticity. AO3: Heidensohn and Carlen explain female crime through control and class, not liberation; recent statistics show most female crime remains low-level (theft, shoplifting). Ethnicity: black people are over-represented in stop-and-search and prison statistics. Hall et al (1978) argued the 1970s 'mugging' moral panic was a myth constructed to legitimate a policing crisis — capitalism in crisis needed a scapegoat. Hood (1992) found black men up to five times more likely to be jailed for the same offence — sentencing bias. Bowling and Phillips (2002) document over-policing and under-protection of ethnic minorities. Self-report studies show smaller differences than official statistics (Sharp and Budd 2005). Mac an Ghaill (1994) examined young black and Asian men's responses to racism. AO3: realists argue some patterns reflect real differences in offending; interactionists argue the statistics are socially constructed; the statistics also under-record white-collar crime committed mostly by the white majority. Age and locality: young men aged roughly 15-24 are most likely to offend and to be victims; crime is concentrated in deprived urban areas and declines with age — biological ageing, life-course changes and peer group effects. AO3: the distribution debates mirror the labelling vs realist divide across all groups. AQA 4.3.1.5 — globalisation and crime: Taylor (1997) argued globalisation creates crime at every level: transnational corporations evade regulation, and global insecurity produces crime in poorer regions. Hobbs and Dunningham (1998) found organised crime now works through glocal networks — locally based but globally connected, organised around a core individual. Castells (1998) described a global criminal economy — drugs, trafficking, cybercrime, money laundering. Beck (1992) framed the global risk society : manufactured risks (pollution, nuclear, climate) cross borders and cannot be contained by nation states. Green crime (South 1998; White 2008) : primary green crime is direct harm to the environment (illegal dumping, emissions); secondary green crime is state or corporate rule-breaking that produces harm (unsafe transport, breaches of regulation). Green criminology defines crime through harm, not law — eco-centric rather than anthropocentric. AO3: transgressive definitions of crime lack legal backing; Beck's risk society is more theory than measurement. State crime: Green and Ward (2004) define state crime through human rights — genocide, torture, detention without trial; McLaughlin (2001) and Ruggiero analyse state-organised crime; the Iraq War and Abu Ghraib are stock examples. States define what counts as crime, so they can conceal their own — hence the human rights definition. AO3: human rights are contested — whose rights, defined by whom? The media and crime: Cohen (1972) documented the moral panic through the mods and rockers: media exaggeration created folk devils, amplified deviance and produced a self-fulfilling spiral. Hall et al (1978) analysed the mugging panic as political legitimation. McRobbie and Thornton (1995) argue moral panics have changed in a media-saturated age — groups now court them. Media representations distort crime: fictional and news media over-represent violent and sexual crime and under-represent property crime (Soothill and Walby 1991 on rape reporting; Greer 2003 on crime news). AO3: the media's role as cause of crime (imitation, moral panics) is contested by pluralists who note audiences interpret actively. AQA 4.3.1.6 — control, prevention and punishment: Right realism: Wilson and Kelling (1982) argued broken windows — visible disorder invites crime, so zero-tolerance policing restores order; Murray (1994) blamed the underclass. Situational crime prevention (Clarke 1997) reduces opportunity through target hardening — locks, CCTV, alarms. Left realism: Lea and Young (1984) argued crime has real victims and real causes — relative deprivation , marginalisation and subculture; prevention must tackle root causes through community policing and the 'square of crime' (state, public, offender, victim). Punishment: Foucault (1977) traced the shift from sovereign power (public execution) to disciplinary power — the panopticon , where constant potential surveillance makes inmates discipline themselves; surveillance has spread through society. Garland (2001) described the 'culture of control' — late-modern crime control combines punitive populism with managerial risk assessment. Restorative justice (Braithwaite 1992) repairs harm and reintegrates offenders. Victims: Christie (1986) argued the 'ideal victim' — weak, respectable, blameless — is a social construction shaping who receives sympathy and support; victims of corporate and state crime (Tombs and Whyte) are largely invisible. The criminal justice system — police, courts, prisons — coordinates control; recidivism (reoffending) rates question prison's effectiveness. Evaluation of prevention and punishment Situational prevention works locally but displaces crime (it moves rather than reduces it) and ignores root causes; broken windows policing produced zero-tolerance controversies in New York and remains contested; Foucault's surveillance thesis explains self-discipline but underplays resistance (Haggerty and Ericson); Garland's culture of control captures late-modern punitiveness but cannot explain why some societies remain lenient. Left realists (Lea and Young 1984) argue prevention must combine opportunity reduction with tackling relative deprivation — the most complete answer weighs both realisms. Exam technique for crime essays AQA Paper 3 : 4- and 6-mark items, a 10-mark 'outline and analyse two...', the 20-mark Methods in Context question (Q6), and a 30-mark 'outline and evaluate...' theory essay. 30-mark skeleton: (1) define the perspective and its logic; (2) three or four developed points, each with a named study and date; (3) three or four evaluations with counter-theorists; (4) a weighed conclusion answering the exact question. Pitfalls: describing theories without studies; confusing Durkheim's functionalism with Merton's strain; citing statistics without discussing their construction (dark figure, labelling); neglecting globalisation, green and state crime (4.3.1.5) in synoptic answers; ending without a judgement.

topics.name: Beliefs in Society
topics.subject: sociology
topics.searchText: sociology Sociology Beliefs in Society Compare religion, science and ideology as worldviews, including Popper's falsification and Horton's open/closed systems (AQA 4.2.1) Set out Durkheim's functionalism, Weber's theodicy and rationalisation, and Marx's account of religion as ideology, with evaluation Classify religious organisations using Troeltsch and Stark & Bainbridge, and explain the church-sect trajectory Assess secularisation evidence (Wilson, Bruce) against supply-side and cultural-defence counter-arguments Explain the postmodernist account of religion (Lyon, Davie) and theories of fundamentalism (Giddens, Bruce) Deploy named studies and reached judgements in 10- and 30-mark answers (AO1/AO2/AO3) Durkheim (1912): religion = separation of sacred and profane; totemism shows society worshipping itself; religion has cognitive and integrative functions. Critique: Worsley - no sharp sacred/profane split in some tribes; works best in small-scale societies. Weber (1905): Calvinist predestination and this-worldly asceticism produced the 'Protestant ethic', fuelling capitalism; rationalisation disenchant the world. Critique: capitalism predates Calvinism in Catholic Italy; multi-causal. Marx: religion as ruling-class ideology, 'opium of the people'; Lenin's 'spiritual gin'. Critique: ignores the meaning religion gives the oppressed (Weber); religion can inspire resistance (liberation theology; MLK). Typologies: Troeltsch (church, sect), Niebuhr (denomination), Stark & Bainbridge (audience/client/cultic-movement cults; sects from schism). Critique: ideal types that blur in reality (e.g. Mormonism fits no box). Secularisation FOR: Wilson (contagion), Bruce (technological worldview; decline of community), attendance fall from ~40% (1851) to ~5-10%. AGAINST: Davie (belief without belonging), religious economy (America), cultural defence and transition (Bruce), Beckford - unsociological meta-concept. Postmodernity: Lyon (Jesus in Disneyland; disembedding), Hervieu-Leger (spiritual shopping, pilgrims/converts). Fundamentalism: Giddens (defensive response to modernity; cosmopolitanism vs fundamentalism), Bruce (product of modernity). Sacred and profane Durkheim's basic distinction: the sacred are things set apart and forbidden, inspiring awe; the profane are ordinary, everyday things. Religion is defined by this split, not by belief in gods. Theodicy of disprivilege Weber's term for religious explanations of suffering (e.g. reward in the afterlife) that appeal especially to deprived groups, making hardship meaningful and tolerable. Disenchantment Weber's description of the outcome of rationalisation: the magical and religious worldview is progressively displaced by scientific, calculated thinking; the world becomes 'disenchanted'. Religion as ideology Marx: religion is the 'opium of the people' - an illusion masking exploitation, promising compensation after death and legitimating class inequality as God-given. Sect A small, exclusive religious group that has split from a larger body (Troeltsch), demanding total membership, rejecting wider society and drawing mainly on the poor; often led by a charismatic leader. Denomination A religious body (Niebuhr) standing between church and sect: less exclusive than a sect, tolerant of other faiths, not tied to the state, with a middle-class following and a bureaucratic ministry. Relative deprivation Stark & Bainbridge: a subjective sense of being deprived compared with others or with expectations - explains why the relatively affluent as well as the poor join sects and cults. Secularisation Wilson: the process by which religious institutions, practices and consciousness lose social significance - declining participation, rationalisation and religion displaced from public life. Belief without belonging Grace Davie: a pattern in Britain where people hold religious beliefs but do not attend church - attendance falls faster than belief, so secularisation is partial. Fundamentalism A literal, uncompromising assertion of a single sacred text as the only truth (Giddens), typically a defensive reaction against modernity and globalisation; Bruce sees it as a product of modern society itself. AQA 4.2 , OCR H580 (Component 03) and Eduqas AC4.1 treat religion as one of three competing worldviews alongside science and ideology. Durkheim (1912) defined religion functionally by the sacred/profane split; his study of the Arunta's totemism argued that when people worship the totem they are really worshipping society - religion reinforces collective conscience and supplies categories for thought. AO3: Worsley found no sharp sacred/profane distinction in some tribes, and the theory fits small-scale societies better than complex plural ones; Mestrovic adds that modern social disorder makes Durkheim's integrative claim harder to sustain. Weber (1905) began from meaning: Calvinist belief in predestination created 'salvation anxiety', answered by a theodicy of disprivilege and this-worldly asceticism - worldly success as a sign of election - which unintentionally fuelled the spirit of capitalism. Rationalisation then progressively disenchanted the world, displacing magic. AO3: capitalism developed in Catholic Italy before Calvin existed, so the causal arrow is contested; and Weber's own multi-causal method lets technology and state-building count too. Marx treated religion as ideology: the 'opium of the people' dulls the pain of exploitation, promises pie in the sky and makes hierarchy appear God-given; Lenin called it 'spiritual gin'. AO3: this ignores the meanings the poor themselves attach to belief (Weber), and religion can inspire resistance - liberation theology in Latin America, the Black clergy in the civil rights movement (MLK). Feminists add that religion is patriarchal: El Saadawi saw veiling as an expression of male control, while Armstrong shows women have also found power within religion (e.g. medieval nuns). Science vs religion: Popper's falsification makes science an open belief system (Horton) that anyone may criticise, against religion's closed self-sealing claims; yet Kuhn (paradigms) and Polanyi (polyfactualism) show science itself rests on unproven assumptions. Deepening Durkheim: Malinowski (1926) refined the functionalist account with the Trobriand islanders: religion deals with life crises (death rituals, canoe magic) where prediction and control fail, reinforcing solidarity at points of stress. Bellah (1970) adds civil religion - American civil religion sacralises the nation itself ('In God We Trust'), functioning as a unifying belief system even for the non-religious. Deepening science: Merton's CUDOS norms (communism, universalism, disinterestedness, organised scepticism) explain why science is institutionally open - knowledge is shared and every claim challengeable - while peer review polices fraudulent claims. AO3: closed systems are not confined to religion: Horton himself notes quasi-scientific dogmatism, and political ideologies (Lenin's Marxism) can be self-sealing too - so the open/closed boundary is blurred, and no worldview has a monopoly on irrationality. Troeltsch (1912) distinguished churches from sects: churches are large, inclusive, universal, tied to the state, with a professional hierarchy and monopoly of truth; sects are small, exclusive, voluntary, hostile to wider society, with charismatic leadership and equality among members. Niebuhr (1929) added the denomination - a middle category, tolerant of other bodies, not claiming a monopoly, recruiting through birth rather than conversion. Cults are looser still: individualistic, without fixed membership. Stark & Bainbridge (1985) replaced the static typology with a spectrum of cult types - audience cults (loose consumer involvement, e.g. astrology), client cults (services for a fee, e.g. transcendental meditation) and cultic movements (full membership) - and argued sects arise by schism from existing churches. Why sects and cults grow - and what happens next Stark & Bainbridge explain growth by relative deprivation : even the materially comfortable may feel spiritually or status-deprived, and sects offer compensators for rewards this world denies. Weber's routinisation of charisma plus Niebuhr's 'the otherworldliness of upwardly mobile sect members' produce the classic trajectory: sect to denomination (Methodism is the textbook case), stable sect (the Amish), or death. AO3: typologies are ideal types that blur in reality - the Church of England behaves denominationally, Mormonism fits no box, and NRMs cut across every category. Wallis (1984) classified NRMs instead by their relationship to the world: world-rejecting (e.g. the Unification Church), world-accommodating (e.g. Neo-Pentecostalism) and world-affirming (e.g. Scientology) - a functional rather than organisational grid that examiners reward as a refinement. Refining the growth explanations: relative deprivation is not only material: the moderately deprived (affluent expectations unmet) are drawn to world-rejecting sects, while the very deprived may lack the resources to join at all; the privileged may experience relative spiritual deprivation (Wallis) - the New Age's world-affirming appeal to the affluent middle class fits this pattern. Heelas & Woodhead (2005) - the Kendal Project - found the traditional congregational domain declining while the holistic milieu (yoga, meditation, self-spirituality) grew: 'self-religion' replacing religion of the church. AO3: their own data show the holistic milieu remains a small minority pursuit, so the growth-of-the-New-Age claim should not be overstated; and sect membership statistics are unreliable because definitions of membership differ between bodies (Bruce), making trend claims contestable. Wilson (1966) defined secularisation as religion losing social influence, arguing it spreads by contagion: once one institution (school, welfare, state) is secularised, others follow. Bruce (2002) gives the strongest modern case: a technological worldview replaces religious explanations; the decline of community (rationalisation plus structural differentiation) removes the social settings where belief is practised; and churches have watered down doctrine to survive. Evidence for: Church attendance fell from around 40% in 1851 to roughly 5-10% today; baptisms, church weddings and Sunday schools have collapsed; clergy numbers fall; mainstream churches have softened doctrine on homosexuality and women priests - secularisation from within . The counter-case: why some sociologists reject the claim Davie (1994): 'belief without belonging' - belief falls far more slowly than attendance, and a residual cultural religion persists. Religious economy (Stark & Bainbridge): demand for religion is constant; supply is the variable - America's deregulated, competitive market keeps participation high (over 40% claim weekly attendance), so low British participation reflects a state-church monopoly, not secularisation. Bruce himself concedes: cultural defence (religion as a symbol of national or group identity, e.g. Poland's Catholic Church under communism) and cultural transition (religion for migrants) produce pockets of high religiosity. Beckford (2003): 'secularisation' is an unsociological meta-concept - observers project their own values and hold religion to a different standard of 'success' than other institutions. AO2/AO3 for essays: the strongest answers treat secularisation as partial and uneven - declining for mainstream churches in Britain, but rising for world-affirming NRMs, megachurches and in contexts of defence and transition; relativise Wilson and Bruce against Davie, the religious economy and Beckford, then reach a judgement (e.g. secularisation is real for institutional religion, contested for belief and demand). Deepening the evidence: Wilson's disengagement theme - religious institutions have lost their hold on wider society: education, welfare and politics are run secularly, and even the monarchy has de-sacralised. Structural differentiation (Parsons' own concept): religion's functions have been transferred to specialised institutions (schools socialise, the welfare state supports), leaving the church a residual role. British Social Attitudes surveys confirm the trend: those identifying as 'no religion' have risen from roughly a third to over half of adults, and church weddings are now a minority of marriages. AO3: identity statistics measure belonging , not belief or practice - Davie's point - and census wording varies, so the trend line is softer than raw numbers suggest. Lyon (2000) - 'Jesus in Disneyland' - argues religion is being disembedded : electronic media lift beliefs out of their physical churches, so faith becomes a consumable choice, sprinkled across cyberspace and consumer culture rather than attached to one organisation. Hervieu-Leger describes spiritual shopping : 'pilgrims' follow individual spiritual journeys while 'converts' join intense revivalist groups; religion becomes a matter of consumption. Postmodernists therefore reject secularisation as a meta-narrative: religion has not vanished, it has been transformed - NRMs, New Age spirituality and healing all fit the consumer pattern. Fundamentalism cuts against both the postmodern celebration of choice and the secularisation story. Giddens (1999) sees it as a defensive assertion of a single sacred text against modernity's cosmopolitanism, provoked by globalisation and uncertainty; fundamentalists reject the relativism the postmodern world celebrates. Bruce (2000) counters that fundamentalism is a product of modernity , not a pre-modern survival: where a whole society is fundamentalist (as in Iran) the cause is a third-world society's experience of modernisation; where it is a minority movement (the Christian Right in the USA) it is a reaction to rapid change and perceived secular decline. Davie notes the global pattern is mixed: a secularising Europe alongside resurgent religion elsewhere. AO3: Haynes argues 'fundamentalism' lumps together movements with different causes (Islamic, Hindu, Christian), and Bruce's own evidence shows fundamentalists use distinctly modern media and technology - consistent with Lyon's disembedding. Deepening fundamentalism: Giddens pairs fundamentalism with cosmopolitanism - the reflective, tolerant openness of late modernity - and calls the two 'cousins': fundamentalism is itself a product of the same globalising forces, a reflexive retreat from uncertainty rather than a return to tradition. Davie's global pattern is threefold (European secularisation; American vitality; Pentecostal growth in the global South), and the worldwide growth of Pentecostalism suggests secularisation is regionally specific, not universal. AO3: the strongest answers avoid treating 'religion' as one thing: institutional decline in Europe, market vitality in the USA, spiritual consumption in postmodernity and fundamentalist reaction can all be true at once - Weber's multi-causal method is the template for holding them together.

topics.name: Social Stratification and Class
topics.subject: sociology
topics.searchText: sociology Sociology Social Stratification and Class Distinguish the four historical forms of stratification (slavery, caste, estate, class) and class/status/party as Weber's three dimensions (AQA 4.3.1) Set out Marxist (bourgeoisie/proletariat), functionalist (Davis & Moore) and feminist accounts of stratification, with evaluation Explain how class is measured (NS-SEC, Registrar-General) and the problems with occupational measurement Apply Weber's concept of life chances to evidence on health, education, wealth and deprivation Analyse patterns and explanations of social mobility using Goldthorpe's studies, including feminist and postmodern critiques Reach weighed judgements between competing explanations in 10- and 30-mark answers (AO1/AO2/AO3) Four forms of stratification: slavery (ownership of persons), caste (birth-ascribed, closed, Hindu varna), estate (feudal, law-defined) and class (achieved, open, market-based) - only class is the modern form. Weber: class is market position, not ownership alone; status can cut across class (black doctors, poor aristocrats); party adds political power. Critique: 'class, status and party' overlap and are hard to operationalise separately. Marx: two-class polarisation, exploitation, ruling-class ideology; neo-Marxists (Wright's contradictory class locations; Gramsci's hegemony) update the picture. Critique: polarisation never happened - middle class grew (Weber; 'embourgeoisement'). Functionalist: Davis & Moore (1945) role allocation - stratification is functionally necessary. Critique: Tumin (1953) - circular, ignores inherited wealth and blocked opportunity, rewards reflect power not functional importance. Feminist: stratification is gendered - Walby's six patriarchal structures; dual-systems theory (capitalism + patriarchy); vertical segregation and the glass ceiling; feminist critique of NS-SEC for scoring women by men's jobs. Life chances: Black Report (1980) class gradients in health; wealth gaps; Townsend's relative deprivation. Postmodern claim (Pakulski & Waters; Bauman) that class is dead is countered by Westergaard - inequality is still class-shaped. Goldthorpe (1972 Oxford Mobility Study, replicated 1992; Sutton Trust 2019): high absolute mobility from white-collar expansion ('upward drift') but stable relative rates - class of origin still shapes destination; long-range 'unjustified' upward mobility into the service class. Social stratification The division of society into hierarchical layers where people have unequal access to resources, power and prestige; the four forms are slavery, caste, estate and class. Class, status and party Weber's three distinct dimensions of stratification: class (market position - economic power over goods and skills), status (social honour or prestige) and party (political power, organised to pursue goals). Bourgeoisie and proletariat Marx's two great classes of capitalist society: the bourgeoisie own the means of production and exploit wage labour; the proletariat own only their labour power, which they sell to survive. Life chances Weber's term for the opportunities individuals have to share in the good things of life - health, education, housing, wealth - which are systematically distributed by class position. NS-SEC The National Statistics Socio-economic Classification, the official UK measure of class based on occupation, employment relations and conditions; it replaced the Registrar-General's scale in 2001. Role allocation Davis & Moore (1945): stratification is a device ensuring the most talented fill the most important positions; unequal rewards ('differential functional importance') motivate effort and training. Social mobility Movement between class positions: inter-generational (between parents and children) or intra-generational (within one person's career); absolute mobility (structural change) differs from relative mobility (chances relative to class of origin). Relative mobility Goldthorpe: mobility chances of one class compared with another - how far class of origin affects one's destination; stable relative rates indicate that class barriers persist even while absolute mobility rises. Glass ceiling An invisible barrier preventing women and ethnic minorities from reaching senior positions despite formal equality of opportunity; measured by pay gaps and boardroom representation. Patriarchy A system of male dominance over women operating through institutions (work, family, culture); feminist theories treat it as a central axis of stratification alongside or above class. AQA 4.3 , OCR H580 (Components 01 and 03) and Eduqas AC5.1 open with the historical forms of stratification: slavery (ownership of persons), caste (birth-ascribed and closed, e.g. the Hindu varna system), estate (feudal layers defined by law, e.g. nobility, clergy, commoners) and class - the open, achieved, market-based form characteristic of capitalism. Weber (1922) then splits class into three dimensions. Class is market position: economic power flowing from skills, qualifications and ownership, creating shared life chances. Status is social honour, which can cut across class - a black doctor suffers status discrimination despite class position, a poor aristocrat enjoys prestige without wealth. Party is organised political power, pursuing goals whether or not they serve economic interests. Marx collapses this into one axis of ownership: capitalist society polarises into bourgeoisie (owners of the means of production) and proletariat (sellers of labour power), with exploitation producing ruling-class ideology that legitimises the system. AO3: the predicted polarisation never arrived - the middle class expanded ('embourgeoisement', Goldthorpe & Lockwood's affluent workers 1968) - so Weber's multi-dimensional model, and neo-Marxist refinements (Wright's contradictory class locations; Erikson & Goldthorpe's class schema), fit modern societies better. The strongest 30-mark answers deploy Weber against Marx and vice versa rather than treating them as rivals on one dimension. Deepening the forms: the four forms differ in openness (can status be achieved?) and ascription (is position given at birth?): slavery and caste are closed and ascribed; estate is semi-open (law-defined but with mobility routes); class is open and achieved - the only form where inequality is theoretically justified by merit. Deepening Weber vs Marx: Goldthorpe & Lockwood's (1968) 'affluent workers' study found manual workers with middle-class incomes still held proletarian traditional norms - supporting Weber's distinction between market situation and consciousness. Wright (1985) tried to reconcile the two with contradictory class locations : managers and semi-autonomous employees occupy positions that are simultaneously capitalist and worker-like, explaining why polarisation never arrived. AO3: Weber's three dimensions overlap and are hard to operationalise separately (status and class blend in the professions), and Wright's locations are contested as arbitrary - use these as refinements, not refutations. Davis & Moore (1945) argue stratification is functional : every society must allocate people to positions; the most important positions require scarce talent and long training, so unequal rewards ('differential functional importance') motivate sacrifice and ensure the best fill them - stratification is therefore universal and, in principle, efficient. AO3 - Tumin (1953) dismantles this: importance is impossible to measure objectively (nurses and cleaners matter more than their pay suggests); rewards reflect power , not function; stratification blocks the talent pool by restricting opportunity to the privileged (inheritance, private education); and it breeds resentment, not motivation - the exact opposite of a functional device. Feminist theories insist stratification is gendered as well as classed. Walby (1990) identifies six patriarchal structures (paid work, household production, culture, sexuality, violence, the state) that systematically subordinate women; dual-systems theorists argue capitalism and patriarchy interlock, so women are exploited as both workers and unpaid domestic labourers. Evidence: vertical segregation concentrates women in junior roles, the gender pay gap persists (~13-14% for full-timers), and the glass ceiling holds despite formal equality. AO3: difference feminists warn against one universal 'women's' experience (intersectionality: class, ethnicity and gender interact), and liberal feminists stress measurable legal progress (Equality Act 2010). Dual-systems theory itself struggles to specify how two systems causally combine - a standard A* evaluation. Deepening functionalism and its critique: the classic Davis & Moore example is the surgeon: long training, scarce talent and life-or-death importance justify high rewards. Tumin's rebuttal has five strands - two worth spelling out: (1) blocked opportunity - the talent pool is restricted by inheritance and private education, so the 'most talented' are partly the most privileged; (2) power not function - rewards reflect the bargaining power of positions, which is why functionally vital cleaners and nurses are paid little. Deepening feminism: vertical segregation concentrates women in the lowest grades even where they dominate the profession (teaching, medicine); intersectionality (Crenshaw) shows gender, class and ethnicity compound - minority women face the steepest ceilings. AO3: evidence of progress (Equal Pay Act 1970; Equality Act 2010; gender pay-gap reporting) supports liberal feminism's reformist claim, while the persistent gap supports the structural account. Measurement: the NS-SEC (National Statistics Socio-economic Classification) replaced the Registrar-General's scale in 2001 and classifies the population (8 classes, from higher managerial/professional to never-employed) by occupation, employment relations and conditions - contract, autonomy, promotion prospects. AO3: occupational measurement has well-known flaws: it ignores wealth (the fastest-growing divide), scores married women by their husband's or their own job inconsistently, misses the informal economy and underclass debates, and - as Weberians would note - captures only class, never status or party. Life chances (Weber's term): class position systematically distributes access to life's goods. Health: the Black Report (1980) showed steep class gradients in morbidity and infant mortality that persist (professionals live roughly a decade longer in good health than routine workers). Wealth and income: the top decile holds a large multiple of the bottom decile's wealth, and inherited advantage compounds. Education and housing: class gaps in attainment and tenure underpin the cyclical reproduction of advantage. Townsend reframed deprivation as relative - lacking what society regards as normal - so life chances are measured against social standards, not subsistence. AO3 for essays: use life-chance evidence to adjudicate between theories - gradients across every domain support Marxist and Weberian accounts of durable class effect, and challenge both the functionalist claim that rewards track talent and the postmodern claim that class no longer matters. Deepening measurement: the NS-SEC's eight classes range from 1 (higher managerial and professional) to 8 (never worked/long-term unemployed), and it underpins everything from exam results to mortality statistics - official statistics operationalise class. Its predecessor, the Registrar-General's scale, ranked occupations by prestige and was criticised as un-theoretical; the NS-SEC is explicitly Weberian (employment relations and conditions), showing how theory shapes measurement. Deepening life chances: relative poverty (households below 60% of median income) has hovered around a fifth of the UK population for decades, with children disproportionately affected; class gradients run through education (attainment gaps between FSM-eligible pupils and others), housing tenure and life expectancy. AO3: life-chance statistics are the strongest empirical adjudicator between theories - they sustain Marxist and Weberian claims of durable class effect, and directly challenge both functionalist meritocracy and the postmodern 'class is dead' claim. Goldthorpe's Oxford Mobility Study (1972, replicated with Erikson 1992) remains the benchmark. Absolute mobility rose across the century - most men did better than their fathers - but Goldthorpe explains this as upward drift : the service class expanded as white-collar and professional jobs grew, so room opened at the top regardless of fairness. Relative mobility - the chances of one class compared with another - was stable : class of origin continued to shape destination, with long-range, 'unjustified' upward mobility into the service class still rare for working-class sons. Later evidence (Sutton Trust 2019; Blanden) confirms stagnant relative rates, and education reproduces rather than interrupts the pattern (Boudon: primary and secondary effects). Critiques: feminist research (Stanworth 1984) showed Goldthorpe's classic study sampled men only , rendering women's mobility invisible - women's patterns differ, and marriage is itself a mobility route. The glass ceiling means upward mobility for women stalls below senior positions. Postmodern challenge: Pakulski & Waters (1996) and Bauman argue class is no longer the main source of identity or inequality - consumption and lifestyle stratify instead. AO3 response: Westergaard (1995) counters that inequality is still demonstrably class-shaped - wealth, life chances and mobility rates remain class gradients - so 'class is dead' mistakes changed language for changed reality . The A* judgement: absolute mobility rose through structural change while relative mobility froze, so the system grew more mobile without growing fairer. Deepening Goldthorpe: the Oxford study used an 11-class schema and the concept of the service class (professionals and managers) with distinct career ladders and advantages; social closure (Parkin) explains why relative rates are stable - privileged classes monopolise positions by excluding others through credentials and culture. Boudon (1974) supplies the education mechanism: primary effects (class differences in attainment) plus secondary effects (class-differentiated choices at transition points) reproduce the class structure even as education expands. Women's mobility was later studied (Heath) showing similar relative rates but steeper ceilings. Deepening the postmodern debate: Bauman argues identity is now chosen through consumption in 'fluid' modernity, and Pakulski & Waters claim property and occupation no longer define the strata. AO3: Westergaard's rebuttal stands - mobility rates, wealth and life chances remain class gradients - and even Bauman concedes inequality persists. The judgement: Britain has become more mobile in absolute terms, not fairer in relative terms. Exam technique: stratification questions reward adjudication between theories, not description. AQA 4.3 and OCR H580 give 30-mark 'outline and evaluate' essays (AO weighting roughly 8/8/14) and 10-mark 'outline and analyse two' items; OCR also asks 'assess the view that...' with an Item (e.g. Item: most people believe social mobility has declined). The A* skeleton: define the concepts (class, status, party; bourgeoisie/proletariat; life chances), deploy two or three competing perspectives each with a named study, evaluate each with a counter-theorist, and finish with a weighed judgement that answers the actual question - e.g. 'class remains the structural skeleton of inequality, but it now operates alongside gender, ethnicity and consumption'.

topics.name: Media
topics.subject: sociology
topics.searchText: sociology Sociology Media Explain the growth of new media, Jenkins' convergence and participatory culture, and the digital divide (AQA 4.7.1) Set out Marxist and hegemonic accounts of ownership and control (Murdock & Golding, Miliband, Gramsci, Herman & Chomsky) against pluralism Analyse representations of gender, ethnicity and age with named concepts (symbolic annihilation, male gaze, tokenism) Compare audience-effect models: hypodermic syringe, two-step flow, uses and gratifications, encoding/decoding Explain moral panics (Cohen 1972), deviancy amplification and their links to labelling theory Assess globalisation debates - cultural imperialism against hybridisation - and deploy reached judgements (AO1/AO2/AO3) New media: Jenkins (convergence, participatory culture, 'fans as producers'); digital divide by age, class, geography ('digital underclass'). Critique: Cornford & Robbins - 'new' media is actually older media repackaged; commercial logics persist. Ownership FOR control: Murdock & Golding - concentration and the profit motive skew content; Miliband - media transmit ruling-class ideology; Herman & Chomsky's five filters; Gramsci's hegemony. AGAINST: pluralism - competition, regulation (Ofcom), and Web 2.0 plurality disperse control. Representations: gender - symbolic annihilation (Tuchman 1978), male gaze (Mulvey 1975), feminised beauty norms; ethnicity - negative stereotypes, tokenism, exclusion (Hall's 'inferential racism'; Gilroy on the 'war on terror'); age - children as innocent/victims, the elderly as frail or invisible (Carrigan & Szmigin). Audience effects: hypodermic syringe (passive audiences) -> two-step flow (Katz & Lazarsfeld 1955, opinion leaders) -> uses and gratifications (active audiences; Blumler & McQuail) -> encoding/decoding (Hall 1973, negotiated and oppositional readings). Evidence: Bandura (1963) supports limited direct effects; Livingston/Gauntlett argue effects research understates audience activity. Moral panics: Cohen (1972) mods and rockers - exaggeration, prediction, symbolisation; folk devils; deviancy amplification; linked to labelling (Becker 1963); 'amplification of deviance' now extends to social media. Globalisation: cultural imperialism (US dominance; Sklair's culture-ideology of consumerism) vs hybridisation and the 'global village' (McLuhan); Ritzer's McDonaldisation; new media accelerate global flows and citizen journalism. New media Digital, interactive, on-demand media enabled by Web 2.0 - user-generated content, convergence and portability - distinct from traditional one-to-many broadcast media. Digital divide Unequal access to and use of digital technology by age, class, income, geography and disability, creating a 'digital underclass' excluded from online services, information and opportunity. Convergence Jenkins: the merging of technologies, industries and audiences - one device (the smartphone) delivers print, broadcast and interactive content, blurring producer and consumer roles. Hegemony Gramsci: ruling-class domination through consent - media win voluntary acceptance of the dominant worldview - which must be continually renewed and can be contested (counter-hegemony). Propaganda model Herman & Chomsky (1988): five filters (ownership, advertising, sourcing, flak, anti-communism/ideology) systematically skew news content towards elite interests without overt conspiracy. Symbolic annihilation Tuchman (1978): women are either absent, trivialised or condemned in media representation, so their social contribution is symbolically erased. Male gaze Mulvey (1975): mainstream film and imagery position women as passive objects of a heterosexual male gaze, constructing femininity for visual consumption. Hypodermic syringe model An early effects theory (Frankfurt School heritage): media 'inject' direct, powerful, uniform messages into passive audiences, producing immediate uniform responses. Moral panic Cohen (1972): an exaggerated, distorted media-driven overreaction to a group ('folk devils') seen as a threat to societal values; produces deviancy amplification spirals. Uses and gratifications Blumler & McQuail (1968); Katz et al (1974): an active-audience theory - audiences use media to gratify needs (surveillance, identity, relationships, diversion) rather than being used by media. AQA 4.7 , OCR H580 (Component 03) and Eduqas AC6.1 expect you to define new media as digital, interactive, on-demand media - user-generated content, convergence, portability, global reach. Jenkins (2006) frames this as convergence : technologies, industries and audiences merge, so the smartphone delivers print, broadcast and interactive content at once, and 'fans become producers' - a participatory culture where audiences co-create what they consume (Wikipedia, fan fiction, YouTube). Digital divide: access and use remain stratified by age (young 'digital natives' against excluded older users), class, income, rurality and disability, producing a digital underclass locked out of online services and opportunity. AO3: the celebratory account has limits. Cornford & Robbins argue 'new' media is largely old media repackaged - the same conglomerates, advertising and commercial logics in new wrappers; interactive platforms still concentrate ownership (a handful of tech giants) and regulation struggles to keep pace. The strongest answers treat new media as an intensification of existing patterns of control, not a rupture - and note the divide itself shows structural inequality persisting into the digital age. Deepening new media: its defining features are digitalisation (content reduced to data, so boundaries between media collapse), interactivity (users respond, comment and co-create), decentralisation (no single gatekeeper) and portability . Optimists (Jenkins) stress democratisation - audiences become participants; pessimists note the same platforms concentrate attention and profit. Prensky's 'digital natives' label the generational divide, but Ofcom data show it is classed as well as aged: income, skills and confidence produce the 'digital underclass', and the divide carries life chances (job applications, services, education). AO3: treating the divide as purely generational mistakes a structural inequality for a cohort effect - the strongest answers link it back to class and age stratification. Murdock & Golding (1977) give the Marxist baseline: media are owned by a shrinking set of conglomerates whose profit motive and cross-ownership skew content towards elite interests; Miliband (1969) adds that media transmit ruling-class ideology , normalising inequality. Gramsci's hegemony refines this: domination works through consent - media renew the dominant worldview daily until it appears common sense - and can be contested by counter-hegemonic voices. Herman & Chomsky (1988) operationalise the claim with the propaganda model : five filters - ownership, advertising, sourcing, flak and ideology - systematically produce elite-friendly news without any conspiracy; studies of Iraq War coverage (Kovach-style sourcing biases) are the standard application. The pluralist counter-case Pluralists argue ownership does not equal control: audiences are sovereign - content must attract them or outlets die; competition, Ofcom regulation, professional values (impartiality norms) and editorial autonomy check owners; and the internet multiplies voices so no one worldview can dominate. Vertical integration may even raise output diversity. AO3: empirical judgement - concentration statistics (a few conglomerates dominate UK national press) and Herman & Chomsky's filters support control; the two-way web and citizen journalism support plurality. The strongest answers argue media give bounded choice: real plurality inside a commercial framework. AO3: the control thesis also underplays audience agency - even if content is skewed, decoding is active (Hall 1973), so ideology must still be accepted, negotiated or resisted by viewers. Deepening ownership: in the UK national press a handful of proprietors dominate circulation, and vertical integration (one company owning TV, print, film and platforms) multiplies their reach; Curran & Seaton document how ownership concentration narrowed the diversity of the press over the twentieth century. Regulation is the pluralist counterweight: Ofcom enforces impartiality rules for broadcasters, and press self-regulation (IPSO) - though critics note its weakness, a finding central to the Leveson Inquiry (2011-12).
