topics.subject: law
topics.searchText: law Law Criminal Law: Actus Reus and Mens Rea Identify and apply the actus reus of an offence, distinguishing conduct, state of affairs and consequence crimes, and the six duty situations where an omission satisfies the actus reus (R v Pittwood; R v Stone & Dobinson; R v Miller) (AQA 3.2.1; OCR H418 Component 3) Apply the two-stage causation test — factual (but-for; R v White) and legal (operating and substantial; R v Pagett; R v Kimsey; R v Cheshire) — including the thin skull rule (R v Blaue) and the victim's own act (R v Kennedy) State the rules of intention — direct (R v Mohan) and oblique (R v Woollin virtual-certainty direction) — and apply them to problem scenarios with the R v Matthews & Alleyne evidential gloss Distinguish subjective recklessness (R v Cunningham; R v G and another) from negligence, and explain the limited role of negligence as mens rea (R v Adomako) Explain the doctrine of transferred malice (R v Latimer; R v Gnango) and its limits (R v Pembliton) Define strict liability, apply the Gammon presumptions, contrast absolute liability (R v Larsonneur) and evaluate the arguments for and against offences of strict liability Deploy the elements, two-stage causation and mens rea ladder accurately in 25-mark AQA problem questions and 20-mark OCR/WJEC scenario questions Actus reus The external, guilty element of a crime: the prohibited act or omission, any prohibited result, and the surrounding circumstances of the offence. Conduct crime An offence completed by the doing of the act itself, with no prohibited result required (e.g. assault, dangerous driving under the Road Traffic Act 1988). State of affairs crime An offence where liability attaches to being in a prohibited situation, even where D acts involuntarily (R v Larsonneur; Winzar v Chief Constable of Kent). Omission A failure to act; generally not criminal, but satisfies the actus reus where a statutory, contractual, relational, assumed-care, danger-created or public-office duty exists (R v Pittwood; R v Gibbins & Proctor; R v Miller; R v Dytham). Factual causation The 'but for' test: the result would not have occurred but for D's act; D must also be a substantial and operating cause of the result (R v White; R v Pagett). Legal causation D's contribution must be more than minimal ('more than a slight or trifling link' — R v Kimsey) and must remain an operating cause unless a novus actus interveniens breaks the chain (R v Cheshire). Thin skull rule D must take the victim as found: pre-existing physical or psychological fragility does not break the chain of causation, even if unforeseeable (R v Blaue; R v Hayward). Direct intention The consequence is D's aim or purpose — 'a decision to bring about... the prohibited consequence, no matter whether the accused desired it' (R v Mohan). Oblique (indirect) intention Where death or serious injury was a virtual certainty as a result of D's act and D appreciated that, the jury may find intention (R v Woollin; R v Matthews & Alleyne). Recklessness D consciously takes an unjustifiable risk, knowing the risk exists or will exist — the subjective Cunningham test restored across the criminal law by R v G and another (2003). Transferred malice Intention or recklessness towards one victim transfers to the actual victim of the same kind of offence (R v Latimer; R v Gnango); different kinds of malice do not transfer (R v Pembliton). Strict liability An offence requiring no proof of mens rea for at least one element, found only where the Gammon presumptions are displaced; absolute liability (R v Larsonneur) admits no defence of any kind. The actus reus is the external, guilty element of an offence: the prohibited act, any prohibited result and the surrounding circumstances. The shape it takes dictates what the prosecution must prove. Conduct crimes — the act itself completes the offence, no result needed: assault, dangerous driving (Road Traffic Act 1988), perjury. Consequence (result) crimes — a prohibited result must be caused: murder (death of a human being in being under the Queen's peace), s.47 OAPA 1861 ABH, criminal damage (Criminal Damage Act 1971, s.1). Causation must be proved. State of affairs crimes — liability attaches to a situation, even without a voluntary act: R v Larsonneur (1933) (deported from England but returned in handcuffs; being 'found' in the UK completed the offence); Winzar v Chief Constable of Kent (1983) (found drunk on hospital premises and carried to the highway). Harsh, but valid — no mens rea required. Omissions. The baseline rule is that there is no liability for failing to act — English law imposes no general duty of rescue. An omission satisfies the actus reus only where a duty to act exists, from one of six sources: Statutory duty — Children and Young Persons Act 1933, s.1 (neglect of a child); Local Government Act 1972 duties. Contractual duty — R v Pittwood (1902) (railway gatekeeper left the gate open; a haycart was hit by a train). Duty from a relationship — R v Gibbins & Proctor (1918) (father and his partner starved the child to death). Voluntarily assumed duty of care — R v Stone & Dobinson (1977) (couple allowed D's anorexic sister, Fanny, to deteriorate; attempts to help insufficient). Duty from creating a dangerous situation — R v Miller (1983) (squatter's cigarette set the mattress alight; the duty to counteract the danger constituted the actus reus); R v Evans (2009) (heroin supplier owed a duty to call an ambulance for the sister who overdosed). Duty through public office — R v Dytham (1979) (off-duty officer watched a fatal beating and drove away). Coincidence of actus reus and mens rea. Both elements must coincide in time, but the courts are pragmatic: Fagan v Metropolitan Police Commissioner (1969) (car parked on the officer's foot; the later-formed intention to leave it there made the actus reus a continuing act over which mens rea coincided); R v Thabo Meli (1954) (a sequence of acts treated as a single transaction). Quick recall — the case bank for the actus reus State of affairs: Larsonneur (1933); Winzar v CC Kent (1983). Omissions duties: Pittwood (contract); Gibbins & Proctor (relationship); Stone & Dobinson (assumed care); Miller and Evans (danger created); Dytham (office); Children and Young Persons Act 1933, s.1 (statutory). Continuing act: Fagan v MPC (1969); R v Thabo Meli (1954). Consequence crimes: murder; s.47, s.20 OAPA 1861; Criminal Damage Act 1971, s.1. Consequence crimes require proof that D caused the prohibited result — a two-stage test. Stage 1: factual causation — the 'but for' test. Would the result have occurred but for D's conduct? R v White (1910): D poisoned his mother's drink, but she died of a heart attack — no factual causation of death, so only attempted murder succeeded. 'But for' alone is not enough where there are multiple contributing causes: R v Pagett (1983): D used his pregnant girlfriend as a human shield while shooting at armed police, who returned fire and killed her — D's acts must be the substantial and operating cause of the result; she would not have died but for his unlawful acts, and police fire was a response to his act, not an independent cause. Stage 2: legal causation. D's contribution must be more than minimal: R v Kimsey (1996): death on a high-speed race — the link must be more than a slight or trifling one (the de minimis principle). D need not be the sole or main cause so long as his act remains operating and substantial at the point of death. Intervening acts (novus actus interveniens) may break the chain of causation: Medical treatment — negligent treatment does not break the chain unless it is independent of D's acts and in itself so potent a cause of death: R v Cheshire (1991) (tracheotomy scarring narrowed the windpipe; the original gunshot wounds remained the operating cause — conviction upheld); R v Malcherek & Steel (1981) (switching off life support after brain death is never a novus actus). The narrow exception is R v Jordan (1956): 'palpably wrong' treatment — the wound had nearly healed and wrongly prescribed drugs plus excessive intravenous fluids caused death. Victim's own condition — the thin skull rule : take the victim as found, physical or psychological, even where unforeseeable: R v Blaue (1975) (Jehovah's Witness refused a blood transfusion after a stabbing; D still caused her death); R v Hayward (1908) (threats caused the wife to run, aggravating a latent heart condition — no break). Victim's reaction to D's act — must be a proportionate and foreseeable response: R v Roberts (1971) (passenger jumped from a moving car to escape sexual advances — injuries caused by D); R v Williams & Davis (1992) (jury must find the reaction was within the range of responses to be expected — hitchhiker leapt at 30mph). Free, deliberate and informed act of the victim breaks the chain: R v Kennedy (No 2) (2007): supplying heroin to a fully informed adult who freely self-injected was not unlawful act manslaughter. Contrast R v Wallace (2018): whether the victim's suicide after an acid attack broke the chain was a matter for the jury. Quick recall — causation cases But-for: R v White (1910). Substantial and operating: R v Pagett (1983). De minimis: R v Kimsey (1996). Medical: R v Cheshire (1991); R v Malcherek & Steel (1981); exception — R v Jordan (1956). Thin skull: R v Blaue (1975); R v Hayward (1908). Victim's acts: R v Roberts (1971); R v Williams & Davis (1992); R v Kennedy (No 2) (2007); R v Wallace (2018) — suicide. The mens rea is the fault element the offence requires: intention, recklessness, negligence or knowledge. For murder it is intention (to kill or to cause grievous bodily harm) alone. Direct intention. The consequence is D's aim or purpose: R v Mohan (1976): 'a decision to bring about, in so far as it lies within the accused's power, the prohibited consequence, no matter whether the accused desired that consequence'. Motive is irrelevant to liability. Oblique (indirect) intention. Covers consequences D did not aim at but foresaw. The modern authority is R v Woollin (1998): where death or serious injury was a virtual certainty (barring some unforeseen intervention) as a result of D's act and D appreciated that was the case , the jury is not obliged but entitled to find intention. R v Matthews & Alleyne (2003): Woollin lays down a rule of evidence , not substantive law — foresight of a virtual certainty is evidence from which the jury may infer intention. This supersedes the earlier Hyam (1976), Moloney (1985) and Nedrick (1986) probability guidelines. Recklessness — the Cunningham (subjective) test. D is reckless where he knows an unjustifiable risk exists or will exist and takes it anyway: R v Cunningham (1957) (tore a gas meter from the wall; gas partially asphyxiated a sleeping woman). The objective Caldwell (1982) version — risk obvious to the reasonable person — was overruled in R v G and another (2003): two boys aged 11 and 12 set fire to newspapers behind a shop; the House of Lords held it unjust to convict where the risk was not obvious to them . Subjective recklessness now governs the Criminal Damage Act 1971, s.1 and the 'Cunningham crimes' (assault, s.47, s.20). Negligence. An objective failure to meet the standard of the reasonable person. In the general criminal law negligence is a low-grade fault; it matters chiefly for gross negligence manslaughter : R v Adomako (1994): (1) a duty of care to the victim, (2) breach of that duty causing death, and (3) the breach so bad as to be criminal (risk of death obvious or serious). Transferred malice. Intention or recklessness towards one victim transfers to the actual victim of the same kind of offence: R v Latimer (1886) (swung a belt, missed the man, hit a woman). The Supreme Court extended the doctrine in R v Gnango (2011) (mutual gunfight; each shooter's intention transferred). Limit : it cannot transfer between different kinds of offence — R v Pembliton (1874) (threw a stone at people, hit a window; no transfer from assault to criminal damage). Quick recall — the mens rea ladder Direct: R v Mohan (1976) — aim/purpose. Oblique: R v Woollin (1998) — virtual certainty + appreciation; jury may find intent. Evidential gloss: R v Matthews & Alleyne (2003). Recklessness: R v Cunningham (1957); R v G (2003) overruled Caldwell — subjective throughout. Negligence: R v Adomako (1994) — gross negligence manslaughter only. Transferred malice: R v Latimer (1886); R v Gnango (2011); limit — R v Pembliton (1874). Some offences require no mens rea for one or more elements of the actus reus: strict liability . Most are regulatory — food hygiene, licensing, health and safety, transport — and carry modest penalties; strict liability attaches to 'true' crimes only if Parliament says so expressly. The starting point is the presumption of mens rea ( actus non facit reum nisi mens sit rea ). Gammon Ltd v A-G for Hong Kong (1985) : mens rea is presumed unless the statute expressly or by necessary implication rules it out; the presumption of strict liability is stronger where (1) the offence is regulatory rather than a true crime, (2) the statute is concerned with an issue of social concern (public safety, food hygiene), (3) strict liability will further the enforcement of the statute by encouraging greater vigilance , and (4) the penalty is not severe. Presumption of mens rea upheld : Sweet v Parsley (1970) (landlady 'concerned in the management' of premises used for cannabis smoking — knowledge required); B (A Minor) v DPP (1995) (similar presumption for a serious offence involving the age of the victim — later reversed by statute: the Sexual Offences Act 2003 made age largely strict). Strict liability found : Harrow LBC v Shah (2000) (selling a lottery ticket to an under-16; the shopkeeper was convicted despite staff training and notices — the protective purpose displaced mens rea). Absolute liability — no mens rea of any kind, and no defence even where D acts involuntarily: R v Larsonneur (1933); Winzar v Chief Constable of Kent (1983); Pharmaceutical Society of GB v Storkwain (1986) (forged prescriptions); Alphacell Ltd v Woodward (1972) (pollution without knowledge). Arguments for strict liability Arguments against Protects the public in areas of social concern (food, water, licensing, safety) Convicts the blameless (Shah; Storkwain) — offends the principle that liability requires fault Easier enforcement — no need to prove a mental state that is hard to evidence No deterrent effect where the defendant is unaware of the risk Encourages greater vigilance and better systems (Gammon) Blurs the criminal/civil boundary; stigma disproportionate to the penalty Raises the profile of the offence and deters cutting corners R v G restored the fault principle for criminal damage — the trend is back towards mens rea Exam technique. Strict liability is a favourite AQA 25-mark evaluate: anchor the answer on the Gammon presumptions, contrast Sweet v Parsley with Harrow LBC v Shah, deploy R v G as the fault-based critique and Larsonneur/Storkwain as the absolute-liability extreme, and finish with a judgement — strict liability is justified for regulatory offences protecting social welfare, but Parliament should signal it expressly and penalties should stay proportionate. Problem questions (AQA 25-mark; OCR/WJEC 20-mark scenario). Structure every answer the same way: Define the offence elements (AO1) — identify the shape of the actus reus and the mens rea required. Apply element by element (AO2) — conduct, omission or state of affairs; then causation in fact (R v White) then in law (R v Pagett; R v Kimsey); then mens rea in order (R v Mohan; R v Woollin; R v Cunningham; R v G), applying authorities to the facts rather than describing them. Run the counter-cases (AO2/AO3) — omission duties, novus actus candidates (R v Cheshire; R v Jordan; R v Roberts; R v Kennedy), the thin skull rule (R v Blaue) and transferred malice (R v Latimer). Conclude liability per defendant — the mark scheme rewards a definite conclusion with reasons, not 'it depends'. Essay questions (AQA evaluate, 25 marks). On strict liability or oblique intention: state the law (Gammon; Woollin), evaluate fault, certainty and fairness (R v G), give a reform direction, and finish with a reasoned judgement. A* answers quote the Woollin formula precisely and use cases as evidence for the evaluation, never as a bare list.

topics.name: Non-Fatal Offences Against the Person
topics.subject: law
topics.searchText: law Law Non-Fatal Offences Against the Person Define and apply the actus reus and mens rea of assault and battery, citing the Criminal Justice Act 1988, s.39 (AQA 3.2.4; OCR 1.2.3; WJEC/Eduqas Component 1) Set out the elements of s.47 OAPA 1861 (ABH) and apply the R v Roberts and R v Savage; R v Parmenter rules on occasioning and mens rea Distinguish a wound from other injury (R v Eisenhower) and define grievous bodily harm for s.20 (DPP v Smith; R v Saunders; R v Bollom) Apply the s.20 mens rea (R v Mowatt; R v Savage) and contrast it with the specific intent required for s.18 (R v Mohan; R v Woollin) Assess the availability and limits of consent as a defence to non-fatal offences (R v Brown; R v Wilson; R v Barnes; A-G's Reference (No 6 of 1980)) Evaluate the OAPA 1861 and the Law Commission (2015) reform recommendations, including the s.47/s.20 sentencing anomaly Deploy offence ladder and case law accurately in 25-mark problem questions (AQA) and scenario questions (OCR/WJEC/Eduqas) Offence ladder by maximum sentence: assault/battery (6 months, CJA 1988 s.39) < s.47 ABH (5 years) = s.20 wounding/GBH (5 years) < s.18 GBH with intent (life imprisonment) Mens rea never rises above the base offence of assault/battery except for s.18, which requires specific intent R v Ireland; R v Burstow: words (even silence) can be an assault, and psychiatric injury can be ABH and GBH Wound = both layers of skin broken (R v Eisenhower); GBH = really serious harm (DPP v Smith; R v Saunders) R v Savage; R v Parmenter fixed the mens rea of s.47 and s.20: recklessness as to some harm suffices; foreseeing GBH is never required R v Woollin: oblique intention requires virtual certainty plus defendant's appreciation — jury may find intention Law Commission report 361 (2015) recommended replacing the OAPA 1861 with a modern statute graded by culpability — use for AO3 Assault A common-law offence (prosecuted summarily under CJA 1988, s.39): any act, word or gesture causing the victim to apprehend the immediate application of unlawful force. Battery The application of unlawful force to another, however slight; no apprehension is required, and contact generally acceptable in everyday conduct (Collins v Wilcock) is excluded. Actual bodily harm (ABH) Harm calculated to interfere with the victim's health or comfort (R v Miller), including recognised psychiatric injury but not mere emotion (R v Chan-Fook); s.47 OAPA 1861, max 5 years. Occasioning The causation word in s.47: the defendant's assault or battery must factually cause the harm; no foreseeability of the harm is needed (R v Roberts). Wound A break in the continuity of both layers of the skin (R v Eisenhower); internal bleeding, bruises and fractured bones are not wounds. Grievous bodily harm (GBH) Really serious harm (DPP v Smith; R v Saunders), which can be the aggregation of injuries assessed against the victim's age and health (R v Bollom); includes serious psychiatric illness (R v Ireland; R v Burstow). Maliciously In s.20 OAPA 1861: intention or subjective recklessness as to some physical harm, not as to GBH itself (R v Mowatt; R v Savage; R v Parmenter). Inflict The s.20 causation word: held not to require a technical assault — inflicting is the same as causing (R v Ireland; R v Burstow). Direct intention The defendant's aim, purpose or decision to bring about the prohibited consequence (R v Mohan). Oblique intention Where the consequence is a virtual certainty of the defendant's act and the defendant appreciated that virtual certainty, the jury may find intention (R v Woollin). Subjective recklessness The defendant foresees a risk of harm and unreasonably goes on to take it (Cunningham approach, adopted for OAPA offences by R v Savage; R v Parmenter). Psychiatric injury A recognised clinical condition (e.g. depression, anxiety states, PTSD) which can constitute ABH (s.47) or GBH (s.20/s.18); mere emotions such as fear, panic or stress do not qualify (R v Chan-Fook; R v Ireland). Assault is a common-law offence, prosecuted summarily under Criminal Justice Act 1988, s.39 (maximum 6 months' imprisonment and/or a fine): any act, word or gesture by which the defendant intentionally or recklessly causes the victim to apprehend the immediate application of unlawful force . The actus reus needs no contact at all — silent telephone calls causing fear can be an assault: R v Ireland; R v Burstow [1998]. Conditional threats still count: R v Martin (1881) — defendant barred theatre exits and told the crowd to hasten or be hurt. Immediacy is applied flexibly: R v Constanza [1997] — letters and a resentful campaign gave the victim well-founded fear that violence might be used at some time not excluding the immediate future. Words can negate apprehension where they make the threat conditional on a lawful act: Tuberville v Savage (1669). Mens rea is intention or subjective recklessness: in R v Lamb [1967] the victim was shot with a revolver the defendant did not know would fire — no assault (no apprehension) and no unlawful act manslaughter because no unlawful act existed. Battery is the application of unlawful force to another , however slight ( Faulkner v Talbot (1981)); touching a skirt hem without more is too trivial ( R v Thomas (1985)). Force can be indirect: pushing a bar door into a fleeing crowd ( R v Martin (1881)); acid spraying from a tampered petrol nozzle ( DPP v K [1990]); punching a mother causing her to drop her baby ( R v Haystead (2000)). Everyday contact — such as generally guiding a person rather than seizing them — is not unlawful: Collins v Wilcock [1984]. Creating a danger then failing to warn can found liability by omission: R v Santana-Bermudez [2003] — defendant told a searching officer there was nothing in his pockets; she was stabbed by a needle. Exam traps: assault and battery Apprehension, not fear: the victim need only be aware force is imminent, not frightened. Battery requires no apprehension and no direct contact; assault requires no contact and may be by words or silence. Charge practice: where there is injury with a lower mens rea, the CPS charges s.39 assault/battery or s.47 ABH rather than s.20 (CPS charging standards) — use for AO3. Mens rea of both offences: intention or subjective recklessness — see R v Parmenter [1991] for the application. s.47 OAPA 1861 (maximum 5 years): an assault or battery occasioning actual bodily harm . Actus reus: a complete assault or battery plus harm — injury calculated to interfere with the health or comfort of the victim ( R v Miller [1954]); it need not be permanent, and scratches, bruising and transient injuries suffice. Psychiatric injury counts if it is a recognised clinical condition beyond mere emotions: R v Chan-Fook [1994] and R v Ireland; R v Burstow [1998] (depressive illness and anxiety from stalking phone calls). Occasioning requires only factual causation between the assault/battery and the harm — the harm need not be reasonably foreseeable: R v Roberts [1971] — the victim jumped from a moving car to escape the defendant's sexual advances; her injuries were still ABH. Mens rea is only the mens rea of the base assault or battery: R v Savage; R v Parmenter [1992] — the House of Lords held that s.47 requires no mens rea as to the harm itself; recklessness as to some unlawful physical contact suffices ( DPP v Spratt [1990] — pellet-gun spraying near passers-by). Why s.47 matters for AO3 Anomaly : s.47 and s.20 carry the same maximum sentence (5 years), yet s.47 requires only the mens rea of a battery while s.20 requires recklessness as to some harm — the Law Commission (2015) treats this as a principal defect of the OAPA 1861. Causation gap : because occasioning requires no foreseeability, an unforeseeable flight reaction can elevate a battery to a 5-year offence. Consent interplay : for serious consensual activity, s.47 charges are used where s.20 would fail for lack of injury — see R v Wilson [1996] (branding initials; consent available where comparable to tattooing). s.20 OAPA 1861 (maximum 5 years): unlawfully and maliciously wounding or inflicting grievous bodily harm . A wound is a break in the continuity of both layers of the skin: R v Eisenhower [1984] — pellet punctures with internal bleeding were not a wound. GBH means really serious harm ( DPP v Smith [1961]; juries today are directed simply with really serious harm — R v Saunders (1985)). Harm can be cumulative : a series of minor injuries aggregated, assessed in light of the victim's age and health ( R v Bollom [2004]; R v Brown and Stratton [2008]). Serious psychiatric illness can be GBH: R v Ireland; R v Burstow [1998] — inflict is satisfied without a technical assault, and for s.20 inflict means cause. Disease transmission can also found s.20 liability where the victim did not knowingly consent: R v Dica [2004] (HIV). Mens rea of s.20: maliciously means intention or subjective recklessness as to some physical harm — not as to GBH: R v Mowatt [1968]; confirmed in R v Savage; R v Parmenter [1992]. The defendant who foresees only a slight injury is still guilty of s.20 if really serious harm results. s.18 OAPA 1861 (maximum life): unlawfully and maliciously by any means wounding or causing GBH with intent to do GBH, or with intent to resist or prevent lawful apprehension or detention. The mens rea is specific intent : direct intention ( R v Mohan [1976]) or oblique intention — where GBH is a virtual certainty of the act and the defendant appreciated that — the jury may find intention ( R v Woollin [1999]). Subjective recklessness is never enough for s.18: the key distinction from s.20. Note the drafting width: s.18 says by any means (so omissions can suffice), while s.20 says inflict. Offence Key AR point Mens rea Maximum Assault / battery (s.39 CJA 1988) Apprehension / unlawful force Intention or subjective recklessness 6 months s.47 ABH Assault or battery occasioning ABH Base offence mens rea only (Roberts; Savage) 5 years s.20 wounding/GBH Wound (Eisenhower) or inflict GBH (Burstow) Intention or recklessness as to some harm (Mowatt; Savage) 5 years s.18 GBH with intent Wound or cause GBH by any means Specific intent only (Mohan; Woollin) Life Consent is no answer where the conduct causes actual bodily harm or worse , except in recognised categories: properly conducted games and sports, horseplay, surgery, tattooing, ear-piercing, and lawful dangerous displays. The baseline rule: R v Brown [1994] — consensual sadomasochistic activities causing injuries were not protected; consent is unavailable for s.47/s.20 assaults beyond the exceptions. Public policy condemns private fights: A-G's Reference (No 6 of 1980) [1981] — a planned fist fight is unlawful, though incidental injury in a spontaneous scuffle is treated differently ( R v Barnes [2004] — sporting consent covers conduct within the rules and what a reasonable player would expect, but not criminal violence off the ball). R v Wilson [1996] allowed a consent defence for branding initials on a wife — activity analogous to tattooing, showing the court's willingness to expand exceptions; R v Richardson and Irwin [1999] allowed consent to dangerous horseplay (dangling a student from a balcony) and took account of what sober participants would have appreciated. Accidental, truly unforeseeable harm during consensual activity may leave no unlawful act: R v Slingsby [1995]; trivial harm with consent is outside the OAPA altogether: R v Donovan [1934]. Using consent for marks Always test consent after establishing the offence — examiners reward order. Link to law reform: the Law Commission (2015) recommended clarifying which consensual activities should remain criminal. Contrast criminal consent limits with civil volenti (see the negligence topic) — knowledge must be real and free in tort too. The non-fatal offences form a ladder matched to culpability and harm : battery/assault (6 months) to s.47/s.20 (5 years) to s.18 (life). The ladder has long been criticised: language — occasioning, maliciously, inflict and grievous are archaic and inconsistently construed; structure — s.47 carries the same maximum as s.20 despite a lower mens rea; wounding — a technical skin rule produces odd results ( R v Eisenhower : internal bleeding worse than a cut is not a wound). The Law Commission report 361 (2015), Reform of Offences Against the Person Act 1861 , recommended a new statute with offences of intentional serious injury, reckless serious injury and intentional/reckless injury, abolishing the distinctions between wounding and other harm; successive governments have not enacted it — a strong AO3 point on law-making inaction. CPS charging standards mitigate some inconsistency by charging the offence that matches culpability. Exam technique. For each suspect act: (1) identify the possible offence from the ladder; (2) work upwards — assault/battery, then s.47, then s.20, then s.18; (3) define AR and MR with one authority per element; (4) apply to facts, including causation; (5) consider consent; (6) conclude on the most likely charge. In evaluation paragraphs, deploy the s.47/s.20 anomaly, the Eisenhower wound rule, Burstow's psychologisation of harm, and the Law Commission recommendations.

topics.name: Tort: Negligence and Occupiers' Liability
topics.subject: law
topics.searchText: law Law Tort: Negligence and Occupiers' Liability Apply the Caparo three-part test for a duty of care and explain the neighbour principle (Donoghue v Stevenson) (AQA 3.3.2; OCR 2.2.2; WJEC/Eduqas Component 2) Assess duty of care for omissions and public bodies, including Robinson v Chief Constable of West Yorkshire, Hill, Michael and Poole Borough Council Evaluate breach against the standard of care, including Bolam v Friern Hospital Management Committee, Bolitho, Nettleship v Weston and Mullin v Richards Apply factual causation (but-for test; material contribution), legal causation, remoteness (The Wagon Mound (No 1); Hughes v Lord Advocate) and intervening acts Distinguish primary and secondary victims for psychiatric injury (Page v Smith; Alcock; White) and the recoverability of pure economic loss (Murphy v Brentwood; Spring v Guardian Assurance) State and apply the common duty of care under the Occupiers' Liability Act 1957 and the s.1(3) conditions of the 1984 Act for trespassers Apply civil defences — volenti non fit injuria, contributory negligence and illegality — with Froom v Butcher, Pitts v Hunt and Revill v Newbery Deploy the structure of a negligence problem answer in 25-mark AQA and 20-mark OCR/WJEC scenario questions Duty of care: Caparo three-part test (foreseeability, proximity, fair/just/reasonable) — but Robinson v Chief Constable of West Yorkshire [2018] reasserted ordinary principles for positive acts, overruling Hill Omissions are generally not actionable (Smith v Littlewoods; Stovin v Wise), even for public bodies (Michael v Chief Constable of South Wales; Poole Borough Council) Breach is fact-sensitive: probability (Bolton v Stone), gravity (Paris v Stepney), precautions vs utility (Latimer v AEC); professions use Bolam with the Bolitho logical caveat; learners and children: Nettleship v Weston; Mullin v Richards Causation: but-for (Barnett); material contribution (Bonnington Castings v Wardlaw); multiple sufficient causes (Fairchild; Barker v Corus); remoteness = foreseeable kind of harm (Wagon Mound; Hughes v Lord Advocate; Jolley v Sutton) Psychiatric injury: primary victims (Page v Smith) vs secondary victims restricted by Alcock; rescuers must satisfy the primary victim rules (White v Chief Constable; contrast Chadwick) Pure economic loss is irrecoverable except where the defendant assumed responsibility, e.g. negligent misstatement (Hedley Byrne; Spring v Guardian Assurance) and some solicitor cases (Ross v Caunters) OLA 1957: visitors, common duty of care, special rules for children (s.2(3)(a)), workers (s.2(3)(b)), warnings (s.2(4)(a)) and independent contractors (s.2(4)(b)) OLA 1984: trespassers protected only where the s.1(3) conditions are met; Tomlinson and Keown show courts refusing duties where the risk arises from the claimant's own activity Defences: volenti is complete but rarely succeeds; contributory negligence reduces damages by a percentage (Froom v Butcher); illegality may bar or reduce (Pitts v Hunt; Revill v Newbery) Duty of care A legal obligation to take reasonable care not to cause foreseeable harm to a neighbour; tested under Caparo Industries plc v Dickman — foreseeability, proximity, fair, just and reasonable. Neighbour principle Donoghue v Stevenson: you must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure your neighbour — persons closely and directly affected by your act. Breach of duty Falling below the standard of the reasonable person: omission to do what a reasonable person would do, or doing what a reasonable person would not (Blyth v Birmingham Waterworks). Causation in fact The but-for test: the damage would not have occurred but for the defendant's breach (Barnett v Chelsea and Kensington Hospital); multiple sufficient causes use the Fairchild exception. Causation in law The breach must be an operative and substantial cause of harm — an intervening act (novus actus interveniens) may break the chain where it is unforeseeable and independent. Remoteness Damage must be of a reasonably foreseeable kind, though the precise manner or extent need not be (The Wagon Mound (No 1); Hughes v Lord Advocate; Jolley v Sutton). Primary victim A person within the zone of physical danger who suffers psychiatric injury; recoverable if physical injury was foreseeable (Page v Smith). Secondary victim A person who suffers psychiatric injury witnessing or hearing of injury to another; recovery restricted by Alcock control mechanisms — ties of love and affection, proximity, perception, sudden shock. Pure economic loss Financial loss unconnected with physical injury or property damage (e.g. a defective product's value, negligent misstatement); generally irrecoverable (Murphy v Brentwood), except negligent misstatement with assumption of responsibility (Hedley Byrne v Heller). Occupier A person with sufficient control over premises (Wheat v Lacon); there may be more than one occupier, each liable for the areas they control. Common duty of care Occupiers' Liability Act 1957, s.2(2): the duty to take such care as in all the circumstances is reasonable to see that visitors are reasonably safe in using the premises for the purposes they are invited or permitted. Volenti non fit injuria A complete defence where the claimant freely and knowingly consented to the risk; knowledge of risk alone is insufficient (ICI Ltd v Shatwell). Contributory negligence Law Reform (Contributory Negligence) Act 1945: where the claimant partly caused their own damage, damages are reduced by the court's assessment of their share of responsibility (Froom v Butcher). Res ipsa loquitur The thing speaks for itself: where the accident is of a kind that ordinarily does not occur without negligence and the defendant controlled the instrumentality, the burden shifts to the defendant to explain. Negligence requires a duty of care , breach and damage caused by the breach, not too remote. The modern starting point is the neighbour principle : Donoghue v Stevenson [1932] — take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure persons closely and directly affected. Caparo Industries plc v Dickman [1990] replaced it with a three-part test : harm of a kind reasonably foreseeable; a relationship of proximity or neighbourhood; and that imposing the duty is fair, just and reasonable. Anns v Merton London Borough Council [1978] had used a looser two-stage test, but the House of Lords retreated from it: Murphy v Brentwood District Council [1991] overruled Anns on defective buildings. Public bodies and omissions. The general rule: there is no liability for omissions — Smith v Littlewoods Organisation [1987]; a highway authority could not be liable merely for failing to act: Stovin v Wise [1996]; Gorringe v Calderdale Metropolitan Borough Council [2004]. Hill v Chief Constable of West Yorkshire [1989] had exempted the police from duties for investigative failures; that immunity was overruled by Robinson v Chief Constable of West Yorkshire [2018] — the Supreme Court held the ordinary principles of negligence apply, and a duty was owed where an officer's positive act (a clumsy arrest) injured a passer-by. But Michael v Chief Constable of South Wales [2015] shows the limits: failing to act on a 999 call created no duty; and R (PNB) v Poole Borough Council [2019] refused duties for child-protection failures absent an assumption of responsibility. For the exam: apply Caparo first; use Robinson for positive acts; use Michael/Poole to refuse omissions-based duties. Exam traps: duty of care Robinson did not make police always liable — it removed a blanket immunity; the Caparo test still governs. Omission claims can succeed where there is control or assumption of responsibility (Barrett v Enfield LBC [2001] — care of a child in council care). Rescuers: a duty is owed to the rescuer foreseeably endangered (Chadwick v British Railways Board [1967]). Breach asks whether the defendant fell below the standard of care : Blyth v Birmingham Waterworks (1856) — negligence is doing something a reasonable person would not do, or omitting something a reasonable person would do. The standard is adjusted by who the defendant is: for professions , the defendant meets the standard by acting in accordance with a responsible body of professional practice: Bolam v Friern Hospital Management Committee [1957], subject to the Bolitho caveat: Bolitho v City and Hackney Health Authority [1998] — the practice must withstand logical analysis. Learners are judged against the competent adult driver, not other learners: Nettleship v Weston [1971]. Children are judged against comparable children: Mullin v Richards [1998] (fencing with plastic rulers). The standard is also fact-sensitive through the risk factors : probability — a very small risk need not be eliminated: Bolton v Stone [1951] (cricket ball over a high fence); gravity — serious potential harm demands more: Paris v Stepney Borough Council [1951] (goggles for a one-eyed welder); precautions against utility — only reasonable precautions are required: Latimer v AEC [1953]. Where the accident is of a kind that ordinarily does not happen without negligence and the defendant had control, res ipsa loquitur shifts the evidential burden to the defendant. Factual causation uses the but-for test: Barnett v Chelsea and Kensington Hospital [1969] — the patient would have died regardless of the hospital's failure, so no causation; the breach must also be a foreseeable cause: Cork v Kirby MacLean [1952]. Where multiple causes each contributed, the claimant need only show a material contribution : Bonnington Castings v Wardlaw [1956] (pneumoconiosis dust). Where science cannot prove which of several exposures caused the disease, the Fairchild exception applies: Fairchild v Glenhaven Funeral Services [2002]; Barker v Corus [2006] — liability is shared among the culpable exposures. Legal causation and remoteness. Damage is recoverable only if it is of a reasonably foreseeable kind: The Wagon Mound (No 1) [1961] — oil spill fouling a dock; fire damage unforeseeable. But the manner of the harm need not be foreseeable: Hughes v Lord Advocate [1963] (paraffin lamp in a manhole); Jolley v Sutton London Borough Council [2000] (injuring a boat; the kind of harm was foreseeable even if the mechanism was not). Intervening acts break the chain only where they are unforeseeable and independent: medical negligence generally does not break it: Robinson v Post Office [1977] — the employer who caused the fracture remained liable for the doctor's misdiagnosis; a claimant's own unreasonable conduct may, unless the reaction was within the range of foreseeable responses. Psychiatric injury is recoverable only as a recognised clinical condition. Primary victims — those within the zone of physical danger — recover if some physical injury was foreseeable: Page v Smith [1996]. Secondary victims — witnesses and those who hear of harm — face the Alcock control mechanisms : Alcock v Chief Constable of South Yorkshire [1992]: close ties of love and affection (presumed only for spouses, parents, children); closeness in time and space to the accident or its immediate aftermath; perception through their own unaided senses; and a sudden shocking event. Rescuers must satisfy the primary victim rules to recover: White v Chief Constable of South Yorkshire [1999] — police officers who suffered psychological injury could not recover as secondary victims; contrast Chadwick v British Railways Board [1967], where the rescuer within the danger zone recovered. Pure economic loss — financial loss unconnected with personal injury or property damage — is generally irrecoverable to avoid indeterminate liability: Murphy v Brentwood District Council [1991] (the cost of replacing defective houses). The exception is negligent misstatement with assumption of responsibility: Hedley Byrne and Co Ltd v Heller and Partners Ltd [1964] (with a disclaimer negating the duty there); Spring v Guardian Assurance plc [1995] — a duty of care is owed in giving references. Some special relationships allow recovery: Ross v Caunters [1980] — a solicitor careless in drafting a will owed a duty to the intended beneficiary. Consequential economic loss flowing from physical injury or property damage is always recoverable. Exam traps: psychiatric injury and economic loss Always classify the claimant first: primary or secondary victim, or economic loss — the rules differ completely. Alcock categories are strict: a friend outside ties of love and affection rarely recovers (contrast spouses and parents). For AO3, criticise the arbitrary divide: pure economic loss often matters more to a claimant than minor personal injury. Occupiers' Liability Act 1957 governs lawful visitors (invitees, licensees, those with contractual permission, those with a right of entry by statute). An occupier is the person with sufficient control: Wheat v Lacon and Co Ltd [1966] — more than one occupier is possible. Section 2(2) imposes the common duty of care : such care as in all the circumstances is reasonable to see that visitors are reasonably safe for the purpose of their visit. Children (s.2(3)(a)): the occupier must be prepared for children to be less careful than adults; a warning must be effective for a child too young to read: Laverton v Kiapasha (1967). Workers (s.2(3)(b)): the occupier may expect workmen to guard against risks incident to their trade: General Cleaning Contractors v Christmas [1953]. Warnings (s.2(4)(a)) discharge the duty only if they enable the visitor to be reasonably safe: Roles v Nathan [1963] (chimney sweep fumes). Independent contractors (s.2(4)(b)): the occupier is liable if the contractor was careless, or the work was improper, or the occupier failed to check: Haseldine v Daw [1941] (negligently maintained lift); Ogwo v Taylor [1988] (firefighter injured; occupier liable); but not where the main contractor directed an unsafe system: Ferguson v Welsh [1988]. Occupiers' Liability Act 1984 protects trespassers . A duty arises only if the s.1(3) conditions are met: the occupier is aware of the danger or has reasonable grounds to believe it exists; knows or has reasonable grounds to believe the person is, or may come, in the vicinity; and the risk is one against which he may reasonably be expected to offer some protection. This codified the duty recognised in British Railways Board v Herrington [1972]. Section 1(5) excludes risks the trespasser willingly accepts. The courts read the Act narrowly where the risk arises from the claimant's own activity : Tomlinson v Congleton Borough Council [2003] (no duty for diving into a lake); Keown v Coventry Healthcare NHS Trust [2006] (climbing a drainpipe); Ratcliff v McConnell [1999] (diving into an unlit pool at night after drinking); Donoghue v Folkestone Properties [2003] (seasonal risk). Where the duty applies, breaches still sound in damages — but reduced: Revill v Newbery [1996] (76-year-old with a gun trap; trespasser recovered, damages cut by 75% for contributory negligence). Defences. Volenti non fit injuria is a complete defence but requires free and knowing consent to the risk, not mere knowledge: ICI Ltd v Shatwell [1965]; spectators accept inherent risks ( Hall v Brooklands Auto Racing Club [1933]); rescuers do not consent: Haynes v Harwood [1935]. Contributory negligence reduces damages by the claimant's share of responsibility (Law Reform (Contributory Negligence) Act 1945): Froom v Butcher [1976] — 25% where a seatbelt would have prevented injury, 50% where it would have made a substantial difference; Sayers v Harlow Urban District Council [1958] — 20% split. Illegality (ex turpi causa) may bar claims arising from the claimant's own crime: Pitts v Hunt [1991] (pillion passenger on a stolen bike encouraging reckless riding); but Revill v Newbery shows it usually reduces rather than bars in modern law.
