Analyse and evaluate metaethical arguments to form reasoned judgements in 25-mark essays (AO2, 'arguing with intent'). Two independent axes: cognitivism (moral judgements truth-apt) vs non-cognitivism (not truth-apt); realism (mind-independent moral facts) vs anti-realism (none). Every theory sits on both. Moral principles may originate in reason (Moore, Ross), emotion/attitudes (Ayer) or society (Mackie: 'inventing' right and wrong). Naturalism: good = natural property — Bentham: pleasure; naturalist virtue ethics: flourishing. Attacked by Moore's open question argument and the naturalistic fallacy. Non-naturalism (Moore, Ross): good is simple, non-natural, known by intuition; Ross adds plural, self-evident prima facie duties. Attacked by Hume's fork, the is-ought gap, the motivation argument and Mackie's queerness. Error theory (Mackie): judgements aim at objective truth but all fail — arguments from relativity and queerness; nihilism charge. Emotivism (boo/hurrah, persuasion) and prescriptivism (universalisable prescriptions) deny truth-aptness; attacked via embedded contexts, disagreement, the fanatic and moral progress. Cognitivism The view that moral judgements express beliefs, state propositions and are truth-apt: 'murder is wrong' is true or false and can be known. Shared by naturalism, non-naturalism and (in modified form) error theory. Non-cognitivism The view that moral judgements express non-cognitive mental states (emotions, prescriptions) and state nothing, so they are not truth-apt. Emotivism and prescriptivism are non-cognitivist theories. Moral realism There are mind-independent moral properties or facts: some moral judgements are true or false independently of what anyone thinks, feels or prescribes. Moral anti-realism There are no mind-independent moral properties or facts — either because moral judgements were never in the business of stating facts (emotivism, prescriptivism) or because, although they aim at objective truth, they systematically fail (error theory). Moral naturalism Cognitivist realism: moral properties are natural properties, reducible to or identical with properties studied by the sciences — e.g. naturalist utilitarianism (Bentham: good = pleasure, right = maximising it) and naturalist virtue ethics (good = traits enabling human flourishing). Open question argument Moore (Principia Ethica, 1903): for any proposed natural property N, the question 'but is N good?' remains open and significant, not self-answering like 'are bachelors unmarried?'; so good is not identical with any natural property — an argument against all reductive metaethical theories. Is-ought gap Hume: no 'ought' follows validly from premises stating only 'is' — a moral conclusion requires a moral premise, so sets of pure facts never entail obligations. Error theory Mackie (Ethics: Inventing Right and Wrong, 1977): moral judgements purport to state objective, mind-independent facts, but there are no objective values, so every positive moral judgement is false; values are projected, not discovered. Emotivism Ayer: moral judgements fail the verification principle (neither analytic nor empirically verifiable), so they are not truth-apt statements but expressions of emotion — 'stealing is wrong' amounts to 'stealing — boo!' (the boo/hurrah theory); Stevenson adds emotive meaning and a persuasive function. Prescriptivism Hare (The Language of Morals, 1952): moral judgements are universalisable prescriptions — imperatives ('do this!') that commit the speaker to prescribing the same for any relevantly similar situation, including their own. Second-order questions. First-order ethics asks 'Is abortion wrong?'; metaethics (AQA 7172 Spec 3.2.3) asks what such a judgement itself is: does it state a fact and aim at truth, or express an attitude and issue a command? Two independent axes organise the theories; a strong answer locates each theory on both. Axis 1 — cognitivism vs non-cognitivism. Cognitivism : moral judgements express beliefs , assert propositions and are truth-apt — 'murder is wrong' is true or false and can be known. Non-cognitivism : moral judgements express non-cognitive states (emotions, prescriptions); they state nothing and are not truth-apt . Both camps agree moral sentences look declarative; the debate is what the utterance does . Axis 2 — realism vs anti-realism. Moral realism : there are mind-independent moral properties or facts, so some moral judgements are objectively true. Moral anti-realism : there are none — either because moral judgements were never in the truth business (emotivism, prescriptivism) or because, though they aim at truth, they systematically fail (error theory). Origins of moral principles. The spec opens 3.2.3 with this question: principles may originate in reason (self-evident truths grasped a priori — Moore, Ross), in emotion and attitudes (approval projected onto the world — Ayer, Mackie) or in society (invented conventions — Mackie's Ethics: Inventing Right and Wrong ). The answer fixes whether moral judgements can be true at all. Cross-classification. The axes combine into a diagnostic grid: Cognitivist (truth-apt) Non-cognitivist (not truth-apt) Realist — mind-independent moral facts Moral naturalism (Bentham; naturalist virtue ethics); non-naturalism / intuitionism (Moore, Ross) — Anti-realist — no mind-independent moral facts Error theory (Mackie) Emotivism (Ayer, Stevenson); prescriptivism (Hare) Examiner-flagged confusions (click to expand) Mackie is not a non-cognitivist: error theory keeps the truth-aim and says it fails. Non-cognitivism is not anti-realism: they answer different questions — semantics vs metaphysics. Moral naturalism. Good, bad, right and wrong are natural properties : reducible to, or identical with, properties studied by the sciences. Two spec-favoured versions. (1) Naturalist utilitarianism (Bentham) : 'good' means pleasure, 'right' means maximising it — moral facts are natural facts about pleasure and pain, discoverable and countable like any other facts (the felicific calculus). (2) Naturalist virtue ethics (Aristotle; Foot): 'good' means what enables a living thing to flourish as the kind of thing it is — good traits are those a well-developed member of the species displays, as good roots draw water. Attractions: it explains moral objectivity (moral claims true or false like scientific ones), moral knowledge (observation of pleasure and flourishing — no special faculty) and moral motivation (natural desires move us). Moore's open question argument. Principia Ethica (1903): 'good' is simple and unanalysable — like 'yellow', it can only be pointed at, not defined. Any proposed natural definition N leaves ' but is N good? ' open : significant, substantive, not self-answering. 'Is pleasure good?' is a genuine question (cruel pleasures seem bad); 'is a bachelor unmarried?' is closed. If good meant pleasure, 'pleasure is good' would be as trivial as 'pleasure is pleasure' — so good is not identical with any natural property. The argument targets all reductive metaethical theories — Bentham's, Foot's, any reduction. Defining good in natural terms is the naturalistic fallacy : deriving value from fact. Critiques. (1) The argument begs the question : the question is open only on the assumption that good is unanalysable — what the naturalist denies. (2) Synthetic identities are open before science closes them: 'is water H2O?' was once a good question, yet water is H2O — natural properties can be discovered , so openness is compatible with identity. (3) Moore's own analysis ('that which we desire to desire') fares no better — the argument proves too much, undermining every definition including his. (4) At most it shows that 'good' and N differ in meaning , not in reference — and the fallacy charge needs the latter. Moore's non-naturalism (intuitionism). If good is simple and unanalysable yet we make true moral judgements, moral properties must be non-natural : simple properties of the world, reducible to no natural property and not studied by science, known by intuition — direct, self-evident, a priori grasping, like seeing that 2+2=4. Ross extends the view: we intuit plural prima facie duties (fidelity, reparation, gratitude, justice, beneficence, non-maleficence, self-improvement), each holding 'unless overridden'; no formula resolves conflicts — judgement decides which duty is most stringent here. Critiques: non-natural properties are metaphysically queer (Mackie, below); a shared faculty of intuition sits badly with persistent disagreement (abortion, capital punishment); intuitions track upbringing, not truth — slavery once seemed 'self-evidently' acceptable; and 'self-evident to whom?' risks subjectivism about the verdicts. Hume's fork and the is-ought gap. Hume's fork (Spec 3.1.3, redeployed): substantive knowledge is either relations of ideas (a priori, analytic, necessary) or matters of fact (a posteriori, contingent). Moral judgements are neither: denying 'murder is wrong' involves no contradiction, yet no wrongness is observable in the act. In the Treatise (Book III, Part 1) Hume notes that writers move from 'is' to 'ought' without explanation: no ought from is — a moral conclusion requires a moral premise, so pure facts never entail obligations. Significance: the naturalist can add a value premise ('pleasure is good'), but then naturalism does not derive value from nature — it presupposes it. Hume's motivation argument. Beliefs are representational and reason alone is inert : 'reason is, and ought only to be, the slave of the passions' — belief cannot by itself move us. But moral judgements are reliably motivating : judging 'I ought to repay the debt' characteristically issues in repayment. So moral judgements are not beliefs — beliefs alone could not motivate us; they involve non-cognitive desire: the classic argument for non-cognitivism. Cognitivist responses: (1) Externalism : motivation needs belief plus desire, and Hume shows only that belief alone is insufficient — the desire can be independent of the belief, present in the normally-constituted and absent in the amoralist who judges 'torturing the child is wrong' and feels nothing; (2) motivational power is no test of truth — we can be moved by false judgements; (3) desire-driven action can be irrational or immoral, so being motivating is no mark of genuine moral judgement. Mackie's error theory. Ordinary moral thought presupposes objective values : categorical, universally binding 'to-be-pursuedness' woven into the fabric of the world. Mackie ( Ethics: Inventing Right and Wrong , 1977): that presupposition is an error — moral judgements aim at objective truth but systematically fail , so every positive moral judgement is false. His positive story is projectivism : we project our desires and attitudes onto the world, as colour-perception projects redness onto the tomato. The nihilism charge: if all positive judgements are false, nothing is morally right or wrong — moral practice looks pointless. Responses: error theory concerns truth , not meaning — moral language still makes sense and attitudes are untouched; and Mackie's title signals the constructive turn: morality should be invented and used as an agreed, useful convention. Counter: nobody can live the theory — deliberating, blaming and promising presuppose that 'wrong' sometimes applies; 'morality as invention' re-describes rather than saves morality. Argument from relativity. Moral codes vary radically and persistently — monogamy, slavery, caste, abortion — and the variation tracks different ways of life , not perceptual conditions. The best explanation of scientific disagreement is misperception of objective facts (hence convergence); the best explanation of moral disagreement is that people approve differently because they live differently ; so objective values are a poor hypothesis. Responses: much moral disagreement is about facts (does the foetus feel pain?); convergence on core prohibitions (murder, betrayal of trust) is real; and persistent disagreement in frontier science has never licensed anti-realism about science. Argument from queerness. Objective values would be metaphysically queer : 'qualities or relations of a very strange sort, utterly different from anything else in the universe', carrying intrinsic to-be-pursuedness — a 'should' built into the world as no natural property is. And epistemologically queer : knowing them would require a special faculty of moral intuition unlike perception, memory or reasoning. Parsimony says they do not exist. Responses: we already accept strange features — consciousness, intentionality — so intrinsically normative properties are less isolated than Mackie suggests; and Moore and Ross accept the faculty, so for them nothing is queer to explain away. Emotivism (Ayer, Stevenson). Ayer ( Language, Truth and Logic , 1946) applies the verification principle : a statement is cognitively meaningful only if analytic or empirically verifiable. Moral judgements are neither — no observation verifies 'murder is wrong' — so they assert nothing and function to express emotions and arouse them: the boo/hurrah theory — 'Stealing is wrong' amounts to 'Stealing — boo!'. Stevenson ( Ethics and Language , 1944) refines this: moral terms carry emotive meaning and a persuasive function — they work to redirect the hearer's attitudes ; and moral reasoning is possible: we cite empirical beliefs as reasons to change attitudes — persuasion by reasons, not proof. Critiques: (1) the embedded-context problem (Frege–Geach): in 'If stealing is wrong, getting your little brother to steal is wrong', the unasserted antecedent expresses no emotion, yet the argument is plainly valid — unasserted moral claims must retain truth-apt meaning ; (2) the disagreement critique : 'Capital punishment is wrong' vs 'Capital punishment is justified' presents itself as genuine contradiction backed by reasons — not two incompatible cheers; (3) the verification principle is self-refuting — itself neither analytic nor verifiable. Prescriptivism (Hare). Hare ( The Language of Morals , 1952): moral judgements are universalisable prescriptions : their meaning is practical — to command and guide action ('do this!') — and their logic is universalisability : whoever prescribes 'ought' for one situation is committed to the same prescription for any relevantly similar situation , including one in which they are the victim. Universalisability makes moral reasoning genuine (prescriptions must be backed by relevant similarities and evidence) and rules out special pleading . Critiques: (1) prescriptions are not truth-apt either, so the embedded-context and disagreement problems return; (2) the fanatic objection: a racist can consistently universalise 'no equal treatment for them' — Hare must insist the fanatic has failed to imagine himself in the victim's position, but universalisability alone does not force that; (3) moral judgements are statements that report , not imperatives that order — 'murder is wrong' can be embedded in arguments and said idly, as commands cannot; (4) moral progress : if judgements only express attitudes, the shift from approval of slavery to its condemnation is a change of fashion, not the discovery of a truth — yet 'progress' is how we describe it.

topics.name: Metaphysics of God: Divine Attributes, Arguments and Religious Language
topics.subject: philosophy
topics.searchText: philosophy Philosophy Metaphysics of God: Divine Attributes, Arguments and Religious Language Explain and evaluate the definitions of God as omnipotent, eternal and omniscient, including the paradox of the stone, Descartes vs Aquinas/Kenny, and Boethius vs Swinburne on eternality (Spec 3.3.1). Explain and evaluate the ontological argument — Anselm (Proslogion 2 and 3), Descartes and Malcolm — with Gaunilo's perfect-island reply and Kant's 'existence is not a predicate' (Spec 3.3.2). Explain and evaluate the teleological argument — Paley's watch, Swinburne's regularity — with Hume's critiques and Darwin's theory of evolution (Spec 3.3.2). Explain and evaluate the cosmological argument — Aquinas' Three Ways, the Kalam argument, Leibniz's principle of sufficient reason — with Hume's and Russell's critiques (Spec 3.3.2). Explain and evaluate the logical problem of evil (Mackie's inconsistent triad, Plantinga's free will defence) and the evidential problem (Rowe's fawn, Hick's vale of soul-making) (Spec 3.3.3). Explain and evaluate religious experience (James, Swinburne's credulity and testimony, Flew's verification challenge) and religious language (via negativa, Aquinas' analogy, Ayer, Hare, Hick) (Specs 3.3.4–3.3.5). Use AQA command words correctly: pure AO1 explanation on 3/5/12-mark questions; 'arguing with intent' and balanced evaluation only on 25-mark essays. Omnipotence (Aquinas/Kenny): every power it is logically possible to have — the stone task is self-contradictory, not a genuine limit; Descartes: God can do the logically impossible, having created the eternal truths. Boethius: God is timeless — 'the whole, simultaneous and perfect possession of unending life'; foreknowledge becomes timeless seeing, imposing only conditional necessity on free acts. Ontological (Anselm Proslogion 2/3, Descartes, Malcolm) vs Kant: existence is not a real predicate (100 thalers) — the crucial debate is whether necessary existence escapes Kant. Cosmological: Aquinas' Three Ways (per se regress), Kalam (no actual infinities), Leibniz (sufficient reason); Hume (fallacy of composition) and Russell ('the universe is just there, and that's all'). Evil: Mackie's triad answered by Plantinga (free will defence + transworld depravity); Rowe's fawn answered by theodicy (Hick) or sceptical theism. Flew's falsification challenge answered by Hare's bliks and Hick's eschatological verification. Paradox of the stone Can an omnipotent God create a stone too heavy for God to lift? If yes, God cannot lift it; if no, God cannot create it — either way a limitation. Aquinas/Kenny: the task is self-contradictory, so not genuinely possible and no limit on power. Boethius' eternity God's eternity is 'the whole, simultaneous and perfect possession of unending life' (Consolation V) — God is timeless, outside time, beholding past, present and future in a single eternal present. Everlasting God Swinburne/Wolterstorff: God is not timeless but everlasting — existing at every moment of time, knowing at each time everything it is then logically possible to know (including past and present, but not future free choices). That than which nothing greater can be conceived Anselm's definition of God (Proslogion 2) — even the fool understands it; since existing in reality is greater than existing in the understanding alone, God must exist in reality as well. Necessary existence Existence that cannot be lacked without incoherence — that which cannot be conceived of as non-existent (Anselm, Proslogion 3). Malcolm: necessary existence cannot be contingent, so God's existence is either impossible or necessary. Existence is not a predicate Kant's critique: 'is' adds no property to a concept, it only asserts that the concept is instantiated (100 real thalers and 100 imagined thalers share one concept) — so defining God as having existence, or counting existence among the perfections, is illegitimate. Principle of sufficient reason Leibniz: everything has a sufficient reason for why it is so and not otherwise; the reason for a contingent thing lies outside it, so the whole series of contingent things requires a sufficient reason outside itself — a necessary being. Per se ordered causal series Aquinas: a series where each member has no independent causal power but only derivatively (hand–stick–stone). Such a series cannot be infinite without a first member; this grounds the First and Second Ways, as opposed to a merely temporal (per accidens) series. Inconsistent triad Mackie ('Evil and Omnipotence'): (1) God is omnipotent, (2) God is wholly good, (3) evil exists — these cannot all be true together, since a wholly good being eliminates evil as far as it can and an omnipotent being can eliminate it entirely. Free will defence / transworld depravity Plantinga: a defence (showing God and evil are logically consistent), not a theodicy. Transworld depravity: it is possible that every creaturely essence goes wrong in at least one action in any world God could actualise, so God cannot create significantly free creatures who never sin. Vale of soul-making Hick (Evil and the God of Love): evil is instrumental — a lawlike world at 'epistemic distance' from God is the environment in which genuinely free persons develop virtues (courage, compassion), with universal salvation ultimately remedying suffering. Principles of credulity and testimony Swinburne: credulity — if it seems to S that X is present, then probably X is present, absent special considerations (known illusions, unreliable witness); testimony — others' reports of their experiences are probably accurate. Religious experience is therefore prima facie evidence of God. Omnipotence and the paradox of the stone. Can an omnipotent God create a stone too heavy for God to lift? Either answer shows a limit: if yes, God cannot lift it; if no, God cannot create it. Aquinas/Kenny: omnipotence is having every power it is logically possible to have — 'a stone an omnipotent being cannot lift' is self-contradictory, not a genuine task, so no limitation (Kenny: God has 'every power which it is logically possible to possess'). Descartes: God can do the logically impossible — God freely created the eternal truths (2+2=4) and could have made them otherwise, so logic does not bind God. Critique: then claims about God cease to be coherent assertions, and the paradox re-runs (can God make himself non-omnipotent?) with no principled answer; for AQA, Aquinas/Kenny is the mainstream line, Descartes the extreme. Eternality: outside time or everlasting? Boethius (Consolation, Book V): God's eternity is 'the whole, simultaneous and perfect possession of unending life' — God is timeless , beholding all times in one eternal present. Swinburne/Wolterstorff: God is everlasting — existing at every moment of time. Against timelessness: a timeless God cannot know tensed truths ('it is now raining'), act at a moment, respond to prayer or relate personally — not the God of worship (Kretzmann, Wolterstorff). Against everlastingness: a God in time changes (learns) as events occur — change implying imperfection — and knows at each time only what is then knowable. Omniscience and free will. Kenny-style definition: God knows everything it is logically possible to know. The problem: if God infallibly knows I will choose tea tomorrow, I cannot do otherwise — not free; if I am free, God lacked the knowledge — not omniscient. Boethius' solution: no fore -knowledge — from outside time God sees my free choice occurring, as I see a friend walking now; and God's seeing does not make it happen. Necessity is conditional , not absolute: if God sees me walk, then I walk — fixing nothing, just as your watching me walk now does not compel me. Response: this trades on timeless knowledge with the problems above; the everlasting alternative (Swinburne) lets God lack knowledge of future free choices — not yet there to be known — but a God who learns is not the immutable, perfect being of classical theism. Either solution buys compatibility with freedom at a cost. Ontological (a priori). Anselm (Proslogion 2): (1) even the fool understands ' that than which nothing greater can be conceived '; (2) it exists in the understanding; (3) existing in reality is greater; (4) if God existed only in the mind, a greater being — God in reality — could be conceived: contradiction; (5) so God exists in reality. Proslogion 3: God cannot be conceived not to exist — necessary existence is greater than contingent. Gaunilo: the same logic 'proves' a most perfect island. Anselm's reply: the form works only where the definition is coherent — for islands a greater is always conceivable; the status is God's alone. Descartes: existence is a perfection — a supremely perfect being lacking it is as incoherent as a triangle without three angles. Malcolm: necessary existence cannot be contingent, so God's existence is either impossible or necessary — and the concept is coherent, so necessary. Kant: existence is not a (real) predicate — '100 real thalers' and '100 imagined thalers' share one identical concept; 'is' only asserts instantiation, so building existence into God's essence as a 'perfection' begs the question. Malcolm's rejoinder: Kant targets contingent existence; necessary existence — not causally dependent — may be a genuine predicate. This Malcolm-vs-Kant exchange is the crucial A* debate. Teleological (a posteriori). Paley: a watch on a heath — parts co-adjusted for purpose — compels a watchmaker; nature shows design qua purpose (the eye) and qua regularity (planetary order) in far greater degree, so its author is a vastly greater intelligence: God. Hume's critiques (Dialogues, pre-Darwin): the analogy is weak — the universe is unique, more organism than machine; even if designed, the effect matches only the cause, licensing a finite, imperfect, possibly plural designer, not the infinite God; order may be internal to the universe itself. Darwin: natural selection explains apparent design (eye, wing) without a designer, undercutting design qua purpose. Swinburne's reply: Darwin explains spatial order, not the temporal regularity of natural laws; regularity 'cries out' for explanation, and theism — one being, simple properties — is the simplest explanation of the whole regular universe. Cosmological (a posteriori). Aquinas' Three Ways (Summa Theologiae I q.2 a.3): First Way — whatever is moved is moved by another, and in a per se series (hand–stick–stone) members have no independent causal power, so the series cannot be infinite: first unmoved mover; Second Way — nothing is its own efficient cause, so a first efficient cause; Third Way — if everything were contingent, at some time nothing existed and nothing would exist now; so there is a necessary being: God. Hume: fallacy of composition — every part having a cause does not give the whole one; the universe itself may be the necessary being; regress is not shown contradictory. Kalam (al-Ghazali, Craig): (1) whatever begins to exist has a cause; (2) the universe began — an actual infinite cannot exist (Hilbert's Hotel) or be traversed by successive addition; (3) the cause is timeless, spaceless, powerful and, freely choosing to create, personal: God — though quantum events lack determinate causes and the Big Bang need not begin time. Leibniz: by the principle of sufficient reason , the series of contingent things needs a reason outside itself: a necessary being. Russell (v Copleston, 1948): the principle is not self-evident, and explaining the parts need not explain the whole — 'the universe is just there, and that's all'. Logical problem (Mackie). Inconsistent triad: (1) God is omnipotent; (2) God is wholly good; (3) evil exists — a wholly good being eliminates evil as far as it can, an omnipotent being can eliminate it entirely, yet evil exists: the three cannot all be true. Solving the logical problem requires only showing the set is consistent. Free will defence (Plantinga): significantly free creatures are a great good; freedom excludes causal determination, so God cannot guarantee free creatures whose free actions are all good. Mackie's counter — why not create people who freely always choose good? — is met by transworld depravity : it is possible that every creaturely essence performs at least one wrong action in any world God could actualise; if so, God could not actualise a world with free creatures and no evil. Conclusion: God and evil are logically consistent — the logical problem fails. Note: a defence shows consistency; a theodicy gives God's actual reasons. Evidential problem (Rowe) and soul-making (Hick). Rowe's fawn: burned in a forest fire, it dies in agony unseen by any human; no apparent good could require such suffering. An omnipotent, wholly good God would prevent pointless evil, so the abundance of apparently gratuitous suffering makes God's existence improbable — a probabilistic, not logical, challenge. Hick's vale of soul-making: a lawlike world at 'epistemic distance' from God is the environment in which free persons develop virtues — courage, compassion — through real challenges; evil is instrumental to soul-making, with universal salvation ultimately remedying suffering. Critiques: dysteleological evil — the fawn, animal suffering before humans, horrendous evils (Phillips) — seems to exceed any soul-making value; and a world with less evil but equal virtue-building seems possible, which Hick must deny. Religious experience. Spec types: corporeal and intellectual visions, voices, the sense of presence. James (Varieties): mystical states are ineffable, noetic, transient and passive; validity is pragmatic — 'by their fruits ye shall know them, not by their roots': transformed, morally serious lives count as evidence. Swinburne: the principle of credulity — if it seems to S that X is present, probably X is present, absent special considerations; the principle of testimony — others' reports are probably accurate. So religious experience is prima facie evidence of God. Flew's verification challenge: Wisdom's explorer's gardener becomes invisible, intangible and scentless through successive 'qualifications' until the claim asserts nothing — 'death by a thousand qualifications'; likewise an 'experience of God' surviving every disconfirmation describes nothing, so it cannot justify belief. Responses: Hare's blik and Hick's eschatological verification (below); and Swinburne's principles, which put the burden on the sceptic to show special considerations apply. Via negativa. Pseudo-Dionysius (Mystical Theology) and Maimonides : God transcends every positive predicate; speak only by denial — 'God is good' means 'God is not evil', protecting transcendence and avoiding anthropomorphism. Critique: negation without affirmation tells us almost nothing — an imperfect being is also 'not evil' — and if no positive claim is legitimate, God-talk fails to identify anything. Examiners reward naming this limit. Aquinas' analogy. Univocal language (same sense) fails: God is not 'wise' as Socrates — anthropomorphic. Equivocal language (entirely different sense) fails: 'God is good' then conveys nothing. Aquinas: religious language is analogical — terms apply proportionately : as 'healthy' is predicated of medicine and urine only by relation to the animal's health (analogy of attribution), God's goodness and wisdom are predicated by relation to God's nature (analogy of proportion). God-talk is meaningful and non-literal. Critique: unclear how much the analogy tells us — 'proportionate to a nature we cannot conceive' may explain too little (Black: analogy 'tells us nothing'). Verification, falsification and bliks. Ayer's verification principle: a statement is meaningful only if analytic or empirically verifiable (in principle); 'God exists' and 'God loves me' are neither — religious language is not false but meaningless . Critiques: the principle is itself neither analytic nor verifiable — self-refuting — and universal scientific laws fail strong verifiability. Hick's eschatological verification: the pious and sceptical lives diverge after death — heaven verifies theism — so religious claims are verifiable in principle, though this is weaker verification than Ayer demands. Hare's bliks: the paranoid and the trusting student see the same dons' behaviour differently; a blik is an unfalsifiable interpretive stance, and religious language expresses bliks, not world-assertions — so Flew's challenge misfires. Critique: Hare concedes religion makes no factual claims, and offers no clear test (beyond pragmatism) for sane vs mad bliks. Exam technique: Paper 2. Paper 2 (3 hours, 100 marks): Section A Metaphysics of God, Section B Metaphysics of mind — five questions per section worth 3, 5, 5, 12 and 25 marks. Everything except the 25-marker is pure AO1 : define terms, set out the argument, illustrate — evaluation on 12-markers is redundant and loses marks . The 25-marker (5 AO1 + 20 AO2) quotes a claim and demands evaluation: argue with intent — thesis in the introduction, best objection met with a weak then a strong response, conclusion with no new ideas. Learn definitions verbatim (Boethius' eternity, Kenny's omnipotence, Mackie's triad) and keep the named debates separate. Common pitfalls and examiner tips (click to expand) Logical vs evidential: the logical problem needs a consistency answer (Plantinga's transworld depravity); the evidential problem (Rowe) needs a probability assessment — do not answer Rowe's fawn with transworld depravity. Ontological ≠ design: the ontological argument is a priori; teleological and cosmological are a posteriori — never answer a 'from reason alone' question with Paley. Boethius precision: quote 'the whole, simultaneous and perfect possession of unending life' and distinguish conditional from absolute necessity before evaluating. Kalam ≠ Aquinas: Kalam argues a temporal beginning (no actual infinities); Aquinas argues per se causal dependence — the critiques differ accordingly. Religious language quad: Ayer = meaninglessness (verification); Flew = empty assertions (falsification); Hare = non-assertive bliks; Hick = eschatological verification.

topics.name: Metaphysics of Mind: Dualism, Physicalism and Functionalism
topics.subject: philosophy
topics.searchText: philosophy Philosophy Metaphysics of Mind: Dualism, Physicalism and Functionalism Explain the mind–body problem and define mental properties via qualia and intentionality (Spec 3.4.1). Explain and evaluate Descartes' conceivability and divisibility arguments for substance dualism, and Elisabeth of Bohemia's interaction objection with the causal closure argument (Spec 3.4.2). Explain and evaluate property dualism via Chalmers' zombie argument, including conceivability-vs-possibility and masking critiques (Spec 3.4.2). Explain and evaluate logical behaviourism (Hempel, Ryle's category mistake) and its circularity, pretence and qualia critiques (Spec 3.4.3). Explain and evaluate type identity theory (Place, Smart), the multiple realizability objection, and eliminative materialism (Churchlands) with the self-refutation critique (Spec 3.4.3). Explain and evaluate functionalism (Putnam) via inverted qualia, philosophical zombies and absent qualia (Spec 3.4.4). Use AQA command words correctly: pure AO1 explanation on 3/5/12-mark questions; argue with intent on 25-mark essays. Qualia Intrinsic, subjective properties of experience — the felt hurtfulness of pain, the redness of red; 'what it is like' to undergo an experience, knowable only from the first person. Intentionality The 'aboutness' or directedness of mental states — beliefs, desires and fears are about things; Brentano's mark of the mental. Substance dualism Descartes' view that mind and body are distinct substances: the mind a thinking, unextended, indivisible thing; the body an extended, divisible, non-thinking one. Property dualism The view that mental properties are non-physical properties had by physical substances (brains): the mind supervenes on the body (Chalmers' naturalistic dualism). Causal closure (of the physical) Every physical event that has a cause has a sufficient physical cause — so immaterial mental causes would violate the closure of physics or the mind is epiphenomenal. Epiphenomenalism The view that mental states are caused by physical states but have no causal power of their own — qualia are causally idle by-products of brain processes. Philosophical zombie A being physically and behaviourally identical to a human but lacking qualia — no inner experience, 'all is dark inside'. Category mistake Ryle: representing items as if they belonged to one logical category when they belong to another — treating 'mind' as a thing alongside the body, like the tourist asking where the University is after seeing all the colleges. Logical (analytical) behaviourism Mental-state statements are translatable without remainder into statements about behaviour (Hempel's hard version) or denote dispositions to behave (Ryle's soft version). Type identity theory Place and Smart: mental-state types are identical with brain-state types — a scientific identity like 'lightning is an electrical discharge', not a mere correlation. Multiple realizability One mental-state type can be realized by many different physical types (human, octopus, silicon) — Putnam's objection to type identity, built into functionalism. Functionalism Putnam: mental states are functional states, individuated by causal role — typical inputs, relations to other mental states and behavioural outputs — realizable in any medium. The problem. Mental properties (belief, desire, pain, seeing red) seem unlike physical properties (mass, charge, neural firing): they are private, qualitative and about things. The mind–body problem asks how the two relate — is the mind a separate substance (dualism), a set of purely physical properties (physicalism), or states to be defined by what they do (functionalism)? Keep substance dualism (two substances) distinct from property dualism (one substance, two kinds of property): examiners report candidates conflating them. Qualia. The intrinsic, subjective properties of experience — the felt hurtfulness of pain, the redness of red, 'what it is like' to see green (Nagel's bat). Qualia seem knowable only from the first person: no third-person description of neural firing appears to capture the feel itself. They power the whole anti-physicalist programme. Intentionality. The 'aboutness' or directedness of mental states: a belief is about Paris, a fear about spiders. Brentano took intentionality as the mark of the mental — no purely physical item is intrinsically about anything (a picture is about Paris only through a mind's use: derived intentionality). Physicalists owe an account of how brain states acquire aboutness. The tests. Every theory below must accommodate qualia, intentionality and mental causation (pain causes wincing) — measure each theory against all three. Substance dualism (Descartes). Mind and body are distinct substances: the mind a thinking, unextended, indivisible thing; the body an extended, divisible, non-thinking one. Conceivability argument ( Meditations VI): (P1) I can clearly and distinctly conceive of myself as a thinking, non-extended thing; (P2) what I clearly and distinctly conceive as separate can be made to exist separately (by God); (C) mind and body are really distinct. Divisibility argument: (P1) every body is by nature divisible; (P2) the mind is not — amputate a limb and nothing is subtracted from the mind; (C) by Leibniz's law (identical things share all properties), mind is not body. Elisabeth of Bohemia's interaction objection (1643 letters). How can an unextended, immaterial mind causally move an extended body? Causation between bodies requires contact and impulsion; a non-spatial thing has no surface to push with. Descartes' reply: the mind is 'intermingled' with the body — a real union, not mere concatenation — acting through the pineal gland; 'mind–body union' is a primitive notion grasped through everyday experience (hunger, pain), not by the pure intellect. Critics reply the defence concedes the point: if interaction needs the brain, the mind is not independent of it. Causal closure. The modern version of Elisabeth: every physical event that has a cause has a sufficient physical cause. Immaterial mind-to-body causation would violate conservation of energy; so either mental causes are physical (physicalism) or the mind is an epiphenomenon — caused by the brain but causally idle, unable to move bodies or exercise free will. Dualists must either reject closure or accept epiphenomenalism. Masking critique of conceivability. Conceivability is a poor guide to possibility: pre-chemistry one could conceive of water that is not H₂O, yet water is necessarily H₂O; conceiving mind as separable may mask an identity. Descartes' reply: he claims complete (clear and distinct) understanding of the mind, not partial — only partial conceivability is unreliable. Property dualism (Chalmers). Mental properties are non-physical properties of physical substances (brains): the mind supervenes on the body. Zombie argument: philosophical zombies are physically and behaviourally identical to us but lack qualia — 'all is dark inside'. Zombies are conceivable; what is conceivable is metaphysically possible; if zombies are possible, physical facts do not fix conscious facts; so physicalism is false. Critiques: (1) conceivability is not possibility (Kripke's necessary a posteriori truths; Dennett: a behaviourally identical being making all our consciousness reports would thereby be conscious — zombies are incoherent); (2) the physicalist denies premise 2: that zombies are impossible is physicalism, so the argument begs the question; (3) interaction problems return — Chalmers' psychophysical laws leave qualia causally idle. Appeal: property dualism explains qualia and leaves science intact, but inherits the interaction problem. Logical (analytical) behaviourism. Mental statements translate without remainder into statements about behaviour. Hempel (hard): 'X is in pain' means X winces, groans, says 'ouch' and reports pain when asked. Ryle (soft): mental concepts denote dispositions to behave (if burned, X would flinch), and Descartes' 'ghost in the machine' rests on a category mistake : treating the mind as one more thing alongside the body when mental vocabulary describes ways bodies behave — like the tourist who, shown the colleges, libraries and labs, asks 'but where is the University?'. Critiques: (1) circularity : dispositions must be defined using other mental terms (desire, belief); (2) perfect actors and super-spartans : behaviourally identical subjects can differ — real pain vs flawless pretence, or pain felt while showing nothing — so behaviour does not exhaust the mental; (3) qualia: behaviourism cannot state what pain feels like, missing the qualitative character of experience. Type identity theory (Place, Smart). Mental-state types are identical with brain-state types — a scientific identity like 'lightning is an electrical discharge' (Place), not a mere correlation. Strengths: parsimony (one substance); interaction solved (pain is C-fibre firing, so mental causation is trivial); science-friendly. Multiple realizability (Putnam): the same mental type is realized by different physical types — pain in humans (C-fibres), octopuses (different wiring), perhaps silicon; by Leibniz's law, pain cannot be identical with any single brain-state type. Responses: token identity (each pain token is some brain state) or species-specific identities; counter: reduction then covers only humans and will not generalize to artificial minds. Eliminative materialism (the Churchlands). Folk psychology (belief–desire explanation) is a radically false empirical theory whose categories — belief, desire, pain — will be eliminated and replaced by mature neuroscience, as phlogiston and caloric fluid were. Evidence: folk psychology fails on sleep, intelligence, memory and mental illness, and has stagnated for 25 centuries. Critiques: (1) self-refutation : 'folk psychology is false' is asserted as a belief, presupposing what it denies; the Churchlands reply that this begs the question — like a phlogiston theorist insisting 'but I believe in phlogiston'; (2) folk psychology is successful : it predicts everyday behaviour superbly, unlike phlogiston; reply: its successes are shallow — it fails precisely where understanding matters. Functionalism (Putnam). Mental states are functional states : individuated by causal role — typical causes (inputs: bodily damage), relations to other mental states (belief that something is wrong; desire to escape) and typical effects (outputs: wincing, saying 'ouch'). A state is pain in virtue of playing the pain role, whatever its material — brains, silicon, or (Putnam's original) the states of a Turing machine. Strengths: builds in multiple realizability (answers type identity's main objection); keeps inner states distinct from behaviour (answers behaviourism's circularity and pretence problems); compatible with scientific psychology. Inverted qualia. Two subjects functionally identical — same inputs, outputs and organization — yet their colour experiences qualitatively inverted. If possible, functional role does not fix qualitative character, so functionalism misses qualia. Functional response (Chalmers' fading/dancing qualia): invert qualia gradually while holding functional organization fixed — the subject could not notice, yet conscious experience cannot systematically fade or flicker without functional change; so inverted qualia are impossible. Counter: the argument assumes phenomenal change requires functional change — exactly what the objection denies. Absent qualia (Block's China brain). A billion Chinese citizens, each playing one 'neuron' and linked by two-way radio, implement the functional organization of a human brain. The functionalist must attribute pain to the nation; intuitively there is no unified conscious subject — so functional organization does not suffice for consciousness. Responses: intuitions about alien systems are unreliable; functionalism need not claim the system is conscious exactly as we are. Zombies: a functional duplicate of you with no inner life is conceivable — functional organization leaves out qualia (with the conceivability caveats from dualism). Exam technique: AQA 7172 Paper 2 Section B (click to expand) Paper 2: Section A Metaphysics of God, Section B Metaphysics of mind — five questions per section worth 3, 5, 5, 12 and 25 marks ; all AO1 except the 25-marker (5 AO1 + 20 AO2, 'Evaluate this claim'). 3/5/12-markers: explanation only — define terms, set out the claim, argument or objection, illustrate. Evaluation is redundant and loses marks. 25-marker top band (21–25): define key terms, state a thesis, develop one or two debates in depth (crucial arguments vs less crucial), give weak then strong responses to objections, finish with a consistent conclusion and no new ideas. Highest-yield 25-marker debates: zombies vs physicalism/functionalism; interaction problem vs dualism; multiple realizability vs type identity; inverted qualia vs functionalism.

topics.name: Persia and the Greek World
topics.subject: ancient-history
topics.searchText: ancient-history Ancient History Persia and the Greek World Ionian Revolt The rebellion of the Greek city-states of Ionia (499-494 BC) against Persian rule, led initially by Aristagoras of Miletus; its suppression triggered Darius' invasion of Greece. Herodotus The 'father of history' (c. 484-425 BC); his Histories are the principal narrative source for the Persian Wars, written in the generation after the events. Hoplite A Greek citizen-soldier equipped with shield (aspis), spear and bronze panoply, fighting in the phalanx formation. Trireme The Greek warship with three banks of oars and a bronze ram; decisive in the naval battle of Salamis. Hellenotamiai The treasurers of the Delian League, which later became the Athenian empire. Spartiate A full citizen of Sparta, entitled to membership of the phalanx and the syssition (mess). Ephor One of five annually elected Spartan magistrates who overseen the kings and exercised extensive power. Satrapy One of the provinces of the Persian Empire, governed by a satrap responsible to the Great King. Background. The Persian Empire under Darius I (522-486 BC) controlled Ionia — the Greek city-states of the Asia Minor coast — through local tyrants and satraps. In 499 BC Aristagoras of Miletus, having failed in an attack on Naxos, launched the Ionian Revolt , appealing for help to mainland Greece. Athens and Eretria sent ships; the Greeks burned Sardis (498 BC) before the revolt was crushed by 494 (the naval defeat at Lade). The revolt matters for three reasons: it gave Persia a pretext to punish Athens and Eretria; it taught Persia the difficulty of coastal campaigning; and Herodotus frames it as the origin (aitiai) of the wars. Darius' expedition (492-490 BC). Mardonius' campaign (492) re-subdued Thrace and Macedonia before the fleet was wrecked at Athos. In 490 a seaborne force under Datis and Artaphernes destroyed Eretria and landed at Marathon . Herodotus' cause-analysis is partial: he omits Persia's wider strategic interest in the Aegean and presents the wars as personal revenge narratives — a standard AO2 evaluation point. Marathon (490 BC). c. 9,000-10,000 Athenians and 1,000 Plataeans under Miltiades defeated a larger Persian force. Herodotus gives the Greek dead as 192 against 6,400 Persian — numbers most historians doubt. The Athenian phalanx charged the Persians (running the mile of arrow-range), thinned its centre and enveloped the wings. The battle's significance: it ended the first invasion, made Athens the saviour of Greece, and — with Themistocles' silver-mines windfall (483 BC, Laurion) — funded the fleet that won Salamis. The lone Spartan march (arrived after the battle, Pheidippides' Spartans celebrating the Carneia) illustrates Greek disunity. Xerxes' invasion (480-479 BC). Xerxes crossed the Hellespont on pontoon bridges with a massive land force (Herodotus' 1,700,000 is impossible; modern estimates 150,000-300,000) and a large fleet, fed by a supply chain along the Thracian coast. Thermopylae (480 BC). Leonidas held the pass with c. 300 Spartiates, 700 Thespians and allied contingents; the pass fell after the local betrayal (Ephialtes' path), and the rearguard died to cover the retreat. Strategically the delay achieved little, but the moral exemplum (Simonides' epitaph: 'go tell the Spartans') shaped Greek memory. The simultaneous naval action at Artemisium damaged the Persian fleet and prepared Salamis. Salamis (480 BC). Themistocles evacuated Athens and trapped the Persian fleet in the narrow strait — either by genuine strategy or by secret message to Xerxes (Herodotus records the alleged trick; the standard essay debate). The Persian fleet, outflanked in confined waters where the heavier Greek triremes and disciplined rams excelled, was destroyed. Salamis' significance: it secured the Greek mainland's sea communications and forced Xerxes to withdraw with Mardonius. Plataea (479 BC). The largest hoplite army yet assembled (Herodotus: 38,700 Spartans and helots among c. 110,000 Greeks) under Pausanias destroyed Mardonius' army and ended the invasion. The parallel victory at Mycale freed Ionia. The wars' aftermath: the Delian League (478 BC) turned Athens' leadership into empire (thesaurus at Delos, phoros tribute), setting up the Peloponnesian War; Sparta's prestige declined. Method. Herodotus (writing c. 440-425 BC) claims autopsy, enquiry (historia) and reportage of what he heard — he names his sources and distinguishes versions. Problems. (1) Chronology : he wrote a generation after the events; oral tradition distorted detail. (2) Numbers : Persian army sizes (1,700,000+) and casualty figures are rhetorical exaggerations. (3) Bias : pro-Athenian framing (Athens as saviour of Greece); anti-Persian moralising (barbarian decadence, e.g. Xerxes' flogging of the Hellespont); the speeches are composed, not recorded. (4) Narrative patterning : divine causation, dreams and omens structure the story — Herodotus balances human and divine causation but the patterns may be literary. Value. Despite this, Herodotus is indispensable: he preserves the only connected narrative, names his informants, and his critical method (testing versions, noting disagreements) is genuine historiography. OCR essays reward the pairing: 'Herodotus says X — but consider the source's problems — the judgement must weigh both'. Arguments: Greek advantages. (1) Hoplite and naval excellence : the phalanx's discipline (Marathon) and the trireme's ram in confined waters (Salamis). (2) Strategy : Themistocles' fleet, the evacuation of Athens, the choice of Salamis' narrows. (3) Motivation : defence of homeland vs conscripted multi-national levies. (4) Unity at crisis points : the Hellenic League's combined command at Plataea. Arguments: Persian weaknesses. (1) Logistics : Xerxes' supply chain along the coast was vulnerable; the fleet needed the army. (2) Command : Xerxes' departure after Salamis; Mardonius' fall at Plataea. (3) Diversity of the levies : reluctant conscripts, language barriers (Herodotus' catalogue). (4) Naval limits : Persian ships crewed by levied Phoenicians, Egyptians, Ionians — quality uneven. Counter-considerations. Greek disunity (the Spartans' Carneia delay, Themistocles' threats to the allies); Persian successes (Eretria's destruction, the Acropolis burn); the wars were close-run (Herodotus' own theme: fortunes reverse). OCR technique : a 30-mark essay needs a thesis, four developed points with named battles/sources, counter-considerations, and a judgement (e.g. Greek tactical brilliance — Salamis' narrows and the phalanx — mattered more than Persian logistical weakness, though both were necessary; the decisive factor was leadership: Themistocles' strategy and Pausanias' command). For source questions, use Herodotus' specifics (numbers, speeches) against the reliability analysis above.

topics.name: Athens in the Age of Pericles
topics.subject: ancient-history
topics.searchText: ancient-history Ancient History Athens in the Age of Pericles Ekklesia The Athenian citizen assembly, meeting on the Pnyx; the sovereign body — all male citizens over 18 could attend, speak and vote. Boule The council of 500 (50 from each of the ten tribes), prepared the assembly's agenda and administered the state; membership by lot for a year. Heliaia The people's jury-courts (dikasteria); large juries (up to 501) of citizen volunteers paid from c. 451 BC (2 obols, later 3). Ostracism Annual vote to exile for ten years any citizen deemed dangerous to the democracy (needed 6,000 quorum); used against Themistocles (471) and Cimon (461). Phoros The tribute paid by Delian League members, assessed by Aristides as 460 talents; the financial base of Athens' navy and building programme. Misthophoria Payment for public service (jury service, later office-holding) — Pericles' reform that opened democracy to the poor (thetes). Kleroterion The stone allotment machine that randomised selection to office and juries — democracy by lot. Pericles Athenian statesman (c. 495-429 BC), dominant from c. 461-429; strategos re-elected annually; Plutarch's subject. The institutions. Athenian democracy rested on three bodies: the ekklesia (assembly — the sovereign decision-making body, ~40 meetings a year, quorum 6,000 for sensitive votes); the boule (council of 500 — agenda-setting and administration, by lot, 50 per tribe, rotated through the pyrtaneis); and the heliaia (jury-courts — up to 501 jurors, paid 2 obols from c. 451, 3 later). Magistracies were filled by lot (the kleroterion) except the strategoi (generals), elected annually and re-electable — Pericles held the generalship continuously. Pericles' reforms : jury pay (misthophoria) opened the courts to thetes (the poorest class), radicalising participation. Radical nature and limits. Direct democracy: citizens voted laws personally, no representatives. Limits: citizenship restricted by Pericles' citizenship law (451/450 BC — both parents Athenian, excluding ~half the population from the democracy: women, metics, slaves had no role); the assembly's susceptibility to demagogues; ostracism's misuse for faction. Thucydides' Pericles (funeral oration) calls Athens 'the school of Hellas' — the standard pro-democracy quotation; the Old Oligarch (Pseudo-Xenophon) supplies the hostile case (the demos rules in its own interest). League to empire. Founded 478 BC (naval defence against Persia), the Delian League's members paid phoros tribute or supplied ships. Athens' leadership hardened: Naxos' secession crushed (c. 470); the treasury moved to Athens (454 BC); tribute became compulsory. The Peace of Callias (c. 449 BC, disputed) ended hostilities with Persia, but Athens kept the tribute — the empire's money now bought Pericles' building programme. The empire's instruments. Cleruchies (Athenian settlements on allies' land), garrisons, the tribute assessment (460 talents by Aristides), the federal courts pulled to Athens, and the Athens Coinage Decree (c. 450 — allies used Athenian weights, measures and silver). Kallias' peace and the empire's economics: Plutarch records the allies' resentment (the 'enslaved' League, per the rhetors); the standard essay debate: protective hegemony vs exploitation — use the tribute lists, the Coinage Decree, and the revolts (Naxos, Thasos 465) as evidence both ways. Leadership (461-429 BC). Pericles dominated Athens for three decades — elected strategos annually, never a tyrant but 'first citizen' (Thucydides). His ascendancy: the Ephialtic reforms (461 — stripped the Areopagus of powers, radicalised democracy); ostracising rivals (Cimon 461, Thucydides son of Melesias 443); his marriage-alliance politics (Aspasia's salon, per Plutarch). Thucydides' assessment: Athens under Pericles 'in name a democracy, in fact rule by the first man' — the standard evaluative quotation. The building programme (447-429 BC). Funded by the phoros: the Parthenon (447-432, Iktinos and Kallikrates, Pheidias' sculptures), the Propylaia, the Temple of Athena Nike, the Hephaisteion. Plutarch's Life defends the programme (the money was for war — spending it on beauty and the gods was legitimate; the allies' resentment is the counter-case). The programme's significance: Periclean Athens' self-image (the imperial capital of Hellas); employment (the poor benefited); the arts' golden age (tragedy: Sophocles, Euripides). Plutarch and Thucydides as sources. Plutarch (c. AD 46-120, writing 500 years later): biographical, moralising, drawn from earlier writers (Stesimbrotus, Ion of Chios); his Life of Pericles preserves anecdotes (Aspasia, the ostracisms, the building programme's defence) but is not a political history — reliability limited by date and moral purpose. Thucydides (c. 460-400): contemporary, exiled general, analytical; his Pericles (Books 1-2) is admiring but written with hindsight and against the post-Periclean demagogues — his praise of Pericles serves his thesis (Athens failed when it lost him). OCR essays weigh both: 'Plutarch preserves the anecdotes, Thucydides the political analysis — neither is neutral'. 'How democratic was Athenian democracy?' FOR: direct participation (ekklesia, heliaia), sortition, pay (misthophoria), the power of the courts (ostracism, euthynai audits). AGAINST: restricted citizenship (451/450 law), women/metics/slaves excluded, demagogue influence, the elite's informal power (Pericles' ascendancy). Judgement: radically democratic for its citizens, unrepresentative of its population — the standard balanced answer. 'Was the Athenian empire tyrannical?' FOR: tribute without consent (post-Callias), crushed revolts (Naxos, Thasos), cleruchies, the Coinage Decree, federal courts in Athens. AGAINST: Persia's continued threat (the Peace of Callias disputed), protection and stability, the League's original purpose, Athens' naval supremacy as the allies' interest. Judgement: the empire began as protection and became extraction — the 454 treasury move is the turning point; say why. OCR method. A 30-mark essay: thesis, four developed points (institutions, empire, individuals, sources), counter-considerations, judgement with the question's wording. For source questions (Plutarch extracts), test the anecdote against Thucydides and the institutional record.

topics.name: Sparta
topics.subject: ancient-history
topics.searchText: ancient-history Ancient History Sparta Agoge The Spartan state education: boys taken at 7 into packs, trained for obedience, endurance and war; the institution that made the Spartiate. Helot The enslaved population of Laconia and Messenia, bound to the land; outnumbered Spartiates several times over and controlled by annual war declarations and the krypteia. Perioikoi Free inhabitants of Spartan towns ('dwellers-around'); craftsmen and traders, no political rights, obliged to military service. Dual kingship Two hereditary kings (Agids and Eurypontids), religious, military and judicial leaders, checked by the ephors and gerousia. Gerousia The council of 28 elders (over 60, elected for life) plus the two kings; prepared business for the assembly and tried capital cases. Ephors Five annually elected magistrates; overseen the kings (oath of monthly swap), could prosecute kings, controlled the krypteia. Krypteia The secret service of young Spartiates who policed the helots — annual war declaration (Plutarch) institutionalised control. Syssition The common mess — Spartiates ate together, contributing food monthly; membership was the mark of full citizenship. Structure. Spartan society had three tiers: the Spartiates (full citizens, ~8,000 adult males at the peak, declining to ~1,000 by Aristotle's day), the perioikoi (free 'dwellers-around' — craftsmen and traders with no political rights, military service obligatory) and the helots (the enslaved majority of Laconia and, after the Messenian Wars, Messenia — outnumbering Spartiates perhaps 7:1). The helots farmed the kleroi (allotments) that fed each Spartiate's syssition contribution — the economic base of the Spartan citizen's freedom for war. Control of the helots. The helots' numbers dictated the constitution's character: Sparta was a garrison state. Controls: the annual war declaration on the helots (Plutarch — institutionalised murder without pollution), the krypteia (young Spartiates' secret police), the obligatory hoplite readiness, and the systemic terror (Xenophon records the helots' willingness to die — their fear of the Spartans). The Messenian revolt (464-460) — the Third Messenian War — showed the system's fragility and Sparta's dependence on allies. The agoge. Boys taken at 7 into age-packs (agelai); trained in endurance (one cloak, barefoot, short rations), obedience (the eirens' discipline), theft tolerated (resourcefulness) but being CAUGHT punished — the standard paradox; the ritual theft of cheese (Plutarch); at 20 into the syssition; at 30 full citizenship (homologoi). Girls too: gymnastics (the running races, per Xenophon and Plutarch) — Sparta's women were famously different (Plutarch on their freedom, the 'thigh-flashers' joke of the comic poets). Military culture. The syssition's messes built the phalanx's cohesion; the agoge's obedience built the discipline that won Plataea's day. Xenophon's Constitution of the Lacedaemonians idealises the system (Lycurgus' design) while admitting decline in his own day (c. 360s). The standard essay debate: Sparta's military excellence (the finest hoplites of Greece) vs its demographic fragility (declining Spartiate numbers, helot control) — the system that made Sparta strong made it rigid. Institutions. The dual kingship : two hereditary kings (Agids and Eurypontids) — religious leaders, military commanders (one on campaign), judges in some cases; checked by the ephors' oath (monthly swap of the mutual oath: king rules by the laws, Sparta keeps the king). The gerousia : 28 elders (over 60, elected for life by acclamation) plus the kings — prepared business, tried capital cases. The ephors : five annually elected — extensive power (prosecuting kings, the krypteia, foreign policy), the real check. The assembly (apella): Spartiates over 30 — voted (by acclamation, no debate) on the gerousia's proposals. Nature. The Spartan constitution (the 'Great Rhetra', per Plutarch/tyrtaios? — Tyrtaios' poems) was a mixed constitution (kingly, aristocratic, democratic elements) — admired by Aristotle and the philosophers as stable. The reality: oligarchic dominance (gerousia + ephors) with a passive assembly. Xenophon idealises Lycurgus' design; the standard essay: how 'Lycurgan' was Sparta really — the reforms attributed to a legendary lawgiver, the institutions evolving over time. Xenophon (c. 430-354 BC). An Athenian aristocrat who admired Sparta (exiled, lived in Scillus near Olympia); his Constitution of the Lacedaemonians is the fullest ancient account of the agoge and syssition — idealising (Lycurgus' divine design) but contemporary-adjacent and detailed; his Hellenica covers Spartan hegemony (404-362). Reliability: idealisation (Sparta as the model constitution), but his detail is unmatched — the standard pairing with Plutarch. Plutarch (c. AD 46-120). Wrote 500+ years later; his Lycurgus and Agis/Cleomenes preserve the traditions (the war declaration, the krypteia, the cheese theft) from earlier writers (Aristotle, Sosibius) — biographical and moralising; reliability limited by date. Tyrtaios (7th century BC, elegies) — the earliest poetic evidence (the messes, the phalanx's ethos, the Messenian Wars). Essay technique. A 30-mark essay: thesis, four developed points (society, agoge, constitution, sources), counter-considerations, judgement. Standard questions: 'How far was Sparta's strength military?' (FOR: the phalanx, the agoge, Plataea; AGAINST: the helot fragility, the declining Spartiate numbers, the rigidity — Leuctra 371 broke the myth); 'How reliable are Xenophon and Plutarch for Spartan society?' (weigh idealisation against detail); 'Was the Spartan constitution democratic?' (the apella's acclamation vs the ephors' power — oligarchic reality, mixed theory).

topics.name: Alexander the Great
topics.subject: ancient-history
topics.searchText: ancient-history Ancient History Alexander the Great Granicus (334 BC) Alexander's first major victory over the Persians in Asia Minor, against a satrapal army under Memnon and Arsames. Issus (333 BC) Alexander's victory over Darius III in person, in a narrow coastal plain; Darius fled, his family captured. Gaugamela (331 BC) The decisive victory over Darius III near Arbela; Alexander's oblique attack broke the Persian line. Companion cavalry The hetairoi — Alexander's elite cavalry, the hammer of his battles; the somatophylakes were his bodyguards. Phalanx The Macedonian infantry formation with the sarissa (5-6m pike); the anvil to the Companion cavalry's hammer. Proskynesis The Persian ritual prostration before the Great King; Alexander's attempt to impose it (327 BC) — Callisthenes' resistance and death. Callisthenes Aristotle's grand-nephew, Alexander's official historian; resisted proskynesis (327 BC), executed in the Pages' Conspiracy. Hephaestion Alexander's closest friend and second-in-command; died 324 BC — Alexander's grief extreme (Plutarch). Granicus (334 BC). Alexander crossed the Hellespont (c. 35,000 Macedonians and allies) and defeated the satrapal army under Memnon and Arsames at the Granicus river — the Companion cavalry's frontal charge across the river broke the Persian line; Alexander fought in the front line (his helmet split, per Plutarch). The victory opened Asia Minor; the Greek cities' liberation (the panhellenic claim). Issus (333 BC). Darius III met Alexander in person in the narrow coastal plain near Issus — the terrain neutralised Persian numbers; Alexander's oblique attack (the Companion wedge at the weakened centre) broke the line; Darius fled (his mother, wife and children captured — treated honourably, the standard propaganda point). The victory opened the Levant and Egypt (the oracle of Siwah, 331 — Alexander declared son of Ammon). Gaugamela (331 BC). The decisive battle: Darius' massive army on open ground (chosen by the Persians); Alexander's oblique advance (the 'Hammer and Anvil' — the phalanx held, the Companion cavalry's wedge found the gap); Darius fled again; Babylon and the Persian capitals (Susa, Persepolis — burned 330, revenge for Athens or accident?) fell. The wars' end: Darius murdered by Bessus (330) — Alexander's pursuit and avenging of Darius (the legitimate successor claim). Military leadership. Alexander fought in the front line (Granicus' split helmet, the siege of Malli's arrow — 325 BC, near-fatal wound); his tactics: the oblique advance, the Companion wedge, the phalanx's discipline; the sieges (Halicarnassus, Tyre's mole — 332, the seven-month siege). His leadership: sharing hardship (the march through Gedrosia's desert — though the cost was extreme), promoting Persians (the epigonoi — 30,000 Persian youths trained in Macedonian style), the mass wedding at Susa (324 — Macedonians married Persians). The mutinies. Alexander's relationship with his Macedonians soured: the Hyphasis mutiny (326 BC — the army refused to cross the Ganges; Alexander sulked in his tent, then turned back); the Opis mutiny (324 BC — the army mutinied at the Persian promotions; Alexander's speech (Arrian), the reconciliation banquet); the purges (Philotas and Parmenion, 330 — the conspiracy; Cleitus, 328 — killed by Alexander in a drunken quarrel). The standard essay debate: Alexander the great commander vs Alexander the autocrat — the mutinies and purges as evidence. Divine sonship. Siwah's oracle (331 — son of Ammon); the panhellenic claim (Zeus-Ammon); the deification push: proskynesis (327 — the Persian prostration imposed on Macedonians; Callisthenes' resistance and execution); the divine honours (the cities' cults); the Gedrosian march's costs. Self-presentation: Homer's model (Achilles — Alexander slept with the Iliad, per Plutarch); the Homeric kingship (the leader in front); Herakles' lineage (the Argead claim). The standard essay: Alexander's deification — genuine belief or propaganda? The sources disagree (Arrian admiring, Curtius hostile). The sources. Plutarch (c. AD 100): biographical, moralising — his Life preserves the anecdotes (Bucephalus, the Gordian knot, Cleitus' murder, the grief for Hephaestion); reliability limited by date (400 years) and moral purpose. Arrian (c. AD 130-150): wrote from Ptolemy and Aristobulus (eyewitnesses) — the most military-detailed; admiring (Alexander 'philitatos' — the divine call), but the admiration colours the account. Curtius Rufus (1st century AD): hostile — the corruption theme (the king corrupted by success); his sources unknown. Reliability: all three wrote centuries later; the eyewitness tradition (Ptolemy, Aristobulus, Callisthenes) survives only in fragments; the standard OCR pairing: 'Arrian for the battles, Curtius for the corruption, Plutarch for the anecdotes — none is neutral'. 'Alexander was a great military commander.' FOR: Granicus, Issus, Gaugamela's tactics (the oblique advance, the wedge); the sieges (Tyre); the front-line leadership (Malli); the march to the Indus. AGAINST: the mutinies (Hyphasis, Opis) and purges (Philotas, Cleitus) — the command's human cost; the Gedrosian march's losses; the empire's fragility after his death. Judgement: the campaigns were brilliant — the oblique tactics and personal leadership unmatched; but 'great' must weigh the cost (the army's suffering, the purges) — the standard balanced answer. 'Alexander's deification was political propaganda.' FOR: Siwah's convenient timing, proskynesis' imposition (Macedonian resistance), the divine honours' political use. AGAINST: Alexander's genuine belief (his mother's cults, the Iliad's model); the Macedonian acceptance of divine kingship. Judgement: both — genuine belief deployed politically; say why the distinction matters. OCR method. A 30-mark essay: thesis, four developed points with named battles/sources, counter-considerations, judgement. For source questions: use the extract's specifics (Arrian's numbers, Curtius' moralising) against the reliability analysis.

topics.name: The Late Republic
topics.subject: ancient-history
topics.searchText: ancient-history Ancient History The Late Republic Consul One of two annually elected chief magistrates of the Republic; commanded armies, presided over the senate — the Republic's executive. Senate The council of ~300 ex-magistrates (seniores); advised the magistrates, controlled finance and foreign policy — the Republic's real power. Tribune One of ten tribunes of the plebs; protected plebeians (veto, auxilium), proposed laws to the plebeian assembly — the Gracchi's office. Dictator The six-month emergency magistracy; Sulla's and Caesar's violations (dictator perpetuus) broke the Republic's rules. Gracchi Tiberius (tribune 133 BC) and Gaius (123-122 BC) Gracchus — land reformers whose deaths began the Republic's crisis. Optimates The senatorial 'best men' faction — defended the senate's traditional power. Populares Politicians who appealed to the people (tribunes, assemblies) against the senate — Caesar's method. Proscription Sulla's purge (82 BC) — lists of enemies executed, property confiscated; the civil war's terror. Magistracies. The consuls (two annually elected, the Republic's executive — armies, the senate's presidency); the praetors (judges); the censors (the census, morality); the tribunes of the plebs (ten — the plebeians' protectors, veto power, proposed laws); the dictator (six months, emergency only). The senate (~300 ex-magistrates): advised (senatus consulta — 'decrees of the senate' = the magistrates' advice), controlled finance, foreign policy and the provinces; the Republic's real power. The assemblies : the comitia centuriata (military — elected consuls, declared war), the comitia tributa and the concilium plebis (tribal — elected tribunes, passed laws — the plebiscites). The cursus honorum. The ladder of offices: quaestor (finance), aedile (games, streets), praetor, consul — with age minima and the two-year gap; competition for office drove faction (the optimates vs populares). Patronage : the clientela (patrons and clients) — the social glue; the nobiles' (nobles') dominance (consulships in families). The Gracchi (133-121 BC). Tiberius Gracchus (tribune 133): land reform (the lex Sempronia agraria — the public land's limit, 500 iugera), funded by Attalus' bequest; bypassed the senate (took the bill to the plebeian assembly, deposed his fellow tribune Octavius — unconstitutional), sought re-election; killed in the senate-house riot (133 — the first political murder in Rome since the kings). Gaius Gracchus (tribune 123-122): grain law (subsidised grain), courts to the equites, citizenship proposals; died in the senatus consultum ultimum's crackdown (121 — the 'final decree', the emergency powers). Significance: the Gracchi normalised political violence, faction and the tribunate's use against the senate — the Republic's crisis begins here (Cicero's and Sallust's claim). Marius and Sulla. Marius (consul 107, 104-100, 86): the military reform (recruited the propertyless — the capite censi; the professional army, loyal to its general, not the state — the Marian reforms' consequence: civil war); the Jugurthine and Cimbrian wars. Sulla (consul 88, dictator 82-79): the march on Rome (88 — the first, against Marius; the civil war 83-82); the proscriptions (82 — ~2,000 senators/equites listed and killed); the dictatorship (unconstitutional duration); the reforms (the senate's powers restored, the tribunate's castration). Significance: Sulla showed that armies could take Rome — Caesar learned from him. The First Triumvirate (60 BC). Caesar, Pompey and Crassus — an unofficial alliance (Caesar's consulship 59, the land bills, the Gallic command). Cicero's opposition : the consul of 63 (the Catiline conspiracy), the optimates' voice; his letters (Ad Atticum, Ad Familiares) preserve the Republic's fall from the inside — the standard source. The fall (49-44 BC). Crassus' death (Carrhae, 53) broke the triumvirate; Julia's death (54) broke the Caesar-Pompey bond; the senate (Pompey's party) ordered Caesar to disband (49); Caesar crossed the Rubicon (49 — civil war); Pompey defeated at Pharsalus (48) and murdered in Egypt; Caesar's dictatorship (dictator perpetuus, 44 — the unconstitutional title); the Ides of March (44 — the assassination by Brutus and Cassius, the Republic's last hope). Caesar's significance: the populares' method (the tribunician laws, the people's support), the army's loyalty (the Marian legacy), the dictatorship's normalisation — the Republic's institutions could not contain him. Cicero's letters (Ad Atticum, Ad Familiares, Ad Quintum): the Republic's fall from the inside — contemporary, candid, but partisan (Cicero's self-image) and fragmentary (the letters survive unevenly). Cicero's speeches (the Catilinarians, Pro Milone): published and edited — not verbatim. Plutarch (c. AD 100): the Lives (Caesar, Pompey, Cicero, Marius, Sulla) — biographical, moralising, from earlier writers (Sallust, Pollio); 500 years' distance. Suetonius (c. AD 120): the Twelve Caesars — anecdotal, gossipy. Appian (2nd century AD): the Civil Wars — the fullest narrative of the period, from earlier sources. Sallust (c. 40 BC): the Catiline conspiracy — contemporary, moralising (the Republic's decadence theme). Reliability: the standard pairing — 'Cicero for the inside view, Sallust for the moralising, Plutarch/Suetonius for the anecdotes, Appian for the narrative — none neutral'. Essay technique. A 30-mark essay: thesis, four developed points, counter-considerations, judgement. Standard questions: 'Was the Republic doomed before Caesar?' (FOR: the Gracchi's violence, the Marian army, Sulla's example; AGAINST: the Republic survived crises, the institutions held until 49); 'Was Caesar a tyrant?' (the dictatorship's normalisation vs the reforms' popularity); 'How reliable are Cicero's letters?' (candid but partisan). Use the sources against each other and the events.

topics.name: Julio-Claudian Rome
topics.subject: ancient-history
topics.searchText: ancient-history Ancient History Julio-Claudian Rome Principate Augustus' settlement (27 BC): rule disguised as the restoration of the Republic — the princeps ('first citizen') with tribunician and proconsular powers. Princeps The 'first citizen' — Augustus' title; the constitutional disguise over monarchical power. Tribunicia potestas The tribune's powers (veto, sacrosanctity) held by the emperor — the legal base of the principate. Imperium maius Greater military command than any governor — Augustus' and Claudius' authority over the provinces. Res Gestae Augustus' own account of his achievements ('the things done'); the principal inscriptional source for his image. Praetorian Guard The emperor's bodyguard (~9 cohorts, Sejanus' command under Tiberius); kingmakers after Caligula's murder (41). Aerarium The public treasury; Augustus' division of finance (the fiscus — the emperor's private treasury) split public and imperial money. Pater patriae 'Father of the fatherland' — Augustus' title (2 BC); the paternal image of imperial rule. The settlement (27 BC). After Actium (31 BC), Augustus 'restored the Republic' (27 — the constitutional settlement: the provinces returned to the senate, the title 'Augustus' granted); the reality: the principate — the princeps' powers: tribunicia potestas (the tribune's veto and sacrosanctity), imperium maius (greater command), the censorial power, the pontifex maximus (12 BC). The Res Gestae (Augustus' own account): 'I transferred the Republic from my power to the dominion of the senate and people of Rome' — the image over the reality (the standard essay point). The working.
