The principate worked through the disguise: the senate's consent (the constitutional forms), the army's loyalty (the donatives), the aerarium's finance (the fiscus split), the succession problem (no constitutional heir — Tiberius, then the dynastic accidents). Augustus' image: pater patriae (2 BC), the moral legislation (the Julian laws — marriage, adultery), the building programme ('I found Rome brick and left it marble', per Suetonius), the pax Romana. Tiberius (14-37 AD). The reluctant princeps (the senate's consent scene, per Tacitus); the Sejanus affair (the praetorian prefect's conspiracy, 31 — Tiberius' withdrawal to Capri); the treason trials (the maiestas cases — Tacitus' theme); characterised as gloomy and suspicious (Tacitus' hostile portrait). Gaius (Caligula, 37-41). The beginning popular (the donatives, the exiles' return); the later madness (Suetonius' anecdotes — the horse consul, the bridge over Baiae; the standard reliability problem); the German bodyguard, the divine honours; assassinated by the praetorians (41). Claudius (41-54). Found hiding behind a curtain after Caligula's murder — the praetorians' kingmaking (the donative); the conquest of Britain (43); the freedmen's administration (Narcissus, Pallas); the Agrippina affair (the marriage, Nero's adoption); characterised as weak (Suetonius) but effective (the administration, the conquest). Nero (54-68). The beginning (the quinquennium — Seneca and Burrus' guidance, the golden age claim); the later descent (Agrippina's murder, 59; the Great Fire, 64 — the Christians blamed; the Golden House; the Senate's hostility); the rebellions (the Pisonian conspiracy, 65; Vindex and Galba, 68); suicide (68 — the Julio-Claudian line ended). Imperial image. The emperors' self-presentation: Augustus' Res Gestae (the achievements' account — the image over reality); the coinage (the emperor's portrait, the victory types); the buildings (the Forum of Augustus, the Golden House's excess); the moral legislation (the Julian laws); the divine honours (the imperial cult). The standard essay: the image vs the reality — 'the princeps disguised the monarch'; the emperors' varying images (Tiberius' gloom, Gaius' divinity, Claudius' weakness, Nero's artistry). The sources. Tacitus (c. AD 100-110): the Annals — the Julio-Claudians' history; hostile to the principate (the liberty theme, the treason trials); stylised (the character sketches, the innuendo); contemporary-adjacent but under Trajan's freed speech — the standard evaluation: Tacitus' hostility colours everything. Suetonius (c. AD 120): the Twelve Caesars — biographical, anecdotal, gossipy (the horse consul, the curtain-hiding); organised by topic not chronology; the archive-based but uncritical. Cassius Dio (c. AD 220): the Roman History — senatorial, later (200 years), from earlier sources (the annals' tradition); balanced but distant. Reliability: all three wrote after the events (Tacitus 40-50 years, Suetonius 60, Dio 150); the senate's perspective (all senators); the standard OCR pairing: 'Tacitus for the political analysis, Suetonius for the anecdotes, Dio for the overview — all senatorial, all hostile to the principate's excesses'. 'Augustus restored the Republic.' FOR: the settlement's forms (27 BC — the provinces returned, the title granted), the senate's consent, the Res Gestae's claim. AGAINST: the powers (tribunicia potestas, imperium maius), the army's loyalty, the dynastic reality (the succession). Judgement: the principate's disguise — the image restored the Republic, the reality founded the monarchy; say why the disguise mattered. 'The Julio-Claudian emperors were increasingly autocratic.' FOR: Tiberius' treason trials, Gaius' divinity, Claudius' freedmen, Nero's Golden House and murders; the praetorians' kingmaking; the senate's decline. AGAINST: the constitutional forms persisted (the senate's consent, the magistracies); the administration's effectiveness (Claudius); the quinquennium's golden age. Judgement: autocratic drift — but the principate's forms constrained it; the standard balanced answer. OCR method. A 30-mark essay: thesis, four developed points with named emperors/sources, counter-considerations, judgement. For source questions: use the extract's specifics (Tacitus' characterisations, Suetonius' anecdotes) against the reliability analysis.

topics.name: The World of the Hero
topics.subject: classical-civilisation
topics.searchText: classical-civilisation Classical Civilisation The World of the Hero kleos Glory or fame won through great deeds, especially in song; kleos aphthiton ('imperishable glory') is the epic's promise that heroic deeds live on in poetry after death. timē Honour — material and social standing expressed through prizes (gera), booty, seats of precedence and public recognition; its loss triggers the plot of the Iliad. mēnis Wrath — the first word of the Iliad; the divine-scale anger of Achilles, distinguished from ordinary anger by its cosmic consequences. nostos Homecoming; the governing theme of the Odyssey, which follows Odysseus' long-delayed return to Ithaca and the restoration of his oikos. mētis Cunning intelligence; Odysseus' defining quality (epithet polutropos, 'of many turns'), deployed through disguise, lies and stratagem rather than force. xenia Guest-friendship: a reciprocal pact protected by Zeus Xenios obliging hosts to shelter, feed and gift guests before questioning them, and guests to behave with restraint. aristeia A hero's peak of battle-excellence; Achilles' aristeia spans Iliad 20–22, culminating in the killing of Hector. formula A repeated phrase fixed to a character or action (e.g. 'swift-footed Achilles', 'rosy-fingered Dawn') that fits the dactylic hexameter and enabled oral composition. type-scene A recurring narrative template (arming, sacrifice, supplication, arrival) varied for each occasion — an oral-compositional building block. moira Fate or allotted portion; it bounds even the gods, as when Zeus weighs the fates of Sarpedon (Iliad 16) and Hector (Iliad 22) on his golden scales. H408/11 The World of the Hero is the compulsory component: 2 hours 30 minutes, 100 marks, 40% of the A Level. You study one of Homer's Iliad or Odyssey in depth, and Virgil's Aeneid, which all candidates study. The paper has three sections: Section A focuses solely on Homer and contains two sets of questions — one on the Iliad, one on the Odyssey — and you answer on the text you studied; Section B contains questions on the Aeneid, all compulsory; Section C offers a stimulus (a passage from Homer and one from Virgil) plus a choice of essays, in which you are expected to make use of secondary sources and academic views. There are three question types: a 10-mark stimulus question , a 20-mark essay and a 30-mark essay . The 30-mark essays are marked against Levels of Response grids that explicitly credit the use of secondary sources, scholars and academic works — so A* answers must weave in scholarship (e.g. Parry and Lord on oral tradition; Griffin; Nicholson's The Mighty Dead ; Weil's The Iliad, or the Poem of Force ) rather than bolt it on. Prescribed books: Iliad 1, 3, 4, 6, 9, 10, 16, 17, 18, 19, 22, 23, 24; Odyssey 1, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 16, 17, 18, 19, 21, 22, 23; Aeneid 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12. Any translation is permitted; printed passages are taken from Rieu (Penguin) and Kline (poetryintranslation.com) for Homer, and West (Penguin) and Kline for Virgil. Plan the paper by weight: the 30-mark essays are marked on Levels of Response grids (knowledge, analysis, evaluation and scholars), the 20-mark essays on knowledge and analysis, the 10-mark stimulus on direct response to the printed passage. On this component AO1 is worth 18% and AO2 22% of the A Level — analysis and evaluation dominate, so A* preparation means practising arguments, not recapping plots. Section C's stimulus questions require you to read the printed Homer and Virgil passages cold and to write with secondary views in support; its essays expect comparison across the epics. The epics were composed orally in dactylic hexameter long before writing was used for literature. Milman Parry and Albert Lord demonstrated that the poems are built from formulae (fixed phrases that fill metrical slots), type-scenes and recurring themes — the toolkit of bards who compose-in-performance, as Lord observed among Yugoslav guslars. Rhapsodes performed Homer at festivals such as the Panathenaia; tradition credits the Athenian tyrant Peisistratus with a 6th-century BC 'recension' that standardised the text. The great unresolved question — one poet or many? — divides Analysts (who detected seams and inconsistencies), Unitarians (who stressed artistic unity) and the oral-formulaic middle ground: consistent characterisation and design (Griffin, Edwards) coexist with formulaic diction, which most scholars now treat as compatible with a single monumental poet working within an oral tradition (Nicholson stresses how the poems preserve Bronze Age memory within an 8th-century BC composition). For analysis, always ask what the technique does : Epithets ('swift-footed Achilles', 'Odysseus of many wiles', 'rosy-fingered Dawn') serve metre first, but also fix characterisation — Hector is still 'glorious' even in defeat, reinforcing the code he dies by. Some formulae are deliberately context-stretching: dead warriors speak words 'fitting the moment'. Type-scenes (arming, sacrifice, supplication, arrival) create expectation and then variation: Achilles' arming in Iliad 19 dwells on the new armour made by Hephaestus; Priam's supplication in 24 inverts the heroic refusal of the embassy in 9. Similes create a second world: lions, storms and fires transfer emotion from battlefield to nature, while domestic similes (the weeping woman of Iliad 22; Odysseus crying like a widow captured at the fall of her city, Odyssey 8) reverse the comparison to expose what war costs. Extended similes can foreshadow and mark significance. Speeches stage debate — the embassy in Iliad 9 is a structured agon of offer and refusal; divine speeches (Athena's restraint of Achilles' sword, Iliad 1) drive dual motivation. Odyssey technique adds flashback : the poem opens in medias res, and Books 9–12 (the Apologoi) retrospectively recount the wanderings. The structure is itself thematic: nostos delayed by divine hostility, achieved by mētis. Ring composition frames both epics: the Iliad opens with Chryses' supplication (a priest dishonoured) and closes with Priam's (a father dishonoured) — the frame is the theme of timē and its limits; Achilles' two speeches in Books 1 and 24 mirror each other. Type-scenes build the structure: the supplication chain runs through the poem (Chryses 1; Lycaon 21; Priam 24), and the arming scenes (Achilles in 19 with divine armour) mark the turning points. The dactylic hexameter itself (six feet, long-short-short) is the engine of formulae — names and phrases chosen for their metrical shape — and the Peisistratean recension tradition is the transmission's evidence that the text was fixed for Panathenaic performance by the 6th century BC. Iliad. The heroic code demands timē — material honour and public standing. Achilles' mēnis begins when Agamemnon strips Briseis, a geras that embodies his timē (Iliad 1); his withdrawal is a protest against dishonour, and Athena's intervention makes his anger simultaneously divine and human (dual motivation). In the embassy of Book 9, Odysseus, Phoenix and Ajax offer restitution, and Achilles articulates the two fates: a long, obscure life at home, or a short life with imperishable kleos (kleos aphthiton). Crucially, he questions the code itself — 'one and the same lot for the man who hangs back and the man who battles hard' — the first crack in the heroic worldview. Patroclus' death converts withdrawal into revenge; the aristeia of Books 20–22 (including the killing of the suppliant Lycaon in 21) shows heroism at its most brutal, before Book 24 transfigures it: Priam's supplication, the kiss of the hands that killed his son, Zeus' two urns of good and evil, and the shared weeping of two men bound by mortality produce pity beyond the code. Weil reads the Iliad as 'the poem of force' — force turns people into things — while Griffin stresses the poem's pathos and humanity. Odyssey. The poem revalues heroism around nostos and mētis . Odysseus' polutropos intelligence — disguise, false tales, the stratagems of Ithaca — replaces brute valour; he refuses Calypso's offer of immortality ( Odyssey 5), choosing wife and home over kleos among the dead, an explicit reversal of Achilles' choice in Iliad 9. Heroism is also endurance (the tortures of Books 5–12; the restraint of the Beggar in his own hall) and justice: the slaughter of the suitors in Book 22 punishes their systemic abuse of xenia. Recognition is progressive — Telemachus (16), Eurycleia's scar (19), the bed test (23), Laertes in the orchard (24) — each testing identity against memory and knowledge. Penelope is the moral centre: her weaving trick (2) and her test of the bed (23) show mētis equal to her husband's, and her fidelity wins 'a fame that reaches the heavens' (24) — kleos for a woman won through virtue, not arms. A* judgement should ask whether the two ideals conflict: the Iliad's hero wins glory by dying young; the Odyssey's by surviving home — Homer seems to expose the cost of the first by dramatising the value of the second. The prescribed books supply the evidence: Patroclus' aristeia and death (16) drive Achilles back to war; the shield of Achilles (18) — Hephaestus' two cities at peace and at war — is the poem's image of the world the war is destroying; Hector's farewell (6) and the ransom (24) frame the family theme. The embassy (9) stages the code's three voices: Odysseus (offer and timē), Phoenix (the story of Meleager — the parable of the hero who waits too long) and Ajax (the appeal to friendship); Achilles' reply questions the code — and Book 24 answers him with pity rather than honour. The immortals are anthropomorphic — they wound (Aphrodite, Iliad 5; Ares), grieve, quarrel and even lose their horses — yet their scope of power exceeds mortals', and they keep the plot in motion. Their relationship with mortals is reciprocal: honour flows upward through sacrifice, prayer and libation; aid flows downward. Motivation is often dual: Athena rouses and restrains Achilles (Iliad 1, 22), but his rage is his own; Zeus weighs the fates of Sarpedon (16) and Hector (22) on the golden scales — fate (moira) binds even Zeus. In the Odyssey , Zeus opens with a theodicy: humans blame the gods for woes they bring on themselves through their own recklessness (1). Athena is Odysseus' advocate and mask-maker; Poseidon the avenging antagonist; Calypso and Circe test the pull of home against divine beds; the slaughtered cattle of Helios (12) prove that divine justice cannot be evaded. Xenia is the Odyssey's moral architecture, protected by Zeus Xenios. The code obliges the host to shelter, feed, bathe and gift a guest before even asking his name, and the guest to respond with gratitude and restraint: Positive: Telemachus received by Nestor (Odyssey 3 — not a prescribed book; cite Menelaus, Odyssey 4) and the Phaeacians (7–8), where the palace sequence stages ideal hospitality; Eumaeus the swineherd offers perfect xenia to a beggar he does not recognise (14–16); Odysseus repays it with life and reward. Negative: Polyphemus eats his guests and has no assemblies or laws (9) — civilisation defined by its absence; the suitors devour Odysseus' oikos and plot his son's murder (1–2, 13–22); Paris' breach of Menelaus' hospitality begins the Trojan War itself. Family is the oikos — the household as social, economic and emotional unit. Hector, Andromache and Astyanax (Iliad 6) give the war its human price: Hector prays his son may outshine him, while the baby fears his horsehair crest — the helmet of timē terrifies the family it protects. Priam and Achilles in Book 24 exchange grief across enemy lines through the shared facts of fatherhood and mortality. In the Odyssey , four generations of one oikos reunite — Penelope, Telemachus, Laertes — through tests of memory and knowledge. Women hold real authority within the oikos but no public role: Penelope's weaving trick and bed test win kleos; Helen is 'dog-faced', beauty and blame inseparable; Clytemnestra is the ever-present foil for female fidelity; Arete's judgement carries weight among the Phaeacians. Slaves are differentiated: the loyal swineherd Eumaeus and cowherd Philoetius are named, trusted and rewarded; the disloyal Melanthius and the twelve maids are executed (22); Briseis' lament for Patroclus (Iliad 19) gives a captive woman interiority. Homer humanises all of these groups while depicting a patriarchal world — the tension A* answers should exploit. The suitors' compound is the anti-oikos: they consume, they court Penelope by force, they plot Telemachus' murder — the poem defines the household by its violation. Helen's self-blame at Hector's funeral (24 — 'shameful me, that Zeus planted a doomed destiny') gives the war's other side a woman's voice; Arete's authority among the Phaeacians (7) shows a queen whose judgement the king obeys; Nausicaa (6 — not a prescribed book) stages guest-friendship from the girl's side. Slaves' loyalty is tested to the end: Eumaeus and Philoetius are rewarded (wives, property and a place in the restored oikos, 24); Melanthius and the twelve maids are executed (22) — the oikos restored by violence as well as reunion.

topics.name: Greek Theatre
topics.subject: classical-civilisation
topics.searchText: classical-civilisation Classical Civilisation Greek Theatre City Dionysia The great Athenian festival of Dionysus Eleuthereus (late March/April) at which tragedies, satyr-plays and comedies competed; the dramatic context of the set plays. choregos A wealthy citizen who funded and trained a chorus as a public duty (liturgy/litourgia) — the financial backbone of Athenian drama. skene The stage building providing the scene's backdrop, doors for entrances/exits and (from the 5th century) a roof usable as a playing area. ekkylema The wheel platform rolled out through the skene doors to reveal interior scenes, usually tableaux of violence (e.g. Agave with Pentheus' head). mechane The crane by which gods appeared above the stage — hence deus ex machina; used for Euripides' divine endings (Bacchae). parabasis The choral interlude in old comedy where the chorus, speaking for the poet, addresses the audience directly and drops the fiction. agon A formal, structured debate in drama (e.g. Aeschylus vs Euripides in Frogs; Dionysus and Pentheus in Bacchae). hamartia Aristotle's term for the protagonist's tragic mistake or error — best read as a miscalculation rather than a moral flaw; central to interpretations of Oedipus. catharsis Aristotle's claim that tragedy purges the emotions of pity and fear in the audience; the standard ancient defence of tragedy's value. peripeteia The reversal of fortune in a tragedy; in Oedipus Tyrannus it coincides with the anagnorisis (recognition) at the shepherd's revelation. Drama at Athens was a civic and religious institution , not secular entertainment. The City Dionysia honoured Dionysus Eleuthereus with a procession (pompe), sacrifice and the display of tribute and orphans before competition began: three tragedians each presented a tetralogy of three tragedies plus a satyr-play, then five comedians a single play each. The archon selected the poets and allotted each a choregos , a rich citizen funding and training the chorus as a liturgy — theatre ran on private wealth spent for public honour. The audience, filling the Theatre of Dionysus (traditionally c.14,000–17,000), comprised male citizens alongside metics, foreigners and (debated) women; ten judges drawn by lot ranked the plays — democracy in the seating, adjudication by lottery. The theatre space evolved through the 5th and 4th centuries BC. The koilon (auditorium, initially wooden banks, later stone) curved round the orchestra (dancing floor for chorus and dithyramb); the skene gave doors and backdrop; the proskenion and its roof extended playing space. Machinery shaped staging: the ekkylema (wheel platform) revealed interior violence, and the mechane (crane) lowered gods — Euripides' Bacchae ends with Dionysus ex machina. The Theatre of Thorikos, a coastal deme theatre with an irregular, elongated auditorium, shows drama rooted below the polis level. The prescribed vases picture the performance itself: the Pronomos Vase shows a victorious team — actors, costumes, masks, aulos-player, playwright, Dionysus; the Choregos Vase (Comic Angels) a comic chorus with choregoi; the Basel Dancers krater a chorus in costume; the British Museum chous (B509, c.480 BC) two chorus-men dressed as birds; the Douris kylix the death of Pentheus; the Phiale Painter pelike tragic actors dressing. These are the evidence base for Section A commentary questions — know appearance, style, content and original location. Competition ran over several days: dithyrambic choruses of 50 men and boys (one for each tribe) opened the festival; tragedy filled the following days in tetralogies; comedy closed it. Before performance the poets held a proagon — presenting their casts without costume — and after it the judges awarded crowns and prizes, with the didaskalika records preserving results. The audience composition is debated: the war orphans paraded in armour, and women, metics and foreigners attended alongside citizens — but the precise proportion of women is genuinely open, since the evidence (Aristophanes' jokes about women in the audience; the vases' seating scenes) is comic or ambiguous. Theatre was also political space: announcements were made to the assembled city — the tribute display, and in Frogs' earlier version the debate on restoring citizen rights to the disenfranchised. Origins and development. Aristotle (Poetics) traced tragedy to improvisation by dithyramb leaders — a hymn to Dionysus — and defined it as the imitation (mimesis) of a serious, complete action in elevated language, effecting catharsis of pity and fear. From satyr-play roots it developed through the 5th century BC: Aeschylus introduced the second actor, reduced the chorus and built connected trilogies (his Agamemnon shows the form at its most ceremonial); Sophocles added the third actor, developed scene-painting and built plays on character in crisis; Euripides brought psychological realism, rhetoric and gods onstage by crane. All three expanded actors' roles against the chorus: tragedy's history is the progressive victory of dialogue over song. Aristotle's theories — peripeteia (reversal), hamartia (tragic mistake), catharsis (purgation) — are tools, not verdicts. Applied to Oedipus Tyrannus : the peripeteia (the shepherd's revelation) coincides exactly with the recognition, which Aristotle thought the plot's ideal shape; but hamartia is contested — is Oedipus rash (killing at the crossroads, cursing the murderer publicly), or simply ignorant of facts no enquiry could spare him? Note also the plot's religious frame: Apollo's oracles drive every character, and the plague in the prologue punishes the unavenged murderer's pollution (miasma). Bacchae : Dionysus' revenge on Thebes for denying his divinity. The prologue epiphany, the palace miracle (Dionysus' escape from bonds), Pentheus' agon with the disguised god, the messenger speeches from Cithaeron, the sparagmos (Agave with her son's head) and the deus ex machina ending structure a plot in which resistance to a god, not ignorance, destroys the house. The two plays give Section B essays their material: fate and free will, prophecy, the polis and its kings, tragic heroism, and the role of women (Jocasta; Agave) and foreigners (the Lydian god and his Asian maenads). Satyr-play is the fourth member of each tragic tetralogy: burlesque with a chorus dressed as satyrs under Silenus, on the same myths treated absurdly — the only complete survivor is Euripides' Cyclops. The development can be tracked through the tragedians' innovations: Aeschylus' second actor (Aristotle credits him), his connected trilogies (the Oresteia's legal and religious resolution), his choral writing; Sophocles' third actor, scene-painting and skene development, and plays built on a single character in crisis; Euripides' rhetorical debates, realistic characters, and prologues that state the myth in advance. Aristotle also transmits the tradition that tragedy's subject matter moved from the satyric and Dionysiac to the heroic — 'it was not long before serious subjects ousted the trivial' (Poetics) — which the exam expects you to weigh against the plays themselves: the Bacchae is nothing if not Dionysiac. Oedipus Tyrannus is the exam's set-text anchor. Plot devices to cite: the plague prologue; Teiresias' accusations; Jocasta's dismissal of prophecy (which triggers the fatal enquiry); the Corinthian messenger's 'relief' that becomes the catastrophe; the old Theban shepherd's refusal to speak, then confession — the recognition; the blinded Oedipus revealed by the ekkylemma. Dramatic irony governs the play: every speech about the murderer is spoken by the murderer to an audience that knows the myth. For religion: Apollo's oracle at Delphi (and to Laius before him) structures fate against free will — Oedipus acts to escape prophecy and so fulfils it; for the polis: the king is saviour (the Sphinx) then pollution; Thebes' health and the king's oikos are one. For tragic heroism: Oedipus the detective — his relentless pursuit of truth is both his greatness and his destruction; punishment falls on eyes that saw too late. Bacchae answers themes of divine justice and the polis: Pentheus, king of Thebes, denies Dionysus' divinity, imprisons him, mocks his rites, and is led — dressed as a maenad — to death on Cithaeron by the god himself; his mother Agave carries back his head. Cite: the prologue (Dionysus states the plot in advance — fate, not suspense); the bonds-miracle of the palace scene; the herdsman's two messenger speeches (the miracle on the mountain, then the sparagmos); the chorus' piety against Pentheus' rationalism; the god's cruelty in the ex machina ending (exile for the survivors — divinity beyond human ethics). The prescribed Douris kylix shows Pentheus' death in red-figure c.480 BC — before either surviving play — proving myth preceded drama and giving AO3-style comparison of visual and literary treatment; the Capodarso krater fragment pictures Jocasta and Oedipus. For both plays, weigh ancient vs modern reception : Aristotle admired Oedipus as the tragic plot; modern readers stress its detective structure and moral ambiguity, or read Bacchae as psychodrama of repression and ecstasy. A* answers hold ancient theory and modern interpretation together. For Oedipus Tyrannus, also cite: the Sphinx backstory — Oedipus' salvation of Thebes is the reason he is king, so his rise and fall are one arc; the self-blinding with Jocasta's brooches, revealed by the ekkylemma; Creon's regency and the exile question; the chorus' closing wisdom — 'count no man happy until he has died free of pain'. For Bacchae, cite: the Teiresias-and-Cadmus scene (old men dressing as worshippers — religion as choice against ridicule); the two herdsman speeches (the mountain miracle, then the sparagmos report); Agave's recognition scene, where the god corrects her illusion with cruelty; and the chorus' hymns — piety in lyric against the palace's rationalism. Nature of old comedy. Aristophanes' own parabases claim comedy began in komos revelry and phallic song; its 5th-century BC development produced a form whose tools are personal invective, obscenity, parody and topical satire, aimed at politicians (Cleon), intellectuals (Socrates in Clouds), poets and the audience itself. Structure: prologue (fantastic premise), parodos, agon (formal debate), parabasis (chorus speaks for the poet), episodes, exodos; plot devices include parody of tragedy, choral interludes and breaking the illusion. Frogs (405 BC) is the set text. Premise: Dionysus, starved of good tragedy since Euripides' death, descends to Hades with slave Xanthias (whose loaded-jokes opening parodies tragedy's solemnity) to bring back a poet — Heracles' street-map of the underworld, the frog-chorus, the Mysteries procession, then the contest: Aeschylus vs Euripides weighed in the scales — style, prologues, lyrics, and finally political utility: which poet can save the city? Aeschylus wins; Pluto sends him home with instructions to advise Athens. Cite for comedy's themes: the satire of tragedy (parody of Euripides' prologues; the weighing of verses); religion (the katabasis, the Eleusinian-flavoured mystic chorus, death and the afterlife as comic geography); the polis (the play was performed in a city losing the Peloponnesian War — its civic advice and reported effect were famous, and later tradition credited it with Athens' decision to recall the exiles). Humour types to name: personal abuse, knockabout slave comedy (Xanthias), literary parody, obscenity, and topical political jokes whose modern loss you should note as an interpretive limit. Styles compared : Aeschylus' grandeur vs Euripides' wit inside the play mirrors the tragedians' real contrast; Aristophanes' Frogs stages the debate the whole component is about — what drama is for. A* answers use the play as evidence for how a 5th-century audience understood tragedy, and weigh it against Aristotle's later theory. For Frogs, also cite: the disguise contest (Dionysus and Xanthias both dressed as Heracles, the lion skin swapped back and forth — a running gag that parodies epic heroism); the underworld geography (Charon's ferry, Aeacus' gatekeeping, the frog-chorus on the lake); the Mysteries chorus whose initiation language frames the descent; the judging scenes — Euripides' prologues tripped up by Aeschylus' oil-flask interruptions, the scales in which verses are physically weighed, and the final test of political utility: Aeschylus wins because his poetry makes men fighting-fit ('Seven Against Thebes filled them with courage') and returns to advise the city. The play's civic advice was topical in a city losing the war, and the reported effect was famous enough for later tradition to credit it with Athens' recall of the exiles.

topics.name: Imperial Image
topics.subject: classical-civilisation
topics.searchText: classical-civilisation Classical Civilisation Imperial Image divi filius 'Son of the Divine (Julius Caesar)' — Octavian's core claim from 42 BC, when the Senate deified Caesar; legitimacy and god-close charisma inherited from his adoptive father. princeps 'Leading citizen' — the republican-sounding title behind the principate: first man of the state, not (nominally) king or dictator. imperator The acclamation of a victorious commander by his troops; Augustus' use (and monopolisation) of it fused military glory with one-man rule. triumph The crowning Roman military-religious ceremony — procession of spoils, captives and the commander in triumphal dress to Jupiter's temple; Augustus celebrated a triple triumph in 29 BC. Res Gestae Divi Augusti Augustus' first-person record of his deeds, inscribed at his Mausoleum and copied across the empire (the Ankara Monument survives); the set text for H408/22. clipeus virtutis The golden shield (27 BC) the Senate hung in the Curia honouring Augustus' virtus, clementia, iustitia and pietas — the virtues as an official image. Ara Pacis Augustae The Altar of Augustan Peace (13–9 BC): procession friezes of the imperial family, myth panels (Aeneas, Roma? — Romulus/Remus, Tellus) and pax-plenty iconography. genius The guardian spirit of a man (or the state/household); after 12 BC? (the Lares reform) Augustus' genius was worshipped alongside the Lares at the crossroads shrines. pater patriae 'Father of the fatherland' — conferred on Augustus by Senate and people in 2 BC, the culminating title of his self-presentation. Carmen Saeculare Horace's hymn commissioned for the Secular Games (17 BC), sung by choirs of boys and girls — the state commissioning poetry for Augustus' new age. Caesar's assassination in 44 BC left an 18-year-old heir: Gaius Octavius, Caesar's adoptive son. The association was essential and dangerous . Benefits: the dead Caesar's popularity with the plebs and the army; the settlement of veterans; the glamour of descent from Venus and Aeneas (the Julian clan's illustrious men and gods); and legitimacy — the will made him heir, the deification (Temple of Divus Iulius, 42 BC) made him divi filius . Dangers: Caesar had been murdered for tyranny; 'king' (rex) was poison in a fundamentally anti-monarchical society. Octavian managed both: the comet at the funeral games (Sidus Iulium) backed the apotheosis — the prescribed denarius with the eight-rayed comet beside Augustus' head; while the aureus pairing his bare head with Caesar's laureate one claims inheritance. The triumvirate (43 BC) was openly unconstitutional — hence the justification of civil war in the Res Gestae: those who murdered his father were punished, and those who waged war on the state ('a faction') were conquered in two battles (Philippi). Antony was never named: the war of 32–31 BC was presented as Rome against a woman and her oriental court — Horace's Odes 1.37 makes Cleopatra a fatale monstrum whose death is no ordinary woman's; Epodes 9 celebrates Actium. The settlement of 27 BC renamed him Augustus, 'the revered one', returning (nominally) the res publica to Senate and people — Res Gestae 34 is the set-text core: 'after I had extinguished civil wars... I transferred the state from my own power to the control of the senate and people of Rome'. The triumvirate itself was openly unconstitutional — a three-man commission of proscription modelled on Sulla's, whose death lists killed Cicero among thousands; the Res Gestae never mentions it. Sextus Pompey's naval blockade starved Italy until Agrippa won Naulochus (36 BC), after which Octavian broke with Lepidus and had only Antony left. The coins are the mass media of the transition: the aureus pairing bare-headed Octavian with the laureate Caesar claims inheritance at the moment of apotheosis; the aureus of Octavian seated on a bench holding a scroll projects clementia and legality; the denarius with Pax holding the olive branch and cornucopia sells peace while civil war still ran. Note how the image meets each audience: the plebs read grain and games, the army read land and pay, the elite read titles, offices and restoration — the same image, different dialects. The image: a capable commander whose wars were glorious, defensive and beneficial. The triple triumph of 29 BC (Dalmatia, Actium, Egypt) staged victory in the Republic's supreme ceremony — its religious pompe, its spoils, its captives; the Res Gestae counts the triumphs, the salutations as imperator, the settlements of veterans and the wars 'won by land and sea'. Reality : Agrippa won Naulochus (36 BC) and commanded at Actium; the Alpine and Balkan campaigns were grinding; the Parthian recovery of the standards (20 BC) was a negotiated settlement, not a war — presented as a triumph (the Prima Porta breastplate's central scene shows a Parthian returning a standard beneath the sky-god, with Apollo and Artemis of Delos below). The prescribed coins package the claims: Pax with olive branch and cornucopia (peace and plenty); sacrificial implements above a tripod and patera (piety as military); the Gaius and Lucius aureus (the heirs as princes of the youth). Justification of civil wars runs through the sources: Philippi avenged the father; the Perusine War is omitted; Sextus Pompey is dismissed as 'a pirate' (Res Gestae 25); Antony's campaign is a war against Cleopatra, not citizens. The Kalabsha Gate relief shows Octavian making offering to Egyptian deities — conqueror as pharaoh, domination dressed as accommodation. For Section B: weigh image against reality — the salutations, triumphs and standard-recovery as image; Agrippa's commands and the body-count as reality; and the Res Gestae's silences as evidence of deliberate shaping. The triumph's regalia made its message visible: the commander in toga picta and laurel crown on the quadriga, spoils and placards displaying the conquests, captives walking before the chariot, the procession climbing to Jupiter Capitolinus — military glory ending in religion. Augustus' triple triumph spread over three days (Dalmatia, Actium, Egypt), and the Res Gestae counts the salutations as imperator (21 in all), the colonies settled and the sums distributed — each a claim to have converted war into public benefit. The Parthian settlement was dressed as victory twice: the standards' return (20 BC) was celebrated with an arch in the Forum, and the Prima Porta breastplate makes the diplomacy the statue's central image — a negotiated return staged as a conquest won under the sky-god's favour. Religious leader. Augustus rebuilt 82 temples (Res Gestae 20), restored lapsed priesthoods, became pontifex maximus (12 BC) and reformed the crossroads cult: the Lares were paired as Lares Praestites and worshipped with the genius Augusti — the state worshipping the ruler's guardian spirit, divinity by association without divinity by claim. His closeness to Apollo was architectural and personal: the Temple of Apollo Palatinus joined his modest house on the Palatine (Suetonius describes the house's plainness as image). The Ara Pacis Augustae (13–9 BC) is the set-text monument: the altar of Augustan peace, its friezes process the imperial family with senators and priests (the real religious elite), its panels flank myth with allegory — Aeneas' sacrifice (pietas), the wolf-and-twins panel and Tellus with babies and plenty (peace's fruits). The Secular Games (17 BC) staged a new age: Horace's Carmen Saeculare, commissioned by the state and sung by choirs of boys and girls, calls on Apollo and Diana for the new saeculum. Culture hero. The myth of Saturn's Golden Age — Augustus as a new Saturn, peace and plenty returning (Horace Odes 4.15; the iconography of Pax, Ceres? — the Ara Pacis' Tellus) — reframed the strongman as restorer. Pater Patriae and the family. The title (2 BC) completes the Res Gestae's arc — 'father of the fatherland', quoted with the Senate's and people's words (ch. 35). The clipeus virtutis (27 BC) fixed the four virtues: virtus, clementia, iustitia, pietas — clementia after civil war is a pointed image. The moral legislation (lex Iulia de maritandis ordinibus and de adulteriis, 18 BC) incentivised marriage and childbearing, criminalised adultery — and was enforced against his own daughter Julia (Suetonius, Life of Augustus, the extracts on his family discipline). The imperial family as role models : the Gaius and Lucius aureus presents the heirs veiled with shields and priestly symbols; the Head of Livia carries the pudicitia iconography of the Roman matron; Augustus himself modelled modest living — the Prima Porta statue's barefoot pose and Cupid (divine descent via Venus) beside a general's breastplate. The Secular Games' machinery made the new age official: heralds summoned everyone to a spectacle no one alive had seen; 27 boys and 27 girls of citizen parents sang the Carmen Saeculare by day and by night; sacrifices to Apollo and Diana (and to Juno, the Fates and Ilithyia) closed each sequence. The genius-worship had its own mechanics: the crossroads shrines (compita) rebuilt, with images of the two Lares and the genius Augusti, served by the neighbourhood magistri — the state's religion reaching every street. The moral legislation's penalties were practical as well as symbolic: adultery became a public crime tried by standing courts, with fathers (and in some cases husbands) bound to prosecute, and the childbearing incentives (ius trium liberorum) gave legal privileges to parents of three. The building programme was image made physical. Suetonius' famous claim — he 'found Rome brick and left it marble' (ch. 28–29) — sums the programme: the Forum of Augustus (built from spoils, its Temple of Mars Ultor avenging both Philippi and the standards, its porticoes lined with statues of summi viri and the Julian family — history as image), the Mausoleum (28 BC, a dynastic tomb on the Campus Martius — the Res Gestae's intended home), the Theatre of Marcellus, aqueducts and the Forum's triumphal arches. The Res Gestae closes with the empire's edges: embassies from India, and the closure of the gates of Janus three times (ch. 13) — peace as military achievement. Evaluating the Res Gestae is the Section B staple. For propaganda: it is first-person, selective and silent where damaging (Antony unnamed; the Perusine War absent; civil wars as 'a faction'); it presents negotiated settlements as victories; its claim to have restored the res publica (ch. 34) coexists with permanent tribunician power and command of army and provinces. For history: its facts check out — the building lists, the dates, the populations enrolled — Mommsen called it 'the queen of inscriptions'; Zanker reads the visual programme (coins, statues, buildings) as a coherent imperial ideology; Wallace-Hadrill stresses its address to every social class; Galinsky treats it as self-conscious self-presentation rather than lying. Its audiences differed: the bronze copies across the empire, bilingual in Greek and Latin, addressed the Greek east as well as Rome; the plebs read grain, games and buildings; the elite read titles and virtue. Later representations test long-term success. The Sebasteion at Aphrodisias (Claudian era) built three-storey porticoes of reliefs: divinities, emperors, and the ethne — conquered peoples of land and sea — an imperial cult complex that takes Augustus' image for granted a generation after his death. Suetonius' Life of Augustus (2nd century AD) balances the image: clementia, modesty, generosity against adultery, cruelty and luxury in the private extracts — evidence that the self-presentation fixed the terms of debate even when contradicted. A* judgement: the image outlasted its contradictions — that is its success; the final topic is assessing how far it lasted beyond his lifetime, and Suetonius is the proof that it did. The Forum of Augustus deserves the detail: its porticoes displayed statues of the summi viri — great Romans of the Republic — each with an elogium (career summary), the Julian family at the centre with Aeneas and Romulus flanking; history as a curated image with Augustus' line as its spine. The Mausoleum was begun in 28 BC — the dynastic tomb intended to house the Res Gestae, and the proof that the image was planned for posterity. The Sebasteion at Aphrodisias, built a generation later under Claudius, is the best test of long-term success: three storeys of reliefs — divinities above, emperors below, with panels of the conquered ethne (peoples of land and sea, Britannia among them) — an imperial cult complex in a Greek city that takes Augustus' entire image for granted. Suetonius' extracts make the terms of debate explicit: clementia and modesty in the public chapters against adultery, cruelty and luxury in the private ones — the image survived its contradictions.

topics.name: Greek Religion
topics.subject: classical-civilisation
topics.searchText: classical-civilisation Classical Civilisation Greek Religion reciprocity (do ut des) 'I give so that you give' — the contractual logic of Greek cult: honour (sacrifice, libation, votives) flows upward; aid, protection and fertility flow downward. anthropomorphism The gods' human-like form and psychology — body, family, jealousy, deceit — as established for the Greeks by Homer and Hesiod (cf. Herodotus 2.53). hero cult Worship of an exceptional dead mortal at or near their tomb, with chthonic-style offerings; heroes protected communities and were prayed to for aid (e.g. Theseus, Brasidas at Amphipolis). mystery cult A cult of initiation (e.g. the Eleusinian Mysteries) promising benefits through secret rites known only to initiates; participation was a matter of personal choice. incubation Ritual sleep in a god's sanctuary — especially that of Asclepius at Epidaurus — during which the god healed the sleeper or prescribed a cure in a dream. asebeia Impiety — a prosecutable offence at Athens (e.g. Socrates, 399 BC); religious authority lay with the polis, its laws and its customs rather than a scripture or church. hecatomb A sacrifice of (originally) a hundred cattle; the great public burnt offerings of state festivals, e.g. on the ash altar of Zeus at Olympia. libation The pouring of wine, water or oil to the gods — at symposia, oaths and sacrifices, in both state and private contexts; the regular renewing of reciprocity. votive offering A dedication (statue, relief, armour, anatomical model) made to a god in thanks or hope — from private anatomical votives at the Asclepieion to state treasures at Delphi and Olympia. Panathenaia Athena's state festival: annual (Lesser) and four-yearly Greater (with games from 566 BC), culminating in the procession to the Acropolis and the hecatomb; the peplos for Athena was woven and presented. The Olympians are anthropomorphic : they have bodies, genealogies (Hesiod's Theogony), moods, jealousies and limitations — but not omnipotence or omniscience. Their scope of power is bounded: Zeus weighs fates on his scales (Iliad 16, 22) rather than simply commanding outcomes; gods cannot reverse what is fated. The relationship with mortals is reciprocal : mortals give honour — sacrifice, libation, votives, festivals — and gods give protection, fertility, victory and healing. Greek cult is contractual (do ut des), not creedal: there is no revealed truth to believe, only powers to honour correctly. Homer and Hesiod were foundational: Herodotus (2.53) credits them with teaching the Greeks the gods' genealogies, epithets and forms barely four centuries before his own writing — the literary sources of the gods' characters. Common epithets map the gods' different roles and contexts: Zeus Agoraios (of the agora), Zeus Phratrios (of the brotherhoods), Zeus Philios (of friendship), Zeus Herkeios (of the courtyard) — one god with many functions; the exam asks how far these were thought of as separate, distinct entities (they were not: one Zeus, many cult titles — but each with its own cult, icon and priest). Hero cults are the other half of Greek worship: exceptional dead mortals — founders, leaders, the glorious dead — received offerings at their tombs and were prayed to for aid, in a chthonic (underworld) register contrasting with Olympian sacrifice. Examples: Theseus' bones translated to Athens by Cimon (c.470s BC); Brasidas buried and honoured as founder-hero at Amphipolis. Worship ranged across Panhellenic (Zeus at Olympia, Apollo at Delphi), localised (Athena Polias at Athens, city-specific cults) and personal (household gods, private vows) — the spectrum the whole component measures. The Olympian roster is fixed by tradition: Zeus, Hera, Poseidon, Demeter, Athena, Apollo, Artemis, Ares, Aphrodite, Hephaestus, Hermes and (in the Athenian list) Hestia or Dionysus — twelve names worshipped Panhellenically, but each with local cults, iconographies and festivals. Hesiod's Theogony supplies the genealogy that orders them; his Works and Days supplies their justice — Zeus who watches all and punishes wrongdoing. Hero cult fills the space between gods and the dead: exceptional mortals received tombs, offerings and prayers for aid — Herakles was worshipped as both hero and god across Greece; city founders (Theseus at Athens) and war dead (Brasidas at Amphipolis) drew cult; and the chthonic register (offerings poured into the earth, at dusk, to the dead below) contrasts with Olympian sacrifice (burnt on the altar, by day, to the gods above). Mystery cults inverted the communal norm: participation was a matter of personal choice and initiation, open across the usual barriers. The Eleusinian Mysteries of Demeter and Persephone (whose Homeric Hymn explains the myth) promised initiates better prospects — for the harvest and for death; the ritual was secret, with two grades (mystes, then epoptes at a later Great Eleusinia). The prescribed red-figure plaque of the cult of Eleusis (c.400–300 BC) shows Demeter and Persephone with initiates — the evidence base. Mystery cults offered what the polis could not: individual religious experience, hope and a personal relationship with the divine. The healing cult of Asclepius blurs the god/hero boundary: a mortal healer deified, worshipped as both god and hero, with incubation (ritual sleep) and miracle cures recorded in the iamata inscriptions at Epidaurus. The prescribed marble anatomical votive from the shrine of Asclepius (British Museum) shows the body parts dedicated in thanks — private piety made material. The oracle at Dodona (Zeus and Dione, in Epirus) served private individuals : questions scratched on lead tablets — will the child be mine? whom should I marry? should I sail? — asked for personal help and advice, contrasted with Delphi's state business. The prescribed Kodros Painter kylix (c.440–430 BC) depicts a consultation of the Pythia at Delphi — the oracle in use, not just in myth. Together these three show the personal face of Greek religion that the polis-centered festivals hide; A* answers use them to complicate any claim that religion was purely civic. The Eleusinian Mysteries rest on the myth of the Homeric Hymn to Demeter: Persephone abducted by Hades, Demeter's grief and withdrawal, the famine that forces Zeus' settlement, and the gift of the Mysteries to Eleusis. The officials are hereditary priestly families: the hierophant (revealer of the sacred things) and the dadouchos (torch-bearer), with the kykeon drink and the two grades of initiation. Asclepius' cult spread from Epidaurus across the Greek world (a temple in Piraeus by 420 BC); his characterisation as both god and hero — a deified mortal healer — and the iamata inscriptions (patients' cures recorded for public display) make the healing cult the best-documented personal religion. At Dodona, the oak's rustling and the bronze cauldrons' humming were read as Zeus' voice; the lead tablets record questions on marriage, children, travel and property — the private questions the polis' festivals never ask. Levels of participation : household (Zeus Ktesios, Hestia, the herm at the door, ancestors), deme (local festivals — the Rural Dionysia, Thesmophoria for women), polis (state sacrifices and festivals, funded by deme and polis) and Panhellenic (Olympia, Delphi, Isthmia, Nemea). Religious authority lay with the polis, its laws and customs — there was no church, no scripture, no dogma; asebeia was a legal offence (Socrates 399 BC; the Mysteries scandals of 415 BC). Politics and religion were intertwined: assemblies consulted oracles before wars (the Sicilian expedition's omens); Sparta's kings needed Delphic approval; sacred wars were fought over Delphi — political decisions were sometimes made on the basis of divine intervention. The Panathenaia is the component's set festival. Structure: the Lesser (annual) and Greater (every four years, penteteric) Panathenaia; contests in athletics, music and (from the 6th century BC) the apobates race, with prizes of Panathenaic amphorae filled with sacred olive oil (the prescribed black-figure Panathenaic amphora, 333–332 BC, British Museum 1856,1001.1, shows the armed Athena between columns and the prize event); the procession (pompe) from the city gate up the Panathenaic Way to the Acropolis, with the hecatomb, the girls (kanephoroi, arrephoroi, ergastinai) who carried baskets and wove the peplos, and the presentation of the robe to Athena Polias. Significance for Athens: Panhellenic spectacle (athletes and visitors from across the Greek world), civic unity (the procession represented all Athenians — the Parthenon frieze depicts it as an eternal procession), and political power (Peisistratus used it; the fifth-century BC Acropolis made it the image of the polis). The impiety cases define the limits of authority: Andocides was prosecuted over the Mysteries scandal of 415 BC (the herms' mutilation and the profanation of the rites); Socrates was tried and executed in 399 BC. Politics and religion intertwined in the other direction too: the Athenian assembly consulted oracles before the Sicilian expedition, Nicias' lunar eclipse delayed the retreat, and Sparta's kings needed Delphic approval for their wars — political decisions were sometimes made on the basis of divine oracular intervention. The Panathenaia's programme also included the ship-cart — the peplos of Athena hoisted like a sail and processed to the Acropolis — and the musical contests added under Pericles; the festival's representation of all Athenians (all tribes, ages and sexes in the procession) is monumentalised in the Parthenon frieze. The prescribed sites are three sanctuaries with different functions. The Athenian Acropolis (Parthenon, Erechtheion, Propylaia) is the polis' civic and religious heart: Athena Polias' cult statue, the city's treasury, the image of Athens to the world. Delphi is the Panhellenic oracle: the Temple of Apollo with its adyton and the Pythia, consulted in a fixed process (purification, fee, lot-order, state business first); the Sacred Way lined with state treasuries and votives (the Siphnian Treasury); the theatre and stadium (Pythian games) — prophecy embedded in festival. Olympia is the Panhellenic games: the Temple of Zeus with Pheidias' chryselephantine statue, the ash altar of Zeus (the hecatombs' ash mound), treasuries, the Echo Stoa and stadium — competition between poleis under a sacred truce (ekecheiria), Panhellenic identity in action. Ritual and priests. Blood sacrifice (thusia) is the central rite — purpose: honour, thanksgiving, communion, divination; process: victim selected and processed, water and barley scattered, the knife concealed, the throat cut, the gods' portion (bones and fat) burned, the meat eaten as a communal feast; significance: the whole social order rehearsed. Libations (wine, water, oil) renewed reciprocity daily, at oaths and symposia; votive offerings — from anatomical models at the Asclepieion to state treasuries — made gratitude permanent. Priests and priestesses were part-time ritual experts, not a preaching class: the priest conducted the rite, often as a hereditary or elected honour; aristocratic families monopolised key posts (the Eteoboutads held the priestess of Athena Polias and the priest of Poseidon-Erechtheus; the Eumolpids and Kerykes ran the Mysteries); women held prominent posts (the Pythia; Athena Polias; the Thesmophoria's priestesses) — religion was the one public arena open to women. Religion and philosophy. From the 6th century BC, philosophical thinking challenged the traditional gods: Xenophanes mocked anthropomorphism — Ethiopians draw their gods snub-nosed, horses would draw horse-gods; there is one god, not like mortals in body or thought. Socrates spoke of a personal divine sign (daimonion), rejected the Homeric gods' immoral behaviour, and was tried and executed for impiety in 399 BC (not believing in the city's gods, introducing new divinities, corrupting the young) — ideas the exam treats as genuinely radical in context, though note the counter-view: philosophers inherited the gods' vocabulary (Xenophanes still posits a god; Socrates still swears by Zeus), temples kept being built, and philosophy coexisted with cult rather than destroying it. The tension — a religion of ritual and reciprocity meeting a philosophy of reason — is the thought half's core evaluation. Delphi's consultation process was fixed and public: purification in the Castalian spring, the pelanos fee, the order by lot with state business first, the Pythia's response from the adyton — and the scholarly debate over how she prophesied (the vapours, the laurel, the verses' ambiguity) is itself examinable. Olympia's games ran under the sacred truce (ekecheiria) with events from the footrace through the combat sports to the chariot races; the ash altar's mound grew with each hecatomb, and Pheidias' Zeus — one of the ancient world's wonders — sat within the temple. On philosophy, the exam's evaluation is the extent to which the ideas were 'truly new': Xenophanes' monotheism still posits a god; Socrates still swears by Zeus and dies obeying the city's gods; Anaxagoras' nous still orders a cosmos — philosophical thinking inherited the gods' vocabulary even as it criticised their stories, and temples kept being built.

topics.name: Greek Art
topics.subject: classical-civilisation
topics.searchText: classical-civilisation Classical Civilisation Greek Art kouros An archaic Greek free-standing marble statue of a nude youth, standing frontal with one foot advanced; developed from geometric rigidity (New York Kouros, c.600 BC) towards naturalism (Aristodikos, c.500 BC). kore The female counterpart — a draped standing maiden, usually a votive offering in a sanctuary (e.g. the Peplos Kore from the Athenian Acropolis); flesh painted white. contrapposto The classical stance: weight on one leg, so hips and shoulders tilt in opposite directions — the naturalistic balance of the Doryphoros. chiastic composition Symmetrical, A-B-B-A balance of body parts (tense/relaxed alternating) that organises Polykleitos' Doryphoros and his Canon of proportions. canon (kanon) Polykleitos' treatise on ideal proportions (symmetria), exemplified by the Doryphoros — 'the' statue by which sculptors learned proportion. foreshortening Representing depth on a two-dimensional surface — receding limbs and shields drawn in perspective (Euthymides' experiments on the Three Men Carousing amphora). torsion Twisting of the torso to imply violent movement in space — Euphronios' Herakles and Antaios; Myron's Diskobolos. black-figure Vase-painting technique: figures painted in slip silhouette on the clay, details incised, added white (female flesh) and purple; dominant to c.530 BC. red-figure The reverse: figures reserved in clay against a black slip ground; details painted with brushes and diluted slip — finer line, foreshortening, emotion; dominant from c.530 BC. chryselephantine A cult statue of gold and ivory over a wooden core — Pheidias' Athena Parthenos (Parthenon) and Zeus at Olympia. Free-standing sculpture had four functions: cult statue (the god's image in a temple — chryselephantine Athena Parthenos, Zeus at Olympia), votive (a dedication to a god — most kouroi and korai stood in sanctuaries), grave marker (the Anavysos Kouros for Kroisos; the Aristodikos) and memorial (the Delphic Charioteer commemorates Polyzalos' victory). Architectural sculpture worked by position: Doric metopes (relief panels between triglyphs, usually fighting scenes), Ionic friezes (continuous narrative bands — the Siphnian Treasury, the Parthenon) and pediments (the gable tympana, where a centrepiece anchors flanking figures that shrink towards the corners). Pot shapes map uses: amphorae for storage and transport, kraters for mixing wine, hydriai for water, oinochoai for pouring, kylikes for drinking, lekythoi for oil — shape dictates which scenes suit which vessel (symposium scenes on kraters and cups; maenads on wine vessels). Materials : marble (block-carving; luminous, but heavy and inflexible) vs bronze (lost-wax casting, hollow and strong — allowing free-standing action poses, chased detail, added metals for lips, teeth and eyes: the Delphic Charioteer's inlaid glass eyes and copper lashes). Limestone survives at Corcyra's pediment; marble dominates later. In vase-painting, clay, slip and added colour (white, purple) carry the design. Limitations drive the exam: damaged pieces (the Antikytheran Youth; the Peplos Kore's missing arm — attribute debated), reconstructions (the Hermes and Dionysus' right arm is a restoration controversy) and copies (most classical bronzes survive only as Roman marble copies — the Diskobolos and Doryphoros; the copy preserves pose and proportion but loses the bronze's surfaces, eyes and balance). Always ask what a piece can and cannot tell us. The Parthenon metopes show the four great battles in position: the Gigantomachy (east), the Amazonomachy (west), the Centauromachy (south — the prescribed XXVI–XXVIII among them) and the Ilioupersis (north) — gods over giants, Greeks over Amazons, Lapiths over Centaurs, Greeks over Trojans. Grave markers could be kouroi (the Anavysos) or stelai with relief scenes; memorial sculpture (the Delphic Charioteer) commemorated victory rather than death. Panathenaic prize amphorae are the shape-function link in action: the shape (wide shoulders, black-figure, armed Athena between columns) was fixed by convention for the prize oil, and prize amphorae kept black-figure long after red-figure conquered the market. The kouros develops from geometric rigidity to naturalism: the New York Kouros (c.600 BC) is frontal, block-like, with geometric anatomy; Kleobis and Biton (c.580 BC, Delphi — Herodotus 1.31 tells their story of a blessed death) are Argive, stockier; the Anavysos Kouros (Kroisos, c.530 BC) shows fleshed musculature and the archaic smile; the Aristodikos Kouros (c.500 BC) is shorter-haired, more proportional — the formula dissolving before the classical pose. The kore develops through drapery and adornment: the Berlin Standing Goddess (c.570 BC) wears layered drapery; the Peplos Kore (c.530–540 BC, Acropolis) is plainer, with painted patterns and added-white flesh — colour, now lost, was central. Bronze moves to action: the Delphic Charioteer (c.470 BC, Severe style, inlaid eyes) stands at rest within his chariot; the Artemision Zeus (or Poseidon — the attribute is debated; c.460 BC) strides with arms extended; the Diskobolos (Myron, c.450 BC) twists at the instant before release; the Doryphoros (Polykleitos, c.440 BC) perfects contrapposto and the Canon; the Antikytheran Youth (c.340 BC) shows late proportional change; the Aphrodite of the Agora, Eirene and Ploutos (Kephisodotos, c.370 BC — allegory of peace and wealth), Hermes and Dionysus (Praxitelean S-curve), the Aphrodite of Knidos (Praxiteles, c.340 BC — the first monumental female nude) and the Apoxyomenos (Lysippos, c.330 BC — smaller head, new eight-head proportions, arms breaking into the viewer's space) complete the arc. Black-figure develops through line and pattern: the Gorgon Painter's dinos (frontal Gorgon faces, profile bodies); Sophilos' dinos and the François Vase (Kleitias, c.570 BC — miniaturist, labelled figures, multiple myth cycles); the Amasis Painter's neck amphora (refined line); Exekias' Achilles and Ajax playing dice (c.540 BC — psychological tension, dignity, the spears' verticals) and Dionysus sailing on the ocean kylix (full-frontal innovation; the mast becomes a vine). Red-figure inverts the technique and unlocks drawing: the Andokides Painter's bilingual amphora (both techniques on one pot); the Pioneers — Euphronios (Herakles and Antaios: torsion, musculature, foreshortened feet; Herakles and the Amazons) and Euthymides (Three Men Carousing — foreshortening 'as never Euphronios [did]'; Hector arming) — compete in experiments and sign their work; the Berlin Painter (Achilles and Hector/Memnon — single figures on black ground) refines; the Kleophrades Painter (the Trojan War hydria — pathos in the sack of Troy; Dionysus and the Maenads) and the Pan Painter (Perseus and Medusa; Boreas pursuing Oreithyia — wit and movement) extend the range. Mannerists deliberately revive archaic manner in red-figure after 480 BC. For each work: appearance, style, content, original location, and what it can and cannot tell us. Details the exam expects: Kleobis and Biton were dedicated by Argos at Delphi, and Herodotus (1.31) tells their story — they drew their mother's cart to the temple and died in their sleep, blessed by the goddess; the Peplos Kore's missing arm once held an attribute that is debated (a bow, a pomegranate, a bird); the Artemision Zeus (or Poseidon) is identified by the attribute the empty hand once held — thunderbolt or trident; the Doryphoros survives through copies (Naples; Pompeii) that transmit pose and proportion; the Aphrodite of Knidos' fame is recorded by Pliny (Natural History 36), with the Knidians' refusal to sell her; the Apoxyomenos' scraping pose breaks the figure's bounds — the arms extend into the viewer's space, completing Lysippos' new proportions (smaller head, taller body). Section A commentary questions reward a fixed method . Analyse in this order: Composition — dominant verticals, horizontals and diagonals: Exekias' dice amphora builds a triangle of cloaks under the spears' verticals; the Doryphoros' chiastic balance (tense right leg/relaxed right arm; relaxed left leg/tense left arm); contrapposto in every classical stance. Pose, anatomy and movement — portrayal of the body from geometric outline (New York Kouros) to musculature (Anavysos) to idealised harmony (Doryphoros); torsion (Diskobolos; Euphronios' Antaios); foreshortening (Euthymides' shields and feet); movement captured between poses (the Artemision Zeus' stride). Emotion — pathos: the Kleophrades Painter's Trojan War hydria (women's grief); Exekias' dice players' concentration; the Hermes and Dionysus' tenderness; the archaic smile's ambiguity. Evaluation — what the piece tells us about function, technique and context, and what it cannot; the range of ancient and modern interpretations. A* answers link technique to effect and effect to context: contrapposto is not just a stance but a claim about the ideal body; foreshortening is not just a trick but a claim about the picture plane. The paper's question types (short answer, 10-mark stimulus, 20- and 30-mark essays) reward this structure at every length. Use the method on the whole range: the Berlin Painter refines red-figure to single figures on the black ground (Achilles and Memnon on the volute krater — the figures' edges against the black field are the technique's clarity at its height); the Kleophrades Painter's Trojan War hydria (a water pot — the sack of Troy on the vessel women used) places pathos at the centre: Neoptolemos swings Astyanax onto Hector's blood; the women grieve; Priam's figure closes the scene. Emotion's portrayal develops with the techniques: the archaic smile's ambiguity, the Severe style's gravity, the classical pathos of the late 5th century BC (the hydria) and the 4th century's grace (Hermes and Dionysus). Mythology dominates, but everyday life is reflected inside it: the Wedding of Peleus and Thetis (Sophilos; the François Vase) mirrors Athenian wedding processions; maenads and symposiasts decorate wine vessels for symposium use; Achilles arming (Euthymides) mirrors the hoplite's own kit. Free-standing themes : mortals and gods (the Delphic Charioteer as a mortal's dedication; the Artemision Zeus' attribute debate); 4th-century concepts — the Aphrodite of Knidos (sensuality and religion; Pliny records the Knidians refusing to sell her), Eirene and Ploutos (peace and wealth as allegory after the Peloponnesian War). Architectural themes : Medusa (Corcyra's west pediment — apotropaic, terrifying at the threshold); the Centauromachy (Olympia and the Parthenon metopes — order over barbarism, read by many as a Persian Wars subtext); the Trojan War (Aphaia's east and west pediments — Greek vs Trojan heroes; the Parthenon's metopes); Olympia's pediments (the chariot race of Pelops and Oenomaus; the Lapiths and Centaurs) and Herakles' labours in its metopes. Vase themes : Achilles (Exekias' dice players; the Berlin Painter's Achilles and Memnon), Athena (on the Panathenaic-type amphorae), Dionysus (Exekias' sailing kylix; the Kleophrades Painter's maenads), Herakles (Euphronios' Antaios and Amazons), and the Trojan War (the Kleophrades Painter's hydria). Contextual analysis is the A* skill. The social, political and religious context shaped the art: the Persian Wars (480–479 BC) turned battle myths (Centauromachy, Amazonomachy, Gigantomachy) into allegories of Greek order over Persian chaos; the Acropolis' rebuilding after the Persian destruction (the Perserschutt buried and preserved the korai); symposium culture dictated vessel shapes; sanctuary economies funded votives. Limits : original paint is lost — the modern white marble and terracotta are illusions; workshop practice is inferred; female painters are unknown. Interpretations differ ancient and modern: cult statues awed worshippers, museums aestheticise them; the Aphrodite of Knidos scandalised and attracted in equal measure (Pliny's anecdote); modern scholarship (Woodford, Boardman, Moignard) reads style chronologically. A* answers evaluate usefulness — what the sources prove about technique, function and context — and mark their limitations honestly. Olympia's pediments pair a local myth with a Panhellenic one: the east pediment's chariot race of Pelops and Oenomaus (the sanctuary's founding myth of the games) and the west's Centauromachy (Lapiths vs Centaurs — order over barbarism); the metopes show the labours of Herakles (the Cretan Bull, the Garden of the Hesperides, the Stables of Augeas among the prescribed) — the Panhellenic hero at the Panhellenic games. The Perserschutt detail is the exam's best example of context preserving art: the Athenians buried the damaged korai and kouroi of the destroyed Acropolis, which preserved them for us; the rebuilt Parthenon replaced the damaged old temple of Athena. On interpretations: cult statues' awe (Pheidias' Zeus) vs museum aesthetics; the Aphrodite of Knidos' scandal and fame (Pliny); and the modern scholarly readings (Woodford's chronological method, Boardman's stylistic surveys, Moignard's vase analysis, Jenkins' architectural sculpture) — cite them to support, not to decorate.

topics.name: Love and Relationships
topics.subject: classical-civilisation
topics.searchText: classical-civilisation Classical Civilisation Love and Relationships epithumia Desire or appetite — the bodily longing that Plato and Seneca distinguish from love (which they give a rational or spiritual definition). sophrosyne Self-control, moderation — the virtue Greek thought demanded of both sexes, but especially policed in women. paiderastia Institutionalised Greek homoerotic courtship between an older lover (erastes) and a younger beloved (eromenos), with norms of gift, shame and restraint. kyrios The male guardian (father, husband, nearest male kin) with legal authority over an Athenian woman and her property. patria potestas The Roman father's legal power over his descendants — life and death authority that marriage (cum manu or sine manu) modified for the wife. pudicitia Roman sexual modesty and chastity — the matrona's defining virtue, policed by law and iconography (the veil; the Head of Livia's imagery). lex Iulia de adulteriis Augustus' adultery law (18 BC): criminalised adultery, gave fathers and husbands the duty to prosecute — the legal double standard against female sexuality. monodic lyric Sappho's genre: songs for solo performance with lyre/aulos accompaniment, composed for her circle of female companions — distinct from public choral poetry. praeceptor amoris 'Teacher of love' — Ovid's didactic persona in the Ars Amatoria, parodying the instructional manuals of farming and rhetoric. apatheia The Stoic ideal of freedom from passion (pathos) — passions as false judgements to be corrected by reason; the frame for Seneca's treatment of love. Greek ideals. The ideal man is self-controlled, brave, publicly useful (andreia and sophrosyne); the ideal woman is chaste, obedient, silent indoors — Pericles' funeral oration gives the classic statement: the best woman's reputation is not to be talked of among men, good or bad (Thucydides 2.45). Status is legally and civically unequal: an Athenian woman needs a kyrios (guardian), cannot vote or own property outright, and her citizen status matters only as the conduit of citizen children (Pericles' citizenship law, 451/450 BC); her public outlets are religious (the Thesmophoria, priesthoods). Roman women sit under patria potestas , though marriage sine manu (without hand) left them in their birth family and, by the late Republic, legally freer than Greek counterparts; the matrona's virtue is pudicitia, the ideal the univira (one-man woman) embodies. Marriage. A good marriage produces legitimate children, joins properties (dowry) and joins families; its joys are companionship and civic continuity. Sexual freedom is double-standard : men in Greece could frequent hetairai and slaves and practise paiderastia; Roman men meretrices; women in both cultures faced enforced monogamy — Augustus' lex Iulia de adulteriis (18 BC) criminalised female adultery and placed prosecution on the family. Adultery is thus theft of another man's property-rights in the Greek frame, and a crime against the state's moral order in the Roman one. Ideal vs reality is the recurring evaluation: funerary monuments and laws praise the silent matron, but literature records real voices — Medea's speech on the desperate bargain of marriage (Euripides, citable as context), Sappho's women who feel, Ovid's women who manipulate. The thought half's question — what makes a 'good' or 'bad' way to love — runs through all four topics. Greek women's religious outlets were real power: the Thesmophoria (the women's festival of Demeter) was organised and run entirely by citizen women; the priestess of Athena Polias (from the Eteoboutad family) held one of the city's most important posts. Xenophon's Oeconomicus gives the Greek training of the wife: Ischomachus marries a girl of fifteen and trains her to run the household — the ideal in a manual, citable as context. Roman women's legal position improved across the Republic: marriage sine manu left them in their birth family's potestas; they could appear in court and manage property; the matrona's veil (the flammeum) and pudicitia remained the ideal, and Augustus' laws (the ius trium liberorum privileges; the adultery courts) policed the ideal by law. Definitions of love — the Symposium stages a competition of speeches: Eryximachus (love as harmony balancing opposites, medical and cosmic); Pausanias (two Aphrodites — Common Love, bodily and venal, vs Heavenly Love, the noble love of character that grounds respectable paiderastia); Aristophanes (the myth of split beings: humans were doubles, cut apart by Zeus, and love is the desire and pursuit of the whole — the physical symptom is the yearning of halves to melt together); Agathon (love as the youngest, most beautiful and virtuous god); and Socrates, reporting Diotima : love is not a god but a great daimon, intermediate between mortal and immortal — the desire for the perpetual possession of the good, expressed as reproduction in beauty, and ascending by the ladder of love from one beautiful body, to all bodies, to souls, to practices and laws, to knowledge, to Beauty itself. Love vs desire. Desire (epithumia) is appetite — for food, drink, sex; love, on Diotima's account, is desire rationally redirected to the good and the everlasting. The distinction grounds the control and resistance of desire: desire should be controlled because it misjudges the good (aiming at the mortal, not the everlasting) and resisted through education, shame and philosophy — the beloved in respectable paiderastia restrains the lover with shame (aidos) and law (nomos), and Socrates resists even Alcibiades' attempt to seduce him (the final speech, where the roles reverse). Homoerotic relationships are thus both the norm being theorised (erastes/eromenos courtship, age asymmetry, gifts) and the object of Plato's refinement: Heavenly Love ennobles them, Common Love disgraces them. Context and reception. Plato's contemporary context shaped the ideas: classical Athens' symposium culture, its elite paiderastia, the aftermath of the Sicilian expedition (Agathon's victory dinner, c.416 BC). His contemporaries would have heard much that was familiar (Pausanias' defence of paiderastia) and much that was new (Diotima's ladder; love as philosophy rather than sex); the women's absence — the flute-girl sent away — is itself evidence of whose relationships the theory is about. A* answers weigh the ladder against the myth: Aristophanes' romantic picture has proved more famous than Diotima's rigorous one — which reception itself is examinable. The Symposium's frame matters for reception: Apollodorus retells the party from a friend's memory; the speeches are staged at Agathon's victory dinner (c.416 BC), with the flute-girl sent away so the men can talk — the women's absence is itself evidence of whose relationships the theory theorises. Socrates' resistance of Alcibiades is the final speech's climax: Alcibiades' drunken entrance (beauty's prize arrives to indict beauty's teacher), his attempt to seduce Socrates (under the cloak), and Socrates' refusal — desire resisted by reason, the theory performed in a character. Note the ambiguity: Socrates' resistance is not pure — he praises and flirts; the exam expects you to weigh the performance against the theory. Stoicism frames everything. The Stoics define passion (pathos) as a false judgement — an impulse that runs ahead of reason; the four categories are distress, fear, appetite and pleasure. Love, for Seneca, belongs to the appetites unless disciplined into rational affection: the Stoic ideal is apatheia, freedom from passion, with virtue as the only good and the body, beauty and pleasure as indifferents (adiaphora). Definitions : love is the desire for union with what appears good — but since beauty is not good (it is indifferent), erotic love is a misjudgement; friendship, by contrast, is rational affection between virtuous partners. Physical symptoms of desire — pallor, trembling, sleeplessness — are evidence of the mind's assent to a false appearance; the first involuntary movements (the blush, the startle) are not yet passions: assent makes them so, and reason can stop the assent. Control and resistance : Stoic technique — premeditation of future ills, habituation away from banquets and luxury, the refusal of the first assent — makes desire resistible; the answer to 'why should desire be controlled' is that passion enslaves the sage's sovereignty of reason. Homoerotic relationships meet the Roman frame: male-male sex was tolerated only in the active role; the passive adult male (the cinaedus of Roman invective) was disgraced — Seneca's moralising reflects and sharpens this; the Stoic critique cuts across both: passion of any direction enslaves. Context and reception. Seneca's contemporary context is Neronian Rome — imperial luxury, the court's excesses, and his own ambiguous position (a Stoic moralist of vast wealth); his contemporaries received the ideas as elite ethics against the court's example, and the irony (Nero as the pupil) is examinable. Good and bad conduct : marriage is a rational partnership (contrast Ovid's game); desire should be governed by judgement, not extinguished by force; the ideal is the sage who feels the first movement and refuses the second. A* answers evaluate the Stoic programme against the reality of Neronian Rome and against Plato: Seneca offers control as therapy; Diotima offers redirection as philosophy. Seneca's Stoic sources matter: the passion taxonomy (distress, fear, appetite, pleasure) comes from the Stoic school; his De Ira is the model treatment — anger as a passion governed by the same techniques (delay, avoid the stimuli, judge the appearance before assent); his Letters apply the method to wealth, grief and love.
