Device-to-effect map Device Effect on the audience Typical use in a group work Motif development Recognition plus freshness Open each section with a new variant of the signature motif Repetition Reinforcement Close a section by restating its motif exactly Contrast Interest; section boundary Break unison into opposing duos Highlights Directed attention A sudden stillness before the climax builds Climax Emotional peak Full-cast unison at maximum intensity in the final section Transitions Flow or fracture Travelling pathways that re-form the cast during a section change Structuring of movement material is a separate assessment criterion: the examiner rewards material structured in a coherent way through sectional use of choreographic structures: Binary (AB): two contrasting sections; effective for opposing moods or question-and-answer material. Ternary (ABA): a return to opening material gives resolution; the reprise should be recognisably altered to avoid pointless repetition. Rondo (ABACA): a recurring principal section alternating with contrasting episodes; strong for group works built on a signature motif. Theme and variation: a theme stated then varied successively; mirrors motif development at structural scale. Narrative: order dictated by a story; the dance idea and the set task's stimulus control the sequence. Episodic: linked episodes, often non-chronological, connected by thematic threads. Chance: ordering determined by chance procedures (associated with Merce Cunningham); if you use chance deliberately, coherence must still be communicated to the audience. Choose the structure that serves the set task and state the intention clearly in the programme note. A common weakness is a structure that exists only on paper: the audience must be able to see section boundaries - through changes of spatial organisation, dynamics, aural setting or use of dancers. Study how practitioners in your area of study structure works (for example, the sectional construction of Bruce's Rooster , one section per Rolling Stones song) and borrow the logic, not the material. Handle transitions as material in their own right: travelling pathways that re-form the cast during a section change keep the work continuous, while a deliberate freeze or blackout break announces a new section. Decide which reading you want and be consistent - an A* choreography shows intentional structure throughout, and the examiner can see every section boundary from the auditorium. If you use an episodic or chance structure, thread a recurring motif or aural cue through the sections so the fragments read as one work. Choosing structure for the task Match structure to stimulus: contrast-rich stimuli suit binary or ternary; a strong recurring idea suits rondo or theme and variation; a story suits narrative; linked episodes suit episodic. Whatever you choose, the set task's wording must still be answered - re-read the task and check your structure delivers every demand it makes. Choreographic intent is the through-line of every criterion: what you want the dance to communicate and how each decision serves it. The programme note (maximum 300 words) must tell the examiner the intention and its relation to the selected task; the choreography must then deliver exactly what the note promises. The aural setting is the dominant constituent feature in group choreography. Know these music-movement relationships and use at least two deliberately: Direct correlation: movement matches the music's beat, phrasing and accents exactly. Music visualisation: movement makes visible the music's colours, textures and instrumentation. Mutual coexistence: music and dance develop independently yet complement one another. Disassociation: movement deliberately ignores or opposes the music - effective for irony or tension. Narrative aural setting: the soundtrack carries or advances the story. Call and response: one voice or part initiates, another answers - mirrored in movement exchange. Also consider tempo, rhythm, mood and atmosphere of the accompaniment, and use physical setting (costume, properties, set, lighting) where appropriate to the task. Dancers are a constituent feature too: communicate with and organise your dancers, utilising their individual skills and attributes (flexibility, partnering strength, performance presence, musicality) to develop the artistic intention - the grid rewards this specifically. Safe practice (spec 3.1.1) applies throughout creating and rehearsing: awareness of correct alignment; technical accuracy; appropriate dancewear and presentation of self; and a healthy approach to training, including the lifestyle of a dancer. Give dancers warm-up time, develop lifts and contact work progressively on a risk-assessed floor, and never choreograph beyond the safe physical capability of your cast. Finally, the specification expects the study of the choreographic approaches (historical or current) of named practitioners in the areas of study to inform your practical work - a synoptic link that also feeds the written paper. Anchoring your process in a practitioner's approach (for example, Bruce's synthesis of Graham and Cunningham techniques, or Alston's Cunningham-based clarity) demonstrates theory informing practice, which is precisely what synoptic assessment demands. Work the rehearsal process in phases: early studio investigation (improvisation tasks from the stimulus, recording promising fragments), then selection and refinement (fixing motif variants, structuring the sections), then production rehearsal (spatial patterns, timing, lifts developed progressively, full runs with the aural setting). Keep the programme note in draft from the start - an intention stated early keeps every later decision answerable to it, and the final version (maximum 300 words) should read as the plan the examiner has just watched, not a retro-fit.

topics.name: Performance
topics.subject: dance
topics.searchText: dance Dance Performance Alignment The correct stacking of head, ribcage, spine, pelvis, knees and ankles; the foundation of safe, efficient technique. Transference of weight Controlled shifting of body weight between points of support; underpins locomotion, falls and partnering. Locomotion Travelling movement across space (walk, run, leap, slide) executed with clear direction and momentum. Elevation Height achieved in jumps and leaps, with controlled, quiet landings. Kinaesthetic awareness The dancer's internal sense of body position, weight and movement in space, enabling continuous self-correction. Neuromuscular coordination The nervous system and muscles working together to produce smooth, accurate movement. Projection Directing movement energy outward to reach the audience; sustaining performance presence to the back of the space. Musicality Sensitivity to the music beyond the beat - phrasing, texture, accent and silence - embodied in movement. Dynamic variation Command of contrast in attack, weight, flow and tempo within performance. Isolation Precise independent movement of one body part while the rest of the body remains controlled or still. Component 1 assesses AO1: perform dance through the application of physical, technical, interpretative and performance skills through two tasks, each marked out of 20 by an external AQA visiting examiner (visits normally March-May): Assessment Task 1 - solo in the style of a specified practitioner: minimum two , maximum three minutes. The practitioner must be the choreographer of a prescribed set work or a named practitioner within one of the prescribed areas of study, from any area of study, and may be the same as or different from your Component 2 choices. The solo can be choreographed by you, your teacher, a dance artist, or a collaboration - but it must encapsulate the practitioner's style without being a reconstruction of existing repertoire. Assessment Task 2 - performance within a quartet: minimum three , maximum four minutes, in any style relevant to the defined genres (modern, ballet, jazz). No practitioner is required; if you use one, it must differ from your solo practitioner. If fewer than four candidates are entered, the centre may add non-examined dancers (including students from other year groups) of appropriate standard and physical maturity. Both tasks require a programme note of no more than 150 words : the solo note identifies the practitioner and reveals insight into the stylistic features explored; the quartet note references the style(s) and the dance idea(s) if applicable. The performance must take place in a live setting, formally risk assessed , with sufficient warm-up time, under teacher supervision for authentication, in the academic year of certification. Under-length or over-length performance incurs a timing penalty scaled to the severity of the infringement. Evidence: a single-camera, unedited recording from an audience perspective, name and candidate number at the start. Choosing your solo practitioner strategically Pick a practitioner whose stylistic vocabulary you can genuinely embody: Graham (contraction and release, floorwork), Alston (Cunningham-based clarity and speed), Bruce (theatrical synthesis of modern, ballet and folk colour), Bournonville (ballon and quick petit batterie) or Fosse (angled lines, isolations, hunched posture). The examiner marks style-embodiment in every column of the grid, so half-embodying a stylistically distant practitioner caps your mark. In the quartet, casting is a performance decision: additional non-examined dancers must have the physical maturity and standard to complete the choreography, and examined dancers must rehearse sensitivity - matching timing, sharing weight safely, holding spacing - since the quartet grid credits spatial awareness including sensitivity to other dancers as its own column. A quartet of strong soloists who ignore each other cannot reach the top band. Task logistics checklist Externally set tasks: the solo and quartet tasks remain unchanged for the lifetime of the specification; the choreography task list is published on Centre Services by 15 September. Live assessment in the academic year of certification; formally risk-assessed setting; sufficient warm-up; teacher supervision for authentication. Evidence: single-camera, audience-perspective, start-to-finish, unedited recording; student named with candidate number; candidate record form signed. Programme notes handed to the examiner at the start of the live assessment. Timing penalties: applied for infringement of minimum/maximum duration, scaled to severity. The specification lists physical skills that underpin both tasks : flexibility, strength, cardiovascular endurance, muscular endurance, agility, neuromuscular coordination and kinaesthetic awareness. These are trained conditions - the examiner sees their product as precision and control. Build them through supplementary conditioning, class technique and progressive rehearsal, not on assessment day. Technical skills credited in the grids: Correct alignment - the stacking of head, ribcage, pelvis, knees and ankles that makes movement safe and efficient. Flexion, extension, rotation - controlled joint actions executed with the range the style demands (turn-out maintained in ballet vocabulary; parallel in much modern work). Whole body participation and/or isolation - integrated movement versus precise isolation of body parts (central to jazz technique). Transference of weight - smooth, controlled shifts between support points; underpins partnering and falls. Locomotion - travelling actions (walk, run, leap, slide) with clarity of direction and momentum. Elevation - height in jumps and leaps, with controlled landing. Balance - sustained stillness on one or few points of support, in the style's required alignment. The grid language matters: top bands demand exceptional and safe demonstration of precision and control in relation to the specified practitioner (solo) or in relation to style/genre (quartet). Safety is embedded in the descriptor - a technically showy but unsafe performance cannot reach the top band. Train each physical skill deliberately: flexibility through progressive stretching after class; strength through resistance and body-conditioning work (core for alignment, legs for elevation); cardiovascular and muscular endurance through sustained full runs of the assessed material; agility through rapid direction-change drills; neuromuscular coordination and kinaesthetic awareness through class technique, partner feedback and video review. The grid's top bands describe a sustained state, not a flash - conditioning underpins everything the examiner sees. Pre-assessment skills audit Check each grid column in rehearsal video: precision and control of technique; spatial control or awareness; dynamics; timing and musicality; focus, projection, emphasis, expression. Any column you cannot evidence in the footage is the one to drill - the grid marks columns separately, so one weak column caps the task. Spatial elements: the solo grid rewards spatial control (personal and stage space) - direction, levels, shape/form - meaning you command both your kinesphere and the stage picture. The quartet grid rewards spatial awareness including sensitivity to other dancers : maintaining formations and spacing, safe partnering, and adapting to the quartet in real time. Dynamic elements (solo): rhythmic control and dynamic variation - command of attack, weight, flow and tempo change, matching the practitioner's dynamic signature (Fosse's controlled isolations against sudden bursts; Graham's percussive contraction against sustained release). Interpretative/performance skills exist to communicate the dance idea(s) in a clear and considered manner - the specification lists projection, focus, expression, emphasis, timing and musicality: Projection: energy reaching the audience; performing to the back row even in a small studio. Focus: deliberate direction of the eyes - focal shifts shape meaning (inward focus for introspection, outward for confrontation). Expression: facial and physical expression consistent with the dance idea and style. Emphasis: giving certain moments weight so the audience reads what matters. Timing: accurate response to the aural setting and to other dancers. Musicality: sensitivity to the music beyond the beat - phrasing, texture, accent, silence. Note the grid splits interpretative skills into two credited columns - timing and musicality , and focus, projection, emphasis and expression - so neglecting one pair caps the mark regardless of brilliance elsewhere. Solo grid (20 marks) at a glance Five columns, 4 marks each: physical/technical skills; spatial elements (personal and stage space); dynamic elements; interpretative skills (timing and musicality); interpretative skills (focus, projection, emphasis and expression). Bands: exceptional (4), highly articulate (3), proficient (2), adequate (1), nothing worthy of credit (0). Quartet grid (20 marks) at a glance Four columns, 5 marks each: physical/technical skills; spatial awareness (including sensitivity to other dancers); timing and musicality; focus, projection, emphasis and expression. Bands: exceptional (5), highly articulate (4), proficient (3), sound (2), adequate (1), nothing worthy of credit (0). Train expressive skills as deliberately as technique: projection through performing phrases to a distant point and filming from the back of the room; focus through rehearsing deliberate focal shifts marked into the choreography; timing and musicality through clapping phrases, marking accents and dancing to silence. In the solo, match your interpretative choices to the practitioner: Fosse's fixed, inward gaze; Graham's dramatic intensity; Alston's clean musical phrasing. Expression inconsistent with style reads as decoration and caps the interpretative columns. Safe practice (spec 3.1.1) is examinable knowledge and a condition of assessment. Know all four requirements: awareness of correct alignment ; technical accuracy (executing movement as intended - inaccurate technique is itself unsafe); appropriate dancewear and presentation of self (correct footwear or barefoot convention for the style, hair secured, no jewellery); and a healthy approach to training, including the lifestyle of a dancer (progressive warm-up and cool-down, hydration, nutrition, sleep, load management, injury reporting). The examiner will only conduct assessments where health and safety requirements are securely in place. Rehearsal process converts skill into performance: learn material accurately, mark through for spacing and safety, build full runs to develop stamina, then rehearse in performance conditions - same floor, same aural setting, entrances and exits rehearsed. For the quartet, rehearse sensitivity deliberately: blind-spot awareness, counterbalance and lift progressions, and recovery from slips without breaking the ensemble picture. Performance environment: the assessed performance happens in a live, formally risk-assessed setting, and the recording must be the performance being assessed - one take, single camera, audience perspective, unedited, in the academic year of certification. Adapt projection and focus to the venue: a studio assessment needs less force than a theatre, but never perform flatly. Treat the examiner as an audience member; do not perform to the examiner. Finally, embodying a specified practitioner means evidencing their style in every credited column: alignment, rotation and balance executed as Graham, Alston, Bruce, Bournonville or Fosse would demand; dynamics matching their signature; timing and musicality inside their aural world; expression consistent with their choreographic intent. Study film of the practitioner's repertoire, take class in the style, and let the programme note signal precisely which stylistic features the examiner should expect to see. The lifestyle of a dancer is named in the spec: sleep for recovery, hydration and nutrition for energy, load management to avoid overuse injury, and honest reporting of niggles before they become injuries. In the performance environment, plan the space: rehearse entrances, exits and spacing to the actual room, check the floor is risk assessed and fit for the style (sprung floor for elevation work), and agree how the aural setting will be played. Walk in as a performer: warm-up complete, dancewear and presentation right, focus already on the dance idea - the assessment begins the moment you enter the space.

topics.name: Dance Appreciation
topics.subject: dance
topics.searchText: dance Dance Dance Appreciation Constituent features The four analytically separable features of a dance: movement components; dancers; aural setting; physical setting. Movement components The action, spatial and dynamic elements of the movement itself. Dynamic elements Qualities of movement - attack, weight, flow, tempo - as distinct from what is done (action) and where (space). Aural setting Everything heard: music, sound, the spoken word, the audible aspect of dance and silence. Physical setting Everything seen that surrounds the movement: costume, properties, set, lighting design, performance environment, film. Choreographic approach A choreographer's particular technique, movement style and choreographic style. Genre A category of dance defined by style, technique and history - modern dance, ballet and jazz dance in AQA 7237. Subject matter The theme or topic of the dance and its treatment. Form The structure of the dance - phrases and sections - and its effectiveness in communicating the subject matter. Leitmotif A recurring musical theme associated with a particular character, incorporated into ballet scores during the romantic period. Component 2: Critical engagement is a written exam of 2 hours 30 minutes , 100 marks , 50% of the A-level , assessing AO3 (knowledge and understanding of performance and choreography from different periods and genres) and AO4 (critically appreciating and assessing performance and choreography through analytical, interpretative and evaluative judgements). You study two set works : one compulsory, one chosen from four options. Section A (50 marks) - compulsory: short answer questions (25 marks) and one essay (25 marks) on the compulsory set work and area of study: Rooster (Christopher Bruce, 1991) and Rambert Dance Company (formerly Ballet Rambert) 1966-2002 . Section B (50 marks) - two essays, 25 marks each: one on your optional set work and one on its corresponding area of study. Options: Giselle / the romantic ballet period; Appalachian Spring / the origins of American modern dance 1900-1945; Singin' in the Rain / American jazz dance 1940-1975; Sutra / the independent contemporary dance scene in Britain 2000-current. The assessment is synoptic : you must draw together knowledge from across the course, demonstrating the relationships between theory and practice - examiners reward answers that connect set works to choreographic and performance understanding, not isolated recall. Command words determine depth demanded: identify/state (recall), describe (account of features), explain (give reasons - how and why), discuss/analyse (interrogate features and their effect), evaluate (AO4 judgement with justification). Short answers reward precise, dated facts; essays reward a thesis supported by constituent-feature evidence and secured by judgement. Timing plan for 2h30 Section A: short answers (25 marks) in about 30 minutes; essay (25 marks) in about 30-35 minutes. Section B: two essays (25 marks each) in about 30-35 minutes each; keep 10 minutes to check dates and terminology. At roughly 1.2 marks per minute, every minute must produce dated, interpretable content - plan each essay in its first two minutes (thesis plus three evidence points) rather than after writing. Also know how the two AOs divide the paper: AO3 (knowledge and understanding of performance and choreography from different periods and genres) dominates the short answers; AO4 (critically appreciating and assessing performance and choreography through analytical, interpretative and evaluative judgements) dominates the essays. An essay with no judgement is capped at mid-band however dense its recall. Command words ladder Identify/state = recall a fact (1-2 marks). Describe = give a precise account of features using action, spatial and dynamic vocabulary. Explain = give reasons - how and why features work. Discuss/analyse = interrogate features, weigh their effect, make links across the work. Evaluate = reach a justified judgement (AO4). Match paragraph length to the command word: short answers earn marks per accurate point; essays earn them per developed, evidenced, judged point. Spec 3.3.1 defines four constituent features - learn this framework as the skeleton of every analysis answer. Each feature must be interpreted in relation to the subject matter , not merely described: Constituent feature Elements Movement components action, spatial and dynamic elements Dancers number, gender, role, physique Aural setting music, sound, the spoken word, the audible aspect of dance, silence Physical setting costume, properties, set, lighting design, performance environment, film Analyse in three moves: describe the feature precisely (what is seen/heard, using action, space and dynamic vocabulary); interpret (what the feature communicates about the subject matter or the character of the dance); evaluate (how effectively it embodies the subject matter - AO4). For example, in Rooster : the men's strutting, cock-of-the-rooster carriage (action) performed with swaggering, syncopated attack (dynamics) to Rolling Stones tracks (aural setting) in 1960s-inspired costume (physical setting) embodies the sexual politics and swagger of the decade - description becomes interpretation once linked to the work's subject matter. Also know the language of form (phrases, sections) and the significance of the character of the dance - both named in the spec as things you must understand about each set work: whether the work is abstract or has a character, how form communicates subject matter, and how the sections build. Build movement vocabulary you can deploy in any work: action - travel, turn, gesture, elevation, stillness, fall, jump, contract, extend; spatial - pathway, direction, level, formation, symmetry/asymmetry, personal versus stage space; dynamic - attack, weight, flow, tempo, sustained/percussive/suspended/swinging. Every set-work answer should name the feature, describe it precisely and interpret its effect on the subject matter in one move. Test the framework on a second work: in Sutra (2008), the dancers move among Antony Gormley's wooden boxes - the physical setting is simultaneously apparatus (boxes are carried, stacked, tipped) and metaphor (a hut, a wall, a void), and the audible aspect of the dance (knocking, sliding) merges with Szymon Brzoska's composed score; in Appalachian Spring (1944), Isamu Noguchi's sculptural set reduces a farmhouse to suggestion, and Graham's dancers work in contraction and release to Aaron Copland's Americana. Both show constituent features embodying subject matter - the pattern every 25-mark answer must expose. Give the dancers feature full treatment too: number (why this many - ensemble weight, symmetry, opposition), gender (casting as meaning - the flirtatious gender play of Rooster ), role (principal, corps, ghost, outsider) and physique (the physique a style demands and displays). Casting choices are interpretation: connect them to the subject matter rather than listing them. Quick check before any set-work answer Can you name: the action, spatial and dynamic features of a key moment; the dancers' number, gender, role and physique; the aural setting elements heard; the physical setting elements seen? If not, that feature is your next revision target - every 25-mark answer draws on all four. Choreographic approach = the choreographer's particular technique, movement style and choreographic style . For each set work you must know the approach, the influences affecting its development , the origins of the dance , its importance in the development of the choreographer and the genre , and similarities and differences with other works by the choreographer. This requires understanding of other related works - selected by your teacher from visual and/or written sources - to place the set work in context within the area of study and the genre. For each area of study you must know the stylistic features of the genre and the choreographic approach of a minimum of two named practitioners , showing the range within the genre, with at least two works from each (subject matter, treatment, form, constituent features of each). The three genres are defined by AQA: Modern dance: theatrical dancing that began in the early 20th century, originally in opposition to the formality of ballet; the term is now sometimes replaced by other labels, e.g. contemporary. Ballet: dancing focused on the technique and style of the danse d'ecole - port de bras, the five positions of the feet, turn-out of the legs. Jazz dance: dancing of African origins focused on complex rhythms and techniques including isolation of body parts; a wide range of styles has evolved, e.g. lyrical jazz and urban dance. Named practitioner lists: Rambert 1966-2002 - Glen Tetley, Robert North, Richard Alston, Siobhan Davies, Ashley Page; romantic ballet - Filippo Taglioni, August Bournonville, Arthur Saint-Leon; American modern 1900-1945 - Loie Fuller, Isadora Duncan, Ruth St Denis, Doris Humphrey; American jazz 1940-1975 - Agnes de Mille, Jack Cole, Jerome Robbins, Bob Fosse; independent contemporary Britain 2000-current - Shobana Jeyasingh, Matthew Bourne, Jasmin Vardimon, Akram Khan, Hofesh Shechter. Structure practitioner comparison by influence, then approach, then work : state the practitioner's influences (training, teachers, companies), define their approach (technique, movement style, choreographic style), then evidence it in two works with subject matter, treatment, form and constituent features. To show the range within the genre, pair practitioners whose approaches genuinely oppose - within the Rambert list, for example, pair a Cunningham-derived, abstract approach with a more theatrical, dramatic one - and make the contrast itself your argument. The spec also asks for similarities and differences between the set work and other works by the choreographer - a cheap source of AO3 content once prepared: Rooster 's celebratory social-dance register against the political gravity of Bruce's other repertoire; Appalachian Spring 's celebratory Americana against Graham's darker psychological works; Sutra 's ritual austerity against Cherkaoui's more overtly theatrical pieces. Prepare one similarity and one difference per set work, each grounded in subject matter, form or constituent features. You must understand the relationship between the dance and its context - the position of the genre within history, culture and society - and the genre's capacity to reflect and challenge society . This is where top-band essays separate from mid-band: connect the work's features to its world. Rooster only makes full sense against 1960s social dance and gender politics; Giselle against Romanticism's supernatural and the ballerina cult; Appalachian Spring against American modern dance's individualism and Copland's American sound; Sutra against Britain's independent, collaborative contemporary scene. Essay craft for the 25-mark questions: Open with a thesis that answers the question directly (one sentence). Build 3-4 paragraphs, each anchored in precise, dated evidence - choreographer, work, year, company, constituent feature. Interpret: link every feature to subject matter, form or character. Judge (AO4): how effectively, how significantly - use evaluative language (the most striking embodiment; this changed the company's direction because...). Use terminology specific to the genre (contraction and release; ballon; isolation; Bharatanatyam) accurately. Cross-reference across the course where possible - synopticity is credited. Practise by converting every fact into a claim: not 'Morrice changed the company in 1966' but 'Morrice's 1966 changes - reducing company size, introducing Graham technique into training, engaging guest choreographers - reoriented Ballet Rambert from ballet towards modern dance, which is why a Bruce work using Rolling Stones and social dance idiom could enter its repertoire by 1994.' Facts + consequence + judgement = AO3 + AO4. Prepare AO4 language deliberately: evaluative sentence openers (the most significant; the decisive change; this crystallised the company's identity), consequence links (which meant that; as a result), and balanced judgement (however; the exception being). Address the genre's capacity to reflect and challenge society with concrete cases: the romantic ballet reflected its era's cult of the unattainable yet, by elevating the ballerina above the male dancer, eventually narrowed ballet's expressive range; jazz on screen democratised dance for mass audiences while drawing on racialised popular forms; Bruce's Rooster both celebrates and gently satirises the sexual politics it reconstructs.

topics.name: Set Works and Anthology
topics.subject: dance
topics.searchText: dance Dance Set Works and Anthology Set work A professional dance work prescribed by AQA for in-depth study in Component 2: Critical engagement. Area of study A prescribed genre-focused period (e.g. Rambert Dance Company 1966-2002) providing historical, cultural and social context for the set work. Compulsory set work Rooster (Christopher Bruce, 1991) with the Rambert Dance Company (formerly Ballet Rambert) 1966-2002 area of study - required of all candidates. Romantic ballet 19th-century ballet style peaking in the 1830s-40s: focus on the ballerina, reality/fantasy contrast, supernatural mystery, illusion of weightlessness, gas lighting, folk colour; formulaic by 1870. Modern dance Theatrical dancing begun in the early 20th century in opposition to ballet's formality; the label is now sometimes replaced by contemporary. Jazz dance Dance of African origins focused on complex rhythms and isolation of body parts; evolved into lyrical jazz, urban and theatre styles. Denishawn The school and company founded by Ruth St Denis and Ted Shaw; students included Martha Graham, Doris Humphrey and Charles Weidman. Contraction and release Martha Graham's technique, based on the act of breathing - percussive contraction of the torso and its release. Fall and recovery Doris Humphrey's technique, built on the arc between surrendering to and resisting gravity. Leitmotif A recurring musical theme associated with a principal character, incorporated into ballet scores during the romantic period. Component 2 requires in-depth knowledge of two set works and their corresponding areas of study . One is compulsory: Rooster (Christopher Bruce, 1991) with Rambert Dance Company (formerly Ballet Rambert) 1966-2002 . One is selected from four options. Learn the credits precisely - short answers reward dated facts: Option Set work Music Area of study 1 Giselle (Jean Coralli and Jules Perrot, 1841) - libretto Gautier, Saint-Georges and Coralli; decor Pierre Ciceri Adolphe Adam The romantic ballet period 2 Appalachian Spring (Martha Graham, 1944) - set Isamu Noguchi; costumes Edythe Gilfond Aaron Copland The origins of American modern dance 1900-1945 3 Singin' in the Rain (Stanley Donen and Gene Kelly, 1952) - lyrics Arthur Freed; screenplay Comden and Green Nacio Herb Brown American jazz dance 1940-1975 4 Sutra (Sidi Larbi Cherkaoui, 2008) - design Antony Gormley; lighting Adam Carree Szymon Brzoska The independent contemporary dance scene in Britain 2000-current Choose by genuine comparative strength: your Section B essays need a minimum of two named practitioners plus two works each from the area of study, so pick the area whose practitioner list and repertoire you can evidence best. Professional works studied must be in the public domain and easily accessible to examiners. For your selected set work you must know: the significance of the character of the dance; the subject matter and its treatment; the form (phrases, sections) and its effectiveness; the constituent features and their relevance to subject matter; the choreographic approach; the influences affecting the development of the choreographer; the origins of the dance; the relationship between the dance and its context; the importance of the dance in the development of the choreographer and the genre; and the similarities and differences between the dance and other works by the choreographer. For short answers, credits win marks: know each work's choreographer, year, company and premiere, music and designers cold. Section A short answers ask for exactly this recall plus constituent-feature identification; the essays ask you to convert it into argument. Also note the spec's list of what you must know about each area of study: the stylistic features of the genre and how they relate to it; the choreographic approach of a minimum of two named practitioners (influences, technique, movement style, choreographic style) with at least two works each; the relationship between the genre's development and its context; the genre's capacity to reflect and challenge society; and terminology specific to the genre. Rooster credits: choreography Christopher Bruce; music - songs recorded by the Rolling Stones; costume designs Marian Bruce; lighting designs Tina MacHugh. First performed 10 October 1991 by the Ballet du Grand Theatre de Geneve; British premiere 28 October 1992 by London Contemporary Dance Theatre; first performance by Rambert Dance Company 8 December 1994 . The work: a suite of sections, each built on one Rolling Stones song, reviving the social dance idiom of the 1960s - strutting, twist- and jitterbug-derived actions, flirtatious gender play. The subject matter is the swagger and sexual politics of the decade: the men preen, the women counter with knowing control, and the mood shifts from celebratory to darker across the sections. The form - one section per song - communicates the decade's shifting moods; the aural setting works through direct correlation and music visualisation with the Stones' syncopated drive. Bruce's approach: technique rooted in Graham-based training with Cunningham influence - the two techniques Rambert institutionalised after 1966; movement style synthesising modern dance, ballet and social dance colour; choreographic style theatrical, musical and humanist - his works frequently address political and social themes (cf. Ghost Dances , 1981, Ballet Rambert, responding to oppression in Latin America). Rooster 's celebratory register shows the range within Bruce's output - a contrast examiners like to see argued. Rambert 1966-2002 chronology - learn as a chain of consequences: 1966: Norman Morrice (associate director) encourages Marie Rambert to change the company - company size, preservation and creation of works, Graham technique in training, involvement of guest choreographers and teachers, development of the touring schedule. The modern-dance reorientation begins. 1974: Morrice leaves; John Chesworth continues his policies - promotes new work from company members, expands the repertoire through guest choreographers, develops Rambert's educational activities. 1975: Christopher Bruce becomes associate director; 1979 associate choreographer. 1975-1985: links between Ballet Rambert and London Contemporary Dance Theatre through choreographers such as Robert North and Richard Alston. 1980s: repertoire focuses on three British choreographers - North, Bruce and Alston. North directs 1981-1986, keen to develop the physicality, musicality and dramatic quality of the dancers. Alston: resident choreographer 1980, artistic director 1986 - consolidating the Cunningham influence. 1987: company renamed Rambert Dance Company . 1994-2002: Bruce returns as artistic director - inclusion of a range of techniques, new works, guest choreographers, and a repertoire of neo-classical and modern works. Rooster enters the repertoire (December 1994). Named practitioners (know two in depth, two works each): Glen Tetley (1926-2007), Robert North (born 1945), Richard Alston (born 1948), Siobhan Davies (born 1950), Ashley Page (born 1956). Option 1 - The romantic ballet period (with Giselle ): Romanticism rebelled against Classicism's focus on form, balance and order, emphasising creativity, emotion and subjectivity; ballet was the last art affected. The romantic ballet peaked in the 1830s-40s. Characteristics: focus on the ballerina; contrast between reality and fantasy; the supernatural and mystery via the illusion of weightlessness, gas lighting and the characteristic romantic tutu; folk or national dances for local colour; leitmotifs for principal characters. Taglioni, Perrot and Bournonville led development - Bournonville alone maintained balance between male and female dancing. The style became formulaic by 1870; female dancers performing male roles signalled decline. Practitioners: Filippo Taglioni (1777-1871), August Bournonville (1805-1879), Arthur Saint-Leon (1821-1870). Option 2 - The origins of American modern dance 1900-1945 (with Appalachian Spring ): America had no tradition of professional ballet; innovators performed barefoot to concert music in freer costume. Loie Fuller led the way in modern stage lighting; Isadora Duncan developed natural movement. Ruth St Denis (eclectic styles, the Delsarte system) with Ted Shawn created a company and the Denishawn school - students included Graham, Humphrey and Weidman. Modern dance stressed individualism: angular asymmetries, aggressive and earthy qualities; early works minimised the importance of music and art; from the 1930s choreography addressed psychological and social issues. German modern dance (Mary Wigman) reached America via tours and via Hanya Holm's branch of the Wigman school. Graham, encouraged by Louis Horst, built technique on breathing - contraction and release ; Humphrey on fall and recovery . University support (e.g. Bennington) accelerated acceptance of modern dance as a distinct art form. Practitioners: Fuller (1862-1928), Duncan (1877-1927), St Denis (1879-1968), Humphrey (1895-1958). Option 3 - American jazz dance 1940-1975 (with Singin' in the Rain ): early 1900s jazz performed by African-American artists showed links to minstrelsy and ragtime via new syncopated rhythms; from the 1930s-60s it became a theatre-based form requiring trained dancers, with choreography from the ballet and modern worlds. Jack Cole developed jazz dance technique and its theatrical form (inspiring Matt Mattox, Jerome Robbins and Bob Fosse); Katherine Dunham founded the anthropological dance movement, introducing African and Caribbean ritual into American choreography; Matt Mattox's teaching shaped future generations' training. Gene Kelly - physique and personality, acrobatic and athletic training, camera-conscious choreography in collaboration with Stanley Donen; Jerome Robbins combined social dance with classical ballet for characterisation, rhythmic complexity and dynamic variation, following Agnes de Mille in making dance of equal importance to drama and music in the storyline; Bob Fosse's style - angled lines, inverted limbs, hunched-over posture. Practitioners: de Mille (1905-1993), Cole (1911-1974), Robbins (1918-1998), Fosse (1927-1987). Option 4 - The independent contemporary dance scene in Britain 2000-current (with Sutra ): several generations of practitioners have achieved international recognition through their own work and commissions for different companies; the work embraces cultural similarities and differences, enhanced by collaborations with designers (Antony Gormley, Anish Kapoor) and composers (Nitin Sawhney, Szymon Brzoska), and responds to social, political and historical issues. Shobana Jeyasingh: Bharatanatyam foundation, multicultural themes of personal identity, relationships and heritage; Matthew Bourne: choreographed body language and a variety of dance and movement styles for storytelling, supported by design and music; Jasmin Vardimon: observations of human behaviour through physical theatre, inventive characterisation, technology, text and dance; Akram Khan: Kathak and contemporary training, constantly exploring other styles through collaborators from a range of backgrounds; Hofesh Shechter: composer involvement - soundscapes providing powerful backgrounds for his contemporary movement and interest in aspects of contemporary life; Cherkaoui: yoga and jazz backgrounds explored from a theatrical starting point. Practitioners: Jeyasingh (born 1957), Bourne (born 1960), Vardimon (born 1971), Khan (born 1974), Shechter (born 1975). Section B demands two essays: one on your optional set work, one on its corresponding area of study (25 marks each). Strong essays do three things the mark scheme rewards: Argue through features: every paragraph anchored in a constituent feature or formal detail of a named work, interpreted in relation to subject matter. Show the range within the genre: contrast two practitioners' approaches (technique, movement style, choreographic style) with at least two works each - e.g. Bournonville's gender-balanced virtuosity against the ballerina-centred romantic norm; Khan's Kathak-contemporary hybridity against Shechter's rock-inflected ensemble drive. Situate and judge: place the genre in history, culture and society, and discuss its capacity to reflect and challenge society - jazz on screen democratised dance but traded on racialised popular forms; the romantic ballet worshipped the unattainable yet narrowed opportunities for male dancers. Use comparison sentences that carry facts : 'Where Graham's Appalachian Spring (1944) stripped the setting to Noguchi's sculptural shorthand, Cherkaoui's Sutra (2008) made Gormley's wooden boxes both set and apparatus - both physical settings concentrate meaning, but Sutra 's is also choreographic infrastructure.' Compare across the two set works you study for synopticity: Bruce's social-dance revival and Cherkaoui's intercultural ritual both reconstruct borrowed movement idioms, but to opposite effect - nostalgia versus inquiry. Finally, connect to practice: the specification states that study of the choreographic approaches of named practitioners in the areas of study informs practical work. Knowing how Graham built material through contraction and release, or how Kelly choreographed for the camera, feeds directly into AO2 decisions in your group choreography - theory informing practice is the stated aim of the area-of-study design.

topics.name: Materials and Performance
topics.subject: design-and-technology
topics.searchText: design-and-technology Design and Technology Materials and Performance Physical property A characteristic measured without changing the composition of the material, e.g. density, thermal conductivity, electrical conductivity. Mechanical property How a material responds to an applied force, e.g. tensile strength, compressive strength, hardness, toughness, malleability, elasticity. Toughness The ability of a material to absorb sudden shock or impact without fracturing; the opposite of brittleness. Hardness Resistance of a surface to scratching, indentation and wear. Malleability The ability of a material to be deformed by compression (hammering, rolling, pressing) without cracking. Thermoset polymer A polymer that cures permanently when heated or mixed with a hardener and cannot be remelted, e.g. epoxy resin, urea formaldehyde. Elastomer A polymer that can be stretched and returns to its original shape, e.g. natural rubber, neoprene, silicone, TPE. Composite Two or more materials combined so the resulting properties are enhanced beyond those of the individual components, e.g. CFRP, GRP, reinforced concrete, glulam. Smart material A material that responds to an external stimulus - a change in temperature, light level or pressure - e.g. shape memory alloy (Nitinol), thermochromic pigment. Case hardening A heat treatment that adds carbon to the surface of a low carbon steel component, producing a hard, wear-resistant skin over a tough core. Paper 1 expects instant, accurate classification. Learn the categories and one or two examples each - examiners award marks for named materials, not vague ones. Category Sub-categories Named examples Metals Ferrous, non-ferrous, alloys Low carbon steel, cast iron (ferrous); aluminium, copper, zinc, titanium (non-ferrous); brass, bronze, duralumin, pewter, stainless steel (alloys) Woods Hardwoods, softwoods, manufactured boards Oak, ash, mahogany, teak, beech; pine, spruce, Douglas fir, larch, cedar; plywood, chipboard, MDF, aeroply, veneers Polymers Thermoplastics, thermosets, elastomers LDPE, HDPE, PP, HIPS, ABS, PMMA, nylon, PVC, PET; urea formaldehyde, melamine formaldehyde, epoxy and polyester resins; natural rubber, neoprene, silicone, TPE Papers and boards By weight and treatment Layout, cartridge, tracing, bleed proof, watercolour, corrugated card, bleached card, duplex, mount board, foil-backed card, moulded paper pulp Composites Polymer matrix, ceramic, engineered CFRP, GRP, tungsten carbide, aluminium composite board, reinforced concrete, fibre cement, glulam Smart and modern Stimulus-responsive; recently developed Nitinol SMA, thermochromic, photochromic and phosphorescent pigments, electroluminescent wire, piezo electric material; Kevlar, precious metal clay, polymorph, high density modelling foam Selection is never a property list on its own. The mark scheme wants a justified explanation referencing six factors: physical and mechanical properties (working characteristics), product function, aesthetics, cost, manufacture and disposal. A 9-mark question on why a material is suitable needs three developed property-function links, each tied to the product's use. Testing (3.1.1) questions ask how a test is set up, what is measured and how data is compared: tensile - specimen clamped in jaws, incremental load applied until fracture, stress-strain graph produced to find yield point and UTS; toughness - pendulum impact test, energy absorbed on fracture measured; hardness - indentation test, depth or diameter of the indent measured; malleability - controlled bending or rolling until cracking occurs; corrosion - exposure to salt spray or weathering, with condition and mass compared against a control; conductivity - current or heat passed through a standardised sample and measured. State that industrial tests are standardised and results are compared against published data so materials can be selected consistently. Two classification nuances earn easy marks. First, why alloy : alloying deliberately mixes metals to enhance properties - duralumin (aluminium plus copper) trades a little corrosion resistance for a large gain in tensile strength, which is why it was developed for aircraft structures; brass (copper plus zinc) gives low friction for fittings; pewter is a low-temperature casting alloy. Second, ferrous selection logic : ferrous metals rust, so low carbon steel is chosen where cost and weldability matter more than corrosion resistance (frames, structures - then protected by coating or galvanising), while stainless steel is chosen where hygiene or appearance under water matters more than cost. On testing data , be ready to analyse rather than describe: destructive tests (tensile, impact) sacrifice specimens to find limits, so they are used on samples, not finished products; results are compared against a control specimen and against published standard data; multiple repeats are averaged to eliminate outliers, and the comparison informs which material is selected. A 3-mark analysis point: the material whose stress-strain curve shows the higher yield point before fracture is selected for the load-bearing application. This is the highest-yield section of Paper 1. Learn the characteristic list and the application pairings - questions routinely give an application and ask which material and why. Material group Performance characteristics to quote Key application pairings Papers and boards Ability to be scored, cutting, folding, surface qualities for printing, impact resistance, recyclability/biodegradability, stability Layout paper - sketching; cartridge - printing; bleed proof - marker rendering; corrugated card - protective packaging; mount board - modelling; duplex - food packaging; moulded paper pulp - eco-friendly packaging Polymer sheet and film Scoring, cutting, folding, moulding, transparency/translucency, flexibility, recyclability Foam board - model making; fluted polypropylene - signs and box construction; styrofoam - modelling formers; LDPE sheet - wrapping and bags; plastazote - protective packaging; PLA film - biodegradable packaging Woods Grain pattern and direction, surface defects, warping, shrinkage, splitting, joining, steam bending, laminating, machining qualities, resistance to decay, moisture resistance, toxicity Softwoods (pine, spruce, larch) - cheap construction and joinery; hardwoods (oak, beech) - quality furniture, wear resistance; plywood - stable panel with no grain weakness across the sheet; MDF - flat uniform surface, machines cleanly Metals Hardness, toughness, malleability, elasticity, tensile strength, density, corrosion resistance, thermal and electrical conductivity, melting points, ability to be alloyed, joined with heat processes, coated Low carbon steel - malleable structural frames, weldable, cheap; stainless steel - corrosion resistance for kitchen and food use; aluminium - low density plus good conductivity; cast iron - compressive strength for machine beds; brass - low-friction fittings Polymers Toughness, elasticity, thermal and electrical insulation, UV resistance, ability to be moulded, chemical resistance, melting points, food-safe suitability, biodegradability, recyclability, self finishing PP - living hinges, chemical containers; HDPE - bottles and jerry cans; ABS - impact-resistant casings; PMMA - optical clarity; nylon - gears and bearings; UF - electrical fittings and adhesives; PET - drinks bottles Know stock forms per category because selection questions often name the form: woods as rough sawn, PSE, PAR, mouldings and manufactured boards; metals as sheet, plate, bar (flat, round, square, hexagonal), tube (round, square, rectangular) and structural sections (H beam, I beam, tee, channel, angle); polymers as sheet, film, granules, rod and other extruded forms, foam, powder. Two economic points are repeatedly examined: efficient 2D net design reduces waste when constructing containers, and material selection should allow recyclability, biodegradability and stability in use - a corrugated card net nests on the sheet with minimal off-cut waste, and PLA film degrades under UV, water or soil enzymes where LDPE does not. Four further 3.1.2 sub-sections sit inside this topic and appear in Paper 1 regularly. Elastomers (natural rubber, polybutadiene, neoprene, silicone, TPE): suitability rests on the ability to be stretched and then return to the original shape, plus texture, self finishing and non-toxicity - used to enhance products such as over-moulded grips for improved ergonomics. Biodegradable polymers (corn starch polymers, Potatopak, biopol bio-batch additive, PLA, PHA, water-soluble Lactel and ecofilm): they can be moulded into 3D products or film and degrade under UV rays, water or enzymes present in soil - quote the degradation trigger, not just biodegradable. Composites (CFRP, GRP, tungsten carbide, aluminium composite board, reinforced concrete, fibre cement, glulam): materials are combined so properties are enhanced - mouldable into varied 3D forms, higher strength-to-weight, and for some uses easier to manufacture against traditional materials. Concrete is strong in compression but weak in tension, so steel reinforcement is added - the classic enhanced-property explanation. Smart materials (Nitinol SMA, thermochromic, phosphorescent and photochromic pigments, electroluminescent wire, piezo electric material): defined by the stimulus they respond to - change in temperature (thermochromic, SMA), light levels (photochromic, phosphorescent) or pressure/force (piezo). Finally modern materials (Kevlar, precious metal clay, high density modelling foam, polymorph) - recently developed materials whose suitability must be explained for given applications, e.g. Kevlar where high impact and cut resistance at low weight is needed. Enhancement questions ask you to describe the method and explain its suitability for a specific product. Learn one enhancement per category plus the mechanism behind it. Polymer enhancement - additives. UV stabilisers prolong the life of polymers used outdoors (garden furniture becomes brittle in sunlight without them); bio-batch additives such as biopol encourage biodegradability in carrier bags and food packaging so they break down after disposal. Pigments added at the moulding stage can also count as enhancement. Wood enhancement - resins, lamination and preservatives. Combining natural timber with resins and laminating (glulam, marine plywood) increases strength and dimensional stability - laminated sections counteract warping and shrinkage because opposing grain directions are glued together. Pressure treating with chemical preservatives and applying oils or varnishes extends outdoor service life. Metal enhancement - heat treatment. Case hardening : low carbon steel is carburised then heat treated, giving a hard, wear-resistant outer skin while the core stays tough - ideal for gear wheels and cam followers subject to surface wear plus shock loading. Hardening and tempering : medium/high carbon steel is heated to critical temperature and quenched (very hard but brittle), then reheated to around 200-300 degrees C and cooled to remove brittleness while retaining hardness - used for chisels, lathe tools and springs. Composites and elastomers can also be framed as enhancement routes: CFRP and GRP mould a high strength-to-weight material into complex 3D forms impossible in plain polymer, and over-moulding a TPE grip onto a rigid substrate enhances ergonomics - a favourite context in Paper 1 extended questions. Tie each method back to the six selection factors; the describe command word earns the method, explain suitability earns the application link. AQA 7552 Paper 1 (2h30m, 120 marks, 30% of A-level) uses a mixture of short answer and extended response. The extended material questions are where A* candidates separate themselves. Structure every justification in three layers: Name plus property. Name the specific material and the specific property - polypropylene has excellent fatigue resistance, not plastic is strong. Property to function link. State what the property does in this product : the fatigue resistance allows an integral living hinge to flex thousands of times without failing. Context - cost, manufacture, disposal. Add the commercial layer: PP is cheap and injection moulds at high volume with zero finishing (self finishing), and is recyclable under polymer code 5, aiding disposal. Where the question offers a comparison (why X rather than Y), score by contrasting one decisive property - choose stainless over low carbon steel for a kitchen sink because corrosion resistance matters more than cost where water is always present. Where a calculation appears (3.1.1 maths links), show working for quantities of material, areas and costs: area = length x width for sheet coverage, cost = quantity x price per unit, and percentages for waste allowances. Marks are lost through generic answers, through properties quoted without a function, and through forgetting the disposal/recycling angle - build all three layers into every practice answer. Common examiner traps Writing strong and durable with no named property or application link. Confusing toughness (impact) with hardness (surface wear) - they frequently oppose each other. Ignoring stock form: selection for a pressed lamp body implies sheet or extruded form, not granules. Missing scale of production: injection moulding only pays off at volume, so a one-off justification should not rely on it. Paper 1 runs 2h30m for 120 marks, so budget roughly one minute per mark plus checking time. Short-answer questions (1-3 marks) need one precise fact per mark - a named material, a named property, one feature of a test. The 9-mark extended questions reward structure and linkage, and typically appear as 'explain why material X is suitable for product Y' or as a comparison. Plan the three layers (property, function, context) in 30 seconds of bullet points before writing - the mark scheme descriptors reward developed links, and a planned answer avoids the generic-property trap that caps marks at 4-5. Where the question says 'justify', a comparison with a rejected alternative is expected; where it says 'explain', the property-to-function chain is enough, but adding cost or disposal still differentiates top answers.

topics.name: Designing and Making Principles
topics.subject: design-and-technology
topics.searchText: design-and-technology Design and Technology Designing and Making Principles Iterative design A cyclic process of designing, modelling, testing and modifying in which each loop informs the next; never a single linear pass through the stages. User-centred design Designing from the needs, wants and values of the user, keeping them closely and regularly involved throughout the process. Anthropometrics The measurement of human body dimensions; percentiles (commonly 5th to 95th) are used to size products so most users are accommodated. Ergonomics The study of the interaction between user and product: comfort, posture, reach, grip and ease of use (human factors). Design specification A set of clear, unambiguous and measurable criteria the design must satisfy; treated as a live working document throughout the project. Prototype A full-size working model of the final design, used to test, evaluate and develop the proposal before commercial manufacture. Jig A guiding device that holds the workpiece or tool to ensure accuracy and repeatability, e.g. a drilling jig with hardened bushes. Fixture A holding device that secures the workpiece in a fixed position during a machining or assembly operation. Template A pattern or guide used to mark out or check a shape repeatedly, ensuring consistency across identical parts. Product life cycle The stages a product passes through: introduction, evolution/growth, maturity, decline and replacement. The specification is explicit that there is no single design process : good design always addresses needs, wants or values, and different approaches to user-centred design exist. What matters in the exam is that you can explain how investigation informs decisions . Primary data - market research, interviews, human factors observation, focus groups, product analysis and disassembly - is collected first-hand; secondary data comes from existing sources such as published reports, books and databases. Questions often ask why both are needed: primary data is specific to the actual user group and context, while secondary data is broader, cheaper and benchmarks against what already exists. Anthropometrics and percentiles are examined almost every year. Designing for the 5th to 95th percentile accommodates about 90% of users: a doorway or chair seat sized for the 95th percentile (largest users) prevents exclusion of tall people, while reach distances based on the 5th percentile (smallest users) keep controls within grasp of most. Adjustable features (seat height, straps, headrests) widen the range further. Ergonomic data then shapes interaction - posture, grip, control placement, force required - and is justified against the user group: a child's scissors have smaller, softer grips sized to child hand anthropometrics. The full design process stages (3.2.4) must be known for the NEA and for discussion questions: investigations and analysis; use of inspiration materials such as mood boards; ideas generation; illustration; development of a design specification; modelling; planning; evaluating and testing. In industrial and commercial contexts , iteration is cyclic and collaborative - design teams work with users, clients and expert practitioners, responding to feedback, and commercial design loops continuously between prototype testing and refinement because the cost of failure at volume makes early testing essential. Be precise about what good design addresses (3.2.1): designing to meet needs, wants or values; investigations that inform the use of primary and secondary data; product analysis and evaluation; the development of a design proposal; the planning and manufacture of a prototype solution; and evaluation of the prototype to inform further development. The specification also expects you to discuss representation of data - how market research and testing data are presented (graphs, tables, charts) to inform design decisions and evaluate outcomes - a small but reliable question type. A classic discussion question contrasts iterative design in school vs industry . In school/NEA the loop is student-driven and documented in a portfolio; in industry it is team-driven, collaborative and cyclic across design and manufacture - feedback comes from users, clients and expert practitioners, and because commercial failure at volume is catastrophic, extensive testing and refinement happen before launch. The mark is in the link: both are iterative, but industry adds collaborative working, cost of failure and cross-functional teams. Avoid claiming industry follows a fixed linear process - the specification explicitly rejects that. Learn each movement with its principles, dates and one signature product or designer - Paper 2 questions ask you to discuss how movements shaped product design, not just describe them. Movement Principles Evidence to quote Arts and Crafts (c.1860-1900) Reaction against industrial mass production; honest use of materials, craftsmanship, simplicity, decoration from construction William Morris; hand-crafted furniture; influenced later designers to value material honesty Art Deco (1920s-30s) Geometric ornament, luxury materials, streamlining, symmetry Chrysler Building; Bakelite radios; streamlined 1930s product styling Modernism (e.g. Bauhaus, 1919-1933) Form follows function; rejection of ornament; design for mass production; honest materials; unity of art and technology Marianne Brandt's metalwork, Wagenfeld lamp; post-WW1 Bauhaus furniture designed for mass production Post-modernism (e.g. Memphis, 1980s) Playful rebellion against modernist rules; colour, pattern, contradiction, decoration returns Memphis Group (Sottsass) furniture; Philippe Starck's decorative yet functional products Named designers (3.2.2): Philippe Starck - post-modern, playful commercial design (Juicy Salif lemon squeezer, styled over function); James Dyson - iterative engineering development (5,127 prototypes for the dual cyclone vacuum), function-driven innovation; Margaret Calvert - graphic/communication design (UK road signage with Jock Kinneir), clarity for the user; Dieter Rams - Braun, functionalist modernism, his ten principles of good design (innovative, useful, aesthetic, honest, unobtrusive and so on); Charles and Ray Eames - moulded plywood and plastic furniture, experimentation with materials for democratic mass production; Marianne Brandt - Bauhaus metalwork and lighting, designed for industrial manufacture. Socio-economic influences (3.2.3): post-WW1 the Bauhaus developed furniture for mass production (cheap, functional, democratic); WW2 brought rationing and utility products (austere, material-efficient design under the Utility scheme); contemporary design reflects fashion and demand for mass-produced furniture plus decorative design. Major technology developments shaping design: microelectronics (product miniaturisation), new materials, new methods of manufacture and advancements in CAD/CAM. Finally, the product life cycle (3.2.3.4): introduction, evolution, growth, maturity, decline and replacement - quote how designers refine and re-develop products to extend maturity (e.g. iterative smartphone updates, the VW Beetle re-launched as the New Beetle). Sharpen the designer profiles with facts you can deploy in 6-mark discuss answers. Dieter Rams (Braun): functionalist modernism; his ten principles - good design is innovative, makes a product useful, is aesthetic, makes a product understandable, is unobtrusive, is honest, is long-lasting, is thorough down to the last detail, is environmentally friendly, involves as little design as possible. James Dyson : 5,127 prototypes for the dual cyclone vacuum - the set-piece example of iterative development and design risk. Margaret Calvert (with Jock Kinneir): the UK road sign typeface and pictograms - clarity, legibility and user-centred graphic design for everyone. Charles and Ray Eames : experiments with moulded plywood and later plastic - material experimentation enabling well-designed furniture for mass production. Marianne Brandt : the only woman in the Bauhaus metal workshop - ashtrays and lighting designed geometrically for industrial manufacture. Philippe Starck : Juicy Salif lemon squeezer - post-modern styling and form over obvious function, a design-as-statement product that divided opinion. For the socio-economic bullet, structure by era: post-WW1 Bauhaus furniture for mass production (functional, affordable, democratic); WW2 rationing and utility products (austere, efficient, standardised); contemporary fashion cycles and demand for mass-produced furniture alongside decorative post-modern design. Link each era to why design responded as it did - economics and materials scarcity shape style, which is exactly the analytical link the discuss questions reward. Prototype development questions ask you to discuss and demonstrate how a prototype grows from design proposals. Expect a narrative chain: design proposal → concept modelling (card, foam, styrofoam, 3D print) → testing against the specification → modification → part-models or technique practice for critical elements → working drawings and plans → final prototype manufacture. Every stage must show that knowledge of the user and specification is driving decisions - AQA states this knowledge should influence NEA development so students make high-quality products that meet the needs of identified users. Selecting tools, equipment and processes (3.2.6) links the prototype to production reality. Key exam points: designs are developed from a single prototype into batch and mass produced products; the need for batch and mass manufacture changes the manufacturing process (one-off hand skills give way to jigs, fixtures, CNC and moulding); the most appropriate process must be selected to realise a design proposal; and safe working practices apply throughout - correct tools for the task, protection of self and others, and in commercial settings workforce training and national safety standards. A strong answer contrasts scales: a one-off birch plywood stool cut by hand and router becomes, at volume, a CNC-nested flat-pack product assembled with KD fittings - same design intent, different process chain chosen by scale. Model with purpose: be ready to justify why a modelling technique suits its stage - card and foam for fast cheap form exploration, 3D printing for accurate functional parts, part-models to prove a single joint or mechanism before committing material to the full prototype. This justification habit is exactly what the NEA Criteria C and D reward, so practicing it in written answers directly lifts coursework marks. Add the commercial chain to your prototype answers: single prototype → batch → mass production changes everything downstream. At batch, jigs and fixtures guarantee repeatability; at mass, processes switch to moulding, pressing and CNC with standardised bought-in components, and the design itself is modified to suit the process (draft angles for moulding, nesting for CNC, knock-down fittings for flat packing). The specification phrase is 'the effect on the manufacturing process brought about by the need for batch and mass manufacture' - be able to name three concrete effects. On safe working (3.2.6): correct tools and equipment for the specific task; ensuring your own safety and that of others in the workshop; and in commercial settings, workforce training plus national safety standards. A 4-mark answer links the hazard to the control: rotating machinery (guards, extraction, eye protection), dust and fumes (LEV extraction, masks under COSHH), and manual handling (technique, aids). Health and safety reasoning also feeds NEA Criterion D evidence, so practicing this link in written answers lifts coursework too. Accuracy in design and manufacture (3.2.7) is examined whatever the scale of production. Learn the mechanism chain: testing eliminates error; measuring aids - templates, jigs and fixtures - ensure consistency and reduce human error; datum points and geometry are used when setting out design drawings and creating templates. Batch and mass production amplify the value of jigs: a jig is made once but guarantees every identical part afterwards is accurate, so the cost per part of the jig falls as volume rises. Be able to give a concrete example - a drilling jig with hardened bushes positions holes identically in every shelf of a flat-pack run. Critical analysis and evaluation (3.2.5) must cover both your own products and commercial products, leading to possible improvements or modifications of the original idea. Commercial products are required to undergo rigorous testing before becoming available for sale - be ready to name testing methods (user trials, endurance and safety testing, standards testing to BSI specifications). Third-party feedback is a favourite question: the views of other interested parties ensure the evaluation is objective and unbiased - the designer is biased towards their own ideas, and users, clients and expert practitioners spot issues the designer cannot see. Feedback then informs future modification and development, completing the iterative loop. Structure evaluation answers as: test → data → judgement against specification → justified modification. That four-step chain mirrors both the written mark scheme and the NEA Criterion E descriptors, so it earns marks in both places. Flesh out commercial testing before sale (3.2.5): products are required to undergo rigorous testing before becoming commercially available - user trials with target users, endurance/fatigue testing beyond normal service conditions, safety testing to BSI standards, and batch sampling during production. Third-party feedback is examined because of objectivity: the views of other interested parties (users, clients, independent testers) ensure evaluation is objective and unbiased, informing future modification and development. A 6-mark answer names the parties, explains the bias they remove, and links the feedback loop to a concrete improvement. For accuracy , add the measurement chain: datum points (a fixed reference edge or face from which all dimensions are taken) prevent cumulative error; geometry creates templates that reproduce curves identically; testing eliminates error before volume manufacture, when the cost of an error multiplies by the batch size. The exam link: an error caught at prototype stage costs one part; the same error at mass production costs thousands - which is why 3.2.7 insists accuracy matters whatever the scale, but the economics justify the jigs and testing at volume.

topics.name: Digital Design and Manufacture
topics.subject: design-and-technology
topics.searchText: design-and-technology Design and Technology Digital Design and Manufacture CAD Computer aided design - software used to develop and present product ideas: 2D CAD for working drawings, 3D CAD for presentation and solid modelling. CAM Computer aided manufacture - computer-controlled machinery converting CAD data directly into machined parts (laser, router, mill, lathe, plotter). CNC Computer numerical control - machine tools controlled by coded digital instructions (e.g. G-code), giving repeatable, accurate production. Rapid prototyping Fast production of a physical model directly from CAD data, typically by additive 3D printing, with no tooling required. FEA Finite element analysis - a component is split into small elements and stress/strain is simulated across them to reveal weak points before manufacture. CFD Computational fluid dynamics - simulation of airflow or liquid flow around or within a product, used for aerodynamics and wind-resistance testing. EPOS Electronic point of sales - till systems that capture sales data, maintain stock levels and collect customer data for marketing and market research. PPC Production planning and control - a networked system coordinating the availability of materials, scheduling of machines and people, and suppliers and customers across manufacture. Just in time (JIT) A system where materials and components are delivered exactly when needed for production, minimising storage costs and waste. Flexible manufacturing system (FMS) A computer-controlled production system that can switch rapidly between different products or variants with minimal downtime. CAD questions split into two forms with two jobs: 2D CAD produces working drawings - orthographic views, dimensions, tolerances - sent straight to CAM; 3D CAD produces presentation drawings, photorealistic renders and solid models that can be tested virtually or 3D printed. Set out drawings from datum points and geometry (edges and faces that everything is measured from) and dimension with tolerances - the permissible variation on a dimension (e.g. 50mm +/- 0.1mm) - so parts assemble interchangeably at volume. Advantages over manual drafting to quote: instant editing and version control without redrawing; guaranteed accuracy and consistent line quality; files share instantly with clients, colleagues and CAM machines; 3D visualisation and photorealistic rendering communicate ideas better than sketches; libraries of standard components drop in; drawings drive CAM directly, removing manual translation errors. Disadvantages balance the answer: expensive software licences and hardware; significant training time; over-reliance can weaken sketching skills; initial modelling is slower than a quick freehand sketch; less tactile exploration of form. Examiners reward balanced answers - a one-sided list caps marks. In industrial applications , CAD is the hub of the digital workflow: design teams collaborate on shared models, client feedback is applied by editing the model rather than restarting, and the same file generates the CAM toolpaths, virtual tests and presentation renders - one source of truth from concept to manufacture. For NEA purposes remember AQA's position: the use of CAD is encouraged but it should not be the only form of design communication used. Deploy concrete examples in CAD answers. 2D CAD for working drawings : orthographic views with dimensions and tolerances sent to the laser cutter or CNC router - the drawing is the manufacturing instruction. 3D CAD for presentation drawings : photorealistic renders for client approval, exploded assemblies to show fixings, and solid models that drive FEA, CFD and 3D printing. Datum points and geometry : setting out from a fixed reference edge prevents cumulative dimensioning error across a drawing; tolerances (e.g. +/- 0.1mm on a housing) guarantee interchangeable assembly at volume. The industrial-application marks come from the digital workflow chain: CAD model → virtual test (FEA/CFD/simulation) → CAM toolpaths → CNC manufacture, with client feedback applied by editing one shared model rather than restarting. Mention parametric modelling where relevant - dimensions are driven by parameters, so a design change propagates automatically through every drawing and toolpath. That single sentence earns the 'how CAD is used in industrial applications' bullet, and contrasts cleanly with manual drafting where every change means redrawing. CAM is the direct link between CAD data and the machine tool. Name the five spec processes and what each does: laser cutting - focused beam cuts or engraves sheet (paper, card, board, polymers, thin metals) with no tool wear and fine detail; routing - rotating cutter follows a toolpath to cut profiles, slots and pockets in sheet and board (e.g. CNC-nested flat-pack parts); milling - rotating multi-point cutter removes metal in controlled passes for accurate flat and profiled surfaces; turning - the workpiece rotates against a single-point tool for cylindrical parts (lathe); plotter cutting - a blade follows the path for vinyl, film and thin sheet, e.g. signage and stencils. Calculating speeds and times is a maths link (3.1.7). Machining time = path length / feed rate; spindle speed follows cutting-speed formulas (speed = (cutting speed x 1000) / (pi x diameter) for a rotating cutter or workpiece). Be ready to show working: a laser cutter moving 1,200mm at 60mm/s takes 20 seconds per pass; a turned bar of 50mm diameter at a cutting speed of 150 m/min needs a spindle speed of about 955 rpm. Even if the exact constants are not recalled, showing the correct method scores the marks.
