The commercial argument is always the same chain: CAM removes manual translation error between drawing and part; produces repeatable accuracy identical across a batch; changes between products by loading a new program rather than retooling; and runs unattended, cutting labour cost. Weigh it against setup cost and programming time - for one-offs, hand skills or a quick manual job can still be faster, which is why scale of production decides the process. Link CAM to scales of production (3.1.6) - the discussion the examiner wants. One-off: a hand-cut or manually machined part can still be faster than programming; CAM adds cost without volume to amortise it. Batch/mass: CAM toolpaths are written once and repeated identically for every part - repeatability and zero manual translation error are the commercial argument, and changeovers between products need only a new program, supporting flexible manufacturing. Standard answer: CAM wins as volume rises because programming and setup costs amortise per part. Worked speed/time example to memorise: a laser cutter runs a 1,200mm pass at 60mm/s - time = 1,200 / 60 = 20 seconds. A turned bar of 50mm diameter at a cutting speed of 150m/min - spindle speed = (150 x 1000) / (pi x 50) = about 955rpm. Showing the formula and substitution scores even if the arithmetic slips. Add the accuracy chain: CAM removes the human translation step between drawing and part; identical programs give identical parts across a batch; this is why jigs and manual setting-out matter less at volume when CNC is used - but machine calibration and tool wear checks still apply. Virtual modelling/testing happens in industry before any product is produced. Learn the three named processes: simulation - the virtual product or assembly is exercised in software to test fit, motion and function; CFD - airflow or liquid flow is simulated around/within the product (aerodynamics and wind resistance, e.g. car bodies and cycle frames, or liquid flow through valves and pipework); FEA - the component is meshed into finite elements and stress/strain is analysed, colour-mapping high-stress zones so the design can be strengthened or lightened before manufacture. Interpreting the data is examined: red zones in FEA show where failure is likely - remove material from blue (low-stress) zones to cut weight, add material or fillets at red zones to cut stress concentration; CFD streamlines show drag or turbulence - modify the geometry and re-run to compare. Rapid prototyping (3D printing) builds the model additively - layer by layer directly from the CAD file, so no tooling is needed. Benefits to designers : overnight iteration from CAD model to testable physical part; complex internal geometry impossible by wasting processes; cheap one-offs - no mould or tooling cost, unlike injection moulding; functional and user testing happens early, informing the next iteration; better communication with clients who handle a real part. Benefits to manufacturers : production tooling, jigs and fixtures can be 3D printed cheaply; spare parts printed on demand instead of stored; small-batch or custom production becomes economical. Volume/time maths links: volume = area x height for a build, time = layers x time per layer - show the method. Draw the comparison the examiner wants: rapid prototyping vs injection moulding - 3D printing has no tooling cost and suits one-offs and prototypes, but per-part cost never falls with volume; injection moulding needs expensive tooling but becomes far cheaper per part at mass production. Scale of production decides, every time. Know the materials and limits of 3D printing for a balanced answer: common filaments are PLA (rigid, biodegradable under industrial composting, brittle), ABS (tougher, temperature-resistant, warps without an enclosed bed) and photopolymer resins (fine detail, brittle). Limits to quote for evaluation marks: layer adhesion makes parts weaker across layers than in-plane, so printed parts do not match the properties of an injection-moulded equivalent; surface finish shows layer lines and needs finishing; build volume restricts size; print time scales with height and layer count - hence the volume/time calculations. For interpreting FEA/CFD data , add the decision loop: FEA colour maps show stress concentration - the designer adds fillets at red zones, removes material from blue zones, then re-runs the simulation to verify; several iterations happen virtually before any material is committed. CFD streamline and pressure maps show drag or turbulence around a product - geometry is modified and re-tested without a wind tunnel session. The evaluation mark: virtual iteration is near-zero marginal cost, so more design options are explored before prototyping, and expensive physical testing (wind tunnels, destructive tests) is reserved for confirming the final design - that economic link is what separates top answers. Computer systems plan and control manufacturing, reduce waste and respond quickly to changes in consumer demand (3.1.6). Learn the named systems: modular/cell production - the line is organised into cells, each completing a sub-assembly or stage; just in time (JIT) - deliveries arrive exactly when needed, so storage cost, waste and obsolete stock fall, and cash is not tied up in inventory; quick response manufacturing (QRM) - the whole system is organised around cutting lead times so the business reacts fast to demand changes; flexible manufacturing systems (FMS) - computer-controlled machines and handling switch between products with minimal downtime. PPC networking (3.1.7) coordinates all of it: availability of materials, scheduling of machines and people, and coordinating suppliers and customers - one networked plan from order to delivery. EPOS feeds the top end of the chain: point-of-sale data maintains stock levels and captures customer data (contact details, buying patterns) used for marketing and market research - sales by region and product tell manufacturers what to make next. Computer-controlled systems also run production, distribution and storage - automated warehouses, pick-and-place handling and logistics scheduling. Finally, standardised and bought-in components from specialist manufacturers (screws, bearings, mechanisms) and sub-assembly - a separate line of manufacture for certain parts of a product - allow the manufacturer to focus on what it does best while guaranteeing component quality. The classic essay weighs digital integration against cost: integrated systems cut waste, lead time and error, but need capital investment, training and supplier discipline - JIT only works with reliable suppliers, because a single late delivery halts the line when there is no buffer stock. Structure discussion answers with that balance, tied to a named system. Two more 3.1.6 points complete this topic. Vertical in-house production : the company owns and controls successive stages of manufacture in-house rather than outsourcing - more control over quality and lead time, but higher capital commitment. Sub-assembly : a separate line of manufacture for certain parts of a product (wiring looms, door cards, pump units) that feed the main line - it shortens the main assembly sequence, lets specialists make complex parts, and pairs with standardised and bought-in components from specialist manufacturers, which guarantee quality and cut cost through their economies of scale. For the automation paragraph, give the concrete chain: computer-controlled production (CNC cells, pick-and-place, robots), storage (automated warehouses with computer-tracked stock, robotic retrieval), and distribution (scheduling and logistics software coordinating suppliers and customers). The system-level argument: EPOS sales data feeds PPC, PPC schedules materials and machines, CAM machines execute - demand at the till propagates automatically through the whole chain, which is exactly how computer systems 'reduce waste and respond quickly to changes in consumer demand' (3.1.6). Quote that chain in any 6-mark systems question.

topics.name: Design in Society
topics.subject: design-and-technology
topics.searchText: design-and-technology Design and Technology Design in Society Inclusive design Designing products that can be used by the widest possible range of users - including disabled people, children and the elderly - without needing adaptation. Circular economy An economic system in which products, components and materials are kept in use through repair, reuse, remanufacture and recycling, designing out waste rather than following take-make-dispose. Six Rs of sustainability Design strategies for reducing environmental impact: reduce, reuse, rethink, recycle, repair, refuse. Product life cycle The stages of a product's commercial life: introduction, evolution/growth, maturity, decline and replacement. Product miles The distance a product and its components travel from raw material source through manufacture to the consumer; global manufacturing increases them and the associated emissions. Fairtrade A certification system ensuring producers in developing countries receive fair prices and decent working conditions; it influences both design decisions and consumer demand. British Standards Institution (BSI) The national standards body whose kitemark certifies that a product has been independently tested to meet safety and quality standards. Registered design Intellectual property protecting a product's visual appearance - its shape, configuration, pattern or ornament - through formal registration. Open design Developing products for the common good of society with designs freely shared, e.g. humanitarian projects and file sharing for 3D printing. WEEE directive Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment directive - places responsibility on producers for the collection, recycling and safe disposal of electrical products at end of life. Consumer choice is shaped deliberately (3.1.13). Marketing and brand identity work through: customer identification - defining exactly who the product targets; labelling and packaging - the legal and persuasive layer of the product that carries branding, information and polymer codes; corporate identification - consistent logos, colours and design language across a product range so consumers recognise and trust the brand; and the concept of global marketing - promoting and advertising products worldwide using new technologies such as social media and viral marketing, where content spreads peer-to-peer at almost no media cost. Product costing and profit, and awareness of the role of entrepreneurs, complete the section: entrepreneurs spot unmet needs and take design risks to serve them, and collaboration between designers (virtual and face-to-face) drives innovation. Socio-economic influences (3.2.3) explain why design looks the way it does: post-WW1 the Bauhaus developed furniture for mass production, making functional design affordable; WW2 rationing produced utility products - austere, material-efficient design under government constraint; contemporary times show fashion cycles and demand for mass-produced furniture alongside decorative design. Major developments in technology - microelectronics, new materials, new methods of manufacture, advancements in CAD/CAM - continually reshape what is possible and what consumers expect. The product life cycle (3.2.3.4): introduction (launch, low sales, high promotion cost), evolution/growth (sales rise as the market adopts), maturity (peak sales, competition, refinement), decline (sales fall as tastes or technology move on) and replacement. The exam wants examples of how designers refine and re-develop products to extend maturity - iterative smartphone updates, cars facelifted between generations, the VW Beetle re-launched as the New Beetle to harvest nostalgia. Link each stage to a marketing response: price cuts and relaunches fight decline; brand extensions stretch maturity. Deepen the global marketing bullet with the mechanism: social media and viral marketing spread content peer-to-peer at negligible media cost, so brand awareness scales fast - but is less controlled than traditional advertising. Corporate identification (consistent logo, colour and design language) builds recognition and trust across a range; packaging and labelling carry both the legal information and the persuasive layer. Entrepreneurs spot unmet needs, take design risks and secure the investment to serve them; collaborative working between designers - virtual and face-to-face - is how new and innovative products are developed, and market research data is interpreted to calculate costs, prices and profit (3.1.13 maths links: profit = revenue - costs; price set against market research on willingness to pay). Add life cycle marketing responses to complete 3.2.3.4: promotion is heaviest at introduction (building awareness); growth relies on widening distribution; maturity is defended by refinement, facelifts, brand extensions and updated specifications; decline is met with price cuts, relaunches or harvesting before replacement. Quote one product refined across its life cycle - iterative smartphone updates or the VW Beetle relaunched as the New Beetle - and link the design refinement to the stage: each iteration extends maturity by re-engaging demand. Inclusive design (3.1.8) means developing products that can be used by a wide range of users including the disabled, children and the elderly . The principle: design out the barriers rather than design a separate specialist product. Classic evidence to quote: lever taps usable by arthritic hands where crosshead taps are not; OXO Good Grips-style oversized soft handles that suit everyone, not just users with reduced grip strength; high-contrast controls and audible feedback for users with impaired vision; step-free access and adjustable-height features. Anchor the answer in aesthetics, ergonomics and anthropometrics (3.1.8): ergonomic data - posture, reach, grip strength, force required - shapes the interaction; anthropometric data with percentiles sizes the product for the 5th to 95th percentile user; aesthetics ensure the inclusive product is not stigmatising - the OXO lesson is that designing for the extreme user produced a mainstream commercial success. Perceptible information (visible, audible, tactile cues) and tolerance for error complete the checklist for exam answers. Questions typically ask you to explain how a given product could be made more inclusive or discuss why designers have a responsibility to design inclusively . Structure: identify the excluded user group and the barrier; propose the design modification (control type, size, force, feedback, adjustability); link to ergonomic/anthropometric data; finish with the commercial and ethical argument - the population is ageing, inclusive products reach bigger markets, and legislation (Equality Act obligations on service provision) increasingly expects accessibility. Avoid the common error of describing accessibility features without naming which user they include - the mark is for the user link. Build the evidence bank with a worked example chain. OXO Good Grips: designed for users with arthritis (reduced grip strength and dexterity) - oversized, cushioned, non-slip handles - and succeeded commercially with everyone, demonstrating that designing for the extreme user produces mainstream products (inclusive design is not niche design). Road signage (Margaret Calvert, 3.2.2): legible typeface and consistent pictograms usable by the widest population at speed - inclusive communication design. Everyday adaptations: lever taps instead of crosshead (arthritic hands), high-contrast controls with tactile and audible feedback (impaired vision), adjustable-height furniture (children to adults), lightweight materials and easy-open packaging (elderly users with reduced strength). Link to fitness for purpose (3.1.8): a product is only fit for purpose if the actual user range can operate it - hence anthropometric percentiles (5th-95th) and ergonomic data drive dimensions, control forces and feedback. The exam phrase is that products must be developed to be inclusive 'so that they can be used by a wide range of users including the disabled, children and the elderly' - name the excluded group, name the barrier, name the modification. The commercial close: ageing populations and legislation on accessibility widen the market for inclusive products, so inclusion is a business argument, not only an ethical one. Responsible design (3.2.8) rests on the circular economy : products designed to conserve energy, materials and components, with minimum environmental impact across raw material extraction, consumption, ease of repair, maintenance and end of life. Sustainable manufacturing uses alternative energy and methods to minimise waste, and considers the waste, surplus and by-products of manufacture itself - reuse of off-cuts, chemicals, heat and water - plus the cost implications of dealing with waste and the impact of global manufacturing on product miles . Design for manufacture, maintenance, repair and disposal (3.1.11) turns the principle into concrete design decisions - learn these as a checklist because discussion questions reward applied specifics: Ease of manufacture: ribs and webbing to reduce material thickness; snap fittings to remove fixings/adhesives; internal moulded screw posts for self-tapping screws; pre-made and standardised components; moulded-in texture to cut process count; self-finishing polymers. Maintenance and repair: temporary and integral fixings; standardised parts; allowing for service and replacement of parts; ability to upgrade with software downloads. Disposal: labelling of materials to aid separation for recycling (polymer codes); making products easy to disassemble or separate; application of the six Rs - reduce the quantity of materials, toxic materials, damaging materials and associated energy use; reuse components; rethink by using eco-friendly alternatives; recycle into new products (plus repair and refuse). Active disassembly: using smart materials such as shape memory alloys so a casing releases itself at end of life, and biodegradable parts that separate naturally. Packaging is a set-piece exam context (3.2.8): the environmental impact of excessive packaging and plastics - design minimal, mono-material, labelled packaging that still protects and sells. Weigh the trade-offs to reach the top band: snap fittings speed assembly and enable recycling but can weaken the joint; reducing material risks product damage in transit, which wastes more than it saves if failure rates rise. Responsible design is a balance, and saying so is what earns the evaluation marks. Structure life cycle thinking as the exam wants it (3.2.8): minimum environmental impact across raw material extraction, consumption, ease of repair, maintenance and end of life - an assessment of the whole life, not just manufacture. Conservation of energy and resources : products designed to conserve energy, materials and components; sustainable manufacturing using alternative energy and methods to minimise waste; the impact of waste, surplus and by-products created in manufacture - reuse of material off-cuts, chemicals, heat and water - plus the cost implications of dealing with waste and the impact of global manufacturing on product miles. A 6-mark answer moves through the stages: extraction (recycled or certified-sustainable inputs), manufacture (waste reuse, alternative energy), use (energy-efficient operation, repairability), end of life (disassembly, labelled materials for recycling). For design for manufacture, maintenance, repair and disposal (3.1.11), add the 'why' behind each feature: ribs and webbing allow thinner walls, cutting material quantity and moulding cycle time; snap fittings remove fixing operations and make separation possible at end of life; internal moulded screw posts accept self-tapping screws without separate nuts; moulded-in texture removes a finishing process; self-finishing polymers need no coating at all; temporary and integral fixings plus standardised parts allow service, repair and part replacement; software-download upgrades extend service life without hardware replacement. Labelling materials (polymer codes) aids separation for recycling, and active disassembly - casings released by smart materials such as shape memory alloy when triggered - automates end-of-life separation. Every feature is an argument that ends 'fewer processes, less material, or easier recovery' - that closing link is the mark. Consumer protection (3.1.9): legislation used to protect consumers and its impact on product design - the Consumer Rights Act (2015) (goods must be as described, of satisfactory quality and fit for purpose) and the Sale of Goods Act (1979) predecessor; the British Standards Institute (BSI) and how specific products are tested to meet safety standards (the kitemark); measures to ensure toy safety such as the Lion Mark; and advice to consumers through manufacturer instructions, safety warnings and aftercare advice. Designers also work within the Health and Safety at Work Act (1974) and COSHH when specifying materials, adhesives and finishes that are hazards. National and international standards (3.2.10) - learn the list with what each does: ISO (International Organisation for Standardisation) international quality/system standards; ROHS directive restricting hazardous substances in electronics; the battery directive (removable/recyclable batteries); polymer codes for identification and recycling; packaging directives (producer responsibility for packaging waste); WEEE directives for e-waste; energy ratings of products; and eco-labelling - the Mobius Loop, the European Eco-label, the EC energy label, the Energy Efficient label and logo, the Forest Stewardship Council (FSC) mark for sustainable timber, and the EPA Energy Star. Intellectual property (3.1.10): copyright and design rights (automatic protection of original work); patents (protecting an invention's function for a fixed term); registered designs (protecting appearance); trademarks and logos (protecting brand identity). Balance with open design : developing products for the common good of society with designs freely shared - humanitarian projects and file sharing for 3D printing. Ethical issues (3.2.3) tie it together: products made using sustainable materials and ethical production methods; products that are culturally acceptable and not offensive to people of different race, gender or religious belief; inclusive products; design addressing social problems such as poverty, health and wellbeing, migration and housing; the impact of Fairtrade on design and consumer demand; and designing to the six Rs. The top band links the ethic to a concrete design decision, not a generic list. Consolidate IP with the differences examiners test: copyright/design right is automatic protection of original work (drawings, designs) without registration; patents protect how an invention works for a fixed term (typically 20 years) and must be applied for; registered designs protect appearance and must be registered; trademarks and logos protect brand identity and can be renewed indefinitely. The designer's stake: protecting IP preserves the commercial value of innovation - which is why open design (3.1.10) is a deliberate exception, developing products for the common good of society with designs freely shared, e.g. humanitarian projects and file sharing for 3D printing. For the ethics bullet (3.2.3), structure the responsibilities: products made using sustainable materials and ethical production methods; products that are culturally acceptable and not offensive to people of different race, gender or religious belief; inclusive products; products that could assist with social problems - poverty, health and wellbeing, migration and housing; the impact of Fairtrade on design and consumer demand; and designing with the six Rs. The top-band link pairs each ethic with a decision: sourcing Fairtrade-certified materials changes the supply chain, not just the label; culturally acceptable design means testing with representative users. Standards close the loop - ISO systems, BSI testing and eco-labels (Mobius Loop, FSC, Energy Star) are how ethical claims become verifiable, which is what makes the consumer trust them.

topics.searchText: design-and-technology Design and Technology Non-Exam Assessment (NEA) Portfolio Context The broad area, selected by the student, from which a design possibility is developed; it must offer the scope and complexity for work worthy of an A-level. Design brief A clearly stated and challenging statement of the problem to be solved, developed by the student from the context and addressing the needs of a user, client or market. Live document A design specification that is constantly referenced and updated throughout the project, rather than written once and forgotten. Iterative process The portfolio is developed through repeated loops of designing, making, testing and evaluating; the five criteria are not a linear checklist to complete in order. Primary investigation First-hand research: questionnaires, surveys, interviews, focus groups, visits, product disassembly and practical experimentation. Candidate Record Form (CRF) The official form recording supervision, use of specialist processes outside school, and any individual support given; marks must be adjusted to reflect assistance. Manufacturing specification A fully detailed set of instructions, referencing quality control checks, that allows a third party to accurately manufacture the prototype. Generic feedback The only teacher feedback permitted during development: oral/written advice on focus and resources; never corrections, templates, model answers or writing frames. Best-fit marking Holistic band assessment: highest mark if the work fully meets all statements, mid-band if mostly, lowest if it just meets the majority. Quality assurance (QA) The procedures and policies put in place before and during manufacture to ensure products are produced accurately and within acceptable tolerances. The NEA is a substantial design-and-make task producing a final prototype based on a context and design brief developed by the student . It is worth 100 marks, scaled by a factor of 2 to 200, and contributes 50% of the A-level. The brief must be of appropriate complexity and contain a degree of uncertainty of the outcome so an iterative process of designing, making, testing and evaluating is genuinely possible. Criterion What it assesses Marks AO A - Identifying and investigating design possibilities Context rationale, investigation, first concepts 20 AO1 B - Producing a design brief and specification Challenging brief, live measurable spec, project management 10 AO1 C - Development of design proposal(s) Justified, innovative development; modelling; manufacturing spec 25 AO2 D - Development of design prototype(s) Justified making; skill, precision, QA/QC, modification 25 AO2 E - Analysing and evaluating Ongoing evaluation, testing, user involvement, final critique 20 AO3 Total: AO1 30, AO2 50, AO3 20 = 100 raw marks. Memorise the split - it dictates where to spend time. Critical rules: the five criteria are not a linear process and criteria should be cross-referenced throughout (work is rewarded wherever it appears in the portfolio); bands are viewed holistically ; no work or work below A-level standard scores zero. The folder should be concise - no more than 45 pages is recommended; exceeding it self-penalises by losing focus, and falling short self-penalises by under-covering the criteria. AOs overall for the qualification: AO1 15%, AO2 25%, AO3 25%, AO4 35% - the NEA carries all of AO1 and AO2, which is why 50 marks of the 100 sit on designing and making. Budget your 45 pages against the marks: Criteria A and B (30 marks) need roughly 8-10 pages of focused context rationale and investigation plus a tight brief/spec; Criterion C (25 marks) is the biggest single block - give it 12-15 pages of developed, justified proposals with modelling evidence; Criterion D (25 marks) is evidenced mainly through photographs of making with brief annotations - 8-10 pages; Criterion E (20 marks) is spread through the portfolio but needs a strong final evaluation of 3-4 pages. Because bands are awarded holistically and work is rewarded wherever it appears, keep evaluation and user involvement visible in every section rather than quarantined at the end. Two marking mechanics matter for strategy. First, best-fit : where work fully meets all statements the highest mark is awarded; mostly meets - mid-band; just meets the majority - lowest mark. So completeness of evidence, not brilliance in one area, decides the band. Second, the zero rule : no work for a criterion, or work below A-level standard, scores zero - so every criterion needs visible, A-level-worthy evidence, and an undeveloped area drags more than a strong area lifts. Criterion A (20 marks) starts with the context. The top band (16-20) demands an excellent rationale for the context selected, with continuous reference throughout the project to the end user and the constraints - not a rationale written once and abandoned. The investigation must employ a comprehensive range of strategies : both primary methods (visits, surveys, questionnaires, interviews) and secondary methods (internet, books, magazines), plus practical experimentation and disassembly where relevant. All sources fully referenced is an explicit top-band statement - keep a source log from day one. First concepts must be fully relevant to the context and feasible for further development , communicated through a fully appropriate variety of methods; at this stage they demonstrate initial thinking and stimulate later, more considered proposals. Criterion B (10 marks) is small but quick to secure. The brief must be clearly stated and challenging , addressing the context and the needs and wants of the intended user. The specification must be fully detailed and well explained , informed by the investigations, with specific measurable outcomes as well as qualitative statements - 'the product must weigh under 2kg', not 'lightweight'. It is a live and working document , constantly referenced throughout. The top band also requires a detailed project management approach - time management and determining quantities and costs of materials - fully integrated into the specification : put a Gantt-style plan and a costed materials list inside the spec, not in an appendix. Common losses at Criterion A: investigation that does not relate directly to the context; issues identified but not addressed; single-strategy research (one questionnaire). At Criterion B: briefs that lack challenge, specs with no measurable statements, and project management bolted on rather than integrated. Make the investigation comprehensive by pairing methods with purposes: a questionnaire quantifies preferences across a sample (present results as graphs or charts); interviews and focus groups explain the why behind the numbers; a visit or observation captures the real context and constraints; product analysis of an existing solution benchmarks features and costs; disassembly reveals how competitors solve joints, fixings and assembly; practical experimentation tests whether a technique or material actually works before you commit a design decision to it. Every method should end in a documented conclusion that a later design decision references - that chain (method → finding → decision) is what the top-band descriptor 'issues are identified and fully addressed' means in practice. For the specification, write measurable and qualitative statements side by side and make them auditable: 'the prototype must support a user weighing up to 110kg without visible deflection' is measurable; 'the product should feel comfortable in one-handed use' is qualitative but testable through a user trial. Include appearance/ aesthetics, function, user requirements, cost of materials, size and weight, safety, manufacture methods and timescale - then integrate the project management: a schedule of activities, quantities and costs of materials, and contingency time. The top band explicitly wants time management and quantities/costs fully integrated into the specification , not appended. Criterion C (25 marks) - development of design proposals. The top band (19-25) requires the rationale for design decisions to be clearly documented and fully justified with constant reference to the design brief, specification and investigations ; originality, creativity and a willingness to take design risks ; excellent use of a variety of modelling techniques - part modelling, practising manufacturing and finishing techniques, scale models, material experimentation; and ongoing development through exploration of and experimentation with different materials, techniques and processes . You must also produce a comprehensive, fully detailed manufacturing specification that makes specific reference to relevant quality control checks and allows fully accurate interpretation by a third party , plus project management that allows for contingency planning . Working drawings, plans and patterns are expected; CAD is encouraged but must not be the only form of design communication. Criterion D (25 marks) - development of the prototype. The top band requires excellent justification for selection of materials, components, techniques and processes, demonstrating excellent understanding of material properties (link this to the materials content of Paper 1); significant complexity or challenge throughout production; excellent manufacturing skills combined with excellent understanding of dimensional accuracy and precision ; selection and use of appropriate tools, machinery and equipment - including CAM where required, though CAM must not be the only form of manufacturing used ; and modifications made in a fully considered manner in light of feedback from user trials and third-party feedback and as a result of testing and evaluation carried out against earlier iterations . Quality assurance must be evident throughout , with it clear where planned quality control checks were applied, and evidence throughout that appropriate health and safety processes were considered and employed . The mechanism is identical in both criteria: justify → evidence → modify. Every design decision is justified against the brief/spec; every justification is evidenced (photos, annotations, test data); every test result produces a documented modification. Photograph every stage of making - Criterion D can only be evidenced through the portfolio plus photographic evidence of the final prototype. Evidence quality control checks in the manufacturing specification by name, because 'makes specific reference to relevant quality control checks' is a top-band statement: measuring with vernier callipers and micrometers against tolerances; go/no-go gauges for repeated holes and slots; laser or probe scanning to check profiles; templates and jigs to guarantee repeatable features; visual checks against the working drawing at each stage; and non-destructive testing (x-ray or ultrasound) where a weld or bond must be verified without destroying the part (3.2.9). Write each check into the plan at the stage where it applies - that is what allows a third party to manufacture accurately, the explicit purpose of the manufacturing specification. In Criterion D , structure the photographic evidence like a test log: each stage photographed with a caption naming the process, the check applied and the outcome; each prototype iteration dated and compared against the previous one with what changed and why. Justify material and process selection against working properties (linking to Paper 1 knowledge), record the QC checks as they are applied, note health and safety controls (guards, extraction, PPE) as they are used, and log every modification with its trigger - user trial feedback, third-party comment, or a test result against an earlier iteration. The top band wants modifications made 'in a fully considered manner' - a dated, triggered, justified modification log is exactly that evidence. Criterion E (20 marks) has one vital instruction: evidence for analysing and evaluating can take place in any part of the NEA - it is not a final chapter. Students should be constantly analysing and recording thoughts to explain their thinking; ongoing evaluation must be seen to inform the decision-making process , particularly by bringing about modifications to design proposals and prototype development. Central to the top band is close and regular involvement of the proposed client/user(s) - ensuring the prototype is fit for purpose for them , not just for the student. The top band (16-20) requires: comprehensive analysis and evaluation throughout; focused and comprehensive testing with clear evidence of how results were used to inform the design and any modifications ; a well-reasoned critical analysis of the final outcome linked clearly to the design brief and specification , with full justification of the extent the prototype is fit for purpose; and a comprehensive critical evaluation identifying how modifications could improve the outcome, with full justification and full consideration of how the prototype could be developed for different production methods (one-off → batch → mass). Evidence and administration rules (4.4.2): the portfolio is written or digital, clearly evidencing how the assessment criteria have been met, with photographic evidence of the final manufactured prototype ; it should not exceed 45 pages. Time limits are not specified because the portfolio is iterative and independent, while the final prototype is made under supervision in school/college; specialist processes or equipment beyond school may be used but must be documented on the Candidate Record Form (CRF) . Feedback rules : students may redraft before final submission; teachers may give generic feedback (oral/written advice on focus, resources, key sections) but cannot correct work, provide templates, model answers or writing frames, or give specific improvement advice against the criteria. Once work is submitted for final assessment it cannot be revised. Any support given to an individual that was not given to the whole class must be recorded on the CRF and the mark adjusted to represent unaided achievement - so record what help you received, and never let assistance inflate work you cannot justify as your own. Structure the final evaluation in four moves, mirroring the top band: (1) critical analysis against brief and spec - go through the specification point by point and judge with evidence how far the prototype satisfies each; (2) fitness for purpose for the client/user - user trial results and third-party feedback decide this, not your opinion; (3) justified modifications - identify how the outcome could be improved, with a full justification for each modification, not a wish list; (4) different production methods - consider how the prototype would be developed for one-off, batch and mass production, changing processes, materials and assembly for the scale. A conclusion that weighs trade-offs and commits to a recommendation completes the AO3 argument. Finally, work the 45-page rule as a discipline: because the band is best-fit against documented evidence, dense justified pages beat sprawling description - every page should end in a decision, a finding or a justification that a marker can point to. Keep sources referenced as you go (all sources fully referenced is an explicit Criterion A top-band statement), keep the spec and project plan live, and remember the CRF: any help beyond generic class feedback must be recorded and the mark adjusted - plan to need none, and record any you do use.
